So the commandment is called a lamp for the less perfect, who do not yet understand divine things clearly; but the law is called a light for the more perfect, for whom the law of God shines more brightly, and who contemplate with clear sight the things that are God's. This is how it is commonly expounded. Nevertheless both may be referred to the same persons, especially since the Prophet says: [[Ps 118:105|Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths|Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, Domine, et lumen semitis meis]] [Denis adds *Domine*, "O Lord"]. So the commandment is compared to a lamp, because it enlightens us and directs us to live well; and the law likewise to light, since it enlightens the mind within.

paras.t: Et via vitæ, increpatio disciplinæ, id est, correptio disciplinaris et ex interiori disciplina procedens, est via pertingendi ad vitam gratiæ in isto exsilio, deinde ad gloriæ vitam in regno : quia per increpationem hanc peccans reducitur, quemadmodum apud Job legitur : Deus instruit disciplina, ut avertat hominem ab his quæ fecit, et liberet eum de superbia. Et alibi dicitur : Etenim multo tempore non sinere peccatoribus ex sententia agere, sed statim ultiones adhibere, magni beneficii est indicium.
paras.en: [[6:23|and reproofs of instruction are the way of life|Et via vitæ, increpatio disciplinæ]] [*disciplina*, which the Douay-Rheims renders "instruction", is also discipline, correction], that is, correction given by discipline and proceeding from inward discipline, is the way of attaining to the life of grace in this exile, and afterwards to the life of glory in the kingdom: because by this reproof the sinner is brought back, as we read in Job: God, [[Job 33:16|teaching instructeth them|instruit disciplina]], that [[Job 33:17|he may withdraw a man from the things he is doing, and may deliver him from pride|avertat hominem ab his quæ fecit, et liberet eum de superbia]]. And elsewhere it is said: [[2 Mach 6:13|For it is a token of great goodness, when sinners are not suffered to go on in their ways for a long time, but are presently punished|Etenim multo tempore non sinere peccatoribus ex sententia agere, sed statim ultiones adhibere, magni beneficii est indicium]].

paras.t: Ut custodiant te a muliere mala, et blanda lingua extranea, id est ab omni fornicaria atque adultera : a quibus se custodit, qui mandata Dei prætacto modo attendit. Non concupiscat pulchritudinem ejus cor tuum ad usum illicitum, ne capiaris nutibus illius, id est, ne per signa lasciviæ oculorum ipsius alliciaris ad culpam ; sed ora cum Propheta : Averte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem ; in via tua vivifica me. Unde et in Ecclesiastico legitur, Averte oculos tuos a muliere compta ; et, Virginem ne inspicias, ne scandalizeris in pulchritudine ejus. Præterea, qualiter per mulierem blandam atque extraneam, spiritualiter intelligatur idololatria pravitasque hæretica, tactum est præcedenti capitulo.
paras.en: [[6:24|That they may keep thee from the evil woman|Ut custodiant te a muliere mala]], [[6:24|and from the flattering tongue of the stranger|et blanda lingua extranea]], that is, from every fornicatress and adulteress: from whom he keeps himself who attends to the commandments of God in the manner just described. [[6:25|Let not thy heart covet her beauty|Non concupiscat pulchritudinem ejus cor tuum]] for unlawful use, [[6:25|be not caught with her winks|ne capiaris nutibus illius]], that is, lest thou be enticed into sin by the wanton signs of her eyes; but pray with the Prophet: [[Ps 118:37|Turn away my eyes that they may not behold vanity: quicken me in thy way.|Averte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem ; in via tua vivifica me]] Hence in Ecclesiasticus too we read: [[Ecclus 9:8|Turn away thy face from a woman dressed up|Averte oculos tuos a muliere compta]] [Denis has "thy eyes" for "thy face"]; and: [[Ecclus 9:5|Gaze not upon a maiden, lest her beauty be a stumblingblock to thee.|Virginem ne inspicias, ne scandalizeris in pulchritudine ejus]] Moreover, how idolatry and heretical depravity are to be understood spiritually by the flattering and strange woman was touched on in the preceding chapter.

paras.t: Pretium enim scorti, id est, quod meretrici datur pro ejus amplexu, vix est unius panis : quia modici est valoris, præsertim quod datur scorto cunctis se exponenti. Atque, ut asserit Glossa, brevis est voluptas fornicationis, et perpetua pœna ipsius : et sicut unus panis solum fugat unius diei esuriem, et paulo post famescit qui fuerat saturatus ; sic qui intrat ad scortum, ad horam quidem evaporat libidinem, sed post paululum redit ardentior. Mulier autem viri pretiosam animam rapit, id est, nobilem viri animam et personam æternæ felicitatis capacem, Christi sanguine liberatam, ad summæ Trinitatis similitudinem factam, donis gratiæ decoratam decipit, et damnationi exponit. Quum ergo tam vile sit pretium scorti, tantumque damnum fornicationis, patet quantum sit contemnenda.
paras.en: [[6:26|For the price of a harlot|Pretium enim scorti]], that is, what is given to a harlot for her embrace, [[6:26|is scarce one loaf|vix est unius panis]]: for it is of little worth, especially what is given to a harlot who offers herself to all. And, as the Gloss asserts, the pleasure of fornication is brief, and its punishment everlasting: and as one loaf drives away the hunger of one day only, and a little later he who had been filled is hungry again, so he who goes in to a harlot vents his lust for an hour, but after a little while it comes back more ardent. [[6:26|but the woman catcheth the precious soul of a man|Mulier autem viri pretiosam animam rapit]] [Denis reads *rapit*, "snatches", for *capit*], that is, the noble soul and person of a man, capable of eternal happiness, set free by the blood of Christ, made to the likeness of the most high Trinity[[Gen 1:26||]], adorned with the gifts of grace: this she deceives and exposes to damnation. Since, then, the price of a harlot is so vile, and the loss from fornication so great, it is plain how much fornication is to be despised.

paras.t: Numquid potest homo abscondere ignem in sinu suo, ut vestimenta illius non ardeant, dum ignis immediate tangit pannum ? aut ambulare super prunas, id est carbones ardentes, nudis plantis, ut non comburantur plantæ ejus? quasi dicat, Hoc per naturam est impossibile : quod tamen miraculose gestum est sæpe in evangelica lege. Sic qui ingreditur ad mulierem proximi sui, ad cognoscendum eam, non erit mundus mente, quum tetigerit eam : imo immundissimus fit ita peccando, quamvis corporalis natura a sua superfluitate purgetur, quemadmodum fertur de Bethsabee : Dormivit David cum ea, statimque sanctificata est ab immunditia sua.
paras.en: [[6:27|Can a man hide fire in his bosom, and his garments not burn|Numquid potest homo abscondere ignem in sinu suo, ut vestimenta illius non ardeant]], while the fire touches the cloth directly? [[6:28|Or can he walk upon hot coals|aut ambulare super prunas]], that is, burning coals, with bare soles, [[6:28|and his feet not be burnt?|ut non comburantur plantæ ejus?]] As if to say: This is impossible by nature; which, however, has often been done by miracle under the law of the Gospel. [[6:29|So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife|Sic qui ingreditur ad mulierem proximi sui]], to know her, [[6:29|shall not be clean|non erit mundus]] in mind [[6:29|when he shall touch her|quum tetigerit eam]]: nay, by sinning so he becomes most unclean, though his bodily nature be purged of its superfluity, as is told of Bethsabee: [[2 Kings 11:4|he slept with her: and presently she was purified from her uncleanness|Dormivit David cum ea, statimque sanctificata est ab immunditia sua]].

paras.t: Non grandis est culpa respectu adulterii, quum quis furatus fuerit, potissime ex quadam necessitate, et non res ecclesiasticas, quia hoc sacrilegium esset, nec ab egeno. Ideo subditur : Furatur enim ut esurientem impleat animam, id est, vitam suam aliunde non habentem sustentaculum vitæ, reficiat. Nihilo minus jura civilia nunc acriter puniunt furtum suspendio, quoniam bonum rei publicæ, securam et pacificam hominum conversationem ad invicem præcipue impedit. Sed in lege Moysis ita non fuit. Ideo subjungitur : Deprehensus quoque, reddet septuplum, si habuerit ; et omnem substantiam domus suæ tradet ei a quo furtim aliquid subtraxit, quousque satisfaciat illi, et liberabit se a pœna furti. Si enim non habuisset unde satisfaceret, jussit lex ut venderetur in servum, et de pretio illo satisfieret damnum passo.
paras.en: [[6:30|The fault is not so great|Non grandis est culpa]], in comparison with adultery, [[6:30|when a man hath stolen|quum quis furatus fuerit]], above all out of some necessity, and not the goods of the Church, since that would be sacrilege, nor from a needy man. Therefore it is added: [[6:30|for he stealeth to fill his hungry soul|Furatur enim ut esurientem impleat animam]], that is, to refresh his life, which has no other support of life. Nevertheless the civil laws now punish theft severely with hanging, because it is chiefly a hindrance to the good of the commonwealth, the safe and peaceful dealing of men with one another. But in the law of Moses it was not so. Therefore it is added: [[6:31|And if he be taken, he shall restore sevenfold|Deprehensus quoque, reddet septuplum]], if he has it; [[6:31|and shall give up all the substance of his house|et omnem substantiam domus suæ tradet]] to him from whom he stealthily took anything, until he satisfies him, and he shall free himself from the penalty of theft [these last words are printed as part of the verse, but they are not in the Vulgate]. For if he had not wherewith to make satisfaction, the law ordered that he be sold as a slave, and that the loss be made good from that price to the one who had suffered it[[Ex 22:3||]].

paras.t: Porro de diversa ac differenti restitutione facienda pro furto, diffuse habetur in Exodo. Nullibi tamen habetur in lege, ut pro ablato septuplum restituatur ; sed pro uno bove furato, et apud furem non invento, redderentur quinque boves, atque pro una ove quatuor. Propter quod David, audita parabola Nathan, dixit : Ovem reddat in quadruplum. Pro inanimatis vero rebus jussit lex duplum restitui. Cur ergo Salomon ait, Deprehensus reddet septuplum? Ad hoc Thomas in prima secundæ respondet, quod præceptis legis judicialibus poterat a regibus additio fieri secundum exigentiam temporis. Unde apparet, quod furto apud Judæos invalescente, ut magis reprimeretur, pœna præfata fuerit aucta tempore Salomonis. Judæi enim semper fuerunt, sicut adhuc sunt, avari et fraudulenti, sicut et Petrus de Alliaco in libro contra superstitiones astronomorum, enarrat. Vel, quum dicitur septuplum, sumitur numerus determinatus pro indeterminato, ut sit sensus : Septuplum restituet, id est, plenarie satisfaciet : sicut in Psalmo dicitur, Redde vicinis nostris septuplum in sinu eorum. Etenim septenario totalitas ac perfectio designantur : quoniam septem dierum circulo totum tempus evolvitur et computatur. Unde et Raphael : Ego sum unus, inquit, de septem, qui adstamus ante Deum. — At vero, de litteralibus rationibus diversimodæ restitutionis pro furto, dictum est plene super Exodum, ex dictis Thomæ, Alexandri de Halés, et Guillelmi Parisiensis.
paras.en: Further, on the various and different restitution to be made for theft, there is much at length in Exodus[[Ex 22:1||]][[Ex 22:7||]] [the margin gives Exod. xxii, 1–4, 7–13]. Nowhere in the law, however, is it laid down that sevenfold be restored for what is taken; but for one ox stolen and not found with the thief, five oxen were to be restored, and for one sheep four[[Ex 22:1||]]. For this reason David, on hearing the parable of Nathan, said: [[2 Kings 12:6|He shall restore the ewe fourfold|Ovem reddat in quadruplum]]. But for inanimate things the law ordered double to be restored[[Ex 22:7||]] [the margin gives Exod. xxii, 7–9]. Why then does Solomon say: [[6:31|And if he be taken, he shall restore sevenfold|Deprehensus reddet septuplum]]? To this Thomas replies, in the Prima Secundae, that additions could be made by kings to the judicial precepts of the law as the needs of the time required. Hence it appears that, as theft grew rife among the Jews, the aforesaid penalty was increased in Solomon's time, so that it might be the more restrained. For the Jews always were, as they still are, avaricious and fraudulent, as Peter of Ailly also relates in his book against the superstitions of the astrologers. Or else, when it says [[6:31|sevenfold|septuplum]], a definite number is taken for an indefinite one, so that the sense is: He shall restore sevenfold, that is, he shall make full satisfaction; as it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 78:12|And render to our neighbours sevenfold in their bosom|Redde vicinis nostris septuplum in sinu eorum]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxviii, 12; the verse is Ps 78:12]. For by the number seven totality and perfection are signified, since the whole of time unrolls and is reckoned in the cycle of seven days. Hence Raphael too: I am one, he says, [[Tob 12:15|of the seven, who stand before the Lord|de septem, qui adstamus ante Deum]]. But as for the literal reasons for the different kinds of restitution for theft, this was dealt with fully on Exodus[[Ex 22:1||]], from the sayings of Thomas, Alexander of Hales and William of Paris.

paras.t: Itaque, quamvis furtum sit mortale peccatum, tamen comparative parvum vocatur : quemadmodum in Ezechiele ad Jerusalem dicitur, Justificata est Sodoma ex te.
paras.en: So, although theft is a mortal sin, it is nevertheless called small by comparison: as it is said to Jerusalem in Ezechiel, Sodom is justified by thee[[Ezech 16:52||]] [the margin gives Ezech. xvi only; Denis's words loosely render Ezech 16:51–52, where Sodom and Samaria are justified by Jerusalem's sins].

paras.t: Qui autem adulter est propter cordis inopiam : nam ex defectu sapientiæ et virtutum contingit, quod a tanto scelere non revocatur, nec anima sensualitatem refrenat ; perdet animam suam : quia peccando æternam meretur damnationem, et ita non solum perdit sua, sed et se ipsum. Adulterium quoque in lege puniebatur corporea morte : sicque adulter perdidit vitam suam animalem ac corporalem. Turpitudinem et ignominiam congregat sibi adulter : quia vitia carnis potissime turpia sunt, diffamativa et probrosa ; et opprobrium illius non delebitur : quia in inferno æterna erit ejus confusio. In præsenti quoque malam post se famam relinquit.
paras.en: [[6:32|But he that is an adulterer, for the folly of his heart|Qui autem adulter est propter cordis inopiam]] [*inopia*, "want, poverty": the heart's poverty of wisdom]: for it comes from a lack of wisdom and of virtues that he is not called back from so great a crime, and that his soul does not rein in his sensuality; [[6:32|shall destroy his own soul|perdet animam suam]]: because by sinning he merits eternal damnation, and so loses not only what is his but himself as well. Adultery too was punished in the law with bodily death[[Deut 22:22||]] [the margin gives Deut. xxii, 22–25]; and so the adulterer lost his animal and bodily life. [[6:33|He gathereth to himself shame and dishonour|Turpitudinem et ignominiam congregat sibi]], the adulterer: because the vices of the flesh are above all foul, defaming and shameful; [[6:33|and his reproach shall not be blotted out|et opprobrium illius non delebitur]]: because in hell his confusion will be everlasting. In the present life too he leaves an evil name behind him.

paras.t: Quia zelus justitiæ, id est amor justæ vindictæ, et furor, id est rigor justitiæ, viri, id est Dei omnipotentis, judicis summi, qui fuit sponsus et vir Synagogæ, sicut ait per Isaiam : Quis est iste liber repudii, quem dedi matri vestræ? De qua re per prophetas Jeremiam, Ezechielem, et Osee multa dicuntur. Deus quoque incarnatus, qui vere est vir, judicabit in forma humana; et Deus frequenter in forma viri apparuit, sicque vir appellatur. Nam et in Exodo, ubi habemus, Dominus quasi vir pugnator; in Hebræo habetur, Dominus vir pugnator. Itaque vir iste non parcet adultero in die vindictæ, id est particularis ac universalis judicii. De quo in Job etiam dicitur, Impius ad diem furoris ducetur; et alibi, Ego autem in die ultionis vindicabo et hoc peccatum eorum.
paras.en: [[6:34|Because the jealousy|Quia zelus]] of justice, that is, the love of just vengeance, [[6:34|and rage|et furor]], that is, the rigour of justice, [[6:34|of the husband|viri]] [*vir*, "man" as well as "husband"], that is, of almighty God, the supreme judge, who was the bridegroom and husband of the Synagogue, as he says by Isaias: [[Is 50:1|What is this bill of the divorce of your mother|Quis est iste liber repudii, quem dedi matri vestræ?]] [Denis has "which I gave to your mother"]. On this matter much is said by the prophets Jeremias[[Jer 3:1||]], Ezechiel[[Ezech 16:15||]] and Osee[[Osee 4:12||]][[Osee 4:13||]] [the margin gives Jer. iii, 1–13; Ezech. xvi, 15–34; Osee iv, 12, 13]. God incarnate too, who is truly a man, will judge in human form; and God often appeared in the form of a man, and so he is called a man. For in Exodus too, where we have [[Ex 15:3|The Lord is as a man of war|Dominus quasi vir pugnator]], the Hebrew has: The Lord is a man of war. So this man [[6:34|will not spare|non parcet]] the adulterer [[6:34|in the day of revenge|in die vindictæ]], that is, of the particular and of the universal judgement. Of which it is also said in Job: [[Job 21:30|he shall be brought to the day of wrath|Impius ad diem furoris ducetur]] [Denis has "the wicked man shall be brought"]; and elsewhere: [[Ex 32:34|And I in the day of revenge will visit this sin also of theirs|Ego autem in die ultionis vindicabo et hoc peccatum eorum]].

paras.t: Nec acquiescet cujusquam precibus, ad ignoscendum iniquis: quia tunc est hora retributionis atque justitiæ, non veniæ aut misericordiæ. Nec suscipiet pro redemptione iniqui dona plurima, sicut in lege per dona et sacrificia placabatur. Unde in Psalmo: Non dabit Deo placationem suam, et pretium redemptionis animæ suæ. Hinc ait sanctus doctor Hieronymus: Judex ille nec gratia prævenitur, nec misericordia flectitur, nec pecunia corrumpitur, nec pœnitentia mitigatur. Imo judicaturo Domino, lugubre mundus immugiet, et tribus ad tribum pectora ferient; potentissimi quondam reges nudo latere palpitabunt, adducetur cum suis Plato discipulis. Tunc Aristotelis argumenta non proderunt, quando veniet ille filius pauperculæ quæstuariæ judicaturus orbem terræ.
paras.en: [[6:35|Nor will he yield to any man's prayers|Nec acquiescet cujusquam precibus]], so as to pardon the wicked: because that is then the hour of retribution and justice, not of pardon or mercy. [[6:35|nor will he accept for satisfaction ever so many gifts|Nec suscipiet pro redemptione iniqui dona plurima]] [*pro redemptione*, "as ransom"; Denis adds *iniqui*, "of the wicked man"], as he was appeased in the law by gifts and sacrifices. Hence in the Psalm: [[Ps 48:8|he shall not give to God his ransom|Non dabit Deo placationem suam]], [[Ps 48:9|Nor the price of the redemption of his soul|et pretium redemptionis animæ suæ]]. Hence the holy doctor Jerome says: That Judge is not forestalled by favour, nor bent by pity, nor corrupted by money, nor softened by penance. Nay, when the Lord comes to judge, the world will bellow in mourning, and tribe after tribe will beat their breasts; kings once most mighty will tremble with naked side; Plato will be brought in with his disciples. Then the arguments of Aristotle will be of no avail, when that son of a poor working woman [*quæstuaria*, a woman who works for hire] comes to judge the world.

paras.t: Præterea, ut apparet, posset forsan hoc loco per virum intelligi proprius maritus adulteræ: qui indignans adultero, ei non pepercit a pœna secundum legem infligenda, in die vindictæ, id est lapidationis, seu legalis punitionis adulteri; nec precibus neque muneribus flectebatur.
paras.en: Moreover, as appears, the *man* [Latin *vir*] in this place might perhaps be taken to mean the adulteress's own husband: who, indignant with the adulterer, did not spare him the penalty to be inflicted according to the law, [[6:34|in the day of revenge|in die vindictæ]], that is, of stoning, or of the legal punishment of the adulterer; and was not swayed by prayers nor by gifts.

paras.t: Ecce rursus hic innotescit, quantum adulteria et cetera carnis vitia sint vitanda. Propter quod in suis Proverbiis ait Cyrillus: Scio quod furibunda luxuria oculos non habet, ideo nequit intueri quo ruit. Nimirum ad occasum amantissimæ vitæ tendit, ad amarissimæ mortis proficiscitur barathrum, ad morsum cruentæ libidinis, duce furore, cæca minatur. Quid namque est coitus, nisi deliciosa pernicies mortis, latens venenositas, blandiens dulcis effusio vitam perdens, amplexus destructionem emolliens, atque suavitas dire fallens?
paras.en: See, here again it is made known how much adulteries and the other vices of the flesh are to be shunned. For this reason Cyril says in his Proverbs [the book of moral fables current in the Middle Ages under Cyril's name]: I know that raging lust has no eyes, and so it cannot see where it is rushing. Truly it tends towards the setting of the dearest life, it sets out for the abyss of the bitterest death, for the bite of bloody lust; with fury for its guide, it is driven on blind. For what is intercourse but a delicious ruin of death, a hidden poisonousness, a sweet, flattering outpouring that destroys life, an embrace that softens destruction, and a sweetness direly deceiving?

7.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI SEPTIMI : FILI MI, CUSTODI SERMONES MEOS.
7.title_en: Explanation of the seventh chapter: My son, keep my words.

paras.t: Sciens Salomon animam hominis incomparabiliter esse corpore præstantiorem, et ad spiritualia bona obtinenda creatam, assidue nos hortatur ad vitandum carnalitatem, atque ut spirituales efficiamur per sapientiam et virtutes.
paras.en: Solomon, knowing that the soul of man is incomparably more excellent than the body, and created for obtaining spiritual goods, constantly exhorts us to shun carnality and to become spiritual through wisdom and the virtues.

paras.t: Fili mi, custodi sermones meos, et præcepta mea reconde tibi in corde, ad tuam utilitatem, ut impleas ea. Scienti enim bonum, et non facienti, peccatum est illi.
paras.en: [[7:1|My son, keep my words, and lay up my precepts with thee|Fili mi, custodi sermones meos, et præcepta mea reconde tibi]] in thy heart, for thy profit, that thou mayest fulfil them. For [[Jas 4:17|To him therefore who knoweth to do good and doth it not, to him it is sin|Scienti enim bonum, et non facienti, peccatum est illi]].

paras.t: Fili, honora Dominum cultu latriæ, adorando, sacrificia offerendo, laudando, contemplando, et eum super omnia diligendo, et valebis; præter eum vero ne timueris alienum, id est, nullum alium quam Deum formides, ita ut Deum summe et principaliter vereris, et ejus vicarios ac ceteros non nisi in Deo, et propter Deum, seu propter rationabilem causam. Nam qui aliter timet hominem, cito corruet. Propter quod Seneca: Tutissima, ait, res est, nil timere præter Deum. Hinc in Isaia monetur: Dominum exercituum sanctificate; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester. Et iterum loquitur Isaias: Quis tu, ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis, qui quasi fœnum arescet? Denique, quum Deus sit majestatis immensæ, a quo finaliter separari est incomparabile malum, et cui placere est via salutis æternæ; idcirco incomparabiliter est timendus etiam filiali timore. Propter quod dixit Apostolus: Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis. Et sanctus Job fassus est: Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus, timui Deum, et pondus ejus ferre non potui; itemque: Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest. Idcirco a facie ejus turbatus sum, et considerans eum, timore sollicitor. Verumtamen versus iste in Hebræo dicitur non contineri.
paras.en: [[7:1|Son|Fili]], honour the Lord with the worship of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone], by adoring, offering sacrifices, praising, contemplating, and loving him above all things, and thou shalt be strong; and besides him fear no other: that is, dread no other than God, so that thou fear God supremely and principally, and his vicars and the rest only in God and for God's sake, or for a reasonable cause. For if anyone fears otherwise, [[Prov 29:25|He that feareth man shall quickly fall|qui aliter timet hominem, cito corruet]]. Wherefore Seneca says: The safest thing is to fear nothing but God. Hence the warning in Isaias: [[Is 8:13|Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself: and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread|Dominum exercituum sanctificate; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester]]. And again Isaias says: [[Is 51:12|who art thou, that thou shouldst be afraid of a mortal man, and of the son of man, who shall wither away like grass?|Quis tu, ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis, qui quasi fœnum arescet?]] [the margin gives Is. ii, 12; the words are Is 51:12]. Finally, since God is of boundless majesty, from whom to be separated at the last is an incomparable evil, and to please whom is the way of eternal salvation, he is therefore to be feared incomparably, even with filial fear. Wherefore the Apostle said: [[Heb 10:31|It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis]]. And holy Job confessed: [[Job 31:23|I have always feared God as waves swelling over me, and his weight I was unable to bear|Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus, timui Deum, et pondus ejus ferre non potui]]; and again: [[Job 23:13|he is alone, and no man can turn away his thought|Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest]]. [[Job 23:15|And therefore I am troubled at his presence, and when I consider him, I am made pensive with fear|Idcirco a facie ejus turbatus sum, et considerans eum, timore sollicitor]]. Yet this verse [that is, the words "Son, honour the Lord … fear no other"] is said not to be contained in the Hebrew.

paras.t: Itaque, Honora Dominum, et valebis, id est, per gratiam confortaberis, ac hostibus animarum fortior eris. Siquidem Dominus alibi contestatur: Quicumque glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum; qui autem contemnunt me, erunt ignobiles. Unde in libris Machabæorum scriptum est: Honora eum qui universa conspicit. Nempe ad hoc conditi sumus, ut Creatorem nostrum toto affectu totisque viribus honoremus.
paras.en: So then, Honour the Lord, and thou shalt be strong: that is, thou shalt be strengthened by grace, and shalt be stronger than the enemies of souls. For the Lord declares elsewhere: [[1 Kings 2:30|whosoever shall glorify me, him will I glorify: but they that despise me, shall be despised|Quicumque glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum; qui autem contemnunt me, erunt ignobiles]]. Hence it is written in the books of the Machabees: [[2 Mach 15:2|reverence him that beholdeth all things|Honora eum qui universa conspicit]]. Indeed we were made for this, that we should honour our Creator with all our affection and all our strength.

paras.t: Serva mandata mea, et vives per gratiam; et legem meam quasi pupillam oculi tui, id est cum diligentia summa, sicut pupilla, id est medium oculi, in quo medio vis visiva consistit, a læsione diligentissime custoditur. Liga eam in digitis tuis, id est, operibus eam cum discretione associa. Quemadmodum enim in manibus vis operativa, ita in digitis vis discretiva mystice designatur. Unde Psalmista fatetur: Benedictus Dominus Deus meus, qui docet manus meas ad prælium, et digitos meos ad bellum. Scribe illam in tabulis cordis tui. Hoc supra scriptum est atque expositum.
paras.en: [[7:2|Keep my commandments, and thou shalt live|Serva mandata mea, et vives]] by grace; [[7:2|and my law as the apple of thy eye|et legem meam quasi pupillam oculi tui]]: that is, with the utmost diligence, just as the apple [pupilla, the pupil], that is, the centre of the eye, in which centre the power of sight resides, is most carefully guarded from injury. [[7:3|Bind it upon thy fingers|Liga eam in digitis tuis]]: that is, join it to thy works with discretion. For as the power of working is mystically signified by the hands, so the power of discernment is signified by the fingers. Hence the Psalmist declares: [[Ps 143:1|Blessed be the Lord my God, who teacheth my hands to fight, and my fingers to war|Benedictus Dominus Deus meus, qui docet manus meas ad prælium, et digitos meos ad bellum]]. And: [[7:3|write it upon the tables of thy heart|Scribe illam in tabulis cordis tui]]. This has been written and expounded above[[Prov 3:3||]].

paras.t: Dic sapientiæ, Soror mea es, id est, cordialiter dilige et amplectere eam; et prudentiam voca amicam tuam, ita ut nil caritati ejus contrarium agas: quemadmodum Sapiens asserit: Hanc amavi, et exquisivi a juventute mea; et quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere, et amator factus sum formæ illius. Ut custodiat te a muliere extranea. Judæi autem ad adulteria erant proni, sicut Jeremias testatur: Unusquisque ad uxorem proximi sui hinniebat.
paras.en: [[7:4|Say to wisdom: Thou art my sister|Dic sapientiæ, Soror mea es]]: that is, love her and embrace her with all thy heart; [[7:4|and call prudence thy friend|et prudentiam voca amicam tuam]], so that thou do nothing contrary to thy love of her, as the Wise Man asserts: [[Wis 8:2|Her have I loved, and have sought her out from my youth, and have desired to take for my spouse, and I became a lover of her beauty|Hanc amavi, et exquisivi a juventute mea; et quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere, et amator factus sum formæ illius]]. [[7:5|That she may keep thee from the woman that is not thine|Ut custodiat te a muliere extranea]]. Now the Jews were prone to adulteries, as Jeremias testifies: [[Jer 5:8|every one neighed after his neighbour's wife|Unusquisque ad uxorem proximi sui hinniebat]].

paras.t: De fenestra enim domus meæ per cancellos prospexi juvenem, et vidi parvulos. Potest hoc accipi de corporali fenestra, corporeoque prospectu; et item spirituali fenestra et ejus cancellis, id est de lumine rationis et industriis ejus ac spirituali intuitu. Considero vecordem juvenem, id est insensatum, et concupiscentiis subditum, quasi sine corde existentem. Fornicatio enim, et ebrietas, et vinum auferunt cor.
paras.en: [[7:6|For I looked out of the window of my house through the lattice|De fenestra enim domus meæ per cancellos prospexi]] at a young man, [[7:7|And I see little ones|et vidi parvulos]]. This can be taken of a bodily window and a bodily looking out; and also of a spiritual window and its lattice, that is, of the light of reason and its workings, and of a spiritual gaze. [[7:7|I behold a foolish young man|Considero vecordem juvenem]]: that is, senseless and subject to concupiscences, as one existing without a heart [vecors, "foolish", means literally "heartless"]. For [[Osee 4:11|Fornication, and wine, and drunkenness, take away the understanding|Fornicatio enim, et ebrietas, et vinum auferunt cor]] [the Latin has "take away the heart"].

paras.t: Qui transit per plateas: quia arctam viam salutis abjecit, et latam perditionis viam incedit; juxta angulum, de quo hinc inde respiciat; et prope viam domus illius, scilicet extraneæ, graditur in obscuro, advesperascente die, in noctis tenebris et caligine. Oculus enim adulteri, teste Job, observat caliginem. Talis quoque in obscuritate est rationis, in excæcatione et nubilo passionis.
paras.en: [[7:8|Who passeth through the street|Qui transit per plateas]]: because he has cast away the narrow way of salvation and walks the broad way of perdition; [[7:8|by the corner|juxta angulum]], from which he may look about this way and that; [[7:8|and goeth nigh the way of her house|et prope viam domus illius]], namely of the strange woman, [[7:9|In the dark when it grows late, in the darkness and obscurity of the night|in obscuro, advesperascente die, in noctis tenebris et caligine]]. For [[Job 24:15|The eye of the adulterer|Oculus enim adulteri]], as Job witnesses, [[Job 24:15|observeth darkness|observat caliginem]]. Such a one, too, is in the darkness of reason, in the blindness and cloud of passion.

paras.t: Et ecce occurrit illi mulier ornatu meretricio, præparata ad capiendas, id est decipiendas, animas: talis namque mulier recte vocatur rete diaboli. Garrula et vaga, quietis impatiens, nec valens in domo consistere pedibus suis; nunc foris, nunc in plateis, nunc juxta angulos insidians, id est versute exquirens, qualiter sibi amatores alliciat. Sic et Apostolus de incontinentibus viduis loquitur: Otiosæ discunt circuire domos; non solum otiosæ, sed et verbosæ et curiosæ, loquentes quæ non oportet.
paras.en: [[7:10|And behold a woman meeteth him in harlot's attire|Et ecce occurrit illi mulier ornatu meretricio]], [[7:10|prepared|præparata]] to catch, that is, [[7:10|to deceive souls|decipiendas, animas]]: for such a woman is rightly called the devil's net. [[7:10|talkative and wandering|Garrula et vaga]], [[7:11|Not bearing to be quiet, not able to abide still at home|quietis impatiens, nec valens in domo consistere pedibus suis]], [[7:12|Now abroad, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners|nunc foris, nunc in plateis, nunc juxta angulos insidians]]: that is, cunningly seeking out how she may allure lovers to herself. So too the Apostle speaks of incontinent widows: [[1 Tim 5:13|being idle they learn to go about from house to house: and are not only idle, but tattlers also and busy bodies, speaking things which they ought not|Otiosæ discunt circuire domos; non solum otiosæ, sed et verbosæ et curiosæ, loquentes quæ non oportet]].

paras.t: Apprehensumque deosculatur juvenem, et procaci, id est impudenti, lascivo, vultu blanditur, dicens: Victimas pro salute devovi, id est, hostias pacificas ac salutares pro obtinenda salute Deo offerre tenebar. Hodie reddidi vota mea, id est, desideria et promissa sacrificia Deo exsolvi. Quasi dicat: Bene mihi convenit cum Deo, ideo non est periculum mihi conjungi. Idcirco egressa sum in occursum tuum, desiderans te videre, et reperi.
paras.en: [[7:13|And catching the young man, she kisseth him|Apprehensumque deosculatur juvenem]], [[7:13|and with an impudent face|et procaci]] (that is, shameless and wanton) [[7:13|flattereth, saying|vultu blanditur, dicens]]: [[7:14|I vowed victims for prosperity|Victimas pro salute devovi]]: that is, I was bound to offer to God peace-offerings and saving victims for obtaining welfare [salus means both welfare and salvation]. [[7:14|this day I have paid my vows|Hodie reddidi vota mea]]: that is, I have discharged to God my desires and the sacrifices I promised. As if she said: I am on good terms with God, so there is no danger in my being joined with thee. [[7:15|Therefore I am come out to meet thee, desirous to see thee, and I have found thee|Idcirco egressa sum in occursum tuum, desiderans te videre, et reperi]].

paras.t: Intexui funibus, id est, chordis composui, lectulum meum: quia lectus sic præparatus, est mollior; stravi tapetibus pictis ex Ægypto, id est, per tapeta curiose in Ægypto depicta lectum meum ornavi. Adspersi cubile meum myrrha, et aloe, et cinnamomo, id est speciebus seu herbis istis aromaticis, ut earum delectati odore, delectabilius misceamur. Porro aloe est suavissima arbor, cujus lignum vice seu loco thymiamatis altaribus adoletur. Est quoque herba amarissimi succi: qui succus instar picis constringit, et valde est medicinalis. Cinnamomum etiam est aromatica arbor, cujus cortex instar cannæ protenditur. Veni, inebriemur uberibus, et fruamur cupitis amplexibus, donec illucescat dies. Non est enim vir in domo sua, via abiit longissima. Sacculum pecuniæ secum tulit. In die plenæ lunæ reversurus est in domum suam.
paras.en: [[7:16|I have woven|Intexui funibus]] with cords, that is, I have put together with cords, [[7:16|my bed|lectulum meum]]: because a bed so prepared is softer; [[7:16|I have covered it with painted tapestry, brought from Egypt|stravi tapetibus pictis ex Ægypto]]: that is, I have adorned my bed with tapestries curiously painted in Egypt. [[7:17|I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon|Adspersi cubile meum myrrha, et aloe, et cinnamomo]]: that is, with these aromatic spices or herbs, so that, delighted by their scent, we may be joined more delightfully. Now aloes is a most sweet-scented tree, whose wood is burnt on altars instead of, or in place of, incense. It is also a herb of a very bitter juice, a juice that binds like pitch and is highly medicinal. Cinnamon, too, is an aromatic tree, whose bark stretches out like a reed. [[7:18|Come, let us be inebriated with the breasts, and let us enjoy the desired embraces, till the day appear|Veni, inebriemur uberibus, et fruamur cupitis amplexibus, donec illucescat dies]]. [[7:19|For my husband is not at home, he is gone a very long journey|Non est enim vir in domo sua, via abiit longissima]]. [[7:20|He took with him a bag of money: he will return home the day of the full moon|Sacculum pecuniæ secum tulit. In die plenæ lunæ reversurus est in domum suam]].

paras.t: Circa hoc scribit Lyra: In Hebræo habetur, In termino constituto. Et addit: Nescio cur translator noster posuit, In die plenæ lunæ: nisi quia antiquitus gentiles et alii eos in hoc sequentes, qui credebant omnia ista inferiora provenire ad corporum cœlestium dispositionem, redeuntes a mercationibus suis, libentius intrabant domos suas in plenilunio, ut sic plenitudo lucri sequeretur. Unde adhuc in aliquibus terris Christiani volentes ædificare domum novam, aut mutare domicilium, non libenter faciunt hoc in defectu lunæ, ne sequatur temporalium bonorum defectus; sed faciunt hoc in augmento aut plenitudine lunæ, ut sequatur bonorum temporalium plenitudo. Et hoc est de gentilitatis reliquiis, ideo potius est cavendum. Hæc Lyra. Ego autem magis credo, sermonem Hebraicum esse æquivocum ad utrumque istorum, et ita translator noster transtulit, sicut in Hebræo habetur. Sæpissime etenim ait Lyra, aliter in Hebræo, quam in nostra translatione haberi. Et tamen ex verbis B. Hieronymi, fratris Raymundi, et Pauli, certissime constat quod verba illa Hebraica sunt æquivoca, et Hieronymus ea juxta suam aptiorem significantiam transtulit. Quamvis interdum sensum e sensu magis, quam verbum e verbo transtulerit, nihil tamen de veritate mutavit Hebraica. Estque credendum, quod propter commune bonum Ecclesiæ, Spiritus Sanctus Hieronymum in transferendo direxerit.
paras.en: On this Lyra writes: In the Hebrew it has, At the appointed time. And he adds: I do not know why our translator put [[7:20|the day of the full moon|In die plenæ lunæ]]; unless it is because in ancient times the gentiles, and others who followed them in this, believing that all these lower things come about according to the disposition of the heavenly bodies, when returning from their trading preferred to enter their houses at the full moon, so that fullness of gain might follow. Hence even now in some lands Christians who wish to build a new house or change their dwelling do not willingly do so when the moon is waning, lest a waning of temporal goods should follow, but do it when the moon is waxing or full, so that a fullness of temporal goods may follow. And this is a relic of paganism, and therefore all the more to be avoided. So far Lyra. But I rather believe that the Hebrew word is equivocal [that is, it can bear more than one meaning], admitting both of these senses, and so our translator rendered it as it stands in the Hebrew. For Lyra very often says that the Hebrew has it otherwise than our translation. And yet from the words of Blessed Jerome, of Brother Raymund and of Paul [probably Raymund Martini, author of the Pugio fidei, and Paul of Burgos, whose Additions to Lyra Denis often cites], it is most certainly established that those Hebrew words are equivocal, and Jerome rendered them according to their more fitting meaning. Although he sometimes translated sense for sense rather than word for word, he changed nothing of the Hebrew truth. And it is to be believed that, for the common good of the Church, the Holy Ghost guided Jerome in his translating.

paras.t: Irretivit eum multis sermonibus, id est, illaqueavit juvenem libidinosum amatoriis verbis, et blanditiis labiorum protraxit illum. Statim eam sequitur, quasi bos ductus ad victimandum, id est ad occidendum, ut immoletur, et quasi agnus lasciviens, id est discurrens ac ludens, quum ducitur ad macellum. Hic itaque agnus in malo accipitur pro adolescente indomito, sicut et ovis in Psalmo: Sicut oves in inferno positi sunt. Et ignorans, id est, juvenis est non advertens et nescit quod ad vincula vitiorum æternaliumque pœnarum, et ad diversa incommoda atque pericula in hac vita, stultus, utpote spirituali et infusa sapientia carens, trahitur, donec transfigat sagitta jecur ejus, id est, jaculum carnalis amoris ac voluptas venerea interiora ejus spiritualiter lædat ac perimat. Vel Sagitta, est divinæ ultionis acerbitas, ei jam imminens. Unde Dominus comminatur: Sagittas meas complebo in eis. Velut si avis festinet ad laqueum desiderio cibi, nesciens laquei fraudem; sic ipse desiderio voluptatis ad mortem præfatam accelerat; et nescit quia de periculo animæ illius agitur: id est, juvenis non considerat quod in omnibus his invisibilis hostis non aliud machinetur, nisi ut eum trahat ad tam enormia scelera, deinde ad inferni tormenta.
paras.en: [[7:21|She entangled him with many words|Irretivit eum multis sermonibus]]: that is, she ensnared the lustful young man with amorous words, [[7:21|and drew him away with the flattery of her lips|et blanditiis labiorum protraxit illum]]. [[7:22|Immediately he followeth her|Statim eam sequitur]], [[7:22|as an ox led to be a victim|quasi bos ductus ad victimandum]], that is, to be killed, to be sacrificed, [[7:22|and as a lamb playing the wanton|et quasi agnus lasciviens]], that is, running about and frisking, when it is led to the shambles. Here, then, the lamb is taken in a bad sense, for an unruly youth, as is the sheep too in the Psalm: [[Ps 48:15|They are laid in hell like sheep|Sicut oves in inferno positi sunt]]. [[7:22|and not knowing|Et ignorans]]: that is, the young man is not heeding, and knows not that [[7:22|to bonds|ad vincula]] of vices and of eternal punishments, and to divers harms and dangers in this life, [[7:22|like a fool|stultus]], as one lacking spiritual and infused wisdom, [[7:22|he is drawn|trahitur]], [[7:23|Till the arrow pierce his liver|donec transfigat sagitta jecur ejus]]: that is, until the dart of carnal love and venereal pleasure spiritually wounds and slays his inward parts. Or, the Arrow is the bitterness of divine vengeance, now hanging over him. Hence the Lord threatens: I [[Deut 32:23|will spend my arrows among them|Sagittas meas complebo in eis]]. [[7:23|as if a bird should make haste to the snare|Velut si avis festinet ad laqueum]] from desire of food, not knowing the deceit of the snare, so he, from desire of pleasure, hastens to the death spoken of; [[7:23|and knoweth not that his life is in danger|et nescit quia de periculo animæ illius agitur]]: that is, the young man does not consider that in all these things the invisible enemy contrives nothing else than to draw him to such monstrous crimes, and then to the torments of hell.

paras.t: Nunc ergo, fili mi, audi me, et attende verba oris mei. Ne abstrahatur in viis illius mens tua, neque decipiaris semitis ejus: id est, cor tuum nequaquam a Deo recedat, acquiescendo, seque immiscendo concupiscentiis ac operibus talis adulteræ.
paras.en: [[7:24|Now, therefore, my son, hear me, and attend to the words of my mouth|Nunc ergo, fili mi, audi me, et attende verba oris mei]]. [[7:25|Let not thy mind be drawn away in her ways: neither be thou deceived with her paths|Ne abstrahatur in viis illius mens tua, neque decipiaris semitis ejus]]: that is, let thy heart in no way depart from God by consenting to, and mingling thyself in, the concupiscences and works of such an adulteress.

paras.t: Multos enim vulneratos vulnere iniqui consensus et concupiscentiæ, dejecit, trahendo in opus nefarium, et fortissimi quique: qui fortissimi erant corpore et anima, hoc est sancti et sapientes, ac validi corpore, ut primus parens, et filii Dei, de quibus in Genesi; Samson quoque et David, ac Salomon iste; interfecti, id est, spiritualiter occisi sunt ab ea, id est ad venerea tracti, aut a rectitudine justitiæ emolliti ab ea, id est a mulieribus, sumendo singulare pro plurali. Viæ inferi domus ejus, id est, ea quæ ipsa agit in domo sua ac sui domestici, sunt viæ inferni, id est scelera ad infernum trahentia. De quibus Christus in Evangelio: Portæ, inquit, inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam. Vitia namque contra Ecclesiam electorum nequeunt finaliter prævalere. Penetrantes in interiora mortis, id est ad obscurissima ac profundissima infernalis calamitatis supplicia.
paras.en: For [[7:26|many wounded|Multos enim vulneratos]] with the wound of wicked consent and concupiscence [[7:26|she hath cast down|dejecit]], drawing them into the abominable deed, [[7:26|and the strongest|et fortissimi quique]]: those who were strongest in body and soul, that is, holy and wise and also strong in body, like the first parent, and the sons of God of whom we read in Genesis[[Gen 6:2||]]; Samson too[[Judg 16:1||]], and David[[2 Kings 11:2||]], and this Solomon[[3 Kings 11:1||]] [the margin gives Judic. xvi; II Reg. xi, 2–4; III Reg. xi, 1–8]; [[7:26|have been slain|interfecti]], that is, spiritually killed, [[7:26|by her|sunt ab ea]]: that is, drawn to venereal pleasures, or softened and turned from the uprightness of justice, by her, that is, by women, the singular being taken for the plural. [[7:27|Her house is the way to hell|Viæ inferi domus ejus]] [literally "her house is the ways of hell"]: that is, the things which she does in her house, she and her household, are the ways of hell, that is, crimes that drag men to hell. Of which Christ says in the Gospel: [[Matt 16:18|the gates|Portæ]], he says, [[Matt 16:18|of hell shall not prevail against it|inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam]]. For vices cannot finally prevail against the Church of the elect. [[7:27|reaching even to the inner chambers of death|Penetrantes in interiora mortis]]: that is, to the darkest and deepest torments of the calamity of hell.

paras.t: Ecce ex his docemur et avisamur, ne quis in pulchritudine et abundantia sermocinationum suarum ac doctrinarum incaute confidat: quoniam Salomon iste, qui tot et tanta tam sapienter et pulchre contra vitia carnis, contra scorta et adulteria ac idololatrias prædicavit ac docuit, ab eisdem præ cunctis hominibus stolidissime ac immoderatissime est devictus. Cum grandi igitur timore et cautela ac humilitate evangelizandum est ac instruendum, hortandum et increpandum, ita ut prædicator ac doctor sic instruat, increpet, exhorteturque proximos, quatenus jugiter memor sit propriæ fragilitatis, ac Dominum deprecetur ne relinquatur ab eo, et quæ loquitur aliis, applicet sibi; et potissime a vitiis abstineat carnis, quum et Innocentius dicat: O extrema libidinis turpitudo, quæ non solum mentem effeminat, sed et corpus enervat; non solum maculat animam, sed etiam fœdat personam! Omne enim peccatum quodcumque fecerit homo, extra corpus est; qui autem fornicatur, peccat in corpus suum. Semper illam præcedit concupiscentiæ ardor, petulantia comitatur, fœtor et immunditia semper sequuntur. Hoc vitium efficit hominem ad ea quæ Dei sunt, insensibilem, acediosum, frontosum, inquietum, inverecundum.
paras.en: See, from these things we are taught and warned that no one should trust incautiously in the beauty and abundance of his discourses and teachings: since this Solomon, who preached and taught so many and such great things, so wisely and beautifully, against the vices of the flesh, against harlots and adulteries and idolatries, was overcome by those same things more stupidly and more immoderately than any other man. With great fear, then, and caution and humility must we preach the Gospel and instruct, exhort and rebuke; so that the preacher and teacher should so instruct, rebuke and exhort his neighbours as to be ever mindful of his own frailty, and pray the Lord that he be not forsaken by him, and apply to himself what he says to others; and above all abstain from the vices of the flesh, since Innocent too says [Pope Innocent III, On the Misery of the Human Condition]: O extreme foulness of lust, which not only makes the mind effeminate but also enervates the body; not only stains the soul but also defiles the person! [[1 Cor 6:18|Every sin that a man doth is without the body: but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body|Omne enim peccatum quodcumque fecerit homo, extra corpus est; qui autem fornicatur, peccat in corpus suum]]. Ardour of concupiscence always goes before it, wantonness goes with it, stench and uncleanness always follow it. This vice makes a man, towards the things of God, insensible, slothful [acediosus: given to acedia, sloth in the things of God], brazen, restless, shameless.

8.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI OCTAVI : NUMQUID NON SAPIENTIA CLAMITAT, ET PRUDENTIA DAT VOCEM SUAM ?
8.title_en: Declaration of the eighth chapter: Doth not wisdom cry aloud, and prudence put forth her voice?

paras.t: Hic Salomon sapientiam multipliciter laudat, actus et fructus ejus explanat, et tandem ad increatæ Sapientiæ, quæ est Verbum Patris, æternam generationem ac contemplationem ascendit.
paras.en: Here Solomon praises wisdom in many ways and sets out its acts and fruits, and at length rises to the eternal generation and the contemplation of the uncreated Wisdom, which is the Word of the Father.

paras.t: Numquid non sapientia clamitat, et prudentia dat vocem suam ? Hoc est quod scriptum est et expositum supra ubi dicitur : Sapientia foris prædicat, et in plateis dat vocem suam. Sic quoque quod subditur, In summis excelsisque verticibus supra viam, in mediis semitis stans, juxta portas civitatis in ipsis foribus loquitur, dicens, concordat cum eo quod scriptum est supra : In capite turbarum clamitat, in foribus portarum urbis profert verba sua. Ibi igitur horum expositio requiratur ; tamen paululum tangam eam. Nempe excelsi vertices, sunt Patriarchæ, Vates, Apostoli ac ceteri sancti prædicatores ac doctores : per quos Sapientia ab exordio clamitavit ac docuit alios.
paras.en: [[8:1|Doth not wisdom cry aloud, and prudence put forth her voice?|Numquid non sapientia clamitat, et prudentia dat vocem suam]]? This is what was written and explained above, where it is said: [[Prov 1:20|Wisdom preacheth abroad, she uttereth her voice in the streets|Sapientia foris prædicat, et in plateis dat vocem suam]]. So too what follows, [[8:2|Standing in the top of the highest places by the way, in the midst of the paths|In summis excelsisque verticibus supra viam, in mediis semitis stans]], [[8:3|Beside the gates of the city, in the very doors she speaketh, saying|juxta portas civitatis in ipsis foribus loquitur, dicens]], agrees with what was written above: [[Prov 1:21|At the head of multitudes she crieth out, in the entrance of the gates of the city she uttereth her words|In capite turbarum clamitat, in foribus portarum urbis profert verba sua]]. Let the explanation of these words, then, be sought there; yet I shall touch on it a little. The highest places, namely, are the Patriarchs, the Prophets, the Apostles and the other holy preachers and doctors, through whom Wisdom has cried aloud from the beginning and taught others.

paras.t: O viri, ad vos clamito, et vox mea ad filios hominum, ut convertamini et salvemini. Intelligite, parvuli, id est imperfecti, astutiam, id est prudentiam. Sicque astutia sumitur hic in bono. Et insipientes, animadvertite. Audite, quoniam de rebus magnis, id est de sublimi materia et generatione æternæ Sapientiæ increatæ ac genitæ, de proprietatibus sapientiæ creatæ infusæ, locutura sum, et aperientur labia mea, ut recta, id est justa documenta præceptaque, prædicent.
paras.en: [[8:4|O ye men, to you I call, and my voice is to the sons of men|O viri, ad vos clamito, et vox mea ad filios hominum]], that ye may be converted and saved [these last words, printed as part of the verse, are not in the Vulgate]. [[8:5|O little ones understand|Intelligite, parvuli]], that is, ye that are imperfect, [[8:5|subtlety|astutiam]], that is, prudence. And so *astutia* [subtlety, cunning, usually a word of blame] is taken here in a good sense. [[8:5|and ye unwise, take notice|Et insipientes, animadvertite]]. [[8:6|Hear, for|Audite, quoniam]] [[8:6|I will speak|locutura sum]] [[8:6|of great things|de rebus magnis]], that is, of a sublime matter, of the generation of the eternal Wisdom, uncreated and begotten, and of the properties of the created, infused wisdom; [[8:6|and my lips shall be opened|et aperientur labia mea]] [[8:6|to preach|prædicent]] [[8:6|right things|ut recta]], that is, just teachings and precepts.

paras.t: Veritatem meditabitur guttur meum internum, scilicet cor, quo verbum intellectuale profertur, guttur quoque corporale, in quantum verba per illud enuntiantur ; et labia mea detestabuntur impium. Justi sunt omnes sermones mei, et non est in eis pravum quid, neque perversum. Pertinent enim verba hæc Salomonis ad Scripturam canonicam, in qua nunquam a veritate et æquitate receditur, quantum ad ea quæ ipsa Scriptura asserit vera esse et æqua. Recti sunt intelligentibus eos, per fidem et illuminationem divinam, aut informationem catholicam : qui in captivitatem redigunt proprium intellectum, et divinæ auctoritati humiliter se subdunt ; et æqui invenientibus scientiam, quæ est donum Dei, per quam veritas noscitur Scripturarum : imo etiam scientiam quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ, per quam ea quæ fidei sunt et Scripturæ, agnoscuntur diffuse ac limpide, et contra perfidos defenduntur. Porro non intelligentibus et perversi sensus hominibus, qui ea quæ fidei sunt, volunt suo intellectu metiri ac penetrare, atque tantumdem credere quantum ipsis apparet credendum, non videntur sermones hi esse veri et justi.
paras.en: [[8:7|My mouth shall meditate truth|Veritatem meditabitur guttur meum]] [*guttur*, "throat"]: the inward throat, namely the heart, by which the word of the intellect is brought forth, and also the bodily throat, inasmuch as words are uttered through it; [[8:7|and my lips shall hate wickedness|et labia mea detestabuntur impium]]. [[8:8|All my words are just, there is nothing wicked, nor perverse in them|Justi sunt omnes sermones mei, et non est in eis pravum quid, neque perversum]]. For these words of Solomon belong to canonical Scripture, in which there is never any departure from truth and equity, as regards what Scripture itself asserts to be true and equitable. [[8:9|They are right to them that understand|Recti sunt intelligentibus eos]], through faith and divine enlightenment, or Catholic instruction: those who bring their own understanding into captivity[[2 Cor 10:5||]] and humbly submit themselves to divine authority; [[8:9|and just to them that find knowledge|et æqui invenientibus scientiam]], the knowledge that is a gift of God, by which the truth of the Scriptures is known; and indeed also the knowledge that is a gift of grace freely given [that is, a grace given for the good of others, not for the sanctification of the one who has it], by which the things of faith and of Scripture are known at large and clearly, and are defended against unbelievers. But to those who do not understand, and to men of perverse mind, who wish to measure and penetrate the things of faith with their own understanding, and to believe just so much as seems to them believable, these words do not seem to be true and just.

paras.t: Accipite disciplinam meam, id est correctionem, informationem, modestiam meam, et non pecuniam meam. Quasi dicat : Spiritualia, non corporalia, bona præbeo vobis. Doctrinam magis quam aurum eligite, id est thesaurum exteriorem : quia quo anima est præstantior corpore, eo doctrina thesauro est incomparabiliter plus optanda. Hinc subditur : melior est enim sapientia cunctis pretiosissimis opibus, videlicet auro, gemmis, et consimilibus rebus ac corporalibus speciebus in suo genere valde pretiosis, ut ea quæ regina Saba legitur tertio Regum detulisse ad Salomonem : et omne desiderabile, ei non potest comparari, id est nullum bonum seu appetibile sensitivum, quum diversorum sint generum : quemadmodum dona naturæ comparari, id est in dignitate æquari, nequeunt donis gratiæ, nec sensitivum intellectivo. Quod si ista de increata Sapientia exponantur, constat quod illa infinite emineat cunctis creatis. Possunt tamen de sapientia creata, ea præsertim, quæ donum est, accipi. De qua scriptum est : Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, bonis consentiens, plena misericordia et fructibus bonis.
paras.en: [[8:10|Receive my instruction|Accipite disciplinam meam]], that is, my correction, my teaching, my discipline of manners, [[8:10|and not money|et non pecuniam]] of mine; as if to say: I offer you spiritual goods, not bodily ones. [[8:10|choose knowledge rather than gold|Doctrinam magis quam aurum eligite]], that is, outward treasure: for as much as the soul is more excellent than the body, so much is knowledge incomparably more to be desired than treasure. Hence it is added: [[8:11|For wisdom is better than all the most precious things|melior est enim sapientia cunctis pretiosissimis opibus]], namely gold, gems and like things, and bodily goods of great price in their kind, such as those the queen of Saba is read in the third book of Kings to have brought to Solomon[[3 Kings 10:2||]][[3 Kings 10:10||]]; [[8:11|and whatsoever may be desired cannot be compared to it|et omne desiderabile, ei non potest comparari]], that is, no good thing or object of the senses' desire, since they are of different kinds: just as the gifts of nature cannot be compared, that is, equalled in worth, with the gifts of grace, nor what belongs to the senses with what belongs to the intellect. And if these words are expounded of the uncreated Wisdom, it is plain that it infinitely surpasses all created things. Yet they can be taken of created wisdom too, above all the wisdom that is a gift [that is, the gift of the Holy Ghost], of which it is written: [[Jas 3:17|the wisdom that is from above, first indeed is chaste, then peaceable, modest, easy to be persuaded, consenting to the good, full of mercy and good fruits|Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, bonis consentiens, plena misericordia et fructibus bonis]].

paras.t: Ego sapientia habito in consilio, et eruditis intersum cogitationibus. Increata Sapientia per gratiam adest et commoratur in consilio, id est inter eos qui ad inquirendum vel dandum salubria consilia ac decreta, sunt congregati. Sic specialiter est in synodo generali, quam credendum est a Spiritu Sancto gubernari ac dirigi ad definiendum ac bene sentiendum de his quæ necessaria sunt saluti, et propter quæ ipsa synodus principaliter est collecta, quum in Evangelio dicat Salvator : Ubi duo vel tres congregati fuerint in nomine meo, ibi in medio eorum sum. Habitat quoque in consilio, id est in salubri et pia inquisitione de agendis, in qua libenter dirigit consulentem, quoniam placet ei talis consultatio. Sapientia quoque creata habitat in consilio, quia formaliter dirigit in eodem ; et sapientia illa quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ, est utique in generali concilio. Similiter sapientia quæ est donum, est in eis qui in caritate exsistunt.
paras.en: [[8:12|I, wisdom, dwell in counsel, and am present in learned thoughts|Ego sapientia habito in consilio, et eruditis intersum cogitationibus]]. The uncreated Wisdom is present by grace and abides [[8:12|in counsel|in consilio]], that is, among those who are gathered together to seek or to give wholesome counsels and decrees. So in a special way it is in a general council, which we must believe to be governed and directed by the Holy Ghost to define and to judge rightly of the things necessary to salvation, for which the council has chiefly been assembled, since the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Matt 18:20|where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them|Ubi duo vel tres congregati fuerint in nomine meo, ibi in medio eorum sum]]. It also dwells in counsel, that is, in a wholesome and devout inquiry into what is to be done, in which it gladly directs the one who takes counsel, since such consultation pleases it. Created wisdom also dwells in counsel, because it is what directs in it, as its form; and that wisdom which is a gift of grace freely given is certainly present in a general council. Likewise the wisdom that is a gift [that is, the gift of the Holy Ghost] is in those who abide in charity.

paras.t: Denique de utraque hac sapientia accipi potest quod ait Apostolus : Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos : sapientiam autem non hujus mundi, nec principum sæculi hujus ; sed loquimur Dei sapientiam in mysterio, quæ abscondita est. Insuper sapientia tam increata quam creata, eruditis, id est prudentibus et sensatis, atque salubribus cogitationibus adest et interest, quia procedunt ex sapientia, et placent supersapientissimo Deo ; cogitationibus vero stultis, vanis, phantasticis et malignis, et imaginationibus frivolis ac insensatis non adest, nec placent ei, sed despicit eas, quemadmodum scriptum est : Spiritus sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum, et auferet se a cogitationibus quæ sunt sine intellectu. Ideo dixit Apostolus : Non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis : quoniam ad cogitandum salubriter ac meritorie, requiritur gratia Dei, imo et actualis motio Spiritus Sancti. Itaque cogitationes eruditæ, sunt, quæ secundum sacræ Scripturæ doctrinam regulantur ac diriguntur, et ex sapientia salutari nascuntur. Qui igitur cupit Deo placere, imo et ipsum suo cordi gratiose præsentem habere, satagat omni exclusa cogitatione inutili, inani, phantastica, perturbativa, perversa, eruditas intra se cogitationes habere, revolvere, possidere, quibus cor coram Deo honeste occupatur, pulchre depingitur, præcipue decoratur.
paras.en: Finally, what the Apostle says can be taken of both these wisdoms: [[1 Cor 2:6|we speak wisdom among the perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, neither of the princes of this world|Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos : sapientiam autem non hujus mundi, nec principum sæculi hujus]]; [[1 Cor 2:7|But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, a wisdom which is hidden|sed loquimur Dei sapientiam in mysterio, quæ abscondita est]]. Moreover wisdom, both uncreated and created, is present and takes part in [[8:12|learned|eruditis]], that is, prudent, sensible and wholesome, thoughts, because they proceed from wisdom and please the all-wise God [*supersapientissimo*, literally "more than most wise"]; but to foolish, vain, fanciful and malicious thoughts, and to frivolous and senseless imaginings, it is not present; they do not please it, but it despises them, as it is written: [[Wis 1:5|the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding|Spiritus sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum, et auferet se a cogitationibus quæ sunt sine intellectu]]. Therefore the Apostle said: [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves|Non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid a nobis, quasi ex nobis]]; for to think wholesomely and meritoriously, the grace of God is required, and indeed the actual motion of the Holy Ghost. And so learned thoughts are those which are ruled and directed according to the teaching of Holy Scripture and are born of saving wisdom. Whoever therefore desires to please God, and indeed to have Him present by grace in his heart, let him take care, shutting out every useless, empty, fanciful, disturbing and perverse thought, to have learned thoughts within him, to turn them over and possess them; with these the heart is worthily occupied before God, beautifully painted and above all adorned.

paras.t: Timor Domini odit malum. Nam timor filialis odit et vitat malum culpæ, eo quod inhonorativum et offensivum sit Dei : sicque ad cogitationes eruditas inducit, et cogitationes abjicit insensatas. Timor vero servilis odit malum pœnæ, quoniam pœnam abhorret, nec amat justitiam. Idcirco, in quantum servilis, dicitur vulnerare. Arrogantiam cordis, et superbiam in verbis et factis, et viam pravam, id est falsam doctrinam, actionem iniquam, et quidquid publice alios scandalizat, et os bilingue detestor : quoniam veræ sapientiæ atque justitiæ contrariantur. Dicitur autem Os bilingue, quasi duabus utens linguis, id est duplici modo loquendi sibi invicem repugnanti : quoniam in præsentia loquitur blande ac placite, aliter vero in absentia. Imo ubique vult loquendo placere : propter quod juxta audientium libitum variat verba. Non enim stabilit se in vero, nec justi est tenax. Hinc Dominus ait : Visitabo super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur. Et alibi legitur : Si ascenderit usque ad cœlum superbia ejus, et caput ejus nubes tetigerit, quasi sterquilinium in fine perdetur. Vitemus itaque universa hæc vitia, ne detestabiles simus Deo ; simus quoque in verbis constantes, veri ac justi, nec quæramus loqui placentia, sed magis expedientia.
paras.en: [[8:13|The fear of the Lord hateth evil|Timor Domini odit malum]]. For filial fear hates and shuns the evil of guilt, because it dishonours and offends God; and so it leads to learned thoughts and casts out senseless ones. But servile fear hates the evil of punishment, because it shrinks from punishment, and does not love justice. Therefore, insofar as it is servile, it is said to wound [so the print]. [[8:13|I hate arrogance|Arrogantiam]] of heart, [[8:13|and pride|et superbiam]] in words and deeds, [[8:13|and every wicked way|et viam pravam]], that is, false doctrine, wicked action, and whatever gives public scandal to others, [[8:13|and a mouth with a double tongue|et os bilingue detestor]]: because they are contrary to true wisdom and justice. A mouth is called double-tongued as if using two tongues, that is, a twofold way of speaking at odds with itself: for to a man's face it speaks smoothly and pleasingly, but otherwise behind his back. Indeed it wishes to please everywhere by its speech, and so it varies its words to suit the pleasure of its hearers; for it does not stand firm in the truth, nor hold fast to what is just. Hence the Lord says: [[Soph 1:9|I will visit|Visitabo]] [[Soph 1:9|upon every one that entereth arrogantly|super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur]]. And elsewhere we read: [[Job 20:6|If his pride mount up even to heaven, and his head touch the clouds|Si ascenderit usque ad cœlum superbia ejus, et caput ejus nubes tetigerit]], [[Job 20:7|In the end he shall be destroyed like a dunghill|quasi sterquilinium in fine perdetur]]. Let us therefore shun all these vices, lest we be hateful to God; and let us be constant, true and just in our words, and not seek to say what pleases, but rather what profits.

paras.t: Meum est consilium, id est, consilium rectum de quo dixi, Ego sapientia habito in consilio, est donum meum. Porro consilium proprie sumptum, non est in Deo, quum in eo non sit inquisitio de agendis, sed æterna et incommutabilis certitudo. Propter quod asserit Damascenus, quod consilium est ignorantis naturæ. Scriptura tamen frequenter attribuit Deo consilium, quantum ad id quod perfectionis est in ratione consilii, quoniam omnia provide agit. Hinc Dominus apud Isaiam ait : Consilium meum stabit. Et in Psalmo asseritur : Consilium Domini in æternum manet. Et Apostolus ait : Deus operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ. Et æquitas ; mea est prudentia, mea est fortitudo : id est, ista omnia plene et cum infinita perfectione consistunt in me, et quidquid veritatis et perfectionis invenitur de his in creaturis, a me fontaliter fluxit. Hinc habetur apud Danielem : Sapientia et fortitudo ejus sunt. Nemo ergo superbiat, aut inaniter glorietur ; sed quidquid boni in se aut in toto fuerit universo, Deo cum omni humilitate et gratiarum actione adscribat.
paras.en: [[8:14|Counsel|Meum est consilium]] is mine, that is, the right counsel of which I said, [[8:12|I, wisdom, dwell in counsel|Ego sapientia habito in consilio]], is my gift. Now counsel taken in its proper sense is not in God, since there is in Him no inquiry into what is to be done, but eternal and unchangeable certainty. For this reason Damascene says that counsel belongs to a nature that does not know. Yet Scripture often attributes counsel to God, as regards what belongs to perfection in the notion of counsel, since He does all things with foresight. Hence the Lord says in Isaias: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand|Consilium meum stabit]]. And in the Psalm it is said: [[Ps 32:11|the counsel of the Lord standeth for ever|Consilium Domini in æternum manet]]. And the Apostle says: God [[Eph 1:11|worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ]]. [[8:14|and equity|Et æquitas]]; [[8:14|prudence is mine, strength is mine|mea est prudentia, mea est fortitudo]]: that is, all these are in me fully and with infinite perfection, and whatever of truth and perfection is found of them in creatures has flowed from me as from its fountain. Hence we have in Daniel: [[Dan 2:20|wisdom and fortitude are his|Sapientia et fortitudo ejus sunt]]. Let no one then be proud or glory in vain; but whatever good there is in himself or in the whole universe, let him ascribe it to God with all humility and thanksgiving.

paras.t: Per me, id est ex dono ac providentia mea, reges regnant. Non est enim potestas nisi a Deo, cui cura est de omnibus, potissime de hominibus. Idcirco ex ejus providentia dependet regimen universi : et palam quod virtuosi præsidentes ex Deo regnent ac præsint ; vitiosi autem superiores saltem permissive regnant ex Deo, qui regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi. Qui et ait : Dabo tibi regem in furore meo, et principes in indignatione mea. Hinc etiam in Daniele dicitur : Ipse transfert regna, atque constituit ; et rursum, Dominatur Excelsus in regno hominum, et cuicumque voluerit, dat illud.
paras.en: [[8:15|By me|Per me]], that is, by my gift and providence, [[8:15|kings reign|reges regnant]]. [[Rom 13:1|For there is no power but from God|Non est enim potestas nisi a Deo]], [[Wis 12:13|who hast care of all|cui cura est de omnibus]], and above all of men[[1 Pet 5:7||]]. Therefore the government of the universe depends on His providence; and it is plain that virtuous rulers reign and govern from God, while vicious superiors reign from God at least by His permission, [[Job 34:30|Who maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people|qui regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi]]. And He it is that says: [[Osee 13:11|I will give thee a king in my wrath|Dabo tibi regem in furore meo]], and princes in my indignation [Denis's reading; the Vulgate has "and will take him away in my indignation"]. Hence also it is said in Daniel: He [[Dan 2:21|taketh away kingdoms, and establisheth them|transfert regna, atque constituit]] [*transfert*, literally "transfers"]; and again: [[Dan 4:14|the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men: and he will give it to whomsoever it shall please him|Dominatur Excelsus in regno hominum, et cuicumque voluerit, dat illud]].

paras.t: Iterum, reges regnant per Sapientiam increatam, quia ut bene et salubriter regnent, ex directione illius procedit, qui etiam per angelos sanctos dirigit præsidentes. Insuper, sancti Apostoli et omnes virtuosi prælati ac præsules, super fideles sibi commissos regnaverunt ex Deo et per Deum : cui ait Propheta, Constitues eos principes super omnem terram. Et legum conditores justa decernunt : id est, ex mea illustratione originaliter manat quod legislatores instituunt justa decreta, et vera dictant judicia. Sicut enim non est potestas nisi a Deo, sic non est sapientia nec justitia, nisi a Deo.
paras.en: Again, [[8:15|kings reign|reges regnant]] through the uncreated Wisdom, because that they reign well and wholesomely comes from the direction of Him who also directs rulers through the holy angels. Moreover the holy Apostles and all virtuous prelates and bishops have reigned over the faithful committed to them from God and through God, to whom the Prophet says: [[Ps 44:17|thou shalt make them princes over all the earth|Constitues eos principes super omnem terram]]. [[8:15|and lawgivers decree just things|Et legum conditores justa decernunt]]: that is, it flows in the first place from my enlightening that lawgivers establish just decrees and pronounce true judgments. For as [[Rom 13:1|there is no power but from God|non est potestas nisi a Deo]], so there is no wisdom or justice but from God.

paras.t: Ego diligentes me diligo. Universos electos et prædestinatos diligit Deus ab æterno in lumine providentiæ suæ ; eos autem qui diligunt Deum per caritatem, ipse etiam diligit secundum præsentem justitiam, non autem secundum æternam prædestinationem, nisi sint electi. Unde ait : Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo, et ego diligam eum. Et rursum Sapientia increata asserit : Pater amat vos, quia vos me amastis. Verumtamen dilectio nostra, non est causa aut ratio prima, quod Deus nos diligit : imo econtra, quoniam ipse dilexit nos, et nos diligimus eum, quia dilectio nostra ad eum, est donum ex sua dilectione ad nos habens ortum. Ideo scriptum est : In hoc est caritas, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos. Eos vero qui diligunt Deum solum naturali dilectione, et ceteros, imo et cuncta creata diligit Deus, quantum ad id quod sunt et quod habent ab ipso, prout in libro Sapientiæ legitur : Diligis omnia quæ sunt.
paras.en: [[8:17|I love them that love me|Ego diligentes me diligo]]. God loves all the elect and predestined from eternity in the light of His providence; and those who love God through charity He also loves according to their present justice, though not according to eternal predestination, unless they are elect. Hence He says: [[John 14:21|he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him|Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo, et ego diligam eum]]. And again the uncreated Wisdom declares: [[John 16:27|the Father himself loveth you, because you have loved me|Pater amat vos, quia vos me amastis]]. Yet our love is not the cause or first reason why God loves us: on the contrary, because He has loved us, we also love Him, since our love for Him is a gift that has its origin in His love for us. Therefore it is written: [[1 John 4:10|In this is charity: not as though we had loved God, but because he hath first loved us|In hoc est caritas, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos]]. And those who love God only with a natural love, and all others, and indeed all created things, God loves as regards what they are and what they have from Him, as we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 11:25|thou lovest all things that are|Diligis omnia quæ sunt]].

paras.t: Et qui mane vigilaverint ad me, id est, celeriter et statim quum gratia eis infunditur, seu divinitus inspirantur, mentem suam direxerint ad me diligenter, invenient me, id est, exaudientur a me, et incrementum gratiæ sortientur, ac contemplari me poterunt. Hora quoque diluculi specialiter apta est ad vacandum Altissimo, sicut Ecclesiasticus ait : Justus cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum. Qui ergo mane, id est protinus in aurora, antequam ad alia agenda processerit, vigilanter ad Deum suam elevaverit mentem, sicut docuit Christus, Primum (inquiens) quærite regnum Dei et justitiam ejus : cito invenient eum. Ideo loquitur Isaias : De mane vigilabo ad te.
paras.en: [[8:17|and they that in the morning early watch for me|Et qui mane vigilaverint ad me]], that is, who quickly and at once, when grace is poured into them or they are inspired from above, direct their mind diligently to me, [[8:17|shall find me|invenient me]], that is, they shall be heard by me, obtain an increase of grace, and be able to contemplate me. The hour of dawn, too, is especially suited to giving oneself to the Most High, as Ecclesiasticus says: The just man [[Ecclus 39:6|will give his heart to resort early to the Lord|cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum]]. Those then who in the morning, that is, straight away at daybreak, before going on to do other things, watchfully raise their mind to God, as Christ taught: [[Matt 6:33|Seek ye therefore first|Primum]] (He says) [[Matt 6:33|the kingdom of God, and his justice|quærite regnum Dei et justitiam ejus]], shall quickly find Him. Therefore Isaias says: [[Is 26:9|in the morning early I will watch to thee|De mane vigilabo ad te]].

paras.t: Mecum sunt divitiæ et gloria. Omnes namque divitiæ corporales ac spirituales profluxerunt a Deo. Et ipse quos vult glorificat et honorat, et in se ipso dives est divitiis infinitis, quæ sunt absoluta et infinita perfectio ejus. Atque, ut asserit Augustinus in libro de Civitate Dei, Deus dives non pecunia, sed omnipotentia ; Apostolus vero ait, Deus dives est in misericordia : sicque de attributis aliis dici potest. Opes superbæ, id est opulentiæ eminentes, scilicet supernaturalia dona ac bona cælestia. Ideo Glossa ait : Opes superbas vocat opes excelsas, ut cælestia dona significet. Græce enim superbus, hyperphanus (id est superapparens) dicitur. Sic ergo superbia accipitur hic in bono, sicut et in Isaia legitur : Ponam te in superbiam sæculorum. Et justitia : quia essentialiter justus est, causa, fons ac regula totius creatæ justitiæ.
paras.en: [[8:18|With me are riches and glory|Mecum sunt divitiæ et gloria]]. For all riches, bodily and spiritual, have flowed from God. And He glorifies and honours whom He will, and in Himself He is rich with infinite riches, which are His absolute and infinite perfection. And, as Augustine says in the book *On the City of God*, God is rich not in money but in omnipotence; and the Apostle says: God, [[Eph 2:4|who is rich in mercy|dives est in misericordia]]; and so it may be said of His other attributes. [[8:18|glorious riches|Opes superbæ]] [*superbæ*, literally "proud"], that is, surpassing wealth, namely supernatural gifts and heavenly goods. Therefore the Gloss says: He calls them proud riches, meaning lofty riches, to signify heavenly gifts. For in Greek *superbus* is called *hyperphanus* (that is, "appearing above"). So *superbia* [pride] is here taken in a good sense, as also we read in Isaias: [[Is 60:15|I will make thee to be an everlasting glory|Ponam te in superbiam sæculorum]] [literally, "I will set thee for the pride of ages"]. [[8:18|and justice|Et justitia]]: because He is just in His essence, the cause, fountain and rule of all created justice.

paras.t: Melior est fructus meus auro et lapide pretioso. Fructus sapientiæ, sunt actus et contemplatio ac delectatio contemplationi annexa, meritum quoque et præmium actibus sapientiæ correspondens : de quibus certum est, quod incomparabiliter rebus corporalibus eminentiora existant. Et genimina mea argento electo, id est, opera exteriora ex me procedentia, meliora sunt auro obrizo.
paras.en: [[8:19|my fruit is better than gold and the precious stone|Melior est fructus meus auro et lapide pretioso]]. The fruits of wisdom are its acts, and contemplation with the delight joined to contemplation, and also the merit and the reward that answer to the acts of wisdom: of which it is certain that they are incomparably more excellent than bodily things.
