Yet there are some parents who love their offspring not spiritually enough, but sensually, who are sometimes gravely saddened over their sons and daughters who are truly wise, who spurn all worldly and carnal things and enter religion [that is, the religious life], and who rejoice over foolish offspring that embraces carnal prudence and seeks out the things of the world and of the flesh. And this is because they reckon true wisdom folly, and the reverse.

paras.t: Nihil proderunt thesauri impietatis, id est divitiæ male adeptæ: quæ non solum non prosunt ad salutem, sed plurimum obsunt, quia non dimittitur peccatum, nisi restituatur ablatum. Vel, Thesauri iniquitatis, sunt temporalia bona collecta, quamvis non male acquisita: quæ dicuntur thesauri iniquitatis propter adjunctum effectum, quoniam sunt materia atque occasio vitiorum multorum. Dives enim currit ad libitum, corruit ad illicitum; ad superbiam, indignationem, iram, impatientiam pronus est; in vitia gulæ atque luxuriæ solet corruere; otiositati loquacitatique vacat. Ideo Christus in Evangelio divitias vocat mammonam iniquitatis. Itaque thesauri terreni per se non prosunt, imo nec per se obsunt saluti: sed sicut justis ac prudentibus, qui eis bene uti noverunt, sunt materia exercitiumque virtutum, quia ex ipsis opera pietatis exercent; sic avaris et insipientibus sunt vitiorum occasio, ac medium damnationis æternæ. Idcirco in suis Proverbiis Seneca loquitur: Pecuniæ imperare oportet, non servire. Pecunia si uti scias, ancilla est; si nescis, domina. Spiritualiter, thesauri iniquitatis sunt, abundantia demeritorum. De quibus ait Apostolus: Secundum duritiam tuam et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram in die justi judicii Dei. Et rursus alibi: Nescierunt agere rectum, thesaurizantes impietatem. Qui thesauri maxime nocent animæ, quamvis quidam per eos in terrenis ditentur. Justitia vero liberabit a morte. Interdum namque liberat a morte corporali, semper autem a morte mortalis peccati et infernalis supplicii, dummodo perseveretur in ea usque in finem.
paras.en: [[10:2|Treasures of wickedness shall profit nothing|Nihil proderunt thesauri impietatis]], that is, riches ill gotten: which not only do not profit unto salvation, but do very great harm, because the sin is not forgiven unless what was taken is restored. Or, treasures of iniquity are temporal goods amassed, even though not ill acquired: which are called treasures of iniquity on account of the effect joined to them, since they are the matter and occasion of many vices. For the rich man runs after what he pleases and falls into what is unlawful; he is prone to pride, indignation, anger, impatience; he is wont to fall into the vices of gluttony and lust; he gives himself to idleness and talkativeness. Therefore Christ in the Gospel calls riches [[Luke 16:9|the mammon of iniquity|mammonam iniquitatis]]. So earthly treasures of themselves do not profit salvation, nor indeed of themselves do they harm it; but as to the just and prudent, who know how to use them well, they are the matter and exercise of the virtues, because with them they practise works of piety, so to the avaricious and foolish they are an occasion of vices and a means of eternal damnation. Therefore Seneca says in his Proverbs: Money ought to be commanded, not served. If you know how to use money, it is a handmaid; if you do not, a mistress. Spiritually, treasures of iniquity are an abundance of demerits. Of which the Apostle says: [[Rom 2:5|according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath|Secundum duritiam tuam et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram]] against the day of [[Rom 2:5|the just judgment of God|justi judicii Dei]]. And again elsewhere: [[Amos 3:10|they have not known to do the right thing|Nescierunt agere rectum]], [[Amos 3:10|storing up iniquity|thesaurizantes impietatem]]. These treasures do the greatest harm to the soul, although some are enriched by them in earthly things. [[10:2|but justice shall deliver from death|Justitia vero liberabit a morte]]. For it sometimes delivers from bodily death, but always from the death of mortal sin and from the pains of hell, provided one perseveres in it to the end.

paras.t: Non affliget Dominus fame animam justi. In lege namque communiter dabatur temporalium copia justis. Unde Moyses fatur: Omnino indigens et mendicus non erit inter vos. (Interdum tamen dispensatione divina evenit oppositum.) Hinc ait Psalmista: Non vidi justum derelictum, nec semen ejus quærens panem. Et tamen ipsemet David inopia ductus, petivit panem et cibos a Nabal. Pensandum ergo quod ait, Non affliget Dominus fame animam justi: quasi dicat, Etsi corpus justi affligatur esurie, animæ tamen patientiam tribuit et gaudium in adversis. Nam et aliqui martyres sancti, fame in carcere obierunt, sed animæ eorum desuper consolabantur. Est quoque spiritualis fames, id est defectus internæ refectionis: qua Dominus justorum animas non affligit. Ideo ait Propheta de Domino: Ut alat eos in fame. Et insidias impiorum subvertet: quia frequenter impedit eas ab intento malignitatis effectu, juxta illud: Deus dissipat cogitationes malignorum, ne possint implere manus eorum quod ceperant. Interdum etiam Deus retorquet impiorum insidias in caput ipsorum, juxta illud Psalmi: In laqueo isto quem absconderunt, comprehensus est pes eorum. Sic Saul aliquoties cecidit in manus David. Finaliter autem impii propter suas peribunt insidias, secundum illud, Iter impiorum peribit. Juxta præhabita, subvertit Deus insidias Judæorum, qui voluerunt nomen ac fidem Christi omnino exstinguere, et tamen in captivitatem redacti sunt Romanorum, et Christianis subjecti.
paras.en: [[10:3|The Lord will not afflict the soul of the just with famine|Non affliget Dominus fame animam justi]]. For under the Law an abundance of temporal things was commonly given to the just. Hence Moses says: [[Deut 15:4|there shall be no poor nor beggar among you|Omnino indigens et mendicus non erit inter vos]]. (Yet sometimes by divine dispensation the opposite happens.) Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 36:25|I have not seen the just forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread|Non vidi justum derelictum, nec semen ejus quærens panem]]. And yet David himself, driven by want, asked bread and food of Nabal[[1 Kings 25:8||]]. We must weigh, then, what he says, [[10:3|The Lord will not afflict the soul of the just with famine|Non affliget Dominus fame animam justi]]: as if to say, Though the body of the just man be afflicted with hunger, yet to his soul he gives patience and joy in adversity. For some holy martyrs too died of hunger in prison, but their souls were consoled from above. There is also a spiritual famine, that is, a want of inward refreshment, with which the Lord does not afflict the souls of the just. Therefore the Prophet says of the Lord: That he may [[Ps 32:19|feed them in famine|alat eos in fame]]. [[10:3|and he will disappoint the deceitful practices of the wicked|Et insidias impiorum subvertet]]: for he often hinders them from the malicious effect they intend, according to that saying: God [[Job 5:12|bringeth to nought the designs of the malignant, so that their hands cannot accomplish what they had begun|dissipat cogitationes malignorum, ne possint implere manus eorum quod ceperant]]. Sometimes too God turns the snares of the wicked back on their own heads, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 9:16|Their foot hath been taken in the very snare which they hid|In laqueo isto quem absconderunt, comprehensus est pes eorum]]. So Saul more than once fell into the hands of David[[1 Kings 24:5||]][[1 Kings 26:8||]]. But at the last the wicked shall perish for their snares, according to that saying, [[Ps 1:6|the way of the wicked shall perish|Iter impiorum peribit]]. In keeping with what has been said, God disappointed the snares of the Jews, who wished to extinguish the name and faith of Christ altogether, and yet were brought into captivity by the Romans and made subject to Christians.

paras.t: Egestatem operata est manus remissa: quia corporalis inopia sequitur operarium pigrum. Qui vero tardus et frigidus est ad exercitia virtuosa, interiorem incurrit inopiam. Manus autem, id est virtus operativa, fortium, qui otia abhorrentes, agiles sunt ad bona, divitias parat, id est acquirit, tam corporales frequenter, quam spirituales semper. — Qui nititur, id est inhæret, mendaciis, hic pascit ventos, id est, vanus atque instabilis est, et verba ventosa roborare et verificare conatur. Idem autem ipse sequitur aves volantes: id est, propria inconstantia circumfertur, et instar avium undique agitatur, nec certum est ubi se figet, quia in veritate non stabilitur. De hoc in Ezechiele multa dicuntur ænigmatice et valde subtiliter, de falsis prophetis Israel, qui liniebant parietem luto sine paleis, et fecerunt pulvillos sub omni cubito, et cervicalia sub omni capite, ad capiendum animas volantes: quia per vaticinia falsa, et promissa mendosa ac blanda, plurimos assecuraverunt ac deceperunt.
paras.en: [[10:4|The slothful hand hath wrought poverty|Egestatem operata est manus remissa]]: for bodily want follows the lazy workman. And he who is slow and cold toward virtuous exercises incurs inward want. [[10:4|but the hand|Manus autem]], that is, the working power, [[10:4|of the industrious|fortium]], who abhorring idleness are quick to good things, [[10:4|getteth riches|divitias parat]], that is, acquires them: bodily riches often, spiritual ones always. — [[10:4|He that trusteth|Qui nititur]], that is, cleaves, [[10:4|to lies|mendaciis]], [[10:4|feedeth the winds|hic pascit ventos]], that is, he is vain and unstable, and tries to strengthen and make true windy words. [[10:4|and the same runneth after birds, that fly away|Idem autem ipse sequitur aves volantes]]: that is, he is carried about by his own inconstancy, and tossed every way like birds, and it is not certain where he will settle, because he is not established in the truth. Much is said of this in Ezechiel, figuratively and very subtly, of the false prophets of Israel, who daubed the wall with mud without straw[[Ezech 13:10||]], and made [[Ezech 13:18|cushions under every elbow|pulvillos sub omni cubito]], and pillows under every head, to [[Ezech 13:20|catch flying souls|animas volantes]]: for by false prophecies and lying and flattering promises they made very many feel secure, and deceived them.

paras.t: Qui congregat in messe, id est tempore prosperitatis, juventutis ac sanitatis, et congruis horis quibus adest facultas meritorie operandi, ac spirituales divitias congregandi: qui, inquam, tunc fortiter agit, spiritualiter proficit, et eos qui sibi commissi sunt, seu proximos suos, Christo lucrifacit, filius sapiens est; qui autem stertit æstate, id est, tali tempore admittit torporem, et negligenter tempus suum expendit, est filius confusionis: quia in se ipso est deordinatus, confusioneque dignus, atque in die judicii sui æternæ confusioni tradetur, sicut de talibus fertur in Psalmo: Erubescant, et conturbentur in sæculum sæculi; et confundantur, et pereant. Non enim dormientibus, et torpori otioque vacantibus, beatitudo æternitatis ingeritur, sed custoditis corde, et sollicitis coram Deo, indefessis ac strenuis in omni observantia præceptorum, ut juxta suæ exigentiam vocationis ambulent digne Deo.
paras.en: [[10:5|He that gathereth in the harvest|Qui congregat in messe]], that is, in the time of prosperity, youth and health, and at the fitting hours when there is opportunity of working meritoriously and of gathering spiritual riches: he, I say, who then acts strongly, makes spiritual progress, and gains for Christ those committed to him, or his neighbours, [[10:5|is a wise son|filius sapiens est]]; [[10:5|but he that snorteth in the summer|qui autem stertit æstate]], that is, gives way to torpor at such a time and spends his time negligently, [[10:5|is the son of confusion|est filius confusionis]]: for he is disordered in himself, and worthy of confusion, and in the day of his judgment he will be given over to eternal confusion, as is said of such in the Psalm: [[Ps 82:18|Let them be ashamed and troubled for ever and ever: and let them be confounded and perish.|Erubescant, et conturbentur in sæculum sæculi; et confundantur, et pereant]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxiii, 18, the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate this is Ps 82:18]. For the bliss of eternity is not bestowed on those who sleep and give themselves to torpor and idleness, but on those who keep watch over their hearts and are careful before God, untiring and strenuous in every observance of the precepts, so that according to the demands of their calling they walk worthy of God[[Eph 4:1||]].

paras.t: Benedictio Domini super caput justi: id est, super justum et in mentem ipsius diffundit Deus atque multiplicat gratiarum suarum charismata. Justus enim Dominus, et justitias diligit: ideo justis tanquam amicis et pro divino honore zelantibus, dat copiam spiritualium munerum, quandoque etiam temporalium rerum. Hinc scriptum est: Non aufert a justo oculos suos. Os autem impiorum operit iniquitas. Nam tot et tanta peccata ore suo committunt, quod propriis iniquitatibus os eorum operiri asseritur. Inquinant enim ora sua, verba scurrilia, mendosa, detractoria, pungitiva, injuriatoria proferendo; item per testimonia falsa, per comessationes et potus superfluos. Econtra, sicut sanctus vir abbas Pambo asseruit, ora monachorum sunt sancta per observantiam discreti silentii, et jugem collocutionem cum Deo, quem orando, laudando, psallendo, assidue occupantur.
paras.en: [[10:6|The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the just|Benedictio Domini super caput justi]]: that is, upon the just man, and into his mind, God pours out and multiplies the gifts of his graces. For [[Ps 10:8|the Lord is just, and hath loved justice|Justus enim Dominus, et justitias diligit]]: therefore to the just, as to friends and to men zealous for the divine honour, he gives an abundance of spiritual gifts, and sometimes of temporal things too. Hence it is written: [[Job 36:7|He will not take away his eyes from the just|Non aufert a justo oculos suos]]. [[10:6|but iniquity covereth the mouth of the wicked|Os autem impiorum operit iniquitas]]. For they commit so many and such great sins with their mouth, that their mouth is said to be covered with their own iniquities. For they defile their mouths by uttering scurrilous, lying, detracting, stinging and injurious words; also by false witness, by revellings and excessive drinking. On the other hand, as the holy man Abbot Pambo declared, the mouths of monks are holy through the observance of discreet silence and continual converse with God, in praying to whom, praising and singing psalms, they are constantly occupied.

paras.t: Memoria justi cum laudibus: id est, homines, recordando justos vivos seu mortuos, laudant eos, et habent eorum nomen honestum; et nomen impiorum putrescet, id est, fama et memoria iniquorum sordescunt et pereunt, et vituperationes habent annexas, præsertim apud sapientes et virtuosos. Aliqui vero sunt ita corrupti mente, quod impios laudant, et justos vituperant, juxta illud Psalmi: Laudatur peccator in desideriis animæ suæ, et iniquus benedicitur. Sed de talium judicio non est curandum. Hinc scriptum est: Nomina eorum vivent in sæculum sæculi; et alibi, Non recedet memoria ejus, videlicet sapientis et justi.
paras.en: [[10:7|The memory of the just is with praises|Memoria justi cum laudibus]]: that is, men, remembering the just, living or dead, praise them and hold their name in honour; [[10:7|and the name of the wicked shall rot|et nomen impiorum putrescet]], that is, the fame and memory of the wicked grow foul and perish, and have reproaches joined to them, especially among the wise and virtuous. But some are so corrupt of mind that they praise the wicked and revile the just, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 9:24|the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul: and the unjust man is blessed|Laudatur peccator in desideriis animæ suæ, et iniquus benedicitur]] [the margin gives Ps. x, 3, according to the Hebrew; in the Vulgate this is Ps 9:24]. But the judgment of such men is not to be heeded. Hence it is written: Their names [[Ps 21:27|shall live for ever and ever|vivent in sæculum sæculi]] [Denis reads *nomina*, "names", where the Vulgate has *corda*, "hearts"]; and elsewhere, [[Ecclus 39:13|The memory of him shall not depart away|Non recedet memoria ejus]], that is, of the wise and just man.

paras.t: Sapiens corde præcepta suscipiet, ut unicuique superiorum suorum obediat, ad minus in his quæ ad illius cathedram pertinent, et Deo absolute in omnibus; stultus cæditur labiis, id est, iniquus et incorrigibilis affligitur verbis corripientium et exhortantium eum quasi flagellis, quia ex habitibus vitiosis inclinatur ad prava. De hoc infra in libris Sapientialibus multa habentur.
paras.en: [[10:8|The wise of heart receiveth precepts|Sapiens corde præcepta suscipiet]], so as to obey each of his superiors, at least in those things that belong to that superior's chair [that is, the authority of his office], and God absolutely in all things; [[10:8|a fool is beaten with lips|stultus cæditur labiis]], that is, the wicked and incorrigible man is afflicted by the words of those who rebuke and exhort him, as by scourges, because from vicious habits he is inclined to evil. Much is found on this further on in the Sapiential books.

paras.t: Qui ambulat simpliciter, id est per tritas vias Sanctorum, et eorum exempla documentaque sequitur, qui sinceriter Deo vixerunt, et ea quæ evidenter bona sunt elegerunt, relinquentes dubiosa et periculosa, in quibus potest esse discrimen; et qui in omni conversatione sua columbinam tenet simplicitatem, vitans omnem duplicitatem, simulationem, hypocrisim; ambulat confidenter, id est secure, vitans singularitatem, et sequens communem justorum viam. Verumtamen Spiritus Sanctus variis modis in suis operatur electis, nec gratia ejus generali restringitur regula. Qui autem depravat vias suas, id est, actiones suas non dirigit secundum legem justitiæ ac divina præcepta, manifestus erit. Aliquando enim in præsenti interior ejus malitia, per exteriorem manifestatur effectum. Porro in judicio ejus, tam particulari quam generali, Judex cœlestis declarabit vitia ejus. Unde ait Salvator: Nihil occultum quod non manifestetur. Apostolus quoque: Deus, inquit, revelabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium.
paras.en: [[10:9|He that walketh sincerely|Qui ambulat simpliciter]], that is, by the trodden ways of the Saints, and follows the examples and teachings of those who lived sincerely for God and chose the things that are evidently good, leaving things doubtful and dangerous in which there may be peril; and who in all his conduct keeps the simplicity of the dove, shunning all duplicity, pretence and hypocrisy: he [[10:9|walketh confidently|ambulat confidenter]], that is, securely, shunning singularity and following the common way of the just. Yet the Holy Ghost works in his elect in various ways, and his grace is not confined by a general rule. [[10:9|but he that perverteth his ways|Qui autem depravat vias suas]], that is, does not direct his actions according to the law of justice and the divine precepts, [[10:9|shall be manifest|manifestus erit]]. For sometimes, in the present life, his inward malice is made manifest by its outward effect. Moreover at his judgment, both the particular and the general, the heavenly Judge will declare his vices. Hence the Saviour says: [[Luke 8:17|there is not any thing secret that shall not be made manifest|Nihil occultum quod non manifestetur]]. The Apostle too: God, he says, [[1 Cor 4:5|will bring to light the hidden things of darkness|revelabit abscondita tenebrarum]], and [[1 Cor 4:5|will make manifest the counsels of the hearts|manifestabit consilia cordium]].

paras.t: Qui annuit oculo, id est, signa impudicitiæ per viam demonstrat, aut nutibus oculorum quemquam deridet, dabit dolorem, id est, dolorosam pœnam pro suo sustinebit peccato. Juxta hunc modum loquendi ait ad Thessalonicenses Apostolus, loquens de impiis: Qui pœnas dabunt in interitu æternas. Talis quoque nutibus suis quandoque ingerit dolorem homini quem irridet, seu viro cujus conjugem provocat. De talibus ait in Psalmo Christus: Qui oderunt me gratis, et annuunt oculis. Et stultus labiis verberabitur. Hoc est quod jam dixit: Stultus cæditur labiis.
paras.en: [[10:10|He that winketh with the eye|Qui annuit oculo]], that is, shows signs of unchastity in the street, or mocks someone with nods of the eyes, [[10:10|shall cause sorrow|dabit dolorem]] [literally "shall give sorrow"], that is, shall suffer a sorrowful punishment for his sin. According to this manner of speaking the Apostle says to the Thessalonians, speaking of the wicked: [[2 Thess 1:9|Who shall suffer eternal punishment in destruction|Qui pœnas dabunt in interitu æternas]] [*pœnas dabunt*, literally "shall give penalties", means "shall suffer them"; the margin gives I Thess. i, 9, but the words are 2 Thess 1:9]. Such a one also, by his nods, sometimes causes sorrow to the man he mocks, or to the husband whose wife he provokes. Of such Christ says in the Psalm: [[Ps 34:19|who have hated me without cause, and wink with the eyes|Qui oderunt me gratis, et annuunt oculis]]. [[10:10|and the foolish in lips shall be beaten|Et stultus labiis verberabitur]]. This is what he has already said: [[10:8|a fool is beaten with lips|Stultus cæditur labiis]].

paras.t: Vena vitæ, os justi: quia ex ore sapientium ac justorum procedunt verba salutis ac gratiæ, salubria documenta, recta consilia: qui etiam propria humiliter confitentur peccata. Unde de Christo scriptum est: Mirabantur omnes in verbis gratiæ, quæ procedebant de ore ejus. Os autem impiorum operit iniquitatem: id est, propria vitia negat, palliat seu excusat, non confitetur: imo magis tuetur. Pro cujus mali evitatione orat Propheta: Non declines cor meum in verba malitiæ, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis. Hinc fertur alio loco: Quum dulce fuerit in ore ejus malum, abscondet illud sub lingua sua; parcet illi, et non derelinquet illud, et celabit in gutture suo. Quocontra sanctus Job de se ipso testatur: Si abscondi quasi homo peccatum meum, et celavi in sinu meo iniquitatem meam. Et Seneca ait: Relinque excusationem, quia nemo peccat invitus; itemque, Proximum innocentiæ tenet locum verecunda peccati confessio.
paras.en: [[10:11|The mouth of the just is a vein of life|Vena vitæ, os justi]]: because from the mouth of the wise and just come forth words of salvation and grace, wholesome teachings, right counsels; and they also humbly confess their own sins. Hence it is written of Christ: All [[Luke 4:22|wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth|Mirabantur omnes in verbis gratiæ, quæ procedebant de ore ejus]]. [[10:11|and the mouth of the wicked covereth iniquity|Os autem impiorum operit iniquitatem]]: that is, it denies, cloaks or excuses its own vices, and does not confess them; nay rather, it defends them. To avoid this evil the Prophet prays: [[Ps 140:4|Incline not my heart to evil words; to make excuses in sins|Non declines cor meum in verba malitiæ, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis]] [the margin gives Ps. cxi, 4; the words are Ps 140:4]. Hence it is said in another place: [[Job 20:12|when evil shall be sweet in his mouth, he will hide it under his tongue|Quum dulce fuerit in ore ejus malum, abscondet illud sub lingua sua]]; [[Job 20:13|He will spare it, and not leave it, and will hide it in his throat.|parcet illi, et non derelinquet illud, et celabit in gutture suo]] Against which holy Job testifies of himself: [[Job 31:33|If as a man I have hid my sin, and have concealed my iniquity in my bosom.|Si abscondi quasi homo peccatum meum, et celavi in sinu meo iniquitatem meam]] And Seneca says: Give up excusing, for no one sins against his will; and again: A shamefaced confession of sin holds the place next to innocence.

paras.t: Odium suscitat rixas: quia ex odio quo quis alium odit, faciliter prorumpit in verba rixosa adversus eum, quoniam appetit ei malum ac læsionem: et universa delicta operit caritas. Jam dictum est, quod os impiorum operit iniquitatem: quomodo ergo caritas operit universa delicta? Respondendum est, quod caritas dicitur peccata operire, id est auferre, ita quod nec Deus imputat ea, quoniam ex caritatis fervore consumuntur peccata, sicut ex igne stipula. Juxta hunc sensum ait Psalmista: Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata. Et Jacobus dicit: Qui converti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suæ, operit multitudinem peccatorum. Denique, sicut impius operit et occultat propriam culpam, sic caritas culpam alterius, ita quod proximum non increpat statim in publico, nec eum diffamat, sed primitus in secreto, ut famæ ejus provideat.
paras.en: [[10:12|Hatred stirreth up strifes|Odium suscitat rixas]]: because from the hatred with which one hates another, a man easily breaks out into quarrelsome words against him, since he desires evil and hurt for him; [[10:12|and charity covereth all sins|et universa delicta operit caritas]]. It has already been said that [[10:11|the mouth of the wicked covereth iniquity|os impiorum operit iniquitatem]]: how then does charity cover all sins? The answer is that charity is said to cover sins, that is, to take them away, so that God does not impute them, since by the fervour of charity sins are consumed as stubble by fire. In this sense the Psalmist says: [[Ps 31:1|Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered|Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata]]. And James says: [[Jas 5:20|he who causeth a sinner to be converted from the error of his way|Qui converti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suæ]], [[Jas 5:20|shall cover a multitude of sins|operit multitudinem peccatorum]]. Lastly, as the wicked man covers and hides his own fault, so charity covers the fault of another, in that it does not at once rebuke one's neighbour in public, nor defame him, but first in secret, so as to provide for his good name.

paras.t: In labiis sapientis invenitur sapientia, id est, sapientialia verba procedunt de lingua hominis sapientis. Nam ea quæ sunt in voce, sunt signa interioris notitiæ; et qualis quisque est, talia loquitur. Unde ait Salvator: Ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. Et virga in dorso ejus qui indiget corde, id est, justa afflictio ei debetur ac imminet, qui excæcatus est corde, propter quod indiget corde, id est usu rationis atque prudentiæ: sicut incredulis contigit Judæis, de quibus Isaias prædixit, Excæcatum est cor populi hujus. Hinc Philistæi propter insipientiam suam in natibus sunt percussi, ut legitur primo Regum.
paras.en: [[10:13|In the lips of the wise is wisdom found|In labiis sapientis invenitur sapientia]], that is, words of wisdom come forth from the tongue of a wise man. For the things that are in the voice are signs of the knowledge within; and as each man is, such things he speaks. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 12:34|out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh|Ex abundantia cordis os loquitur]]. [[10:13|and a rod on the back of him that wanteth sense|Et virga in dorso ejus qui indiget corde]] [*indiget corde*, literally "wanteth heart"], that is, a just affliction is due to him and hangs over him who is blinded in heart, so that he wants heart, that is, the use of reason and prudence: as befell the unbelieving Jews, of whom Isaias foretold: Blinded is [[Is 6:10|the heart of this people|cor populi hujus]] [Denis reads *Excæcatum est cor*, "the heart is blinded", where the Vulgate has *Excæca cor*, "Blind the heart"]. Hence the Philistines, for their folly, were struck in their hinder parts, as we read in the first book of Kings[[1 Kings 5:6||]].

paras.t: Sapientes abscondunt scientiam tempore opportuno, nec sapientiam suam jactant: est enim tempus tacendi; nec illusoribus et incapacibus eam proponunt. Ex humilitate ergo eam abscondunt. Nihilo minus tempore apto, ex caritate ostendunt, communicant, et prædicant eam. Sapientia enim abscondita et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utrisque? Os autem stulti, confusioni proximum est: quia a reprehensibilibus verbis diu non abstinet, et inordinate in loquendo se habet.
paras.en: [[10:14|Wise men lay up knowledge|Sapientes abscondunt scientiam]] [*abscondunt*, literally "hide"] at the fitting time, and do not boast of their wisdom: for there is [[Eccles 3:7|a time to keep silence|tempus tacendi]]; nor do they set it before mockers and those incapable of it. So they hide it out of humility. Nevertheless at a suitable time, out of charity, they show it, impart it, and preach it. For [[Ecclus 41:17|wisdom that is hid, and a treasure that is not seen, what profit is there in them both?|Sapientia enim abscondita et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utrisque?]] [[10:14|but the mouth of the fool is next to confusion|Os autem stulti, confusioni proximum est]]: because he does not long abstain from reprehensible words, and behaves without order in speaking.

paras.t: Substantia divitis, urbs fortitudinis ejus: id est, dives in suis confidit divitiis, quasi in civitate munita, et sicut is qui in urbe est, in murorum fortitudine sperat. Porro qui spiritualiter dives est, in meritis suis confidit, id est, per ea sperat in Domino. Spes namque est certa exspectatio futuræ felicitatis, ex gratia Dei meritisque procedens. Pavor pauperum, egestas eorum: id est, ideo timent opprimi atque deficere, quia sciunt se inopes esse. Spiritualiter quoque, qui pauper est, id est virtutibus carens ac meritis, timet inordinato, carnali, mundano timore; et merito formidaret damnari. Multi etiam pauperes propriam paupertatem abhorrent.
paras.en: [[10:15|The substance of a rich man is the city of his strength|Substantia divitis, urbs fortitudinis ejus]]: that is, the rich man trusts in his riches as in a fortified city, and as one who is in a city hopes in the strength of its walls. But he who is spiritually rich trusts in his merits, that is, through them he hopes in the Lord. For hope is the certain expectation of future happiness, proceeding from the grace of God and from merits [the definition of hope given by the Master of the Sentences, Peter Lombard]. [[10:15|the fear of the poor is their poverty|Pavor pauperum, egestas eorum]]: that is, they fear to be oppressed and to fail, because they know they are needy. Spiritually too, he who is poor, that is, lacking virtues and merits, fears with an inordinate, carnal, worldly fear; and he would rightly dread being damned. Many poor men also abhor their own poverty.

paras.t: Opus justi, id est justa actio ejus, tendit ad vitam gloriæ, et vitam gratiæ perficit; fructus autem impii, id est delectatio ejus seu actus interior, est ad peccatum. Concupiscentia enim quum conceperit, parit peccatum, ut Jacobus ait apostolus. Et ex interiori culpa ad exteriorem proceditur.
paras.en: [[10:16|The work of the just|Opus justi]], that is, his just action, tends to the life of glory, and perfects the life of grace; [[10:16|but the fruit of the wicked|fructus autem impii]], that is, his delight, or inward act, is [[10:16|unto sin|ad peccatum]]. For [[Jas 1:15|when concupiscence hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin|Concupiscentia enim quum conceperit, parit peccatum]], as the apostle James says. And from the inward fault one proceeds to the outward.

paras.t: Via vitæ est custodienti disciplinam: quoniam disciplinæ acquiescendo, vivit per gratiam, estque in via ad patriam; qui autem increpationes relinquit, id est, increpari de suis peccatis non vult, vel facta increpatione, ad solita vitia redit, errat: quia superbus et fatuus est.
paras.en: [[10:17|The way of life|Via vitæ]] is [[10:17|to him that observeth correction|custodienti disciplinam]]: since by yielding to correction he lives by grace and is on the way to the fatherland; [[10:17|but he that forsaketh reproofs|qui autem increpationes relinquit]], that is, will not be rebuked for his sins, or, when rebuked, returns to his accustomed vices, [[10:17|goeth astray|errat]]: because he is proud and foolish.

paras.t: Abscondunt odium labia mendacia: id est, mendosi rancorem suum occultant, dum dicunt se diligere eum quem odiunt. Odium namque quærit occulte nocere, idcirco absconditur. Ira vero aperta est, et publice appetit lædere, ut ait Philosophus. Hinc in Proverbiis suis Seneca loquitur: Odia multorum sub osculo latent. Et rursus: Pejora sunt, inquit, tecta odia quam aperta. Propterea loquax inimicus te minus offendit, quam taciturnus. Istud in Joab et Juda patuit proditore. Qui profert contumeliam, id est, alteri convitiatur, insipiens est, id est impatiens, passionatus et improbus, non attendens se ipsum, et proximum lædere non formidans: quod caritati atque justitiæ est contrarium.
paras.en: [[10:18|Lying lips hide hatred|Abscondunt odium labia mendacia]]: that is, liars hide their rancour while they say they love him whom they hate. For hatred seeks to harm in secret, and therefore it is hidden. But anger is open, and seeks to hurt publicly, as the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle] says. Hence Seneca says in his Proverbs: The hatreds of many lie hidden under a kiss. And again: Hidden hatreds, he says, are worse than open ones. Therefore a talkative enemy harms you less than a silent one. This was seen in Joab[[2 Kings 3:27||]] and in Judas the betrayer[[Matt 26:49||]]. [[10:18|he that uttereth reproach|Qui profert contumeliam]], that is, reviles another, [[10:18|is foolish|insipiens est]], that is, impatient, passionate and wicked, not looking to himself and not fearing to hurt his neighbour: which is contrary to charity and justice.

paras.t: In multiloquio non deerit peccatum: quia aliquid mali se miscet, et indiscretionis est plus loqui quam expedit. Multiloquium autem dicitur, non quia multa, sed quia superflua verba promuntur. Nam et Paulus in Actibus legitur usque in mediam noctem protraxisse sermonem. Similiter Christus in monte et post Cœnam, longum fecit sermonem. Qui autem moderatur labia sua, loquendo vera, salubria, justa, cum discretione, circumstantiisque virtutum, videlicet loco et tempore opportuno, recta intentione, et taliter ut oportet; prudentissimus est: quia hoc signum est et effectus magnæ prudentiæ ac virtutis.
paras.en: [[10:19|In the multitude of words there shall not want sin|In multiloquio non deerit peccatum]]: because something evil mixes itself in, and it is a mark of indiscretion to speak more than is expedient. It is called *multiloquium* [much speaking] not because many words are brought out, but because superfluous ones are. For Paul too, we read in the Acts, prolonged his discourse until midnight[[Acts 20:7||]]. Likewise Christ made a long discourse on the mount[[Matt 5:1||]] and after the Supper[[John 13:1||]]. [[10:19|but he that refraineth his lips|Qui autem moderatur labia sua]], by speaking things true, wholesome and just, with discretion and with the circumstances of virtue, that is, at the fitting place and time, with right intention, and in such a manner as is right, [[10:19|is most wise|prudentissimus est]]: for this is a sign and effect of great prudence and virtue.

paras.t: Argentum electum, lingua justi, id est pretiosa et instar optimi argenti, a macula verborum pravorum immunis, ac splendens per pulchram doctrinam, atque sonora loquendo salubriter; cor [autem] impiorum pro nihilo est habendum, in quantum hujusmodi. Nam et peccatum nihil est, et nihil fiunt homines peccando. Unde de justo cantatur: Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus. Etiam de iniquo inducitur apud Job: Habitent in tabernaculo illius socii ejus, qui non est.
paras.en: [[10:20|The tongue of the just is as choice silver|Argentum electum, lingua justi]], that is, precious, and like the best silver, free from the stain of evil words, and shining with fair doctrine, and sonorous in speaking wholesomely; but [[10:20|the heart|cor]] [[10:20|of the wicked|impiorum]] is to be held as [[10:20|nothing worth|pro nihilo]], in so far as they are such. For sin too is nothing, and men become nothing by sinning. Hence it is sung of the just man: [[Ps 14:4|In his sight the malignant is brought to nothing|Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus]]. Of the wicked man too it is set forth in Job: [[Job 18:15|Let the companions of him that is not, dwell in his tabernacle|Habitent in tabernaculo illius socii ejus, qui non est]].

paras.t: Labia justi erudiunt plurimos, corripiendo, hortando, consulendo seu prædicando. Aliqui tamen sunt justi, quibus non suppetit gratia eruditionis ad prædicandum. Qui autem indocti sunt, in cordis egestate morientur, id est, ex defectu informationis internæ morientur modo per culpam, deinde per pœnam æternam. Necesse est enim scire ea quæ sunt necessaria ad salutem, nec præcepta queunt impleri, nisi sciantur. Necesse est quoque donum scientiæ a Spiritu Sancto habere. Hinc ait Apostolus: Qui ignorat, ignorabitur. Et de electis ait Salvator: Erunt omnes docibiles Dei. Omnis qui audivit a Patre et didicit, venit ad me.
paras.en: [[10:21|The lips of the just teach many|Labia justi erudiunt plurimos]], by rebuking, exhorting, counselling or preaching. Yet there are some just men to whom the grace of learning for preaching is not granted. [[10:21|but they that are ignorant, shall die in the want of understanding|Qui autem indocti sunt, in cordis egestate morientur]] [*in cordis egestate*, literally "in want of heart"], that is, through lack of inward instruction they shall die, now by fault, and afterwards by eternal punishment. For it is necessary to know the things necessary for salvation, and the precepts cannot be fulfilled unless they are known. It is necessary also to have the gift of knowledge from the Holy Ghost. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 14:38|if any man know not, he shall not be known|Qui ignorat, ignorabitur]]. And of the elect the Saviour says: [[John 6:45|they shall all be taught of God|Erunt omnes docibiles Dei]]. [[John 6:45|Every one that hath heard of the Father and hath learned|Omnis qui audivit a Patre et didicit]], cometh to me.

paras.t: Benedictio Domini divites facit homines in virtutibus: quia benedictio Domini est collatio munerum ejus, et multiplicatio eorumdem; nec sociabitur eis afflictio, id est pœna inordinata, aut damnatio sempiterna: imo cum gaudio serviunt Deo. Attamen de peccatis suis ac aliorum tristantur. Nam et alibi scriptum est: Qui addit scientiam, addit et dolorem. De talibus ait Apostolus: Divites facti estis in illo, in omni verbo et in omni scientia.
paras.en: [[10:22|The blessing of the Lord maketh men rich|Benedictio Domini divites facit homines]] in virtues: for the blessing of the Lord is the bestowal of his gifts and their multiplication; [[10:22|neither shall affliction be joined to them|nec sociabitur eis afflictio]], that is, inordinate pain, or everlasting damnation; nay rather, they serve God with joy. Yet they are sorrowful over their own sins and those of others. For it is written elsewhere too: [[Eccles 1:18|he that addeth knowledge, addeth also|Qui addit scientiam, addit et]] sorrow [Denis reads *dolorem*, "sorrow", where the Vulgate has *laborem*, "labour"]. Of such the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 1:5|you are made rich in him, in all utterance and in all knowledge|Divites facti estis in illo, in omni verbo et in omni scientia]].

paras.t: Quasi per risum stultus operatur scelus, id est, impie agit cum gaudio vano, sicut præhabitum est: Lætantur quum malefecerint. Imo quidam sunt ita obtenebrati ac habituati in vitiis, quod etiam peccata mortalia facere, reputant quasi ludum, nec ponderant plus quam risum. Potest et ita exponi: Quasi per risum stultus operatur scelus, id est, proximum graviter lædit, idque faciendo risum quemdam et jucundum vultum assumit, ne malignandi animo hoc egisse putetur, sed potius improvise, aut ludendi intentione, ita quod commisso facinore, dicit: Ludens feci. Sapientia autem est viro prudentia, id est causa discretionis et provisionis. Quamvis enim sapientia et prudentia distinguantur, tamen in divinorum cognitione illuminati, ex ipsa contemplatione æternorum incitantur ad habendum se prudenter et ordinate in rebus actibusque humanis. Nam et teste Apostolo, Spiritualis homo omnia judicat. Philosophus quoque testatur, quod sapientia tanquam capitanea judicare habet de inferioribus intellectualibus habitibus.
paras.en: [[10:23|A fool worketh mischief as it were for sport|Quasi per risum stultus operatur scelus]], that is, acts wickedly with vain joy, as was said before: They [[Prov 2:14|are glad when they have done evil|Lætantur quum malefecerint]]. Nay, some are so darkened and so habituated in vices that they reckon even the committing of mortal sins as it were a game, and weigh it no more than a laugh. It can also be expounded thus: [[10:23|A fool worketh mischief as it were for sport|Quasi per risum stultus operatur scelus]], that is, he gravely hurts his neighbour, and in doing so puts on a kind of laugh and a cheerful face, so that he may not be thought to have done it with intent to harm, but rather unawares, or meaning it in play; so that when the deed is done he says: [[Prov 26:19|I did it in jest|Ludens feci]]. [[10:23|but wisdom is prudence to a man|Sapientia autem est viro prudentia]], that is, a cause of discretion and foresight. For although wisdom and prudence are distinct, yet those who are enlightened in the knowledge of divine things are moved by the very contemplation of eternal things to conduct themselves prudently and in order in human affairs and acts. For, as the Apostle witnesses, [[1 Cor 2:15|the spiritual man judgeth all things|Spiritualis homo omnia judicat]]. The Philosopher too testifies that wisdom, as the chief, has to judge of the lower intellectual habits.

paras.t: Quod timet impius, veniet super eum, videlicet debita pœna, quam vel in præsenti, aut in futuro sustinebit: præsertim qui peccat cum servili timore, et scit se peccare, ille nisi pœniteat, damnationem incurret perpetuam. Verumtamen, sicut in Ecclesiaste asseritur, multi sine ullo timore perpetrant mala: quibus tamen tandem supervenit hora, in qua vel in extremis concutientur horrore, atque peribunt. Desiderium suum justis dabitur, id est rem desideratam, videlicet æternam consequentur salutem, donaque gratiæ in præsenti. Etenim oculi Domini super justos, et aures ejus in preces eorum.
paras.en: [[10:24|That which the wicked feareth, shall come upon him|Quod timet impius, veniet super eum]], namely the punishment due, which he will suffer either in the present or in the future: especially he who sins with servile fear [that is, fear of punishment, not of offending God], and knows that he sins; unless he repents, he will incur everlasting damnation. Yet, as is said in Ecclesiastes, many commit evils without any fear[[Eccles 8:11||]]: on whom nevertheless the hour at length comes when, at least at the last, they will be shaken with horror, and will perish. [[10:24|to the just their desire shall be given|Desiderium suum justis dabitur]], that is, the thing desired: namely, they shall obtain eternal salvation, and the gifts of grace in the present. For the [[Ps 33:16|eyes of the Lord are upon the just: and his ears unto their prayers|oculi Domini super justos, et aures ejus in preces eorum]].

paras.t: Quasi tempestas transiens non erit impius, id est, cito tolletur de medio, juxta illud: Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt. Unde dicitur in Job: Recordare, obsecro, quis unquam innocens periit? Quin potius vidi iniquos Domino flante perisse. Hinc loquitur Isaias: Et quidem neque satus, neque radicatus in terra truncus eorum; repente flavit in eos, et aruerunt. Et dato quod in vita hac usque ad debitam subsistant ætatem, tamen omne hoc respectu futuræ æternitatis, vix est momentum. Justus [autem] quasi fundamentum sempiternum: quia in omni eventu constans manet in Domino, et stabilitur in Creatore, modo per gratiam, deinde per gloriam. Hinc ait Salvator: Omnis qui audit verba mea, et facit ea, assimilabitur viro sapienti, qui ædificavit domum suam supra petram; et descendit pluvia, et venerunt flumina, et flaverunt venti, et irruerunt in domum illam, et non cecidit: fundata enim erat supra petram.
paras.en: [[10:25|As a tempest that passeth, so the wicked shall be no more|Quasi tempestas transiens non erit impius]], that is, he shall quickly be taken out of the way, according to that saying: [[Ps 72:19|How are they brought to desolation? they have suddenly ceased to be|Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt]]. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 4:7|Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished being innocent?|Recordare, obsecro, quis unquam innocens periit?]] [[Job 4:8|On the contrary, I have seen|Quin potius vidi]] the wicked perish at the blast of the Lord[[Job 4:9||]]. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 40:24|And surely their stock was neither planted, nor sown, nor rooted in the earth|Et quidem neque satus, neque radicatus in terra truncus eorum]]: [[Is 40:24|suddenly he hath blown upon them, and they are withered|repente flavit in eos, et aruerunt]] [the margin gives Is. xi, 24; the words are Is 40:24]. And granted that in this life they last until the due age, yet all this, in respect of the eternity to come, is scarcely a moment. But [[10:25|the just|Justus]] [[10:25|is as an everlasting foundation|quasi fundamentum sempiternum]]: because in every event he remains constant in the Lord, and is established in the Creator, now by grace, afterwards by glory. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:24|Every one therefore that heareth these my words, and doth them, shall be likened to a wise man that built his house upon a rock|Omnis qui audit verba mea, et facit ea, assimilabitur viro sapienti, qui ædificavit domum suam supra petram]]; and [[Matt 7:25|the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and they beat upon that house, and it fell not, for it was founded on a rock|descendit pluvia, et venerunt flumina, et flaverunt venti, et irruerunt in domum illam, et non cecidit: fundata enim erat supra petram]].

paras.t: Sicut acetum dentibus molestiam ingerit, quos acidos facit, et fumus oculis, quos affligit, obscurat, amaricat: sic piger his qui miserunt eum in via. Nam sua tarditate ac negligentia ipsos affligit, dum nec causas propter quas missus est, expedit, nec statuto revertitur tempore.
paras.en: [[10:26|As vinegar to the teeth|Sicut acetum dentibus]], which it troubles and sets on edge, [[10:26|and smoke to the eyes|et fumus oculis]], which it afflicts, darkens and makes smart, [[10:26|so is the sluggard to them that sent him|sic piger his qui miserunt eum]] on the way. For by his slowness and negligence he afflicts them, since he neither dispatches the business for which he was sent, nor returns at the appointed time.

paras.t: Timor Domini apponet dies: id est, homo Deum filialiter timens, vitæ prolongationem meretur, et ad annos æternitatis perducitur: de quibus in Psalmo habetur, Annos æternos in mente habui. Vitamque gratiæ et ipsas virtutes, quæ sunt dies cordis, timor Dei adducit ac auget. Et anni impiorum breviabuntur: quoniam sæpe propter sua scelera occiduntur, et gulose turpiterque vivendo suam abbreviant vitam.
paras.en: [[10:27|The fear of the Lord shall prolong days|Timor Domini apponet dies]] [*apponet dies*, literally "shall add days"]: that is, the man who fears God filially merits the lengthening of his life, and is brought to the years of eternity, of which it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 76:6|I had in my mind the eternal years|Annos æternos in mente habui]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxvi, 6; the words are Ps 76:6]. And the life of grace, and the virtues themselves, which are the days of the heart, the fear of God brings and increases. [[10:27|and the years of the wicked shall be shortened|Et anni impiorum breviabuntur]]: since they are often slain for their crimes, and by living gluttonously and shamefully they shorten their own life.

paras.t: Expectatio justorum, lætitia, id est, æternam præstolantur jucunditatem a Domino: et ipsa eorum expectatio est consolatoria et jucunda, sicut ait Apostolus: Spe gaudentes. Spes autem impiorum peribit, id est, privabitur effectu seu bono sperato. Nam et sine virtuosis actibus salvari confidunt; et frequenter sperant in vita hac diu subsistere, prosperari, et suis concupiscentiis deservire, tandemque ante finem vitæ pœnitentiam agere: et tamen subito auferuntur, quemadmodum fertur de divite quodam, dicente: Anima, habes multa bona reposita in annos plurimos; requiesce, comede, bibe, epulare. Dixit autem illi Deus: Stulte, hac nocte animam tuam repetunt a te; quæ autem parasti, cujus erunt?
paras.en: [[10:28|The expectation of the just is joy|Expectatio justorum, lætitia]], that is, they await from the Lord eternal gladness: and their very expectation is consoling and pleasant, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 12:12|Rejoicing in hope|Spe gaudentes]]. [[10:28|but the hope of the wicked shall perish|Spes autem impiorum peribit]], that is, it shall be deprived of its effect, or of the good hoped for. For they trust to be saved even without virtuous acts; and they often hope to last long in this life, to prosper, and to serve their lusts, and at length, before the end of life, to do penance: and yet they are suddenly taken away, as is told of a certain rich man, who said: [[Luke 12:19|Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years. Take thy rest: eat, drink, make good cheer|Anima, habes multa bona reposita in annos plurimos; requiesce, comede, bibe, epulare]]. [[Luke 12:20|But God said to him: Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee. And whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?|Dixit autem illi Deus: Stulte, hac nocte animam tuam repetunt a te; quæ autem parasti, cujus erunt?]]

paras.t: Fortitudo simplicis, via Domini, id est, observantia viæ seu legis Dei, est spiritualis confortatio simplicis hominis, simplicitate columbina micantis: qui etsi altiora nequit scrutari, nec magnæ exsistit scientiæ, hoc tamen ei sufficit, quod in sua manens simplicitate, servet præcepta. Et pavor his qui operantur malum, id est, horrenda formido imminet eis, et inordinati timores sunt in ipsis frequenter, dum metuunt deprehendi, sicut de furibus, adulteris et consimilibus constat.
paras.en: [[10:29|The strength of the upright is the way of the Lord|Fortitudo simplicis, via Domini]] [*simplicis*, literally "of the simple"], that is, the keeping of the way or law of God is the spiritual strengthening of the simple man, who shines with the simplicity of the dove: who, though he cannot search out higher things, nor is of great learning, yet this suffices him, that abiding in his simplicity he keeps the precepts. [[10:29|and fear to them that work evil|Et pavor his qui operantur malum]], that is, a dreadful terror hangs over them, and inordinate fears are often in them, while they fear to be caught, as is plain in thieves, adulterers and the like.

paras.t: Justus in æternum non commovebitur a via justitiæ, sicut Job dicit: Donec deficiam, non recedam ab innocentia mea; justificationem quam cœpi tenere, non deseram. Atque Apostolus ad Romanos: Quis, inquit, nos separabit a caritate Dei? Verumtamen istud non est intelligendum quasi justus non possit peccare; sed quod justus, in quantum talis, magis vult vitam quam justitiam perdere, et quod viri perfecte justi, parati sint pro justitia mori. Impii autem non habitabunt super terram cœlestis patriæ: de qua fertur in Psalmo, Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium.
paras.en: [[10:30|The just shall never be moved|Justus in æternum non commovebitur]] from the way of justice, as Job says: [[Job 27:5|till I die I will not depart from my innocence|Donec deficiam, non recedam ab innocentia mea]]; [[Job 27:6|My justification, which I have begun to hold, I will not forsake|justificationem quam cœpi tenere, non deseram]]. And the Apostle to the Romans: [[Rom 8:35|Who|Quis]], he says, [[Rom 8:35|shall separate us from the love of|nos separabit a caritate]] God? [Denis reads *Dei*, "of God", where the Vulgate has *Christi*, "of Christ"] But this is not to be understood as if the just man could not sin; but that the just man, in so far as he is such, would rather lose his life than his justice, and that men perfectly just are ready to die for justice. [[10:30|but the wicked shall not dwell on the earth|Impii autem non habitabunt super terram]] of the heavenly fatherland: of which it is said in the Psalm, [[Ps 26:13|I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living|Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium]].

paras.t: Os justi parturiet sapientiam, id est, justa ac sapientialia proferet verba; lingua pravorum peribit: quia propter vitia sua damnabitur; sicut et epulo in inferno petiit linguam suam refrigerari, insinuans se in ea gravius cruciari.
paras.en: [[10:31|The mouth of the just shall bring forth wisdom|Os justi parturiet sapientiam]], that is, it will utter just and wise words; [[10:31|the tongue of the perverse shall perish|lingua pravorum peribit]]: because it will be damned for its vices; as the feaster [*epulo*, the rich man of the parable who feasted every day] in hell asked that his tongue be cooled[[Luke 16:24||]], hinting that he was more grievously tormented in it.

paras.t: Labia justi considerant placita: id est, justus sua discretione perpendit, ut labia sua loquantur ea quæ Deo et proximis merito debent placere, ut non nisi ædificatoria atque salubria proferant. Unde monet Apostolus: Omnis sermo malus ex ore vestro non procedat; sed qui utilis est ad ædificationem, ut det gratiam audienti. Et os impiorum perversa, id est, considerant impii qualiter possint vana, frivola et nociva effari: et ex industria evomunt talia, quia in sua loquacitate ac perversitate delectantur; et sæpe libentius proferunt ea quæ audientibus displicent, quam quæ placent.
paras.en: [[10:32|The lips of the just consider what is acceptable|Labia justi considerant placita]]: that is, the just man weighs with his discretion that his lips may speak those things that ought rightly to please God and his neighbours, so that they utter nothing but what is edifying and wholesome. Hence the Apostle warns: [[Eph 4:29|Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth|Omnis sermo malus ex ore vestro non procedat]]; but that which is useful [[Eph 4:29|to the edification|ad ædificationem]], [[Eph 4:29|that it may administer grace to the hearers|ut det gratiam audienti]]. [[10:32|and the mouth of the wicked uttereth perverse things|Et os impiorum perversa]], that is, the wicked consider how they may utter vain, frivolous and harmful things: and they vomit forth such things on purpose, because they delight in their talkativeness and perversity; and often they more gladly utter what displeases their hearers than what pleases them.

11.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI UNDECIMI : STATERA DOLOSA ABOMINATIO EST APUD DOMINUM.
11.title_en: Exposition of the eleventh chapter: A deceitful balance is an abomination before the Lord.

paras.t: Justitia cum actibus suis hic specialiter commendatur, et vitia eis opposita reprobantur.
paras.en: Here justice with its acts is especially commended, and the vices opposed to them are condemned.

paras.t: Statera dolosa abominatio est apud Dominum, id est, divino judicio multum est abominanda statera fraudulenter formata, qua proximi clam falluntur. Talis namque statera, id est usus seu mensuratio facta per eam, est Deo odibilis, quum sit directe contra legem naturalem atque divinam, et contra caritatem et æquitatem. Spiritualiter quoque dolosa statera, hoc est ponderatio seu judicium rationis, quæ vel ex personarum acceptione, vel affectione sinistra seu aversione perversa, judicat male de se ipsa et aliis, propria vitia non ponderando, ut requirit justitia, et facta aliorum bona, judicando non bona, vel mala, nimis mala: hæc statera est abominabilis Deo. Similiter statera utuntur dolosa, qui onera gravia et importabilia aliis portanda imponunt, quæ digito suo nolunt movere. Hinc Dominus jussit: Nolite facere iniquum aliquid in judicio, in regula, in pondere, in mensura. Nihilo minus multi intimorati et cupidi dolosis utuntur ponderibus, stateris, mensuris, sicut ait Psalmista: Mendaces filii hominum in stateris, ut decipiant ipsi de vanitate in id ipsum. Hæc mensuratio fraudulenta est furtum, specie seu apparentia justitiæ coloratum: qua qui utuntur, ad restitutionem tenentur.
paras.en: [[11:1|A deceitful balance is an abomination before the Lord|Statera dolosa abominatio est apud Dominum]]: that is, a balance fraudulently made, by which one's neighbours are secretly cheated, is greatly to be abhorred in the judgment of God. For such a balance, that is, its use or the measuring done with it, is hateful to God, since it is directly against the natural and the divine law[[Lev 19:35||]][[Lev 19:36||]], and against charity and equity. Spiritually, too, a deceitful balance is the weighing or judgment of the reason which, whether from respect of persons [that is, partiality: favouring someone for who he is rather than for the merits of the case], or from a wrong affection or a perverse aversion, judges ill of itself and of others, not weighing its own vices as justice requires, and judging the good deeds of others to be not good, or evil ones too evil: this balance is abominable to God. Likewise they use a deceitful balance who lay [[Matt 23:4|heavy and insupportable burdens|onera gravia et importabilia]] on others to carry, which they themselves will not move [[Matt 23:4|with a finger of their own|digito suo]]. Hence the Lord commanded: [[Lev 19:35|Do not any unjust thing in judgment, in rule, in weight, or in measure|Nolite facere iniquum aliquid in judicio, in regula, in pondere, in mensura]]. Nevertheless many who have no fear of God, and covetous men, use deceitful weights, balances and measures, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 61:10|the sons of men are liars in the balances: that by vanity they may together deceive|Mendaces filii hominum in stateris, ut decipiant ipsi de vanitate in id ipsum]]. This fraudulent measuring is theft coloured with the look or appearance of justice: and those who use it are bound to restitution.

paras.t: Et pondus æquum, id est justa mensura, voluntas ejus, id est, Deo essentialiter justo placet, qui jussit: Statera justa, et ephi justum, et batus justus erit vobis. Itaque qui in cunctis juste ac sinceriter agit ac judicat, qui causam ac causam æqua lance discernit, summi Judicis voluntati concordat.
paras.en: [[11:1|and a just weight|Et pondus æquum]], that is, a just measure, [[11:1|is his will|voluntas ejus]]: that is, it pleases God, who is just in his very essence, and who commanded: [[Ezech 45:10|You shall have just balances, and a just ephi, and a just bate|Statera justa, et ephi justum, et batus justus erit vobis]]. And so he who in all things acts and judges justly and sincerely, who weighs case against case in an even scale, is in accord with the will of the supreme Judge.

paras.t: Ubi fuerit superbia, ibi erit et contumelia. Superbi namque, quum sint magni in oculis suis, faciliter arbitrantur sibi factam injuriam, quamvis quandoque non sit; et injuriam sibi factam, reputant nimis magnam: sicque in contumeliosa verba prorumpunt. Alios quoque non humiliter, sed contumeliose solent corripere, sicut Eliu sanctum Job. Talis fuit Rabsaces, qui a servis Ezechiæ humiliter rogatus, respondit: Numquid ad dominum tuum misit me dominus meus, et non potius ad viros qui sedent super murum, ut comedant stercora sua, et bibant urinam suam vobiscum? Denique valde vitandum est vitium istud: quia, ut Thomas in secunda secundæ, quæstione 72, declarat, contumelia ex suo genere est peccatum mortale; et quamvis superbia disponat ad contumeliam, propria tamen origo contumeliæ dicitur esse ira. Nam finis iræ est vindicta. Contumeliosus autem, per verba contumeliæ communiter intendit se vindicare, alteriusque honorem auferre. Hinc Seneca in suis ait Proverbiis: Contumelia a contemptu dicta est, quoniam nemo, nisi quem contempsit, tali notat injuria. Solent etiam verba contumeliosa citius proferri in eos, qui minus timentur. Unde et Seneca: Ingenuitas, inquit, contumeliam non suscipit; in vita miseri, contumelia est.
paras.en: [[11:2|Where pride is, there also shall be reproach|Ubi fuerit superbia, ibi erit et contumelia]]. For the proud, being great in their own eyes, readily think that a wrong has been done them, even when sometimes it has not; and a wrong done them they reckon far too great: and so they break out into insulting words. They are wont, too, to rebuke others not humbly but insultingly, as Eliu did holy Job[[Job 32:1||]] [the margin gives Job xxxii–xxxvii, Eliu's speeches]. Such was Rabsaces, who, when humbly asked by the servants of Ezechias[[4 Kings 18:26||]], answered: [[4 Kings 18:27|Hath my master sent me to thy master|Numquid ad dominum tuum misit me dominus meus]], [[4 Kings 18:27|and not rather to the men that sit upon the wall, that they may eat their own dung, and drink their urine with you?|et non potius ad viros qui sedent super murum, ut comedant stercora sua, et bibant urinam suam vobiscum?]] In short, this vice is much to be avoided: for, as Thomas declares in the Secunda Secundæ, question 72, contumely [that is, insult: dishonouring a person to his face by words] is of its kind a mortal sin; and though pride disposes to contumely, yet its proper origin is said to be anger. For the end of anger is revenge. And the man given to insult commonly means, by words of insult, to avenge himself and to take away the other's honour. Hence Seneca says in his Proverbs: Contumely is named from contempt, since no one marks another with such a wrong unless he has despised him. Insulting words, too, are wont to be uttered more readily against those who are less feared. Whence Seneca again: Noble birth, he says, does not admit of insult; in the life of the wretched, there is insult.

paras.t: Ubi autem humilitas, ibi et sapientia. Humilitas namque ad illuminationem divinam specialiter præparat mentem, ut dictum est sæpe. Ideo scriptum est: Revelasti ea parvulis; itemque, Testimonium Domini fidele, sapientiam præstans parvulis. Imo per Isaiam Dominus loquitur fons sapientiæ adorandus: Super quem requiescet spiritus meus, nisi super quietum et humilem?
paras.en: [[11:2|but where humility is, there also is wisdom|Ubi autem humilitas, ibi et sapientia]]. For humility especially prepares the mind for the divine enlightenment, as has often been said. Therefore it is written: Thou [[Matt 11:25|hast revealed them to little ones|Revelasti ea parvulis]]; and again, [[Ps 18:8|the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones|Testimonium Domini fidele, sapientiam præstans parvulis]]. Nay, through Isaias the Lord, the adorable fount of wisdom, says: Upon whom shall my spirit rest, but upon him that is quiet and humble?[[Is 66:2||]] [Denis quotes Is 66:2 in an older Latin form; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have: "to whom shall I have respect, but to him that is poor and little, and of a contrite spirit"]

paras.t: Simplicitas columbina justorum dirigit eos, id est, recte faciet incedere ad finem salutis æternæ. Nam facit deverticula duplicitatis, simulationis, hypocrisisque vitare, et per suam simplicitatem merentur justi desuper dirigi. Semper quoque connexæ sunt simplicitas ista et vera justitia: sicut Job fuit vir simplex et rectus; idcirco in omnibus direxit eum Altissimus. Et supplantatio perversorum vastabit eos. Sæpe enim contingit, quod qui impotentiores se supplantant, a potentioribus se supplantantur, et in judicio Dei debita punitione vastentur. Ideo Tullius dixit: Quod alteri feceris, scito ac præstolare tibi ab alio fieri.
paras.en: [[11:3|The simplicity|Simplicitas]], the dove's simplicity, [[11:3|of the just shall guide them|justorum dirigit eos]]: that is, it will make them walk aright to the end of eternal salvation. For it makes them shun the byways of duplicity, pretence and hypocrisy, and through their simplicity the just deserve to be guided from above. This simplicity and true justice are also always joined together: as Job was a man [[Job 1:1|simple and upright|simplex et rectus]][[Job 1:8||]][[Job 2:3||]]; therefore the Most High guided him in all things. [[11:3|and the deceitfulness of the wicked shall destroy them|Et supplantatio perversorum vastabit eos]] [Latin *supplantatio*, a tripping-up or supplanting, which Denis takes literally in what follows]. For it often happens that those who supplant men weaker than themselves are supplanted by men stronger than themselves, and are laid waste with due punishment in the judgment of God. Therefore Tully said: What thou hast done to another, know and expect to be done to thee by another.

paras.t: Non proderunt divitiæ temporales in die ultionis divini judicii, in quo solum merita prosunt; justitia autem liberabit a morte culpæ atque gehennæ, et etiam sæpe a corporali occisione.
paras.en: [[11:4|Riches shall not profit|Non proderunt divitiæ]] (temporal riches) [[11:4|in the day of revenge|in die ultionis]] of the divine judgment, in which merits alone avail; [[11:4|but justice shall deliver from death|justitia autem liberabit a morte]] of sin and of hell, and often also from bodily slaughter.

paras.t: Justitia simplicis dirigit viam, id est actum et conversationem ejus, ut perseveret in medio, non divertens ad vitiosa extrema; et in impietate sua corruet impius. Nam ipsa impietas, spiritualiter ruina est, qua ab altitudine gratiæ et dignitate virtutis, et a statu salutis, ad profunditatem excæcationis, vilitatem culpæ et statum damnationis corruitur; deinde a vita hac in ima inferni, per impietatem suam peccator dilabitur.
paras.en: [[11:5|The justice of the upright shall make his way prosperous|Justitia simplicis dirigit viam]] [Latin *dirigit viam*, "directs his way"], that is, his acts and his manner of life, so that he keeps to the mean, not turning aside to the vicious extremes; [[11:5|and the wicked man shall fall by his own wickedness|et in impietate sua corruet impius]]. For wickedness itself is spiritually a fall, by which one falls from the height of grace, the dignity of virtue and the state of salvation, to the depth of blindness, the baseness of sin and the state of damnation; and then the sinner slips through his wickedness from this life into the depths of hell.

paras.t: Justitia rectorum liberabit eos, perducendo ad vitam felicem, in qua nullum potest esse periculum, nulla adversitas; et in insidiis suis capientur iniqui, id est, quod aliis moliuntur, ipsimet incident, et eorum versutia redundat in eos, et maxime nocet eis: quod si in vita ista evaserint, ab Omnipotente comprehendentur, et manifesti omnibus fient in die furoris Dei adversus insidiatores. Ideo scriptum est: In laqueo isto quem absconderunt, comprehensus est pes eorum. Isaias quoque ait: Qui explicuerit pedes suos de laqueo, cadet in foveam.
paras.en: [[11:6|The justice of the righteous shall deliver them|Justitia rectorum liberabit eos]], by bringing them to the happy life, in which there can be no danger and no adversity; [[11:6|and the unjust shall be caught in their own snares|et in insidiis suis capientur iniqui]]: that is, they will themselves fall into what they plot against others, and their cunning recoils upon them and does them the greatest harm: and if they escape in this life, they will be seized by the Almighty, and made manifest to all in the day of God's fury against those who lie in wait. Therefore it is written: [[Ps 9:16|Their foot hath been taken in the very snare which they hid|In laqueo isto quem absconderunt, comprehensus est pes eorum]]. Isaias too says: He that shall rid his feet out of the snare, shall fall into the pit[[Is 24:18||]] [the margin gives "Cf. Is. xxiv, 18"; the Vulgate has the reverse: "he that shall rid himself out of the pit, shall be taken in the snare"].

paras.t: Mortuo homine impio, nulla erit ultra spes de sua salvatione, quia in mortali decessit, et tempus merendi in eo finitum est. Hoc non attenderunt, qui damnatis finem promiserunt pœnarum. Verumtamen ex gratia speciali, quidam in mortali culpa defuncti, ad vitam istam reducti sunt, pœnitentiamque egerunt. Sunt autem quasi innumerabilia testimonia Scripturarum, quibus monstratur æternitas infernalis supplicii.
paras.en: [[11:7|When the wicked man is dead, there shall be no hope any more|Mortuo homine impio, nulla erit ultra spes]] of his salvation, since he died in mortal sin, and for him the time of meriting is ended. Those who promised the damned an end of their pains did not heed this. Nevertheless, by a special grace, some who died in mortal sin have been brought back to this life and have done penance. And there are well-nigh countless testimonies of the Scriptures by which the eternity of the punishment of hell is shown.

paras.t: Et expectatio sollicitorum peribit. Quædam est sollicitudo spiritualis, id est diligentia custodiendi se coram Deo, vitandi pericula animæ, proficiendi in gratia atque virtutibus. De qua dicit Michæas: Indicabo tibi, homo, quid sit bonum: utique facere justitiam, et sollicitum ambulare cum Deo tuo. Alia est sollicitudo de corporalibus rebus: et illa est duplex, videlicet moderata, et immoderata. Moderata est, qua temporalia quæruntur et conservantur, quantum necessaria aut utilia sunt per respectum ad spiritualia bona. Unde et princeps Apostolorum in prima sua epistola: Omnem, inquit, sollicitudinem vestram projicientes in Deum, quoniam ipsi cura est de vobis. Immoderata est, qua quæruntur superflua, aut cum nimia anxietate occupationeque cordis quæruntur aut conservantur temporalia, sive sint necessaria vel utilia, sive non. De qua ait Salvator: Nolite solliciti esse in crastinum. Vult etenim Deus, ut in eo tanquam in piissimo ac providissimo patre, filialem habeamus fiduciam, sic tamen, ut id quod in nobis est, moderate agamus. Itaque de immoderata et carnali sollicitudine dicitur: Exspectatio sollicitorum peribit, id est, tanquam vitiosa damnabitur, et frequenter in vita hac suo privatur effectu. Immoderate namque solliciti pro terrenis, exspectant ditari, diuque vivere: quorum utroque sæpe privantur. Ideo loquitur Paulus: Nihil solliciti sitis.
paras.en: [[11:7|and the expectation of the solicitous shall perish|Et expectatio sollicitorum peribit]]. There is a spiritual solicitude, that is, diligence in keeping oneself before God, in shunning the dangers of the soul, and in advancing in grace and the virtues. Of it Michæas says: [[Mich 6:8|I will shew thee, O man, what is good|Indicabo tibi, homo, quid sit bonum]]: [[Mich 6:8|Verily to do|utique facere]] justice [the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have "judgment"], [[Mich 6:8|and to walk solicitous with thy God|et sollicitum ambulare cum Deo tuo]]. Another is solicitude about bodily things: and this is twofold, namely moderate and immoderate. The moderate is that by which temporal things are sought and kept so far as they are necessary or useful with regard to spiritual goods. Whence the prince of the Apostles also, in his first epistle: [[1 Pet 5:7|Casting all your care|Omnem]], he says, [[1 Pet 5:7|upon him, for he hath care of you|sollicitudinem vestram projicientes in Deum, quoniam ipsi cura est de vobis]]. The immoderate is that by which superfluous things are sought, or temporal things, whether necessary or useful or not, are sought or kept with excessive anxiety and preoccupation of heart. Of this the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:34|Be not therefore solicitous for to morrow|Nolite solliciti esse in crastinum]]. For God wills that we have a filial trust in him as in a most loving and most provident father, yet so that we do moderately what lies in us. And so it is said of immoderate and carnal solicitude: [[11:7|the expectation of the solicitous shall perish|Exspectatio sollicitorum peribit]], that is, it will be condemned as sinful, and often in this life it is robbed of its effect. For those who are immoderately solicitous for earthly things expect to grow rich and to live long: and of both they are often deprived. Therefore Paul says: [[Phil 4:6|Be nothing solicitous|Nihil solliciti sitis]].

paras.t: Justus de angustia liberatus est, id est de inordinata tristitia atque formidine, aut etiam de corporali persecutione, sicut in Psalmo habetur: Multæ tribulationes justorum, et de his omnibus liberabit eos Dominus. Hinc in Job dicitur: Salvabit te de ore angusto latissime. David quoque fatetur: Vivit Dominus qui eripuit me de omni angustia. Sicut et sacratissimus Petrus ab Herode incarceratus ac vinctus, ab angelo est eductus. Et tradetur impius pro eo, id est, iniquus in angustias cadet, et pro malis quæ intulit justo, damnabitur: sicut Herodes ab angelo est percussus, vermibusque consumptus, qui summum incarceraverat Apostolum, decollavitque Jacobum. Hinc scriptum est: A facie malitiæ collectus est justus.
paras.en: [[11:8|The just is delivered out of distress|Justus de angustia liberatus est]], that is, out of disordered sadness and fear, or even out of bodily persecution, as we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just; but out of them all will the Lord deliver them|Multæ tribulationes justorum, et de his omnibus liberabit eos Dominus]]. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 36:16|he shall set thee at large out of the narrow mouth|Salvabit te de ore angusto latissime]]. David too declares: [[2 Kings 4:9|As the Lord liveth, who hath delivered my soul out of all distress|Vivit Dominus qui eripuit me de omni angustia]] [Denis has "who hath delivered me"]. So too the most holy Peter, imprisoned and bound by Herod, was led out by an angel[[Acts 12:3||]][[Acts 12:4||]][[Acts 12:7||]] [the margin gives Acts xii, 3, 4, 7–11]. [[11:8|and the wicked shall be given up for him|Et tradetur impius pro eo]]: that is, the unjust man will fall into straits, and will be condemned for the evils he brought upon the just man: as Herod was struck by an angel and consumed by worms[[Acts 12:23||]], who had imprisoned the chief Apostle[[Acts 12:3||]][[Acts 12:4||]] and beheaded James[[Acts 12:2||]]. Hence it is written: [[Is 57:1|the just man is taken away from before the face of evil|A facie malitiæ collectus est justus]].

paras.t: Simulator, qui aliud gerit in corde, et aliud prætendit in ore, ore decipit amicum suum, id est verbis aut factis, dicendo aut fingendo in opere quod diligat illum et quærat profectum ipsius, quum tamen quærat propria commoda cum proximi damno. De talibus asseritur: Sagitta vulnerans lingua eorum; in ore suo pacem cum amico suo loquitur, et occulte ponit ei insidias. Sic et falsi doctores et hæretici fallunt Catholicos, asserendo se esse vere fideles. Tales sunt Deo valde odibiles, juxta illud: Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei. Justi autem liberabuntur scientia, id est, per veram discretionem catholicamque doctrinam evadent simulatorum deceptiones et fraudes.
paras.en: [[11:9|The dissembler|Simulator]], who bears one thing in his heart and shows another in his mouth, [[11:9|with his mouth deceiveth his friend|ore decipit amicum suum]], that is, by words or deeds, saying or pretending in his conduct that he loves him and seeks his advancement, when all the while he seeks his own advantage to his neighbour's loss. Of such it is asserted: [[Jer 9:8|Their tongue is a piercing arrow|Sagitta vulnerans lingua eorum]]; [[Jer 9:8|with his mouth one speaketh peace with his friend, and secretly he lieth in wait for him|in ore suo pacem cum amico suo loquitur, et occulte ponit ei insidias]]. So also false teachers and heretics deceive Catholics, asserting that they are truly of the faith. Such men are greatly hateful to God, according to the saying: [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]]. [[11:9|but the just shall be delivered by knowledge|Justi autem liberabuntur scientia]]: that is, through true discernment and Catholic doctrine they will escape the deceits and frauds of dissemblers.

paras.t: In bonis justorum exaltabitur civitas, id est, per prudentiam et facultates virtuosorum civium oppida prosperabuntur: quoniam justi consilio et auxilio laborant pro bono politiæ communi, prout de Catone recitat Cicero. Et in perditione impiorum erit laudatio: id est, justi laudant jura, justumque judicem, imo et Deum omnipotentem, dum impii secundum leges puniuntur ac tolluntur de medio, ne amplius perturbent rem publicam: et talis laudatio procedit ex zelo justitiæ et amore boni communis. Nam et impiis expedit hic puniri. Unde in Psalmo: Lætabitur justus quum viderit vindictam.
paras.en: [[11:10|When it goeth well with the just, the city shall rejoice|In bonis justorum exaltabitur civitas]] [Denis reads *exaltabitur*, "shall be exalted"; the margin gives the Vulgate's *exsultabit*, "shall rejoice"]: that is, through the prudence and the means of virtuous citizens the towns will prosper: since the just labour with counsel and help for the common good of the commonwealth, as Cicero relates of Cato. [[11:10|and when the wicked perish, there shall be praise|Et in perditione impiorum erit laudatio]]: that is, the just praise the laws and the just judge, nay, Almighty God himself, when the wicked are punished according to the laws and taken out of the way, so that they may no longer disturb the commonwealth: and such praise proceeds from zeal for justice and love of the common good. For it is good even for the wicked to be punished here. Whence in the Psalm: [[Ps 57:11|The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge|Lætabitur justus quum viderit vindictam]].

paras.t: Benedictione justorum, id est per dona et merita justis collata, exaltabitur civitas: quoniam politia juvatur civium meritis, in tantum quod Dominus dixit se parcere Sodomæ, si essent in ea decem justi. Vel: Benedictione, id est imprecatione et oratione, qua justi imprecantur civibus pacem et prosperitatem, exaltabitur civitas: sicut in libris Regum ac Paralipomenon leguntur habitatores Jerusalem bona plurima consecuti precibus et meritis David, Asa, Josaphat, Ezechiæ, Josiæ, ac Prophetarum contemporaneorum regibus illis. Et ore impiorum subvertetur. Impii enim seditiosi et fraudulenti, variis modis pacem communitatis impediunt, urbem tradunt. Sic quoque Ecclesia per hæreticos inquietatur.
paras.en: [[11:11|By the blessing of the just|Benedictione justorum]], that is, through the gifts and merits bestowed on the just, [[11:11|the city shall be exalted|exaltabitur civitas]]: since the commonwealth is helped by the merits of its citizens, so much so that the Lord said he would spare Sodom if there were ten just men in it[[Gen 18:32||]]. Or: [[11:11|By the blessing|Benedictione]], that is, by the invocation and prayer by which the just call down peace and prosperity upon the citizens, [[11:11|the city shall be exalted|exaltabitur civitas]]: as we read in the books of Kings and of Paralipomenon that the inhabitants of Jerusalem obtained very many good things through the prayers and merits of David, Asa, Josaphat, Ezechias and Josias, and of the Prophets who were contemporary with those kings. [[11:11|and by the mouth of the wicked it shall be overthrown|Et ore impiorum subvertetur]]. For the wicked, seditious and deceitful, hinder the peace of the community in various ways, and betray the city. So too the Church is disquieted by heretics.
