paras.t: Qui despicit amicum suum ex elatione: quem deberet diligere ex caritate, et propter communionem naturæ, Religionis quoque ac fidei unitatem; indigens corde est, id est defectuosus, carens sapientia atque virtutibus: quibus si perficeretur, proximis suis etiam peccantibus compateretur, non elate aspernaretur, sicut ait Apostolus: Debemus nos firmiores, imbecillitates infirmorum sustinere, et non nobis placere. Vir autem prudens tacebit, considerando propriam defectuositatem, et aliorum peccata non publicando, dummodo corrigibiles se exhibeant in secreto.
paras.en: [[11:12|He that despiseth his friend|Qui despicit amicum suum]] out of haughtiness, whom he ought to love out of charity, and because of their common nature, and also the unity of religion and faith, [[11:12|is mean of heart|indigens corde est]] [Latin *indigens corde*, "wanting in heart"]: that is, he is defective, lacking wisdom and the virtues: if he were made perfect in them, he would have compassion on his neighbours even when they sin, and would not haughtily spurn them, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 15:1|we that are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak and not to please ourselves|Debemus nos firmiores, imbecillitates infirmorum sustinere, et non nobis placere]]. [[11:12|but the wise man will hold his peace|Vir autem prudens tacebit]], considering his own defectiveness, and not making public the sins of others, provided they show themselves open to correction in private.

paras.t: Qui ambulat fraudulenter, simulans se fidelem ac probum, quum sit loquax et improbus, revelat arcana, quæ sibi in secreto sunt patefacta cum obligatione celandi, seu alia proximorum peccata sibi soli cognita. Secretorum autem revelatio, præsertim quæ alicui in fide sunt patefacta, est ex suo genere mortale peccatum, repugnans caritati atque justitiæ, quum sit contra fidelitatem quam quis alteri servare tenetur: nisi forsan talium secretorum celatio redundaret aperte in detrimentum ac periculum boni communitatis. Idcirco incautum est, aliquid sine causa prægnanti in secreto accipere. Similiter viri prudentis est, secreta sua non faciliter alteri pandere: quia si ipsemet ea celare non valet, quomodo alius ea celabit? Ideo Seneca in Proverbiis suis dixit: Quod tacitum esse vis, nemini dixeris: quia non poteris ab alio exigere silentium, si tibi ipse non præstas. Nihilo minus interdum ratione obtinendi consilium, aut ex alia causa urgente, potest quis alteri viro probo ac sapienti, cujus fidelitatem expertus est, secretum suum insinuare. Nam subditur: qui autem fidelis est animi, fidelitate quæ est pars justitiæ, vel fide quæ per dilectionem cum discretione notabili operatur, celat amici commissum, id est secretum sui amici sibi in fide ab alio notificatum.
paras.en: [[11:13|He that walketh deceitfully|Qui ambulat fraudulenter]], pretending to be faithful and upright when he is a babbler and dishonest, [[11:13|revealeth secrets|revelat arcana]] that were disclosed to him in confidence under an obligation of keeping them hidden, or other sins of his neighbours known to him alone. Now the revealing of secrets, especially of those disclosed to someone in confidence, is of its kind a mortal sin, contrary to charity and justice, since it is against the fidelity which one is bound to keep towards another: unless perhaps the concealing of such secrets would plainly redound to the harm and danger of the good of the community. Therefore it is unwise to receive anything in secret without weighty cause. Likewise it belongs to the prudent man not to open his secrets readily to another: for if he himself cannot keep them hidden, how will another keep them? Therefore Seneca said in his Proverbs: What thou wouldst have kept quiet, tell no one: for thou canst not demand silence of another if thou dost not keep it thyself. Nevertheless, sometimes, for the sake of obtaining counsel or for some other pressing cause, one may confide one's secret to another man, upright and wise, whose fidelity one has tried. For it is added: [[11:13|but he that is faithful|qui autem fidelis est animi]] [literally "faithful of mind"], by the fidelity that is a part of justice, or by the faith which works through charity[[Gal 5:6||]] with notable discretion, [[11:13|concealeth the thing committed to him by his friend|celat amici commissum]]: that is, the secret of his friend, made known to him in confidence by the other.

paras.t: Ubi non est gubernator, populus corruet: quia non habet ducem et correctorem ac instructorem, et est sicut oves sine pastore. Ideo dicit in regula sua Hieronymus, quod nec congregatio, nec politia, nec domus diu potest subsistere, si desit cujus voluntati obediatur. Salus autem, id est periculorum evasio ac regimen bonum, est ubi sunt multa consilia, id est inter homines assidue inter se inquirentes, vel a prudentioribus investigantes quid sit agendum, quid evitandum. Ideo Tobias docetur: Consilium semper a sapiente perquire.
paras.en: [[11:14|Where there is no governor, the people shall fall|Ubi non est gubernator, populus corruet]]: because they have no leader, corrector and instructor, and are as sheep without a shepherd. Therefore Jerome says in his rule that neither a community, nor a commonwealth, nor a household can long subsist if there is no one whose will is obeyed. [[11:14|but there is safety|Salus autem]], that is, escape from dangers and good government, [[11:14|where there is much counsel|ubi sunt multa consilia]], that is, among men who constantly inquire among themselves, or seek out from those more prudent, what is to be done and what avoided. Therefore Tobias is taught: [[Tob 4:19|Seek counsel always of a wise man|Consilium semper a sapiente perquire]].

paras.t: Affligetur malo, id est, curam, timorem seu tristitiam in se patietur, qui fidem facit pro extraneo, id est, qui fidejubet pro alio: quia veretur ne ille satisfacere nequeat, aut non velit, sicque ipse pro illo satisfacere compellatur. De hoc, et qualiter caute habere se debeat homo fidejubendo pro proximo, dictum est plenius supra, capitulo sexto. Qui autem cavet laqueos, id est dispositiones propinquas et occasiones periculorum, deceptionum, damnorum, securus erit ab ipsis periculis. Laqueos ergo invisibilium ac visibilium hostium fugiamus, similiter fidejussiones incautas, societates perversas, fallaces divitias, oscula et amplexus, tactus et respectus morosos, ad concupiscentiam provocantes.
paras.en: [[11:15|He shall be afflicted with evil|Affligetur malo]], that is, he will suffer care, fear or sadness within himself, [[11:15|that is surety for a stranger|qui fidem facit pro extraneo]], that is, who goes bail for another: for he fears that the other will be unable or unwilling to pay, and that he himself will so be forced to pay for him. Of this, and of how cautiously a man ought to behave in going surety for his neighbour, it was said more fully above, in the sixth chapter[[Prov 6:1||]]. [[11:15|but he that is aware of snares|Qui autem cavet laqueos]], that is, the near dispositions and occasions of dangers, deceits and losses, [[11:15|shall be secure|securus erit]] from those very dangers. Let us therefore flee the snares of enemies invisible and visible, and likewise incautious suretyships, perverse company, deceitful riches, kisses and embraces, lingering touches and looks that provoke to concupiscence.

paras.t: Mulier gratiosa, id est pia, proba, accepta, inveniet gloriam, id est, delectationem bonam habebit, et erit famosa, ac tandem gloriam obtinebit cœlestem; et robusti in gratia et virtutibus, habebunt divitias spirituales, interdum etiam corporales.
paras.en: [[11:16|A gracious woman|Mulier gratiosa]], that is, devout, upright, well-pleasing, [[11:16|shall find glory|inveniet gloriam]]: that is, she will have good delight, and will be of good repute, and at length will obtain heavenly glory; [[11:16|and the strong|et robusti]] in grace and the virtues [[11:16|shall have riches|habebunt divitias]], spiritual ones, and at times bodily ones too.

paras.t: Benefacit animæ suæ vir misericors, id est, aliis miserendo ac succurrendo, meretur sibi ipsi misericordiam desuper fieri, juxta illud: Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. Sic qui aliis ignoscit, meretur sibi ignosci. Rursus, qui misericors est, opera misericordiæ spiritualia ac corporalia exercendo pro posse, in primis miseretur propriæ animæ, dolendo de ejus peccatis: sicque properat pœnitere, confiteri, et a vitiorum miseriis liber exsistere, prout in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Miserere animæ tuæ placens Deo. Nempe sicut caritas, sic et misericordia ista incipit a se ipsa. Qui autem crudelis est, proximos abjicit, negando eis consilium atque auxilium: quod est specialiter contra legem naturæ et naturalem amorem.
paras.en: [[11:17|A merciful man doth good to his own soul|Benefacit animæ suæ vir misericors]]: that is, by having mercy on others and succouring them, he merits that mercy be shown to himself from above, according to the saying: [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy|Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur]]. So he who forgives others merits to be forgiven. Again, he who is merciful, practising the spiritual and bodily works of mercy as far as he can, has mercy first of all on his own soul, grieving for its sins: and so he hastens to repent, to confess, and to be free of the miseries of the vices, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 30:24|Have pity on thy own soul, pleasing God|Miserere animæ tuæ placens Deo]]. Indeed, as charity, so this mercy too begins with oneself. [[11:17|but he that is cruel|Qui autem crudelis est]] [[11:17|casteth off|abjicit]] his neighbours [Denis reads *proximos*, "neighbours", where the Vulgate has *etiam propinquos*, "even his own kindred"], denying them counsel and help: which is especially against the law of nature and natural love.

paras.t: Impius facit opus instabile, id est a firmitate virtutum, et a rationis constantia alienum. Nam impius, quum passionibus sit subjectus, secundum diversitatem alterationis passionum suarum et diversimode et instabiliter agit, de uno vitio ruens in aliud. Seminanti autem justitiam, id est opera justa exercenti, merces erit fidelis, id est salus æterna, sicut a Deo promissum est.
paras.en: [[11:18|The wicked maketh an unsteady work|Impius facit opus instabile]], that is, one foreign to the firmness of the virtues and to the constancy of reason. For the wicked man, being subject to his passions, acts variously and unsteadily according to the varying changes of his passions, falling from one vice into another. [[11:18|but to him that soweth justice|Seminanti autem justitiam]], that is, to him who does just works, [[11:18|there is a faithful reward|merces erit fidelis]], that is, eternal salvation, as it has been promised by God[[Jas 1:12||]][[Jas 2:5||]].

paras.t: Clementia, per quam quis dimittit reo debitam pœnam in parte aut in toto, præparat vitam: quia per hanc meretur clemens sibi conferri aut augeri vitam gratiæ in hoc mundo, et gloriæ vitam in cœlo. Reo quoque quandoque relaxat mortis sententiam. Ideo hortatur Apostolus: Donantes invicem, si quis adversus aliquem habet querelam, sicut et Deus in Christo donavit vobis. Interdum tamen, imo et sæpe, servare oportet, propter bonum commune, rigorem justitiæ. Hinc Seneca loquitur: Quam magnarum virium est, lædentem negligere, id est non advertere! [Et] sectatio malorum, mortem, id est, frequens imitatio pravitatum parit gehennalem interitum.
paras.en: [[11:19|Clemency|Clementia]], by which one remits to the guilty the punishment due, in part or in whole, [[11:19|prepareth life|præparat vitam]]: for by it the clement man merits that the life of grace be granted or increased to him in this world, and the life of glory in heaven. It also sometimes remits the sentence of death to the guilty. Therefore the Apostle exhorts: [[Col 3:13|forgiving one another, if any have a complaint against another|Donantes invicem, si quis adversus aliquem habet querelam]], [[Eph 4:32|even as God hath forgiven you in Christ|sicut et Deus in Christo donavit vobis]] [the margin gives Col. iii, 13; these last words are as in Eph 4:32]. Yet at times, nay often, the rigour of justice must be kept for the sake of the common good. Hence Seneca says: How great a strength it is to disregard the one who wrongs us, that is, not to take notice of him! And [[11:19|the pursuing of evil things, death|sectatio malorum, mortem]]: that is, the frequent imitation of wickedness brings forth the destruction of hell.

paras.t: Abominabile Domino cor pravum, quum Deus sit naturaliter et incircumscriptibiliter bonus; et voluntas ejus in his qui simpliciter, id est columbina simplicitate, ambulant.
paras.en: [[11:20|A perverse heart is abominable to the Lord|Abominabile Domino cor pravum]], since God is good by nature and without limit; [[11:20|and his will is in them|et voluntas ejus in his qui]] [[11:20|that walk|ambulant]] [[11:20|sincerely|simpliciter]], that is, with the simplicity of the dove.

paras.t: Manus in manu non erit innocens malus: id est, homo pravus, exsistens manus in manu, id est cessans ab opere exteriori, sicut qui unam manum tenet in alia, nullam extendens in opus: talis non erit innocens, quoniam corde peccabit cogitando et appetendo, bonaque omittendo. Semen autem, id est operatio bona, seu virtuosa posteritas, justorum salvabitur.
paras.en: [[11:21|Hand in hand the evil man shall not be innocent|Manus in manu non erit innocens malus]]: that is, the wicked man, being hand in hand, that is, ceasing from outward work, like one who holds one hand in the other and stretches out neither to work: such a man will not be innocent, since he will sin in his heart by thinking and desiring, and by leaving good undone. [[11:21|but the seed|Semen autem]], that is, good works, or virtuous offspring, [[11:21|of the just shall be saved|justorum salvabitur]].

paras.t: Circulus aureus in naribus suis, mulier pulchra et fatua: id est, femina incontinens et formosa, ita se habet, ut aureus circulus in naribus porcæ: quoniam porcea seu sus circulum aureum naso suo innexum, luto et sordibus mox infigit. Sic mulier stulta ac speciosa, pulchritudinem et ornatum sibi concessum convertit ad cœnum libidinis. Spiritualiter, mulier pulchra et stulta, est hæreticorum collectio, quæ venustate gaudet eloquii, et eam cum notitia veritatis sibi concessa, vertit ad suorum fœditates errorum, tanquam spurcissima porca.
paras.en: [[11:22|A golden ring in a swine's snout, a woman fair and foolish|Circulus aureus in naribus suis, mulier pulchra et fatua]] [the Vulgate has only "in its nostrils"; Denis explains of what beast]: that is, a woman who is unchaste and beautiful is like a golden ring in the nostrils of a sow: for the sow, or swine, soon thrusts the golden ring fastened in its snout into the mud and filth. So the foolish and comely woman turns the beauty and adornment granted her into the mire of lust. Spiritually, [[11:22|a woman fair and foolish|mulier pulchra et stulta]] is the assembly of heretics, which delights in beauty of speech, and turns it, together with the knowledge of the truth granted it, to the foulness of its errors, like a most filthy sow.

paras.t: Desiderium justorum, omne bonum est, id est, bonitatem et æquitatem in omnibus cupiunt observari, atque in omni gratia et virtute optant proficere; Deum quoque, in quo est omnium bonorum et pulchrorum superplena possessio, desiderant finaliter obtinere. Præstolatio impiorum, furor, id est, cum immoderantia iræ cupiunt et exspectant mala inferre, et vitiosæ eorum exspectationi furoris flamma sæpe miscetur, ac pro eorum excessibus imminet eis furor Dei, id est rigor ultionis divinæ.
paras.en: [[11:23|The desire of the just is all good|Desiderium justorum, omne bonum est]]: that is, they long for goodness and equity to be kept in all things, and they wish to advance in every grace and virtue; and they desire in the end to obtain God, in whom is the overflowing possession of all good and beautiful things. [[11:23|the expectation of the wicked is indignation|Præstolatio impiorum, furor]] [Latin *furor*, "fury"]: that is, with unbridled anger they long and wait to inflict evils, and the flame of fury is often mingled with their sinful expectation; and for their excesses the fury of God hangs over them, that is, the rigour of the divine vengeance.

paras.t: Alii dividunt propria, id est, bona spiritualia ac temporalia eis concessa communicant proximis; et ditiores fiunt: quia pro hac eorum caritativa communicatione, piaque liberalitate, Deus auget in eis spiritualia ac temporalia bona. Alii rapiunt non sua, scilicet temporalia aliorum, seu virtutes quibus carent, sibi adscribunt; et semper in egestate sunt: nam veris divitiis mentis privantur, et temporalia male consumunt. Nihilo minus, sicut in Job legitur, abundant interdum tabernacula prædonum.
paras.en: [[11:24|Some distribute their own goods|Alii dividunt propria]], that is, they share with their neighbours the spiritual and temporal goods granted them, [[11:24|and grow richer|et ditiores fiunt]]: for in return for this charitable sharing and devout liberality of theirs, God increases their spiritual and temporal goods. [[11:24|others take away what is not their own|Alii rapiunt non sua]], namely the temporal goods of others, or they ascribe to themselves virtues they lack; [[11:24|and are always in want|et semper in egestate sunt]]: for they are deprived of the true riches of the mind, and they squander their temporal goods. Nevertheless, as we read in Job, at times [[Job 12:6|The tabernacles of robbers abound|abundant interdum tabernacula prædonum]].

paras.t: Anima quæ benedicit, id est, Deum laudat, et proximis prædicat bona, impinguabitur donis Spiritus Sancti, prout orat Psalmista: Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea. Unde in Jeremia loquitur Dominus: Inebriabo animas sacerdotum pinguedine, eritque anima eorum quasi hortus irriguus. Et qui inebriat auditores verbo sacræ doctrinæ seu gaudio spirituali, ipse quoque inebriabitur charismatibus Dei, qui tanto liberalius gratiam inserit et refundit, quanto quis proximis suis magis caritative ac pie communicat dona sibi concessa. Porro nonnulli ex industria inebriant socios suos poculo corporali: quod faciendo, vanitate et impietate inebriantur, et postea suppliciis replebuntur.
paras.en: [[11:25|The soul that blesseth|Anima quæ benedicit]], that is, that praises God and proclaims good things to its neighbours, [[11:25|shall be made fat|impinguabitur]] with the gifts of the Holy Ghost, as the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 62:6|Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness|Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea]]. Whence the Lord says in Jeremias: [[Jer 31:14|I will fill the soul of the priests with fatness|Inebriabo animas sacerdotum pinguedine]] [Latin *inebriabo*, "I will inebriate", the word of the verse that follows here], [[Jer 31:12|their soul shall be as a watered garden|eritque anima eorum quasi hortus irriguus]]. [[11:25|and he that inebriateth|Et qui inebriat]] his hearers with the word of sacred doctrine or with spiritual joy, [[11:25|shall be inebriated also himself|ipse quoque inebriabitur]] with the gifts of God, who instils and pours back grace the more liberally, the more charitably and devoutly a man shares with his neighbours the gifts granted him. But some deliberately make their companions drunk with a bodily cup: and in so doing they are made drunk with vanity and wickedness, and afterwards will be filled with torments.

paras.t: Qui abscondunt frumenta, id est, ea non exponunt venalia tempore opportuno, sed ex immoderata sollicitudine ea in proprium usum reservant, aut ex cupiditate apud se retinent, ut postea carius vendant; maledicentur in populis indigentibus. Benedictio autem super caput vendentium, id est, vendentibus populi bona imprecabuntur, præsertim si pro competenti dent pretio. Sicque abscondentes frumenta tempore quo sunt venditioni exponenda, peccant non solum ex cupiditate et immoderata sollicitudine, sed etiam alios graviter scandalizando; nec faciunt proximis quemadmodum sibi in casu simili cuperent fieri: quod est legi contrarium naturali; imo periculosum est valde, quia si pauperes aliqui ex inopia morerentur, timendum quod imputaretur divitibus illis a Deo. Nempe, ut sancti patres Ambrosius Basiliusque testantur, qui periclitantibus et indigentibus non succurrit, occidit. Seneca quoque: Qui perituro, inquit, succurrere potest, quum non succurrit, occidit.
paras.en: [[11:26|He that hideth up corn|Qui abscondunt frumenta]], that is, those who do not put it up for sale at the fitting time, but out of immoderate solicitude keep it back for their own use, or out of covetousness hold it back with them so as to sell it more dearly afterwards, [[11:26|shall be cursed among the people|maledicentur in populis]] that are in need. [[11:26|but a blessing upon the head of them that sell|Benedictio autem super caput vendentium]]: that is, the people will call down good things upon those who sell, especially if they sell at a fair price. And so those who hide up corn at a time when it ought to be put up for sale sin not only by covetousness and immoderate solicitude, but also by giving grave scandal to others; nor do they do to their neighbours as they would wish done to themselves in a like case[[Tob 4:16||]][[Matt 7:12||]]: which is contrary to the natural law; nay, it is very dangerous, for if any poor people died of want, it is to be feared that God would lay it to the charge of those rich men. Indeed, as the holy Fathers Ambrose and Basil testify, he who does not succour those in danger and in need, kills. Seneca too: He who can succour one about to perish, he says, and does not succour him, kills.

paras.t: Spiritualiter frumenta abscondit, qui dona gratiæ sibi collata non communicat proximis, nec verbum Dei prædicat sibi commissis, nec fructuose utitur creditis sibi talentis. Talis maledictionem meretur. Cui et judex in Evangelio loquitur: Serve male et piger. Benedictio autem super caput vendentium, id est fructuose exponentium, atque implentium quod jubet Salvator: Negotiamini dum venio. Quorum unicuique dicitur: Euge, serve bone et fidelis, etc.
paras.en: Spiritually, he hides up corn who does not share with his neighbours the gifts of grace bestowed on him, nor preaches the word of God to those entrusted to him, nor uses fruitfully the talents lent him. Such a man deserves a curse. To him the judge in the Gospel says: [[Matt 25:26|Wicked and slothful servant|Serve male et piger]]. [[11:26|but a blessing upon the head of them that sell|Benedictio autem super caput vendentium]], that is, of those who lay them out fruitfully and fulfil what the Saviour commands: [[Luke 19:13|Trade till I come|Negotiamini dum venio]]. To each of whom it is said: [[Matt 25:21|Well done, good and faithful servant|Euge, serve bone et fidelis]][[Matt 25:23||]], etc.

paras.t: Bene consurgit diluculo, qui quærit bona, id est, feliciter mane surgit, qui cupit et nititur tempus fructuose expendere, proximis subvenire, et semper boni aliquid operari. Qui autem investigator malorum est, id est, facta et defectus proximorum malitiose aut curiose inquirit, ad accusandum seu persequendum vel diffamandum, aut simili intentione perversa, opprimetur ab eis, id est, illorum pondere a propria impedietur salute. Grave enim, ut ait Gregorius, est vitium curiositatis: quod dum mentem circa aliorum defectus investigandos occupat, eam sibi ipsi abscondit, ut tanto minus propria cernat peccata, quanto curiosius discutit aliena: sicque in superbia fovet miseram animam, atque ad temeraria judicia efficit eam pronam.
paras.en: [[11:27|Well doth he rise early who seeketh good things|Bene consurgit diluculo, qui quærit bona]]: that is, he rises happily in the morning who desires and strives to spend his time fruitfully, to help his neighbours, and always to be doing some good. [[11:27|but he that seeketh after evil things|Qui autem investigator malorum est]], that is, who maliciously or curiously searches out the deeds and failings of his neighbours, in order to accuse or pursue or defame them, or with some like perverse intention, [[11:27|shall be oppressed by them|opprimetur ab eis]]: that is, by their weight he will be hindered from his own salvation. For, as Gregory says, the vice of curiosity is grievous: for while it busies the mind with searching out the failings of others, it hides the mind from itself, so that it sees its own sins the less, the more curiously it examines those of others: and so it nurses the wretched soul in pride, and makes it prone to rash judgments.

paras.t: Vel: Qui investigator malorum est, id est, excogitat quæ mala dicat aut faciat, opprimetur ab eis, id est, eorum demeritis in supplicia demergetur. Rursus, qui investigat mala, id est illicita, ut faciat ea, aut instruatur ex eis, sicut qui artibus magicis quærunt juvari, quemadmodum Saul qui pythonissam consuluit: opprimetur ab eis, quia suæ adversantur saluti, et sæpe decipitur. Verumtamen qui præsunt, præsertim episcopi, ex caritate et zelo justitiæ debent subditorum mala per se ipsos, et per condignos ministros inquirere.
paras.en: Or: [[11:27|he that seeketh after evil things|Qui investigator malorum est]], that is, who thinks out what evil things he may say or do, [[11:27|shall be oppressed by them|opprimetur ab eis]], that is, he will be plunged into punishments by their demerits. Again, he who searches out evil things, that is, unlawful ones, in order to do them or be instructed by them, like those who seek help from the magic arts, as Saul did who consulted the pythoness[[1 Kings 28:7||]] [the margin gives 1 Kings xxviii, 7–12; that is, the witch of Endor]: [[11:27|shall be oppressed by them|opprimetur ab eis]], because they are against his salvation, and he is often deceived. Yet those who are in authority, especially bishops, ought out of charity and zeal for justice to inquire into the evils of their subjects, by themselves and through fit ministers.

paras.t: Qui confidit in divitiis suis temporalibus et terrenis, corruet in culpam et pœnam. Idcirco ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus: Divitibus præcipe non sperare in incerto divitiarum. Similiter qui in spiritualibus suis divitiis, id est meritis, magis quam in pietate et gratia Dei confidit, corruet et peribit. Et ad utrumque istorum spectat quod fertur in Psalmo: Ecce homo qui non posuit Deum adjutorem suum, sed speravit in multitudine divitiarum suarum. Justi autem quasi virens folium germinabunt, id est, fructum virtutum producent ex interiori mentis virore, et crescent in melius, quemadmodum folium virens extenditur ad congruam quantitatem. Est etenim tanquam lignum quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum, et folium ejus non defluet.
paras.en: [[11:28|He that trusteth in his riches|Qui confidit in divitiis suis]], temporal and earthly ones, [[11:28|shall fall|corruet]] into sin and punishment. Therefore the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[1 Tim 6:17|Charge the rich|Divitibus præcipe]] not [[1 Tim 6:17|to trust in the uncertainty of riches|sperare in incerto divitiarum]]. Likewise he who trusts in his spiritual riches, that is, his merits, more than in the goodness and grace of God, shall fall and perish. And to both of these belongs what is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 51:9|Behold the man that made not God his helper: But trusted in the abundance of his riches|Ecce homo qui non posuit Deum adjutorem suum, sed speravit in multitudine divitiarum suarum]]. [[11:28|but the just shall spring up as a green leaf|Justi autem quasi virens folium germinabunt]]: that is, they will bring forth the fruit of the virtues from the inner greenness of the mind, and will grow for the better, as a green leaf spreads out to its due size. For he is like [[Ps 1:3|a tree which is planted near the running waters|lignum quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum]], [[Ps 1:3|And his leaf shall not fall off|et folium ejus non defluet]].

paras.t: Qui conturbat domum suam, id est, suos domesticos seu cognatos, aut plebem seu congregationem sibi commissam irrationabiliter inquietat, et impatientia, ira seu inquietudine sua molestat, quos debuit tranquillos reddere, pacare atque dirigere; possidebit ventos, id est, fructum non consequetur ex hoc, sed impietatem, inquietudinem et rancorem, aut etiam expulsionem a statione mansioneque sua. Hinc in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Noli esse quasi leo in domo tua, evertens domesticos tuos. Spiritualiter qui conturbat domum suam, et habitaculum cordis sui pravis cogitationibus, passionum tumultibus, desideriis inordinatis, apprehensionibus phantasmaticis implet; possidet ventos, id est, flatus diabolicarum suggestionum intra se suscipit ac reservat. De talibus Dominus loquitur per Osee: Ventum seminabunt, et turbinem metent.
paras.en: [[11:29|He that troubleth his own house|Qui conturbat domum suam]], that is, who unreasonably disquiets those of his household or his kin, or the people or community entrusted to him, and vexes with his impatience, anger or restlessness those whom he ought to have made tranquil, set at peace and guided, [[11:29|shall inherit the winds|possidebit ventos]]: that is, he will gain no fruit from this, but ill will, unrest and rancour, or even expulsion from his post and dwelling. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 4:35|Be not as a lion in thy house, terrifying them of thy household|Noli esse quasi leo in domo tua, evertens domesticos tuos]] [Latin *evertens*, "overturning"]. Spiritually, [[11:29|He that troubleth his own house|qui conturbat domum suam]], and fills the dwelling of his heart with wicked thoughts, the tumults of the passions, disordered desires and fantastic imaginings, possesses the winds: that is, he receives and keeps within himself the blasts of the devil's suggestions. Of such the Lord speaks through Osee: [[Osee 8:7|they shall sow wind, and reap a whirlwind|Ventum seminabunt, et turbinem metent]].

paras.t: Et qui stultus est, serviet sapienti. Hoc equidem est de jure naturali, ut sapiens præsit, et insipiens sit subjectus, sicut et primo Politicorum docet Philosophus. Frequenter tamen in rebus humanis contingit contrarium. Sapientes autem, qui sciunt qualiter sit jubendum, et quomodo homines sint regendi, atque in virtutibus sunt fundati, passionibus dominantes, digni sunt præcipere et præesse.
paras.en: [[11:29|and the fool shall serve the wise|Et qui stultus est, serviet sapienti]]. This indeed is of natural right, that the wise should rule and the unwise be subject, as the Philosopher also teaches in the first book of the Politics. Yet in human affairs the contrary often happens. But the wise, who know how to command and how men are to be ruled, and are grounded in the virtues, masters of their passions, are worthy to command and to rule.

paras.t: Fructus justi, lignum vitæ: id est, operatio virtuosa reficit operantem, sicut lignum vitæ edentem. Unde ait Salvator: Meus cibus est ut faciam voluntatem Patris mei. Iterum, fructus justi est justo pro ligno vitæ, atque ad beatificam fruitionem Christi, qui est lignum vitæ, perducit. Hinc fatetur: Vincenti dabo edere de ligno vitæ, quod est in paradiso Dei mei. [Et] qui suscipit animas, sapiens est, id est, qui animas proximorum spiritualiter diligit, et eis pro posse succurrit, atque in sinu caritatis amplectitur eas, ut nutrix infantulum, unicuique subveniendo secundum quod indiget, sapiens est. Talis namque est vere illuminatus a Deo; et quo animæ præstantiores sunt corporibus, eo ferventior est ad exhibendum spiritualia misericordiæ opera animabus, quam corporalia misericordiæ opera corporibus, implens illud Apostoli: Corripite inquietos, consolamini pusillanimes, suscipite infirmos, patientes estote ad omnes. Talis sequitur Deum, cui in libro Sapientiæ dicitur: Qui amas animas.
paras.en: [[11:30|The fruit of the just man is a tree of life|Fructus justi, lignum vitæ]]: that is, virtuous work refreshes the one who does it, as the tree of life refreshes the one who eats of it. Whence the Saviour says: [[John 4:34|My meat is to do the will|Meus cibus est ut faciam voluntatem]] of my Father [the Vulgate has "of him that sent me"]. Again, the fruit of the just man is to the just man in place of the tree of life, and leads him to the beatifying enjoyment of Christ, who is the tree of life. Hence he declares: [[Apoc 2:7|To him that overcometh I will give to eat of the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God|Vincenti dabo edere de ligno vitæ, quod est in paradiso Dei mei]]. And [[11:30|he that gaineth souls is wise|qui suscipit animas, sapiens est]] [Latin *suscipit*, "takes up" or "receives", which Denis expounds as taking souls to oneself]: that is, he who loves the souls of his neighbours spiritually, and succours them as far as he can, and embraces them in the bosom of charity as a nurse her little child, helping each according to his need, is wise. For such a man is truly enlightened by God; and the more excellent souls are than bodies, the more fervent he is in showing the spiritual works of mercy to souls than the bodily works of mercy to bodies, fulfilling that saying of the Apostle: [[1 Thess 5:14|rebuke the unquiet: comfort the feeble minded: support the weak: be patient towards all men|Corripite inquietos, consolamini pusillanimes, suscipite infirmos, patientes estote ad omnes]]. Such a man follows God, to whom it is said in the book of Wisdom: O Lord, [[Wis 11:27|who lovest souls|Qui amas animas]].

paras.t: Si, pro quia, justus in terra recipit persecutiones, tentationes et debitas pro suis culpis correptiones et pœnas, aut etiam absque suis demeritis, ut patet de sanctis martyribus, et de Job, Tobia, ac aliis multis; quanto magis impius, qui peccat directe in Deum, et peccator peccans in proximum, recipiet justam punitionem, vel in præsenti sæculo, aut futuro? Unde per Jeremiam Dominus ait: Ecce domum in qua invocatum est nomen meum, ego incipio affligere, et vos eritis immunes? Non eritis immunes. Et per Ezechielem ad Jerusalem dixit: Pro eo quod occidi in te justum et impium, egredietur gladius meus ad omnem carnem. Hinc et princeps Apostolorum dignissimus, in prima sua ait Canonica: Tempus est ut incipiat judicium a domo Dei. Si autem primum a nobis, quis finis eorum qui non credunt Dei Evangelio? Et si justus vix salvabitur, impius et peccator ubi parebunt? Quod, secundum Glossam, ex hoc loco acceptum est secundum translationem antiquam.
paras.en: [[11:31|If|Si]], put for *since*, [[11:31|the just man receive in the earth|justus in terra recipit]] persecutions, temptations, and the rebukes and punishments due for his faults, or even without any demerit of his own, as is plain of the holy martyrs, and of Job, Tobias and many others[[Job 1:13||]][[Tob 2:10||]] [the margin gives Job i, 1, 8, 13–20; Tob. i, 2, 12, 13, 15, 19, 20; ii, 3–12]; [[11:31|how much more the wicked|quanto magis impius]], who sins directly against God, [[11:31|and the sinner|et peccator]] who sins against his neighbour, will receive just punishment, either in the present world or in the world to come? Whence the Lord says through Jeremias: Behold, the house [[Jer 25:29|wherein my name is called upon|in qua invocatum est nomen meum]], [[Jer 25:29|I begin to bring evil|ego incipio affligere]] [Latin *affligere*, "to afflict"; Denis has "the house" where the Vulgate has "the city"], and shall you be free? [[Jer 25:29|you shall not escape free|Non eritis immunes]]. And through Ezechiel he said to Jerusalem: [[Ezech 21:4|forasmuch as I have cut off in thee the just and the wicked|Pro eo quod occidi in te justum et impium]], [[Ezech 21:4|shall my sword go forth|egredietur gladius meus]] [[Ezech 21:4|against all flesh|ad omnem carnem]]. Hence the most worthy prince of the Apostles too says in his first Canonical epistle: [[1 Pet 4:17|the time is, that judgment should begin at the house of God. And if at first at us, what shall be the end of them that believe not the gospel of God?|Tempus est ut incipiat judicium a domo Dei. Si autem primum a nobis, quis finis eorum qui non credunt Dei Evangelio?]] [[1 Pet 4:18|And if the just man shall scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?|Et si justus vix salvabitur, impius et peccator ubi parebunt?]] Which, according to the Gloss, was taken from this place according to the old translation [that is, the Greek Septuagint, which reads this verse: "If the just man is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?"].

paras.t: Postremo, ex his sumitur evidens argumentum divinæ providentiæ ac futuri judicii, et quod post vitam præsentem sit alia vita, in qua finalis est retributio malorum atque bonorum. Apertissime namque videmus, multos perfectos ac justos in sæculo isto variis adversitatibus persecutionibusque affligi omni tempore vitæ hujus, impios vero et sceleratissimos assidue prosperari: quo constat, quod in sæculo isto non sit retributio ultimata, sed alia restet secundum forum divini judicii. Propter quod habetur: Peccator ex eo quod centies facit malum, et per patientiam sustentatur, ego cognovi quod bene erit timentibus Deum, qui verentur faciem ejus.
paras.en: Lastly, from these things an evident argument is drawn for divine providence and the judgment to come, and that after the present life there is another life, in which is the final requital of the wicked and the good. For we see most plainly that many perfect and just men are afflicted in this world with various adversities and persecutions through the whole time of this life, while the wicked and most criminal prosper continually: from which it is clear that in this world there is no final requital, but that another remains, before the court of the divine judgment. For which reason we have: [[Eccles 8:12|though a sinner do evil a hundred times, and by patience be borne withal, I know from thence that it shall be well with them that fear God, who dread his face|Peccator ex eo quod centies facit malum, et per patientiam sustentatur, ego cognovi quod bene erit timentibus Deum, qui verentur faciem ejus]].

12.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI DUODECIMI : QUI DILIGIT DISCIPLINAM, DILIGIT SCIENTIAM.
12.title_en: Elucidation of the twelfth chapter: He that loveth correction, loveth knowledge.

paras.t: Qui diligit disciplinam, id est informationem magistrorum ac sapientiorum, diligit scientiam, quæ per informationem magistrorum acquiritur, quamvis interdum propria adinventione aut studio obtineatur. Vel : Qui diligit disciplinam, id est correptionem et castigationem pro suis peccatis, diligit scientiam quæ est donum Spiritus Sancti, quæ purgatis a vitiis infunditur et augetur. Diligit quoque talis scientiam, id est veritatis notitiam, et profectum in ea. Qui autem odit increpationes, insipiens est : quoniam amat vitia sua, et curationem animæ suæ ab eis abhorret, nec acquiescit Scripturis ; et sapientiam veram quæ est donum, non habet, quoniam illa suasibilis est, et bonis consentiens, ut Jacobus ait apostolus. Sicque quasi incomparabiliter insipientior est corporaliter vulnerato atque letaliter læso, et tamen corporalem medelam refugienti.
paras.en: [[12:1|He that loveth correction|Qui diligit disciplinam]] [*disciplina* means both 'instruction' and 'correction, chastisement'; Denis takes it first one way, then the other], that is, the instruction of masters and of wiser men, [[12:1|loveth knowledge|diligit scientiam]], which is acquired through the instruction of masters, though it is sometimes obtained by a man's own discovery or study. Or: [[12:1|He that loveth correction|Qui diligit disciplinam]], that is, correction and chastisement for his sins, [[12:1|loveth knowledge|diligit scientiam]], which is a gift of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]], poured into those who are cleansed of vices, and increased in them. Such a man loves knowledge also in the sense of the acquaintance with truth, and progress in it. [[12:1|but he that hateth reproof, is foolish|Qui autem odit increpationes, insipiens est]]: for he loves his vices and shrinks from the healing of his soul from them, and does not yield to the Scriptures; and he has not the true wisdom which is a gift, since that wisdom is [[Jas 3:17|easy to be persuaded, consenting to the good|suasibilis est, et bonis consentiens]], as the apostle James says. And so he is, as it were, incomparably more foolish than a man wounded in body and mortally hurt who yet flees from bodily medicine.

paras.t: Qui bonus est, hauriet gratiam a Domino, id est, Deo acceptabilis est, et gratiæ incrementum sortietur ab eo ; qui autem confidit in cogitationibus suis, id est in propriis industriis et conceptionibus, amplius quam in directione ac ope Spiritus Sancti, impie agit : quia meretur a Deo relinqui, sicque errat et peccat. Unde de quibusdam ait Apostolus : Evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis. Et per Isaiam Dominus contestatur : Averti faciem meam ab eo, et abiit vagus in cogitationibus suis.
paras.en: [[12:2|He that is good, shall draw grace from the Lord|Qui bonus est, hauriet gratiam a Domino]], that is, is acceptable to God and will obtain from him an increase of grace; [[12:2|but he that trusteth in his own devices|qui autem confidit in cogitationibus suis]] [*cogitationes*, 'thoughts'], that is, in his own efforts and notions, more than in the guidance and help of the Holy Ghost, [[12:2|doth wickedly|impie agit]]: for he deserves to be abandoned by God, and so he errs and sins. Hence the Apostle says of certain men: They [[Rom 1:21|became vain in their thoughts|Evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis]]. And by Isaias the Lord protests: [[Is 57:17|I hid my face from thee|Averti faciem meam ab eo]], and [[Is 57:17|he went away wandering in his own heart|abiit vagus in cogitationibus suis]] [Denis's text reads 'I turned away my face from him, and he went away wandering in his thoughts', *in cogitationibus suis*, the very words of the verse expounded; the Vulgate has *in via cordis sui*, 'in the way of his heart'].

paras.t: Non roborabitur homo ex impietate. Peccatum enim naturalia vulnerat, et lædit naturam. Et radix justorum, id est fides seu caritas, vel stabilitas bonorum, non commovebitur, sed tentationibus et peccatis resistit, ac Deo stabiliter innititur : et ita nec ex parte Dei, nec ex parte virtutis, sed ex fragilitate conditionis humanæ contingit ruina peccati, et commotio a virtutum constantia.
paras.en: [[12:3|Man shall not be strengthened by wickedness|Non roborabitur homo ex impietate]]. For sin wounds man's natural goods and hurts his nature. [[12:3|and the root of the just|Et radix justorum]], that is, faith or charity, or the steadfastness of the good, [[12:3|shall not be moved|non commovebitur]], but resists temptations and sins and leans steadfastly upon God: and so the fall into sin, and the moving away from the constancy of the virtues, comes neither from God's side nor from virtue's, but from the frailty of the human condition.

paras.t: Mulier diligens, id est in factis bonis et domus suæ regimine vigilans, et virum suum sinceriter amans, corona est viro suo, id est causa lætitiæ et honoris. Talisquoque mulier sæpe trahit ad gratiam et salutem suum maritum, sicut ait Apostolus : Salvatus est vir infidelis per mulierem fidelem. Unde in Ecclesiastico scriptum est : Mulieris bonæ beatus vir. Et putredo in ossibus ejus, quæ confusione res dignas gerit, id est, putrefactio interior atque exterior debetur mulieri incontinenti, præsertim adulteræ : quemadmodum etiam in Numeris narratur de pœnis adulteræ, aquas in quas maledicta erant congesta potantis, ut putrescat femur ejus, et tumens uterus dirumpatur.
paras.en: [[12:4|A diligent woman|Mulier diligens]], that is, watchful in good deeds and in the governing of her house, and loving her husband sincerely, [[12:4|is a crown to her husband|corona est viro suo]], that is, a cause of joy and honour. Such a woman also often draws her husband to grace and salvation, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 7:14|the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the believing wife|Salvatus est vir infidelis per mulierem fidelem]] [Denis reads *salvatus*, 'saved', where the Vulgate has *sanctificatus*, 'sanctified']. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 26:1|Happy is the husband of a good wife|Mulieris bonæ beatus vir]]. [[12:4|and she that doth things worthy of confusion, is as rottenness in his bones|Et putredo in ossibus ejus, quæ confusione res dignas gerit]]: that is, rottenness within and without is owed to the incontinent woman, above all to the adulteress: as is also told in Numbers of the punishments of the adulteress who drinks the waters on which curses were heaped[[Num 5:19||]], so that her thigh may rot and her swollen belly burst[[Num 5:21||]][[Num 5:22||]].

paras.t: Cogitationes justorum, judicia, id est judicialiter examinatæ, et cum discretione directæ. Justi enim et sapientes, cogitationes suas discutiunt et refrenant, ne Deo displiceant ; quia, ut ait Apostolus, Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Sic cogitationes suas discrevit, qui dixit : Meditatio cordis mei in conspectu tuo semper. Rursus, Cogitationes justorum, judicia, id est, ad hoc tendunt cogitationes eorum, ut judicium justitiamque conservent. Et consilia impiorum fraudulenta : quoniam quærunt propria commoda, ideo consulunt quod eorum utilitati plus congruit, et perverso eorum fini magis concordat. Nec habent veram prudentiam, sed vulpinam versutiam : imo sæpe fingunt se scire quod nesciunt, quatenus consulendo, aliquid utilitatis ab eo cui præstant consilium, consequantur.
paras.en: [[12:5|The thoughts of the just are judgments|Cogitationes justorum, judicia]], that is, examined as in a court, and directed with discretion. For the just and the wise sift their thoughts and rein them in, lest they displease God; for, as the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. So he weighed his thoughts who said: [[Ps 18:15|the meditation of my heart always in thy sight|Meditatio cordis mei in conspectu tuo semper]]. Again, [[12:5|The thoughts of the just are judgments|Cogitationes justorum, judicia]], that is, the thoughts of the just tend to this, that they may keep judgment and justice. [[12:5|and the counsels of the wicked are deceitful|Et consilia impiorum fraudulenta]]: since they seek their own advantage, they counsel what best suits their interest and most agrees with their perverse end. Nor have they true prudence, but a fox's cunning: indeed they often pretend to know what they do not know, so that by giving counsel they may get some profit from the one to whom they give it.

paras.t: Verba impiorum insidiantur sanguini : quia ad læsiones et homicidia provocant, et pro temporali commodo falsa testimonia dicunt, falsam quoque et injustam sententiam proferunt. Os justorum liberabit eos, id est, sanguinem innocentem excusando eruet justos, et pro eorum ereptione faciendo quidquid potuerit. Vel, Os justorum liberabit eos, id est, impios convertet ad Deum : sicque ab eorum iniquitatibus eruet eos.
paras.en: [[12:6|The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood|Verba impiorum insidiantur sanguini]]: for they provoke to injuries and murders, and for temporal advantage they bear false witness, and pronounce a false and unjust sentence as well. [[12:6|the mouth of the just shall deliver them|Os justorum liberabit eos]], that is, it will rescue the just by clearing their innocent blood, doing whatever it can to rescue them. Or: [[12:6|the mouth of the just shall deliver them|Os justorum liberabit eos]], that is, it will convert the wicked to God, and so deliver them from their iniquities.

paras.t: Verte impios, id est, ab iniquitate eorum eos averte orando aut exhortando. Qui enim converti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suæ, salvabit animam ejus a morte, ut dicit Jacobus. Et non erunt impii sicut ante. Hinc Paulus de persecutore in Apostolum versus : Vivo, inquit, jam non ego. Vel : Verte impios, id est, statum et prosperitatem eorum immuta; et non erunt, id est, cito deficient. Antiqua translatio habet : Quocumque se vertit impius, exterminabitur. Nam et cito perit ac putrescit eorum memoria, juxta illud Job : Memoria vestra comparabitur cineri. Ideo ait Glossa : Multa impietas in diis gentium, in sectis hæreticorum, in præstigiis magorum, in persecutionibus paganorum ; sed his a Deo subversis, subversa est et memoria impietatis istorum. Domus autem justorum, id est congregationes justæ, Ecclesiæ Christi, personæ fideles, permanebunt in gratia, et salvabuntur.
paras.en: [[12:7|Turn the wicked|Verte impios]], that is, turn them away from their iniquity by prayer or exhortation. For [[Jas 5:20|he who causeth a sinner to be converted from the error of his way shall save his soul from death|Qui enim converti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suæ, salvabit animam ejus a morte]], as James says. [[12:7|and they shall not be|Et non erunt]] wicked as before. Hence Paul, the persecutor turned Apostle, says: [[Gal 2:20|I live|Vivo]], he says, [[Gal 2:20|now not I|jam non ego]]. Or: [[12:7|Turn the wicked|Verte impios]], that is, change their state and prosperity; [[12:7|and they shall not be|et non erunt]], that is, they will quickly fail. The old translation [that is, the Old Latin version, made from the Greek] has: Whithersoever the wicked man turns, he shall be destroyed. For their memory too quickly perishes and rots, according to that word of Job: [[Job 13:12|Your remembrance shall be compared to ashes|Memoria vestra comparabitur cineri]]. Therefore the Gloss says: There was much wickedness in the gods of the Gentiles, in the sects of the heretics, in the illusions of the magicians, in the persecutions of the pagans; but when these were overthrown by God, the memory of their wickedness was overthrown too. [[12:7|but the house of the just|Domus autem justorum]], that is, the just congregations, the Churches of Christ, the faithful, [[12:7|shall stand firm|permanebunt]] in grace and be saved.

paras.t: Doctrina sua noscitur vir : quia ex viri doctrina ostenditur an sit vere catholicus; et si ea quæ docet salubriter, implet viriliter, constat quod bonus sit. Doctrina quoque ostendit an sit multum subtilis ac eruditus. Qui autem vanus, id est soliditate virtutis carens, nec ad ultimum finem per iter salutis tendens, et excors est, id est sine prudentia, patebit contemptui, id est, per verba et opera sua contemptibilem se esse monstrabit. Itaque vanus est, qui summum et incommutabile bonum non quærit sed ea quæ avertunt ab illo, et levis est corde, atque inanis gloriæ cupidus.
paras.en: [[12:8|A man shall be known by his learning|Doctrina sua noscitur vir]]: for by a man's teaching it is shown whether he is truly catholic; and if what he teaches soundly he fulfils manfully, it is plain that he is good. His teaching also shows whether he is very subtle and learned. [[12:8|but he that is vain|Qui autem vanus]], that is, lacking the solidity of virtue and not making for the last end along the way of salvation, [[12:8|and foolish|et excors est]] [*excors*, literally 'without heart'], that is, without prudence, [[12:8|shall be exposed to contempt|patebit contemptui]], that is, he will show by his words and works that he is contemptible. And so he is vain who does not seek the highest and unchangeable good, but the things that turn men away from it; and he is light of heart, and greedy of empty glory.

paras.t: Melior est pauper, id est de temporalibus aut spiritualibus gratiæ donis aliquantulum habens, et sufficiens sibi, ita quod satis habet pro necessitate corporis, et de necessariis animæ ad salutem, quam gloriosus, id est insignis in divitiis ac scientiis, et indigens pane, eo quod bona sua consumat superflue, vel humilitatem et caritatem non habeat scientiis suis annexas. Propter quod corporali vel spirituali eget refectione. Itaque melior et incomparabiliter desiderabilior est scientia parva cum humilitate et vita bona, quam grandis scientia cum vanitate et detestabili vita.
paras.en: [[12:9|Better is the poor man|Melior est pauper]], that is, one having a little of temporal goods or of the spiritual gifts of grace, [[12:9|that provideth for himself|et sufficiens sibi]] [literally 'and sufficient for himself'], so that he has enough for the needs of the body, and of what the soul needs for salvation, [[12:9|than he that is glorious|quam gloriosus]], that is, distinguished in riches and learning, [[12:9|and wanteth bread|et indigens pane]], because he spends his goods wastefully, or has not humility and charity joined to his learning; for which reason he lacks bodily or spiritual refreshment. And so a little learning with humility and a good life is better, and incomparably more to be desired, than great learning with vanity and a detestable life.

paras.t: Novit justus animas jumentorum, id est servorum ac subditorum suorum, qui instar jumenti pergunt quo pastor et dominus eorum dirigit illos. Unde ait obediens : Ut jumentum factus sum apud te. Justus ergo hebetudini et simplicitati crediti sibi gregis ac familiæ condolet et succurrit; capacitatem et mores et labores singulorum considerat servorum, quatenus unicuique, prout capax seu indigens est, aut meretur, auxilietur vel præmium largiatur. Viscera autem impiorum crudelia : quia subditis indignari, irasci, molestiasque inferre noverunt; non condolere, indulgere, auxiliari. Talibus Dominus ait : Cum austeritate imperabatis eis, et cum potentia. Quod valde vitandum est, ut in suis epistolis copiose docet Apostolus, inter cetera loquens : Vos, domini, eadem facite illis (quæ vobis fieri vultis), remittentes minas; scientes quia et illorum et vester Dominus est in cœlis. Nam et Seneca in suis fatetur Proverbiis : Qui servis crudelis est, ostendit sibi in aliis voluntatem non deesse, sed potestatem. Et rursus: Fulmen est, ubi cum potestate habitat iracundia.
paras.en: [[12:10|The just regardeth the lives of his beasts|Novit justus animas jumentorum]] [literally 'the just knoweth the souls of his beasts'], that is, of his servants and subjects, who like beasts go wherever their shepherd and lord directs them. Hence the obedient man says: [[Ps 72:23|I am become as a beast before thee|Ut jumentum factus sum apud te]]. The just man therefore pities and relieves the dullness and simplicity of the flock and household entrusted to him; he considers the capacity, the ways and the labours of each of his servants, so as to help each one, or give him a reward, as he is capable or in need, or deserves. [[12:10|but the bowels of the wicked are cruel|Viscera autem impiorum crudelia]]: for they know how to be indignant with their subjects, to be angry, to inflict troubles on them; not how to pity, forgive and help. To such the Lord says: [[Ezech 34:4|you ruled over them with rigour, and with a high hand|Cum austeritate imperabatis eis, et cum potentia]]. This is greatly to be avoided, as the Apostle teaches at length in his epistles, saying among other things: [[Eph 6:9|you, masters, do the same things to them|Vos, domini, eadem facite illis]] (the things that you would have done to you), [[Eph 6:9|forbearing threatenings: knowing that the Lord both of them and you is in heaven|remittentes minas; scientes quia et illorum et vester Dominus est in cœlis]]. For Seneca too admits in his Proverbs: He who is cruel to his slaves shows that in other matters he lacks not the will but the power. And again: Where wrath dwells with power, it is a thunderbolt.

paras.t: Qui operatur terram suam, satiabitur panibus. Hoc in corporalibus communiter sic contingit, quod qui per se ipsum aut suos ministros congrue colit agros suos, colligit inde fructus sufficientes, et panibus, id est cibis, sufficienter se potest reficere, quamvis interdum ex intemperie auræ, seu hostium devastatione, infirmitate aut morte, inde impediatur. Porro spiritualiter, qui operatur terram suam, id est, plebem seu Ecclesiam sibi commissam, aut proprium corpus, sensitivamque partem exercet spiritualibus disciplinis, virtuosis directionibus, assiduis curis paternis; satiabitur panibus : quia de illorum profectu gaudebit, et jam per merita, deinde per præmia feliciter reficietur. Imo pro cunctis quos ad salutem adduxerit, coronam gloriæ sortietur.
paras.en: [[12:11|He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread|Qui operatur terram suam, satiabitur panibus]]. In bodily things this commonly happens so: he who tills his fields fittingly, himself or by his servants, gathers enough fruit from them, and can refresh himself sufficiently with bread, that is, with food, though he is sometimes hindered in this by bad weather, the ravages of enemies, sickness or death. Spiritually, [[12:11|he that tilleth his land|qui operatur terram suam]], that is, exercises the people or Church committed to him, or his own body and sensitive part, with spiritual disciplines, virtuous guidance and constant fatherly care, [[12:11|shall be satisfied with bread|satiabitur panibus]]: for he will rejoice in their progress, and will be happily refreshed, now by merits, afterwards by rewards. Indeed, for all whom he has brought to salvation he will obtain a crown of glory.

paras.t: Qui autem sectatur otium, stultissimus est, præsertim si præsit aliis. Quum enim possemus omni hora in spiritualibus donis tam vehementer proficere, ac tantum nobis in cœlis thesaurum reponere, futura tormenta redimere, atque per opera virtuosa non modo nobis ipsis ac proximis, sed etiam in purgatorio existentibus subvenire : nonne stultissimum est otium sequi, præsertim quum ignoremus diem et horam? Nam et qui otio præstat locum, non solum non crescit in divitiis animæ, sed et valde decrescit in eis, quum in Ecclesiastico scriptum sit : Multa mala docuit otiositas. Ex ea namque sequuntur distractio cordis, concupiscentiæ motus, inordinata affectio, loquacitas, tædium boni, torpor, lascivia. Vide si mercator otio vacet, dum multum auri valet lucrari, nonne insipiens putabitur? Quanto magis stulti et fatui sumus censendi, qui dum in pretiosissimis donis gratiæ et gloriæ possemus valde proficere, hoc ipsum otiando negligimus, et insuper multa mala committimus?
paras.en: [[12:11|but he that pursueth idleness is very foolish|Qui autem sectatur otium, stultissimus est]], especially if he is set over others. For since we could at every hour advance so mightily in spiritual gifts, lay up for ourselves so great a treasure in heaven, redeem the torments to come, and by virtuous works help not only ourselves and our neighbours but also those who are in purgatory: is it not most foolish to pursue idleness, above all since we know not the day and the hour[[Matt 25:13||]]? For he who gives place to idleness not only does not grow in the riches of the soul, but even greatly decreases in them, since it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 33:29|idleness hath taught much evil|Multa mala docuit otiositas]]. For from it follow distraction of heart, stirrings of concupiscence, disordered affection, talkativeness, weariness of good, torpor, wantonness. See: if a merchant sits idle while he could gain much gold, will he not be thought foolish? How much more are we to be judged fools and simpletons, who, when we could advance greatly in the most precious gifts of grace and glory, neglect it by idling, and commit many evils besides?

paras.t: Qui suavis est in moderationibus, in suis monitionibus, relinquit contumeliam. Iste versiculus non est in Hebræo. Sed sensus est, quod homo per moderamen discretionis ac mansuetudinem dulcis, non per verba contumeliosa, sed pia atque humilia, admonet alios, juxta illud Apostoli : Si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, hujusmodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis, considerans te ipsum, ne et tu tenteris. Nempe, ut asserit Augustinus, objurgationes raro, et pro magna necessitate sunt faciendæ : in quibus etiam insistendum est, non ut nobis, sed ut Domino serviatur.
paras.en: [[12:12|He that is delighted in passing his time over wine, leaveth a reproach in his strong holds|Qui suavis est in moderationibus, in suis monitionibus, relinquit contumeliam]] [Denis's text reads *Qui suavis est in moderationibus, in suis monitionibus, relinquit contumeliam*, 'He that is gentle in his moderation, in his admonitions, leaveth off reproach', where the Vulgate has *in vini demorationibus, in suis munitionibus*; his gloss follows his own reading. The Vulgate prints this sentence at the end of v. 11, the Douay-Rheims at the head of v. 12]. This little verse is not in the Hebrew. But the sense is that a man who is gentle through the governance of discretion and through meekness admonishes others not with insulting words but with kind and humble ones, according to that word of the Apostle: [[Gal 6:1|if a man be overtaken in any fault, you, who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness, considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted|Si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, hujusmodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis, considerans te ipsum, ne et tu tenteris]]. For, as Augustine asserts, rebukes are to be made seldom and for great necessity; and in them too we must take care that not we but the Lord be served.

paras.t: Desiderium impii monumentum est pessimorum : id est, de impiis factis eorum qui præcesserunt, et in sepulcro sunt positi, impius appetit loqui : quæ et cupit sectari. Prava quoque desideria impii, ad mortem et monumentum propinquant. Vel, Monumenta pessimorum, sunt memorialia eorumdem opera vitiosa, circa quæ desiderium versatur iniqui. Radix autem, id est fides vel caritas, justorum proficiet. Etenim tanto plus crescit caritas, quantoplus decrescit cupiditas, id est amor privivatus, cujus minoratio, est caritatis augmentatio, et cujus mera exstirpatio, est caritatis perfectio.
paras.en: [[12:12|The desire of the wicked is the fortification of evil men|Desiderium impii monumentum est pessimorum]] [Denis reads *monumentum*, 'tomb, memorial', where the Vulgate has *munimentum*, 'fortification'; his gloss follows his reading]: that is, the wicked man longs to speak of the wicked deeds of those who went before him and have been laid in the tomb, and he desires to follow them. The depraved desires of the wicked also draw near to death and the tomb. Or: the memorials of the worst men are their vicious works, about which the desire of the wicked man turns. [[12:12|but the root|Radix autem]], that is, faith or charity, [[12:12|of the just shall prosper|justorum proficiet]]. For charity grows the more, the more covetousness decreases, that is, private love [that is, a man's love of his own good apart from God], whose lessening is the increase of charity, and whose complete uprooting is the perfection of charity.

paras.t: Propter peccata labiorum : quæ sunt mendacium, falsum testimonium, detractio, susurratio, contentio, seminatio discordiæ, et consimilia ; ruina proximat malo, id est, æterna damnatio imminet peccatori. Non ergo parva quis reputet vitia linguæ. Effugiet autem justus de angustia : quia meritis suis æternam consequetur securitatem, et virtuose conversando, conscientiæ vitat remorsum, et mille evadit pericula.
paras.en: [[12:13|For the sins of the lips|Propter peccata labiorum]], which are lying, false witness, detraction, whispering, contention, the sowing of discord and the like, [[12:13|ruin draweth nigh to the evil man|ruina proximat malo]], that is, eternal damnation hangs over the sinner. Let no one, then, think the vices of the tongue small. [[12:13|but the just shall escape out of distress|Effugiet autem justus de angustia]]: for by his merits he will gain eternal security; and by living virtuously he avoids the remorse of conscience and escapes a thousand dangers.

paras.t: De fructu oris sui unusquisque replebitur bonis : id est, pro verbis bonis salutaribusque doctrinis, pro oratione et laudibus Dei, habebit homo profectum gratiæ ac meritorum in via, incrementumque gloriæ in futuro. Nam et prædicatoribus atque doctoribus datur aureola, et subditorum profectus in superiores redundat. Hinc et in Evangelio loquitur Christus : Ex verbis tuis justificaberis. Non tamen sufficiunt sola verba, sed oportet ut consonent opera, et ut ipsemet loquens faciat bona quæ docet proximos. Ideo subditur : et juxta opera manuum suarum, id est virium practicarum, retribuetur ei. Unde apud Job dicitur : Absit a Deo impietas, et ab Omnipotente iniquitas ; opus enim hominis reddet ei, et juxta vias singulorum restituet.
paras.en: [[12:14|By the fruit of his own mouth shall a man be filled with good things|De fructu oris sui unusquisque replebitur bonis]]: that is, for good words and wholesome teaching, for prayer and the praises of God, a man will have progress in grace and merits on the way, and increase of glory hereafter. For an aureole [a special crown of reward, given over and above the essential reward, to virgins, martyrs and doctors] is given to preachers and doctors, and the progress of subjects overflows upon their superiors. Hence in the Gospel too Christ says: [[Matt 12:37|by thy words thou shalt be justified|Ex verbis tuis justificaberis]]. Yet words alone are not enough, but deeds must agree with them, and the speaker himself must do the good he teaches his neighbours. Therefore it is added: [[12:14|and according to the works of his hands|et juxta opera manuum suarum]], that is, of his practical powers, [[12:14|it shall be repaid him|retribuetur ei]]. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 34:10|far from God be wickedness, and iniquity from the Almighty|Absit a Deo impietas, et ab Omnipotente iniquitas]]; [[Job 34:11|For he will render to a man his work, and according to the ways of every one he will reward|opus enim hominis reddet ei, et juxta vias singulorum restituet]].

paras.t: Via stulti, recta in oculis ejus, id est, actio seu locutio vel conversatio sua sibi bona videtur : quoniam ratio ejus passionibus victa, et vitiis atque erroribus obscurata, judicat valde perverse, sicut febricitans omnem cibum judicat quasi amarum. Talibus dicitur : Væ qui convertistis in amaritudinem judicium, et fructum justitiæ in absinthium. Quod enim quis amat, hoc judicat bonum. Nam amor privatus et odium pervertunt judicium. Idcirco Dominus protestatur : Numquid vestrum est scire judicium, qui odio habetis bonum, et diligitis malum? Qui autem sapiens est, audit consilia, id est, diligenter ea advertit, considerat, et, si expedientia sunt, adimplet. Nemo ergo tam sapiens sit in suis oculis, ut aspernetur audire consilia. Non enim unus homo potest omnia considerare; nec homo in propria causa semper bonus est judex. Deus quoque frequenter suggerit et revelat uni, imo et inferiori, quod non inspirat alteri, nec superiori; et facilius invenitur, quod a pluribus quæritur.
paras.en: [[12:15|The way of a fool is right in his own eyes|Via stulti, recta in oculis ejus]], that is, his action or speech or manner of life seems good to him: for his reason, overcome by the passions and darkened by vices and errors, judges very perversely, as one in a fever judges all food bitter. To such it is said: Woe! [[Amos 6:13|you have turned judgment into bitterness, and the fruit of justice into wormwood|convertistis in amaritudinem judicium, et fructum justitiæ in absinthium]]. For what a man loves, that he judges good; for private love and hatred pervert judgment. Therefore the Lord protests: [[Mich 3:1|Is it not your part to know judgment|Numquid vestrum est scire judicium]], [[Mich 3:2|You that hate good, and love evil|qui odio habetis bonum, et diligitis malum?]]? [[12:15|but he that is wise hearkeneth unto counsels|Qui autem sapiens est, audit consilia]], that is, he attends to them diligently, considers them, and, if they are expedient, carries them out. Let no one, then, be so wise in his own eyes as to scorn to hear counsel. For one man cannot consider everything, nor is a man always a good judge in his own cause. God too often suggests and reveals to one, even to an inferior, what he does not inspire in another, even a superior; and what is sought by many is more easily found.

paras.t: Fatuus statim indicat iram suam, id est, foris erumpit per iracundiæ signa, et flammam suæ commotionis evaporat per verba et gestus distortos, non attendens quam inhonestum sit hoc. Nam passioni subjectus est, nec per mansuetudinem refrenare se didicit : idcirco per iram totaliter excæcatur ejus ratio, propter quod recte stultus vocatur. Nec advertit quam nociva sit ira. De qua ait Hieronymus : Fuge, o homo, iram, quæ est hostis naturæ, confundit justitiam, amicitiam rumpit, concordiam dissipat, aufert pacem pectoris, et tollit gaudium æternitatis. Janua quædam est ira omnium vitiorum : qua janua clausa, datur cordi tranquillitas et quies virtutibus; et qua aperta, ad omne facinus firmabitur animus. Ideo recte disseruit Seneca : Iracundiam qui vincit, maximum superat hostem.
paras.en: [[12:16|A fool immediately sheweth his anger|Fatuus statim indicat iram suam]], that is, it breaks out in the signs of wrath, and he lets the flame of his agitation off in words and distorted gestures, not heeding how unseemly this is. For he is subject to passion, and has not learned to rein himself in by meekness: hence his reason is wholly blinded by anger, and for this he is rightly called a fool. Nor does he consider how harmful anger is, of which Jerome says: Flee anger, O man, which is the enemy of nature: it confounds justice, breaks friendship, scatters concord, takes away peace of heart, and removes the joy of eternity. Anger is a kind of door to all the vices: when this door is shut, tranquillity is given to the heart and quiet to the virtues; and when it is open, the mind is made firm for every crime. Therefore Seneca rightly taught: He who conquers wrath overcomes the greatest enemy.

paras.t: Qui autem dissimulat injuriam sibi factam, callidus est. Callidus communiter in malo accipitur, scilicet pro versuto, juxta illud : Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei. Sicque loquendo de callido, iste est sensus : Qui dissimulat injuriam, id est, fingit se non advertere nec curare injuriam sibi illatam, quatenus postea improvise gravius vindicet eam, est callidus: qualis præcipue fuit Joab, qui injuriosum sibi reputans quod Amasa fieret princeps militiæ loco ipsius, dissimulavit se inde dolere, et paulo post proditorie Amasam magis strenuum se, occidit. Talis quoque fuit et Absalon, qui violata sua sorore ab Amnon, nihil locutus est ei; sed expleto biennio, ipsum peremit. Interdum vero accipitur callidus pro astuto seu sagace. Sicque, Qui dissimulat injuriam suam, habendo se ac si eam nesciret, atque ut penitus eam obliviscatur, callidus est, id est astutus et sagax. Unde antiqua translatio continet : Stultus pronuntiat eadem hora iram suam; occultat autem ignominiam suam astutus. Circa quod ait Glossa : Callidus non vult occultare iram seu injuriam suam ut duret, sed ut omnino deleatur. Est enim natura iræ, ut prolata plus ferveat, occultata languescat. Hoc modo Saul adhuc bonus, in principio regni sui dissimulavit se audire verba injuriantium sibi : quæ nec postea voluit vindicare, data opportunitate, ut primo Regum habetur. Hinc Seneca loquitur : Res magnæ gloriæ est, indulgendo peccata corrigere, magis quam vindicando.
paras.en: [[12:16|but he that dissembleth injuries|Qui autem dissimulat injuriam]] done to him, [[12:16|is wise|callidus est]] [*callidus*, 'shrewd' or 'crafty'; the Douay-Rheims has 'wise']. *Callidus* is commonly taken in a bad sense, namely for crafty, according to that word: [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]]. Speaking so of the crafty man, the sense is this: [[12:16|he that dissembleth injuries|Qui dissimulat injuriam]], that is, pretends not to notice or care about an injury done to him, so that afterwards he may avenge it the more heavily and unexpectedly, is crafty: such above all was Joab, who, thinking it an injury to himself that Amasa should be made captain of the army in his place, hid his grief at it, and shortly after treacherously slew Amasa, a more valiant man than himself. Such too was Absalom, who, when his sister had been violated by Amnon, said nothing to him; but when two years were past, killed him. But sometimes *callidus* is taken for astute or shrewd. And so, [[12:16|he that dissembleth injuries|Qui dissimulat injuriam suam]], behaving as if he did not know of the injury, so that he may forget it altogether, [[12:16|is wise|callidus est]], that is, astute and shrewd. Hence the old translation has: The fool declares his anger in the same hour; but the astute man hides his shame. On which the Gloss says: The shrewd man does not wish to hide his anger or injury so that it may last, but so that it may be wholly blotted out. For it is the nature of anger that, uttered, it boils the more, and hidden, it languishes. In this way Saul, while still good, at the beginning of his reign pretended not to hear the words of those who insulted him: nor would he avenge them afterwards when he had the chance, as is told in the first book of Kings. Hence Seneca says: It is a thing of great glory to correct sins by pardoning rather than by avenging.

paras.t: Qui quod novit loquitur, id est, quod verum esse scit, suo tempore profert ac attestatur, index justitiæ est, id est, indicat justum se esse, et ipsam veritatem justitiæ pandit; qui autem mentitur in foro judicii, quo testimonium perhibet, testis est fraudulentus. Similiter qui libenter faciliterque mentitur, cito ad hoc inducitur ut testimonium proferat falsum.
paras.en: [[12:17|He that speaketh that which he knoweth|Qui quod novit loquitur]], that is, brings forth and attests in its time what he knows to be true, [[12:17|sheweth forth justice|index justitiæ est]] [literally 'is a pointer-out of justice'], that is, shows that he is just, and lays open the very truth of justice; [[12:17|but he that lieth|qui autem mentitur]] in the court of judgment, where he bears witness, [[12:17|is a deceitful witness|testis est fraudulentus]]. Likewise he who lies willingly and easily is soon brought to bear false witness.

paras.t: Est qui promittit se aliquid dare aut facere, et quasi gladio pungitur conscientiæ, id est, remorsum conscientiæ patitur, dum quod promisit, renuit adimplere; vel quia promisit indiscrete atque illicite. Quemadmodum enim, juxta Hieronymum, tres sunt comites juramenti, ita et promissionis seu voti, videlicet judicium (id est discretio), justitia, veritas. Et quidquid contra hæc aut horum aliquid promittitur aut juratur, non tenet ; peccatque homo ita illicite jurando aut promittendo, non autem juramentum seu promissum non adimplendo. Idcirco in Jeremia habetur : Jurabis, Vivit Dominus, in veritate et judicio et justitia. Lingua autem sapientium sanitas est : quia per verba sapientialia curat audientes a vulnere vitiorum et læsione errorum, et a morte perfidiæ ; et quod jurat, promittit, vel asserit, verificare conatur. Sicque in ea inter verba et facta est proportio, quemadmodum sanitas adæquatio seu proportio est humorum. Hinc scriptum est : Multitudo sapientium sanitas est orbis terrarum. Et in Isaia fertur : Dominus dedit mihi linguam eruditam, ut sciam sustentare eum qui lapsus est, verbo.
paras.en: [[12:18|There is that promiseth|Est qui promittit]] to give or do something, [[12:18|and is pricked as it were with a sword of conscience|et quasi gladio pungitur conscientiæ]], that is, suffers remorse of conscience when he refuses to fulfil what he promised; or because he promised indiscreetly and unlawfully. For as, according to Jerome, there are three companions of an oath, so too of a promise or vow, namely judgment (that is, discretion), justice and truth. And whatever is promised or sworn against these, or against any of them, does not bind; and a man sins by swearing or promising so unlawfully, not by failing to fulfil the oath or the promise. Therefore it is said in Jeremias: [[Jer 4:2|thou shalt swear: As the Lord liveth, in truth, and in judgment, and in justice|Jurabis, Vivit Dominus, in veritate et judicio et justitia]]. [[12:18|but the tongue of the wise is health|Lingua autem sapientium sanitas est]]: for by words of wisdom it heals the hearers from the wound of vices, from the hurt of errors and from the death of unbelief; and what it swears, promises or asserts, it strives to make true. And so in it there is a proportion between words and deeds, as health is the balance or proportion of the humours. Hence it is written: [[Wis 6:26|the multitude of the wise is the welfare of the whole world|Multitudo sapientium sanitas est orbis terrarum]]. And in Isaias we read: [[Is 50:4|The Lord hath given me a learned tongue, that I should know how to uphold by word him that is weary|Dominus dedit mihi linguam eruditam, ut sciam sustentare eum qui lapsus est, verbo]] [Denis reads *lapsus*, 'fallen', where the Vulgate has *lassus*, 'weary'].

paras.t: Labium veritatis firmum erit in perpetuum, id est, veritati stabiliter inhærebit, et pro hoc perpetuam consequetur mercedem ; qui autem testis est repentinus, id est, sine debita deliberatione aut pro propria commoditate ex aliorum persuasione profert testimonium, concinnat linguam mendacii, id est, linguam suam componit ad mentiendum, et ad colorandum pro posse falsum testimonium suum, sicut apud Isaiam habetur : Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt ; ipse enim cogitationes concinnabit ad perdendos mites in sermone mendacii. Tales fuerunt, qui tertio Regum leguntur contra Naboth testimonium falsum dixisse.
paras.en: [[12:19|The lip of truth shall be steadfast for ever|Labium veritatis firmum erit in perpetuum]], that is, it will cleave steadfastly to the truth, and for this will gain an everlasting reward; [[12:19|but he that is a hasty witness|qui autem testis est repentinus]], that is, who gives testimony without due deliberation, or for his own advantage at the persuasion of others, [[12:19|frameth a lying tongue|concinnat linguam mendacii]] [*concinnare*, 'to put together, to trim up'], that is, fits his tongue for lying, and for colouring his false testimony as best he can, as we read in Isaias: [[Is 32:7|The vessels of the deceitful are most wicked|Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt]]; [[Is 32:7|for he hath framed devices to destroy the meek, with lying words|ipse enim cogitationes concinnabit ad perdendos mites in sermone mendacii]]. Such were those who, as we read in the third book of Kings, bore false witness against Naboth.

paras.t: Dolus in corde cogitantium mala : id est, qui excogitant qualiter nocent aliis, sæpe confingunt in se vias quibus dolose implere id valeant. Qui autem pacis ineunt consilia, sequitur eos gaudium : id est, qui inter se conferunt et inquirunt qualiter invicem pacificentur, et pactum super hoc statuunt, ac fœderi pacis consentiunt, ex hoc deinceps jucunditatem, quietem et securitatem adipiscuntur. Unde et Christus : Beati, inquit, pacifici. Zachariæ quoque dicitur de electis : Consilium pacis erit inter illos.
paras.en: [[12:20|Deceit is in the heart of them that think evil things|Dolus in corde cogitantium mala]]: that is, those who devise how they may harm others often contrive within themselves ways by which they may accomplish it by deceit. [[12:20|but joy followeth them that take counsels of peace|Qui autem pacis ineunt consilia, sequitur eos gaudium]]: that is, those who confer among themselves and inquire how they may be reconciled with one another, and make a covenant upon it, and consent to a treaty of peace, gain from it thereafter gladness, quiet and security. Hence Christ too: [[Matt 5:9|Blessed|Beati]], he says, [[Matt 5:9|are the peacemakers|pacifici]].
