And in Zacharias it is said of the elect: [[Zach 6:13|the counsel of peace shall be between them|Consilium pacis erit inter illos]].

paras.t: Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit, id est, quidquid adversitatis seu mali pœnæ ei evenerit. In adversis enim patientiam habet, et omne gaudium æstimat quum in varias inciderit tentationes ; ac certus de providentia Patris æterni, quidquid sibi adversi contigerit, quasi donum de manu capit Omnipotentis. Verumtamen de malo culpæ tristatur, et sua quotidiana quotidie deflet peccata. De adversitate quoque et turbatione rei publicæ, et detrimento boni communis, mœrore afficitur. Attamen tristitiam dejicientem, carnalem, inordinatam et sæcularem, evitat, de qua ait Apostolus : Sæculi tristitia mortem operatur ; et de qua in Ecclesiastico edocetur : Tristitiam longe expelle a te, multos enim occidit tristitia. Itaque in omni eventu stemus firmi in Domino, et nec prosperis inaniter gloriemur, neque adversis dejiciamur, quum et Seneca dicat : Feras quod lædit, ut prosit ; et rursus : Injuriæ et honores vulgi, in promiscuo sunt habendi ; nec his gaudendum, nec illis dolendum. Hinc ait gloriosus Hieronymus : Per bonam et malam famam a dextris et a sinistris, Christi miles progreditur. Nec laude extollitur, nec vituperiis frangitur ; non ex divitiis tumet, nec paupertate confunditur ; et læta contemnit, et tristia. His concordat illud Tullii : Vir est, qui contra biformes fortunæ eventus, uniformi mentis constantia militat præmunitus. De hoc super illud Job, Vir erat in terra Hus, plenius scribit Gregorius. Impii autem replebuntur malo : quia variis passionibus, inordinato timore, pravo mœrore, ac consimilibus affliguntur ; et de malis culpæ, ruunt in mala infernalis miseriæ. Ideo ait Apostolus : Impii proficient in pejus, errantes, et in errorem mittentes.
paras.en: [[12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]], that is, whatever adversity or evil of punishment [*malum pœnæ*, suffering, as distinguished from *malum culpæ*, the evil of guilt, that is, sin] befalls him. For in adversity he has patience, and counts it all joy when he falls into divers temptations[[Jas 1:2||]]; and, sure of the providence of the eternal Father, whatever adverse thing befalls him he takes as a gift from the hand of the Almighty. Yet he is saddened by the evil of guilt, and daily bewails his daily sins. He is also stricken with grief at the adversity and disturbance of the commonwealth and at loss to the common good. But he avoids the sadness that casts down, carnal, disordered and worldly sadness, of which the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 7:10|the sorrow of the world worketh death|Sæculi tristitia mortem operatur]]; and of which Ecclesiasticus teaches: [[Ecclus 30:24|drive away sadness far from thee|Tristitiam longe expelle a te]], [[Ecclus 30:25|For sadness hath killed many|multos enim occidit tristitia]]. So in every event let us stand firm in the Lord, neither glorying vainly in prosperity nor cast down by adversity, since Seneca too says: Bear what hurts, that it may profit; and again: The insults and the honours of the crowd are to be held alike: neither are these to be rejoiced at, nor those grieved over. Hence the glorious Jerome says: Through good report and evil report, on the right hand and on the left, the soldier of Christ goes forward. He is not lifted up by praise nor broken by reproaches; he does not swell with riches nor is he confounded by poverty; he despises both the glad and the sad. With these agrees that saying of Tully: He is a man who, armed beforehand, fights with a uniform constancy of mind against the two-faced chances of fortune. Gregory writes of this more fully on that verse of Job: [[Job 1:1|There was a man in the land of Hus|Vir erat in terra Hus]]. [[12:21|but the wicked shall be filled with mischief|Impii autem replebuntur malo]]: for they are afflicted with divers passions, disordered fear, evil grief and the like; and from the evils of guilt they rush into the evils of the misery of hell. Therefore the Apostle says: The wicked [[2 Tim 3:13|shall grow worse and worse: erring, and driving into error|proficient in pejus, errantes, et in errorem mittentes]] [the Apostle has 'evil men and seducers'].

paras.t: Abominatio est Domino labia mendacia, id est, mendaces Deo sunt abominabiles, quum ipse sit fons, causa, finis, mensura ac regula omnis veritatis creatæ, qui in se ipso essentialiter verus, et verax est, ac veritas ipsa. Qui autem fideliter agunt, ex fide, quæ est virtus theologica, et fidelitate, quæ ad justitiam pertinet, placent ei: quia ei sunt similes : de quo ait Psalmista, Fidelis Dominus in omnibus verbis suis. Similitudo autem per se est ratio complacentiæ et amoris.
paras.en: [[12:22|Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord|Abominatio est Domino labia mendacia]], that is, liars are abominable to God, since he is the fountain, cause, end, measure and rule of all created truth, he who in himself is essentially true and truthful, and truth itself. [[12:22|but they that deal faithfully|Qui autem fideliter agunt]], out of faith, which is a theological virtue, and out of fidelity, which belongs to justice, [[12:22|please him|placent ei]]: for they are like him, of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 144:13|The Lord is faithful in all his words|Fidelis Dominus in omnibus verbis suis]]. And likeness is of itself the ground of being well pleased, and of love.

paras.t: Homo versutus celat scientiam. Alibi legitur : Vir versutus odiosus est. Si ergo versutus in malo accipiatur, pro callido et vulpino, talis celat scientiam suam, quando deberet eam caritative proximis communicare, et constitutos in periculo avisare. Unde, secundum Augustinum, qui negat se scire quod scit, ingratus est; et qui non vult communicare quod accepit, invidus est. Porro, si versutus sumatur in bono, pro astuto seu sagace, talis interdum ex humilitate, quandoque ex discretione, celat scientiam suam, ne eam videatur jactare, aut ubi non est auditus, effundere, ne sanctum det canibus. Idcirco Corinthiis scribit Apostolus : Non judicavi me aliquid scire inter vos, nisi Jesum Christum, et hunc crucifixum. Hinc namque Ezechieli locutus est Dominus : Linguam tuam adhærere faciam palato tuo. Et cor insipientium provocat stultitiam, id est, ad inanem lætitiam, risum, cachinnum et vanitatem excitat alios. Frequenter etiam decipit, et erronee instruit proximos, ac sua improbitate provocat eos ad vitia sapientiæ veræ contraria.
paras.en: [[12:23|A cautious man concealeth knowledge|Homo versutus celat scientiam]] [Denis's text reads *versutus*, 'wily', where the Vulgate has *versatus*, 'experienced', which the Douay-Rheims renders 'cautious'; he takes *versutus* first in a bad sense, then in a good one]. Elsewhere we read: [[Prov 14:17|the crafty man is hateful|Vir versutus odiosus est]]. If, then, *versutus* is taken in a bad sense, for crafty and foxlike, such a man hides his knowledge when he ought to share it charitably with his neighbours and warn those who stand in danger. Hence, according to Augustine, he who denies that he knows what he knows is ungrateful; and he who will not share what he has received is envious. But if *versutus* is taken in a good sense, for astute or shrewd, such a man hides his knowledge sometimes out of humility, sometimes out of discretion, lest he seem to boast of it, or pour it out [[Ecclus 32:6|where there is no hearing|ubi non est auditus]], lest he give [[Matt 7:6|that which is holy to dogs|sanctum det canibus]]. Therefore the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 2:2|I judged not myself to know anything among you, but Jesus Christ: and him crucified|Non judicavi me aliquid scire inter vos, nisi Jesum Christum, et hunc crucifixum]]. And hence the Lord spoke to Ezechiel: [[Ezech 3:26|I will make thy tongue stick fast to the roof of thy mouth|Linguam tuam adhærere faciam palato tuo]]. [[12:23|and the heart of fools publisheth folly|Et cor insipientium provocat stultitiam]] [*provocat*, 'calls forth, stirs up'], that is, stirs others up to empty mirth, laughter, guffawing and vanity. Often too it deceives its neighbours and teaches them wrongly, and by its wickedness provokes them to vices contrary to true wisdom.

paras.t: Manus fortium dominabitur. Nam principes fortes ac strenui solent prævalere in bellis, ac latius præsidere. Similiter qui virtutibus fortes sunt, solent fratribus præfici et præesse, sensitivo quoque appetitui et ejus passionibus imperare. Unde Seneca dixit : Vis habere honorem? Dabo tibi magnum imperium : impera tibi. Quæ autem remissa est, tributis serviet. Principes quippe ignavi ac desides, solent adversariis suis sub tributo servire. Spiritualiter vero, qui dissoluti et negligentes consistunt, implentur peccatis, et principi serviunt tenebrarum, cujus exactioni seu tentationi dant assidue pro tributo consensum in malo. Propter quod tandem cum illo mittentur in carcerem infernalem, non egressuri quousque reddiderint novissimum quadrantem : quod nunquam fiet.
paras.en: [[12:24|The hand of the valiant shall bear rule|Manus fortium dominabitur]]. For strong and vigorous princes usually prevail in wars and rule more widely. Likewise those who are strong in virtues are usually set over their brethren and preside over them, and they also command the sensitive appetite and its passions. Hence Seneca said: Do you wish to have honour? I will give you a great empire: rule yourself. [[12:24|but that which is slothful shall be under tribute|Quæ autem remissa est, tributis serviet]] [*remissa*, 'slack']. For slothful and idle princes usually serve their enemies under tribute. Spiritually, those who are dissolute and negligent are filled with sins and serve the prince of darkness, to whose exaction or temptation they constantly pay consent to evil as their tribute. Wherefore at last they will be cast with him into the prison[[Matt 5:25||]] of hell, not to come out until they have repaid [[Matt 5:26|the last farthing|novissimum quadrantem]]: which will never be.

paras.t: Mœror in corde viri humiliabit eum. Justus enim de suis ac proximorum mœret peccatis, et ex pœnitentiali mœrore valde humiliat se coram Deo, fragilitatem et vilitatem ac culpam suam et alienam ex totis præcordiis recognoscens, et veniam postulans. Quum etenim in peccato sit quædam inordinata sui ipsius erectio, oportet ut in contritione sit ordinata et humilis sui dejectio. Unde scriptum est : Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali, et incedit curva et infirma, et oculi deficientes, dant gloriam et justitiam tibi, Domine. Et sermone bono lætificabitur, id est, ex promissione et spe veniæ, ex consolatione Scripturæ, ex confessoris instructione, et sacramentali absolutione, jucunditatem et consolationem accipiet, ita ut dicat : Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua! Idcirco Apostolus : Consolamini, inquit, invicem in verbis istis.
paras.en: [[12:25|Grief in the heart of a man shall bring him low|Mœror in corde viri humiliabit eum]]. For the just man grieves for his own sins and for his neighbours', and by penitential grief humbles himself greatly before God, acknowledging from the bottom of his heart his frailty and vileness and his own guilt and others', and begging pardon. For since in sin there is a certain disordered lifting up of oneself, in contrition there must be an ordered and humble casting down of oneself. Hence it is written: [[Bar 2:18|the soul that is sorrowful for the greatness of evil she hath done, and goeth bowed down, and feeble, and the eyes that fail|Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali, et incedit curva et infirma, et oculi deficientes]], [[Bar 2:18|giveth glory and justice to thee the Lord|dant gloriam et justitiam tibi, Domine]]. [[12:25|but with a good word he shall be made glad|Et sermone bono lætificabitur]], that is, from the promise and hope of pardon, from the consolation of Scripture, from the confessor's instruction and the sacramental absolution, he will receive gladness and consolation, so that he says: [[Ps 118:103|How sweet are thy words to my palate|Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua!]]! Therefore the Apostle: [[1 Thess 4:17|comfort ye|Consolamini]], he says, [[1 Thess 4:17|one another with these words|invicem in verbis istis]].

paras.t: Qui negligit, id est, parvi pendit et æquanimiter sustinet, damnum temporale propter amicum, id est ad subveniendum proximo suo in necessitate, præsertim ut eum liberet a morte corporali aut spirituali; justus est. Hoc namque requirunt caritas atque justitia, ut amor, vita et salus proximi, præferatur temporalium rerum amori. Propter quod in prima sua Canonica ait Joannes : Qui habuerit substantiam hujus mundi, et viderit fratrem suum necessarium habere, et clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo caritas Dei manet in illo? At vero qui propter Deum et Christi amorem, temporalia damna et rapinam bonorum suorum æquanimiter ferunt, imo se ipsos et omnia sua morti exponunt, vere sunt justi : quoniam quidquid a Creatore sortiti sunt, in ejus amorem, cultum et confessionem rependunt. Iter autem impiorum decipiet eos : quoniam sua delectatione iniqua allicit eos ad perseverandum in vitiis, et ad diligendum ea quæ adversantur saluti, sicque in tartarum detrahit ipsos.
paras.en: [[12:26|He that neglecteth|Qui negligit]], that is, makes light of and bears with an even mind, [[12:26|a loss|damnum]] in temporal things [[12:26|for the sake of a friend|propter amicum]], that is, to help his neighbour in his need, above all to free him from bodily or spiritual death, [[12:26|is just|justus est]]. For charity and justice require this, that the love, life and salvation of our neighbour be preferred to the love of temporal things. Wherefore John says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 3:17|He that hath the substance of this world and shall see his brother in need and shall shut up his bowels from him: how doth the charity of God abide in him?|Qui habuerit substantiam hujus mundi, et viderit fratrem suum necessarium habere, et clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo caritas Dei manet in illo?]] But those who, for God's sake and for the love of Christ, bear with an even mind temporal losses and the plundering of their goods, indeed expose themselves and all they have to death, are truly just: since whatever they have received from the Creator they pay back in his love, worship and confession. [[12:26|but the way of the wicked shall deceive them|Iter autem impiorum decipiet eos]]: since by its wicked delight it entices them to persevere in vices, and to love the things that are contrary to salvation, and so drags them down to hell.

paras.t: Non inveniet fraudulentus lucrum : quia etsi ex verbis suis dolosis aut mendosis obtineat temporale lucrum ad tempus, ut patet secundo Regum de Siba accusatore doloso ac impio virtuosi Miphiboseth ; postea tamen experietur incomparabile detrimentum et damnum perpetuum. Hoc attendant mercatores ac ceteri venditores. Et substantia hominis erit auri pretium, id est, ipsum aurum est facultas seu possessio hominis, non id quod dolose acquirit, et restituere obligatur. Vel : Substantia, id est vita seu anima hominis, est auri pretium, id est pretiosior auro, et id pro cujus ereptione expenditur aurum, sicut apud Job inducitur : Pellem pro pelle, et cuncta quæ habet homo, dabit pro anima sua. Spiritualius autem loquendo, Substantia hominis, id est interior opulentia ejus in actibus virtuosis, erit auri pretium, quia pro illa exponendum est aurum in operibus pietatis et æquitatis; vel, Erit auri pretium, id est id per quod mercatur et obtinet homo claritatem regni cœlestis, de quo in Apocalypse asseritur : Civitas erat ex auro mundo, simili vitro mundo.
paras.en: [[12:27|The deceitful man shall not find gain|Non inveniet fraudulentus lucrum]]: for though by his deceitful or lying words he obtain temporal gain for a time, as is plain in the second book of Kings of Siba, the deceitful and wicked accuser of the virtuous Miphiboseth[[2 Kings 16:3||]][[2 Kings 16:4||]][[2 Kings 19:27||]], yet afterwards he will find incomparable loss and everlasting harm. Let merchants and other sellers attend to this. [[12:27|but the substance of a just man shall be precious gold|Et substantia hominis erit auri pretium]] [Denis's text reads *substantia hominis … auri pretium*, 'the substance of a man shall be the price of gold'; his glosses follow it], that is, the gold itself is a man's means or possession, not what he acquires by deceit and is bound to restore. Or: [[12:27|the substance|Substantia]], that is, the life or soul of a man, [[12:27|shall be precious gold|est auri pretium]], that is, it is more precious than gold, and that for whose rescue gold is spent, as is brought in in Job: [[Job 2:4|Skin for skin; and all that a man hath, he will give for his life|Pellem pro pelle, et cuncta quæ habet homo, dabit pro anima sua]]. Speaking more spiritually, [[12:27|the substance|Substantia]] of a man, that is, his inward wealth in virtuous acts, [[12:27|shall be precious gold|erit auri pretium]], because for it gold must be laid out in works of piety and equity; or, [[12:27|shall be precious gold|Erit auri pretium]], that is, it is that by which a man buys and obtains the brightness of the heavenly kingdom, of which it is asserted in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:18|the city itself pure gold like to clear glass|Civitas erat ex auro mundo, simili vitro mundo]].

paras.t: In semita, id est observatione seu præcepto et lege, justitiæ, id est cujuscumque virtutis, secundum quod justitia est virtus communis, et quodammodo omnis virtus : nam unaquæque virtus est quædam justitia, quia per eam habet se homo ut debet ; vita consistit, id est vita gratiæ in præsenti, et vita gloriæ in futuro. Iter autem devium, id est error a veritate discedens, actio vitiosa a rectitudine æquitatis deflectens, et omne peccatum, quod est transgressio rectissimæ legis Dei, ducit ad mortem æternæ damnationis, quæ omni morte, naturali et corporali ac temporali ineffabiliter exstat amarior : imo minima pœna inferni pro mortali peccato inflicta, creditur esse major ipsis puncturis atque angustiis diræ ac transitoriæ mortis, quæ tamen inæstimabiliter premit ac torquet.
paras.en: [[12:28|In the path|In semita]], that is, in the observance, or precept and law, [[12:28|of justice|justitiæ]], that is, of any virtue whatever, inasmuch as justice is a general virtue, and in a manner every virtue: for each virtue is a kind of justice, since by it a man stands as he ought; [[12:28|is life|vita]], that is, the life of grace in the present and the life of glory in the future. [[12:28|but the bye-way|Iter autem devium]], that is, error departing from the truth, vicious action turning aside from the rightness of equity, and every sin, which is a transgression of the most righteous law of God, [[12:28|leadeth to death|ducit ad mortem]], the death of eternal damnation, which is unspeakably more bitter than every death, natural, bodily and temporal: indeed the least pain of hell inflicted for mortal sin is believed to be greater than the very pangs and agonies of dire and passing death, which yet presses and tortures beyond reckoning.

13.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI TERTIIDECIMI : FILIUS SAPIENS, DOCTRINA PATRIS.
13.title_en: Explanation of the thirteenth chapter: A wise son heareth the doctrine of his father.

paras.t: Filius sapiens, doctrina patris. Filius sapiens dicitur esse doctrina sui patris sive doctoris : primo, quia paulatim proficiendo ad hoc potest pertingere, ut sapientior fiat patre, et sic doceat eum ; secundo, quia in filio sapiente relucet sui patris doctrina. Spiritualiter autem, Filius in divinis est sapientia et doctrina Patris æterni, quia Pater per Filium nos informat. Qui autem illusor est, id est, sapientiam et virtutes irridet, nec se docilem ac dirigibilem exhibet, non audit auditu mentis, quum arguitur. Sæpe quoque exteriorem auditum a verbis increpatoriis salubribusque avertit. Tales fuerunt Audiunt verba mea ex te, et non faciunt, quia in canticum oris sui verterunt illa; et factus es eis quasi carmen musicum, quod suavi dulcique sono canitur. Horum vestigia multi sequuntur, qui quidquid exhortationis correptionisque audiunt, in risum et jocum vertunt.
paras.en: [[13:1|A wise son heareth the doctrine of his father|Filius sapiens, doctrina patris]] [the Latin has no verb, literally "a wise son, the doctrine of his father", and Denis takes it so]. A wise son is said to be the doctrine of his father or teacher: first, because by advancing little by little he can come so far as to become wiser than his father, and so teach him; secondly, because the doctrine of his father shines forth in a wise son. Spiritually, however, the Son in the Godhead is the wisdom and doctrine of the eternal Father, because the Father instructs us through the Son. [[13:1|but he that is a scorner|Qui autem illusor est]], that is, who mocks at wisdom and the virtues, and does not show himself teachable and ready to be guided, [[13:1|heareth not|non audit]] with the hearing of the mind [[13:1|when he is reproved|quum arguitur]]. Often too he turns his outward hearing away from words of rebuke and of healing. Such were those who [[Ezech 33:31|hear thy words, and do them not: for they turn them into a song of their mouth|Audiunt verba mea ex te, et non faciunt, quia in canticum oris sui verterunt illa]]; [[Ezech 33:32|And thou art to them as a musical song which is sung with a sweet and agreeable voice|et factus es eis quasi carmen musicum, quod suavi dulcique sono canitur]]. Many follow in their footsteps, who turn into laughter and jest whatever exhortation and correction they hear.

paras.t: De fructu oris sui homo satiabitur bonis. Hoc est quod in præcedenti capitulo legitur, De fructu oris sui unusquisque replebitur bonis. Anima autem impiorum, id est in Deum peccantium, est iniqua, id est injusta, quia a Deo, qui est mensura ac regula omnis rectitudinis, est aversa. Hinc in prima sua epistola scribit Joannes : Omnis qui peccatum facit, et iniquitatem facit; et peccatum iniquitas est.
paras.en: [[13:2|Of the fruit of his own month shall a man be filled with good things|De fructu oris sui homo satiabitur bonis]]. This is what is read in the preceding chapter: [[Prov 12:14|By the fruit of his own mouth shall a man be filled with good things|De fructu oris sui unusquisque replebitur bonis]]. [[13:2|but the soul of transgressors|Anima autem impiorum]] [Denis reads *impiorum*, "of the wicked", where the Vulgate has *prævaricatorum*, "of transgressors"], that is, of those who sin against God, [[13:2|is wicked|iniqua]], that is, unjust, because it is turned away from God, who is the measure and rule of all rightness. Hence John writes in his first epistle: [[1 John 3:4|Whosoever committeth sin committeth also iniquity. And sin is iniquity.|Omnis qui peccatum facit, et iniquitatem facit; et peccatum iniquitas est]]

paras.t: Qui custodit os suum corporale ab omni culpabili locutione, et multo plus qui custodit os suum mentale, videlicet intellectum, quo verbum cordis profertur, ab omni prava cogitatione, providendo ne oriatur in se, vel ortam mox reprimendo et expellendo ; custodit animam suam a multis vulneribus vitiorum, ab insidiis hostium, et a gravaminibus, damnis, periculis, quæ homines solent incidere ex incustodia oris. Ideo scriptum est : Si quis in verbo non offendit, hic perfectus est vir. Hinc in Proverbiis suis ait Cyrillus : Doctus sis loqui, et avarus verbi. Clausura namque quæ raro aperitur, est fortior; et lingua minus frequentata, solidior. Nam quod diu rectum tenetur, difficilius obliquatur : sed dum lingua non loquitur, recta tenetur. Revera mentis conceptus est verbum. Ubi ergo verbum nimis effunditur, internum rationis est vinculum dissolutum. Qui autem inconsideratus est ad loquendum, non præmeditando qualiter sit loquendum, nec providendo ne Deum offendat loquendo, sentiet mala. Nam sæpe incurrit ex hoc aliorum offensam, et inquietudinem propriæ mentis, conscientiæ quoque remorsum; et si fuit in eo devotio et recollectio aliqua mentis in Deo, mox perdit eas, læditque animam suam, ac debitas luet pœnas. Ideo ait Cyrillus : Pro certo qui vento loquacitatis effunditur, indigestis verbis prolatis conturbat alios, aut turbatur. Quamobrem antiquis Prophetis semper placuit parce loqui. Nempe qui multum loquitur, modicum ruminat, ideoque verbum otiosum eructat. Et ideo secundum legem immundum est animal.
paras.en: [[13:3|He that keepeth his mouth|Qui custodit os suum]], his bodily mouth, from all blameworthy speech, and much more he that keeps his mental mouth, namely the understanding, by which the word of the heart is brought forth, from every evil thought, by taking care that it does not arise in him, or by quickly checking and driving it out once it has arisen, [[13:3|keepeth his soul|custodit animam suam]] from the many wounds of the vices, from the snares of enemies, and from the troubles, losses and dangers into which men commonly fall through an unguarded mouth. Therefore it is written: [[Jas 3:2|If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man|Si quis in verbo non offendit, hic perfectus est vir]]. Hence Cyril says in his Proverbs: Be skilled in speaking, and sparing of words. For a door that is seldom opened is the stronger; and a tongue less used, the sounder. For what is long held straight is the harder to bend: and while the tongue does not speak, it is held straight. Truly the word is the mind's conception. Where, then, the word is poured out too freely, the inward bond of reason is loosed. [[13:3|but he that hath no guard on his speech|Qui autem inconsideratus est ad loquendum]], not premeditating how he should speak, nor taking care not to offend God by speaking, [[13:3|shall meet with evils|sentiet mala]]. For through this he often incurs the displeasure of others, disquiet of his own mind, and remorse of conscience as well; and if there was in him any devotion and recollection of mind in God, he soon loses them, wounds his soul, and will pay the penalties due. Therefore Cyril says: Certainly he who is poured out on the wind of talkativeness, by uttering undigested words, either troubles others or is troubled. For this reason it always pleased the ancient Prophets to speak sparingly. For he who talks much ruminates little, and therefore belches out idle words. And so according to the Law he is an unclean animal[[Lev 11:26||]] [that is, like the beasts that do not chew the cud].

paras.t: Vult, et non vult piger, id est, remisse cupit bonum agere et sortiri, non autem vult hoc efficaciter et intense : sicque habet voluntatem optativam, non imperativam. Itaque vult finem, sed media ad finis adeptionem necessaria non vult amplecti : vult perfectionem et beatitudinem obtinere; sed non vult jejunare, abstinere, in vigiliis, disciplinis, orationibus perdurare, cunctas vanitates et delectationes pravas relinquere, injurias, persecutiones et contemptus propter Deum gaudenter perferre : vult regnare cum Christo; sed non vult se profunde in omnibus humiliare, et pati cum ipso. In quo impletur illud apostoli Jacobi : Vir duplex animo, inconstans est in omnibus viis suis. Talis pigra voluntas, non acceptatur a Deo pro opere bono; sed voluntas plena et imperativa, quæ statim quum facultas aut opportunitas adest, procedit in opus, a quo si impediatur aliunde, acceptatur pro opere. Anima autem operantium, id est exsequentium divina præcepta, impinguabitur spirituali profectu et suavitate interna, quemadmodum scriptum est : In custodiendis illis retributio multa ; itemque, Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea.
paras.en: [[13:4|The sluggard willeth, and willeth not|Vult, et non vult piger]], that is, he desires slackly to do good and to obtain it, but does not will it effectively and intensely: and so he has a wishing will, not a commanding one. Thus he wills the end, but will not embrace the means needed to attain the end: he wills to obtain perfection and beatitude, but will not fast, abstain, persevere in vigils, disciplines and prayers, give up all vanities and wicked pleasures, and bear injuries, persecutions and contempt gladly for God's sake: he wills to reign with Christ, but will not humble himself deeply in all things and suffer with Him. In this is fulfilled that saying of the apostle James: [[Jas 1:8|A double minded man is inconstant in all his ways.|Vir duplex animo, inconstans est in omnibus viis suis]] Such a sluggish will is not accepted by God for a good work; but a full and commanding will, which goes forth into the work as soon as the means or the opportunity is there, and which, if it is hindered from it by something else, is accepted for the work. [[13:4|but the soul of them that work|Anima autem operantium]], that is, of those who carry out the divine commandments, [[13:4|shall be made fat|impinguabitur]] with spiritual progress and inward sweetness, as it is written: [[Ps 18:12|in keeping them there is a great reward|In custodiendis illis retributio multa]]; and again, [[Ps 62:6|Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness|Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxi, 6; the words are Ps 62:6].

paras.t: Verbum mendax justus detestabitur : quoniam odit quidquid justitiæ contrariatur. Impius autem confundit, et confundetur. Alios enim mentiendo, irridendo, demonstrando confundit : ideo confundetur a Domino, et sæpe confunditur in præsenti. Unde beato Job dicitur : Quum ceteros irriseris, a nullo confutaberis? quasi dicat, Ita non erit.
paras.en: [[13:5|The just shall hate a lying word|Verbum mendax justus detestabitur]]: since he hates whatever is contrary to justice. [[13:5|but the wicked confoundeth, and shall be confounded|Impius autem confundit, et confundetur]]. For he confounds others by lying, by mocking, by pointing them out: therefore he shall be confounded by the Lord, and is often confounded in this present life. Hence it is said to blessed Job: [[Job 11:3|when thou hast mocked others, shall no man confute thee?|Quum ceteros irriseris, a nullo confutaberis?]] as if to say: It shall not be so.

paras.t: Justitia custodit innocentis viam : id est, innocens merito suæ justitiæ custoditur a Domino, et ipse per justitiam, suam custodit conversationem, ne Deum offendat. Ideo scriptum est : Junior fui, etenim senui; et non vidi justum derelictum. Hinc Daniel ait : Misit Dominus angelum suum, et conclusit ora leonum, quia justitia coram eo inventa est in me. Impietas vero peccatorem supplantat.
paras.en: [[13:6|Justice keepeth the way of the innocent|Justitia custodit innocentis viam]]: that is, the innocent man is kept by the Lord through the merit of his justice, and he himself through justice keeps his manner of life, so as not to offend God. Therefore it is written: [[Ps 36:25|I have been young and now am old; and I have not seen the just forsaken|Junior fui, etenim senui; et non vidi justum derelictum]]. Hence Daniel says: The Lord [[Dan 6:22|hath sent his angel, and hath shut up the mouths of the lions|Misit Dominus angelum suum, et conclusit ora leonum]], [[Dan 6:22|forasmuch as before him justice hath been found in me|quia justitia coram eo inventa est in me]]. [[13:6|but wickedness overthroweth the sinner|Impietas vero peccatorem supplantat]].

paras.t: Est quasi dives, quum nihil habeat : id est, quidam parum de temporalibus rebus habentes, sunt quasi divites, quia hoc ipsum modicum quod habent, sufficit eis, nec quærunt superflua. Unde dixit Apostolus : Quasi nihil habentes, et omnia possidentes. Et est quasi pauper, quum in multis divitiis sit. Avari enim qui multa habent, sunt quasi pauperes, quia non contentantur habitis, et vix audent uti eisdem, et quærunt plura. Hinc Seneca in suis deprompsit Proverbiis : Quæ sunt maximæ divitiæ? non desiderare divitias. Quis plurimum habet? is qui minimum cupit. Quidam exponunt sic : Est quasi dives, quum nihil habeat : id est, qui temporalibus rebus abundat, dives putatur, quum meritis vacuus sit coram Deo, quemadmodum dives epulo. Et est quasi pauper, quum in multis divitiis sit : sicut Lazarus, qui fuit meritis opulentus, et pauper in rebus terrenis. Unde ait Scriptura : Dives quum dormierit, nil secum auferet; apprehendet eum quasi aqua, inopia, etc. Hieronymus quoque : Diviti, inquit, deest tam quod habet, quam quod non habet.
paras.en: [[13:7|One is as it were rich, when he hath nothing|Est quasi dives, quum nihil habeat]]: that is, some who have little in the way of temporal things are as it were rich, because the very little they have is enough for them, and they do not seek what is superfluous. Hence the Apostle said: [[2 Cor 6:10|as having nothing and possessing all things|Quasi nihil habentes, et omnia possidentes]]. [[13:7|and another is as it were poor, when he hath great riches|Et est quasi pauper, quum in multis divitiis sit]]. For the avaricious, who have much, are as it were poor, because they are not content with what they have, scarcely dare to use it, and seek more. Hence Seneca put forth in his Proverbs: What are the greatest riches? Not to desire riches. Who has the most? He who desires the least. Some expound it thus: [[13:7|One is as it were rich, when he hath nothing|Est quasi dives, quum nihil habeat]]: that is, he who abounds in temporal things is thought rich, while he is empty of merits before God, like the rich feaster[[Luke 16:19||]]. [[13:7|and another is as it were poor, when he hath great riches|Et est quasi pauper, quum in multis divitiis sit]]: like Lazarus[[Luke 16:20||]][[Luke 16:21||]], who was rich in merits and poor in earthly things. Hence Scripture says: [[Job 27:19|The rich man when he shall sleep shall take away nothing with him|Dives quum dormierit, nil secum auferet]]; [[Job 27:20|Poverty like water shall take hold on him|apprehendet eum quasi aqua, inopia]], etc. Jerome too: The rich man, he says, lacks what he has as much as what he has not.

paras.t: Redemptio animæ viri, divitiæ suæ, id est, spiritualis opulentia meritorum, valet homini pro redemptione animæ suæ a pœnis gehennæ, et ad evadendum rigorem divini judicii. Opera enim eorum sequuntur illos. Exteriores quoque divitiæ, si in opera misericordiæ expendantur, valent ad expiationem animæ a peccatis, sicut ad Nabuchodonosor Daniel ait : Consilium meum placeat tibi, et peccata tua eleemosynis redime, et iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum. Unde legitur in Tobia : Fiducia magna apud Deum est eleemosyna, et non patietur animam ire in tenebras.
paras.en: [[13:8|The ransom of a man's life are his riches|Redemptio animæ viri, divitiæ suæ]] [*animæ*, "of the soul", which the Douay-Rheims renders "life"], that is, the spiritual wealth of merits avails a man for the redemption of his soul from the pains of hell, and for escaping the rigour of the divine judgement. [[Apoc 14:13|For their works follow them|Opera enim eorum sequuntur illos]]. Outward riches too, if they are spent on works of mercy, avail for the cleansing of the soul from sins, as Daniel says to Nabuchodonosor: [[Dan 4:24|let my counsel be acceptable to thee, and redeem thou thy sins with alms, and thy iniquities with works of mercy to the poor|Consilium meum placeat tibi, et peccata tua eleemosynis redime, et iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum]]. Hence we read in Tobias: [[Tob 4:12|Alms shall be a great confidence before the most high God|Fiducia magna apud Deum est eleemosyna]], [[Tob 4:11|and will not suffer the soul to go into darkness|et non patietur animam ire in tenebras]].

paras.t: Qui autem pauper est, id est virtutibus inops et imperfectus, increpationem non sustinet : quod ex defectu sapientiæ et patientiæ provenit. Nam increpationem considerat non quasi animæ suæ medelam, sed quasi suæ personæ injuriam et contemptum : et in hoc graviter errat. Vel sic : Qui pauper est, id est pauper spiritu, seu humilis aut voluntarie terrena despiciens, ac Domino in tali paupertate deserviens, increpationem non sustinet, id est, a Deo in futuro judicio non redarguetur, neque damnabitur, sed consequetur quod Judex promisit : Beati, inquiens, pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Insuper sæpe contingit, quod pauperes et mendici increpationem patienter non ferunt, quum sint pusillanimes et afflicti. Ideo non sunt durius increpandi, nisi forsan magnitudo excessus aliud exigat. Nam, ut Seneca testatur, Dura est in afflictione increpatio. Atque communiter dicitur, quod afflicto non est addenda afflictio.
paras.en: [[13:8|but he that is poor|Qui autem pauper est]], that is, destitute of virtues and imperfect, [[13:8|beareth not reprehension|increpationem non sustinet]]: which comes from a lack of wisdom and patience. For he regards rebuke not as a medicine for his soul, but as an injury and an insult to his person: and in this he errs gravely. Or thus: [[13:8|he that is poor|Qui pauper est]], that is, poor in spirit, or humble, or willingly despising earthly things and serving the Lord in such poverty, [[13:8|beareth not reprehension|increpationem non sustinet]] [*sustinet* means both "bears" and "undergoes": here, he does not undergo rebuke], that is, he will not be reproved by God at the judgement to come, nor condemned, but will obtain what the Judge promised: [[Matt 5:3|Blessed|Beati]], He says, [[Matt 5:3|are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]. Moreover it often happens that the poor and beggars do not bear rebuke patiently, since they are faint-hearted and afflicted. Therefore they are not to be rebuked too harshly, unless perhaps the greatness of the fault demands otherwise. For, as Seneca testifies, Rebuke is hard in affliction. And it is commonly said that affliction is not to be added to the afflicted.

paras.t: Lux justorum lætificat. Lux justorum, est sapientia, gratia, virtus, spes, contemplatio et moderata prosperitas eorumdem : quæ tam eos, quam alios qui diligunt justos, exhilarat, quia congaudent justis. Lucerna autem impiorum, id est temporalis eorum prosperitas, fama et ornatus exterior, exstinguetur : juxta illud Job, Nonne lux impii exstinguetur? Et rursus, Exstinguetur in mediis tenebris lucerna illius.
paras.en: [[13:9|The light of the just giveth joy|Lux justorum lætificat]]. The light of the just is their wisdom, grace, virtue, hope, contemplation and moderate prosperity: which gladdens both them and others who love the just, since they rejoice together with the just. [[13:9|but the lamp of the wicked|Lucerna autem impiorum]], that is, their temporal prosperity, fame and outward adornment, [[13:9|shall be put out|exstinguetur]]: according to that saying of Job, [[Job 18:5|Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished|Nonne lux impii exstinguetur]]? And again, [[Prov 20:20|his lamp shall be put out in the midst of darkness|Exstinguetur in mediis tenebris lucerna illius]].

paras.t: Inter superbos semper jurgia sunt : quoniam unusquisque eorum vult suam fieri voluntatem, aliumque excedere. Itaque, sicut humilitas parit pacem, ita superbia lites. Interdum tamen superbi et ambitiosi concordes sunt, quia eosdem habent inimicos, contra quos interim concorditer prœliantur. Sed quum ab extraneis cessaverint, bellis intestinis, pugnis ac jurgiis se invicem lacerabunt : ut patuit in Romanis, qui semper ambitiosi fuerunt. Qui autem omnia agunt cum consilio, reguntur sapientia. Hoc enim consilii est, nil magni sine prævio consilio operari. Ideo in Proverbiis suis ait Cyrillus : Diligentiori ruminatione omnia digeras, antequam agas. Summa enim et increata ars, sapientem docuit ruminare in mente : quæ ars animalia munda docuit ruminare in corpore. Cuncta namque subtili meditatione ruminat prudens, quæ dicit aut facit : ideo digesta loquitur, et examinata purgataque operatur. Ad quid enim communicatum est homini clarum rationis consilium, tanquam carissimum meditationis bonum? Nonne ut his salubriter in agendis utatur? Unde præmeditationis atque consilii masticatio præponenda est semper actibus cunctis humanis, si sapientia gubernentur, ut digestiora ac puriora opera subsequantur.
paras.en: [[13:10|Among the proud there are always contentions|Inter superbos semper jurgia sunt]]: since each of them wants his own will to be done, and to outdo the other. And so, as humility gives birth to peace, so pride gives birth to strife. Sometimes, however, the proud and ambitious are of one mind, because they have the same enemies, against whom they fight together for a time. But when they have done with outsiders, they will tear one another with civil wars, fights and quarrels: as was seen in the Romans, who were always ambitious. [[13:10|but they that do all things with counsel, are ruled by wisdom|Qui autem omnia agunt cum consilio, reguntur sapientia]]. For it is the part of counsel to do nothing great without counsel beforehand. Therefore Cyril says in his Proverbs: Digest all things by careful rumination before you act. For the highest and uncreated Art, the same Art that taught the clean animals to ruminate in the body, taught the wise man to ruminate in the mind. For the prudent man ruminates with subtle meditation everything that he says or does: therefore he speaks things digested, and does things examined and purged. For to what end has the clear counsel of reason been imparted to man, as the most precious good of meditation? Is it not that he may use it wholesomely in what he does? Hence the chewing of forethought and counsel must always come before all human acts, if they are to be governed by wisdom, so that better digested and purer works may follow.

paras.t: Substantia festinata, id est cito ac faciliter acquisita, minuetur, id est, a suo possessore inutiliter consumetur. Sæpe quippe contingit, quod hi qui divitias celeriter et faciliter adipiscuntur, eas parum appretiantur, prodigaliterque expendunt; et sicut eis accesserunt, sic ab ipsis recedunt. Filii etiam, quorum parentes temporalia cupide collegerunt, emerunt, auxerunt, solent ea dilapidare. Quæ autem paulatim colligitur manu, id est, studio et labore successive acquiritur, multiplicabitur : quia a suo possessore diligenter custoditur et augmentatur, sicut videmus in his qui ex paupertate ad opulentiam per officia sua creverunt. Istud quoque Aristoteles ait. In spiritualibus item conspicimus, quod hi qui grandi exercitatione, abstinentia et labore ad virtutum incrementa, seu perfectionem perducti sunt, timorati exsistunt, ne per negligentiam suis priventur profectibus; qui vero gratiose præventi, ad spiritualem alacritatem, sensibilem devotionem, ac lacrimas, celeriter atque faciliter devenerunt, sæpe per incautelam et incustodiam dilabuntur, nec data sibi charismata debite appretiantur. Hinc etiam pius ac supersapientissimus Deus, desideratam gratiæ affluentiam multis non statim largitur, sed paulatim eos exaudit, ne repente evacuentur, sed diutius orando ac laborando magis promercantur, et firmiores cautioresque fiant.
paras.en: [[13:11|Substance got in haste|Substantia festinata]], that is, quickly and easily acquired, [[13:11|shall be diminished|minuetur]], that is, will be uselessly consumed by its owner. For it often happens that those who come by riches quickly and easily set little value on them and spend them lavishly; and as they came to them, so they leave them. Sons too, whose parents greedily gathered, bought and increased temporal goods, commonly squander them. [[13:11|but that which by little and little is gathered with the hand|Quæ autem paulatim colligitur manu]], that is, is acquired step by step by effort and labour, [[13:11|shall increase|multiplicabitur]]: because it is carefully kept and increased by its owner, as we see in those who have risen from poverty to wealth through their own employments. Aristotle says this too. In spiritual things likewise we observe that those who have been brought to growth in the virtues, or to perfection, by great exercise, abstinence and labour, remain fearful of being deprived of their progress through negligence; whereas those who, anticipated by grace, have come quickly and easily to spiritual eagerness, sensible devotion and tears, often slip away through want of caution and of watchfulness, and do not value as they should the gifts given them. Hence also the loving and supremely wise God does not at once bestow on many the abundance of grace they desire, but hears them little by little, so that they may not suddenly be emptied, but by praying and labouring longer may earn it the more, and become firmer and more cautious.

paras.t: Spes quæ differtur, id est, a desiderati boni adeptione retardatur, affligit animam cupientis, quam facit avide et anxie adspirare ad bonum speratum, præsertim ad beatificam Altissimi fruitionem : ipsaque dilatio tanti boni affligit. Unde dixit Propheta : Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est. Itemque : Fuerunt mihi lacrimæ meæ panes die ac nocte, dum dicitur mihi quotidie : Ubi est Deus tuus? Ex tali dolore clamavit Apostolus : Infelix ego homo! Quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? Verumtamen, sicut spes dilata, et boni cupiti dilatio, mentem affligunt sperantis; sic consideratio præmii, et confidentia pertingendi ad illud, exhilarant animam anhelantis. Propter quod admonet Paulus : Spe gaudentes. Porro prædictis consonat Seneca, dicens : Etiam celeritas in desiderio mora est; et rursus, Mora molesta est, sed parit sapientiam.
paras.en: [[13:12|Hope that is deferred|Spes quæ differtur]], that is, is held back from obtaining the good desired, [[13:12|afflicteth the soul|affligit animam]] of him who longs for it, which it makes aspire eagerly and anxiously to the good hoped for, above all to the beatific enjoyment of the Most High: and the very delay of so great a good afflicts it. Hence the Prophet said: [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] And again: [[Ps 41:4|My tears have been my bread day and night, whilst it is said to me daily: Where is thy God?|Fuerunt mihi lacrimæ meæ panes die ac nocte, dum dicitur mihi quotidie : Ubi est Deus tuus?]] From such grief the Apostle cried out: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo! Quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]] Yet, as hope deferred and the delay of the good longed for afflict the mind of him who hopes, so the thought of the reward and the confidence of reaching it gladden the soul of him who yearns for it. For this reason Paul admonishes: [[Rom 12:12|Rejoicing in hope|Spe gaudentes]]. Seneca, moreover, agrees with what has been said: Even speed is delay to desire; and again, Delay is irksome, but it gives birth to wisdom.

paras.t: Lignum vitæ, desiderium veniens : id est, desiderati et sperati boni impletio, præsentia ac possessio, dulciter reficit appetentem, ut lignum vitæ : et in fruitione Christi, qui est lignum vitæ, consistit delectatio ista; qui amatori suo repromisit : Ego ostendam ei me ipsum. De quo in prima sua Canonica ait sacratissimus apostolici chori vertex : In Christum non videntes creditis, videntes autem, exsultabitis lætitia inenarrabili et glorificata.
paras.en: [[13:12|desire when it cometh, is a tree of life|Lignum vitæ, desiderium veniens]]: that is, the fulfilment, presence and possession of the good desired and hoped for sweetly refreshes him who longs for it, like the tree of life: and this delight consists in the enjoyment of Christ, who is the tree of life; who promised His lover: I [[John 14:21|will manifest myself to him|ostendam ei me ipsum]] [Denis has *ostendam*, "I will shew", for the Vulgate's *manifestabo*]. Of Him the most holy head of the apostolic choir says in his first canonical epistle: In Christ, [[1 Pet 1:8|though you see him not, you believe|non videntes creditis]], but seeing, you [[1 Pet 1:8|shall rejoice with joy unspeakable and glorified|exsultabitis lætitia inenarrabili et glorificata]] [Denis has *videntes*, "seeing", where the Vulgate has *credentes*, "believing"].

paras.t: Qui detrahit alicui rei, obloquendo alicui, ipse se in futurum obligat, id est, ad luendum debitam pœnam pro suæ detractionis culpa adstringit se. Obligat quoque se ad vitandum in se ipso quod vituperavit in alio, dicente Apostolo : Qui prædicas non furandum, furaris? Quidam exponunt sic : Qui detrahit alicui rei, eam vituperando, ipse in futurum se obligat ad non commendandum eam, quia sic inhoneste veniret contra proprium verbum : quæ expositio videtur inepta, quoniam qui alterius famam detrahendo denigrat, ad famæ illius restitutionem tenetur. Ideo si mendaciter vituperavit, tenetur suum revocare ac fateri mendacium; si autem vere, nihilo minus, quia inordinate et detractorie alium vituperare præsumpsit, tenetur dicere inordinate ac male se esse locutum. Qui autem timet præceptum, id est, præcepta Dei et vicariorum ejus prævaricari veretur ex caritate et zelo justitiæ, in pace versabitur : quia habebit in se pacem internam, secundum illud, Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam. Cum superioribus quoque suis et proximis habebit pacem fraternam, deinde in regno cœlesti pacem supernam cum Deo.
paras.en: [[13:13|Whosoever speaketh ill of any thing|Qui detrahit alicui rei]] [*detrahit*: "detracts from"], by speaking against someone, [[13:13|bindeth himself for the time to come|ipse se in futurum obligat]], that is, binds himself to pay the penalty due for the guilt of his detraction. He also binds himself to avoid in himself what he blamed in another, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 2:21|thou, that preachest that men should not steal, stealest|Qui prædicas non furandum, furaris]]? Some expound it thus: [[13:13|Whosoever speaketh ill of any thing|Qui detrahit alicui rei]], by blaming it, [[13:13|bindeth himself for the time to come|ipse in futurum se obligat]] not to commend it, since he would thus shamefully go against his own word: but this exposition seems unfitting, since he who blackens another's good name by detraction is bound to restore that good name. Therefore, if he blamed him falsely, he is bound to take it back and confess his lie; and if truly, he is bound none the less, because he presumed to blame another inordinately and by way of detraction, to say that he spoke inordinately and wrongly. [[13:13|but he that feareth the commandment|Qui autem timet præceptum]], that is, who out of charity and zeal for justice fears to transgress the commandments of God and of His vicars, [[13:13|shall dwell in peace|in pace versabitur]]: because he will have inward peace in himself, according to that saying, [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]. He will also have brotherly peace with his superiors and his neighbours, and afterwards, in the heavenly kingdom, peace on high with God.

paras.t: Lex sapientis, id est lex divina a sapientissimo Deo collata, vel lex cujuscumque legislatoris prudentis; vel, Lex sapientis, id est lex Dei, quam sapiens homo custodit, est fons vitæ : quia ex lege accipitur forma bene vivendi, et ipsa lex dirigit in agendis; ut declinet a ruina mortis, id est, ut per legem homo recedat a casu peccati et morte æterna, ad quod lex ipsa instigat.
paras.en: [[13:14|The law of the wise|Lex sapientis]], that is, the divine law given by the most wise God, or the law of any prudent lawgiver; or, [[13:14|The law of the wise|Lex sapientis]], that is, the law of God which the wise man keeps, is [[13:14|a fountain of life|fons vitæ]]: because from the law is received the pattern of living well, and the law itself directs us in what we do; [[13:14|that he may decline from the ruin of death|ut declinet a ruina mortis]], that is, that through the law a man may withdraw from the fall of sin and from eternal death, to which the law itself urges him.

paras.t: Doctrina bona dabit gratiam : quia ex ea crescit in gratia, tam docens quam audiens. In itinere contemptorum, id est in verbis et factis eorum qui despiciunt alios et documenta salubria, est vorago, id est præcipitium periculosum, quia usque in foveam infernalem præcipitari merentur. Hinc ait in Proverbiis suis Cyrillus : In rebus etiam minimis vim quamdam natura distribuit : quamobrem nihil est a sapiente spernendum, quoniam habet unaquæque res suo loco et tempore suum juvamentum et commodum.
paras.en: [[13:15|Good instruction shall give grace|Doctrina bona dabit gratiam]]: because through it both the one who teaches and the one who hears grow in grace. [[13:15|in the way of scorners|In itinere contemptorum]], that is, in the words and deeds of those who despise others and wholesome teaching, is [[13:15|a deep pit|vorago]], that is, a perilous precipice, because they deserve to be cast headlong right down into the pit of hell. Hence Cyril says in his Proverbs: Even in the smallest things nature has placed a certain power: wherefore nothing is to be despised by the wise man, since each thing, in its own place and time, has its own help and use.

paras.t: Astutus omnia agit cum consilio : quia in omni re potest occurrere aut latere periculum, cui per consilium obviatur; nec quidquam præcipitanter agendum. Qui autem fatuus est, aperiet stultitiam, id est, irrationabiliter aget, et impetum passionis sequetur.
paras.en: [[13:16|The prudent man doth all things with counsel|Astutus omnia agit cum consilio]]: because in every matter danger can arise or lie hidden, and it is met by counsel; nor is anything to be done headlong. [[13:16|but he that is a fool, layeth open his folly|Qui autem fatuus est, aperiet stultitiam]], that is, he will act without reason, and follow the impulse of passion.

paras.t: Nuntius impii cadet in malum. Dum enim pro causa prava scienter egreditur, peccat, et interdum ab adversariis sui domini capitur. Nuntii impii, id est diaboli, fuerunt hæresiarchæ maledicti, qui corruerunt, et secum traxerunt quamplures in malum perfidiæ et tormenta gehennæ. Legatus autem fidelis est sanitas : quia commissam sibi causam bene exsequitur, atque bonam inter homines dispositionem procurat, quemadmodum sanitas est bona dispositio corporis.
paras.en: [[13:17|The messenger of the wicked shall fall into mischief|Nuntius impii cadet in malum]] [*malum*: "evil"]. For when he goes out knowingly on a wicked errand, he sins, and is sometimes taken by his master's adversaries. The messengers of the wicked one, that is, of the devil, were the accursed heresiarchs, who fell, and dragged very many with them into the evil of unbelief and the torments of hell. [[13:17|but a faithful ambassador is health|Legatus autem fidelis est sanitas]]: because he carries out well the business entrusted to him, and brings about a good disposition among men, as health is a good disposition of the body.

paras.t: Egestas, id est spiritualium divitiarum seu virtutum carentia ac defectus, et ignominia debentur ei qui deserit disciplinam, id est, correctionem et informationem dedignatur suscipere, aut susceptas non retinet. Talis enim est incorrigibilis, et omni carens prudentia, cujus prima pars est docilitas. Qui autem acquiescit arguenti, id est rationabiliter increpanti, glorificabitur, id est, coram Deo et Sanctis ejus erit gloriosus et laude dignus, tanquam vere virtuosus ac sapiens, defectuositates suas perpendens, curarique cupiens.
paras.en: [[13:18|Poverty|Egestas]], that is, the want and lack of spiritual riches or virtues, [[13:18|and shame|et ignominia]] are due [[13:18|to him that refuseth instruction|ei qui deserit disciplinam]] [*disciplina* is both "instruction" and "correction"], that is, who disdains to receive correction and instruction, or does not keep them once received. For such a man is incorrigible and lacks all prudence, the first part of which is teachableness. [[13:18|but he that yieldeth to reproof|Qui autem acquiescit arguenti]], that is, to one who rebukes him with reason, [[13:18|shall be glorified|glorificabitur]], that is, he will be glorious and worthy of praise before God and His Saints, as one truly virtuous and wise, who weighs his own failings and desires to be cured.

paras.t: Desiderium si compleatur, id est, ad effectum perducatur, delectat animam. Delectabile enim est, bono desiderato uniri, et cupitam perfectionem sortiri. Detestantur stulti eos qui fugiunt mala, id est periculosa eorum consortia atque carnalia oblectamenta, quæ ipsi stulti appretiantur ac diligunt. Hinc beatissimus Petrus in prima sua ait Canonica de iniquis : Qui mirantur, non concurrentibus vobis in eamdem luxuriæ confusionem.
paras.en: [[13:19|The desire that is accomplished|Desiderium si compleatur]], that is, brought to effect, [[13:19|delighteth the soul|delectat animam]]. For it is delightful to be united to the good desired, and to obtain the perfection longed for. [[13:19|fools hate them that flee from evil things|Detestantur stulti eos qui fugiunt mala]], that is, their dangerous company and the carnal pleasures which the fools themselves prize and love. Hence most blessed Peter says of the wicked in his first canonical epistle: Who [[1 Pet 4:4|think it strange that you run not with them into the same confusion of riotousness|mirantur, non concurrentibus vobis in eamdem luxuriæ confusionem]].

paras.t: Qui cum sapientibus graditur, id est, conversatur per vitæ conformitatem, sapiens erit : juxta quod scriptum est, Cum sancto sanctus eris. Ideo dicit Cyrillus : Cum electo socio proficiscaris ac converseris; fuge luminis hostem. Cum amatore sapientiæ, zelatore justitiæ, atque amicitiæ fideli cultore vive. Seneca quoque : Optimum, inquit, est majorum sequi vestigia, si recte præcesserint. Amicus stultorum, qui scilicet vanos et impios amat, non quia homines sunt felicitatis capaces, ac propter Deum, sed quoniam vani et stulti, jocosi et ludicres sunt; similis illis efficitur : quia communicat eis in vitiis per consensum; nec juste redarguit, sed arridet. Contra quod jubet Apostolus : Nolite communicare infructuosis operibus tenebrarum; magis autem redarguite. Nequaquam ergo spectacula cum complacentia, risu aut delectatione sunt intuenda, sed magis deflenda.
paras.en: [[13:20|He that walketh with the wise|Qui cum sapientibus graditur]], that is, keeps company with them by likeness of life, [[13:20|shall be wise|sapiens erit]]: according to what is written, [[Ps 17:26|With the holy thou wilt be holy|Cum sancto sanctus eris]]. Therefore Cyril says: Travel and keep company with a chosen companion; flee the enemy of the light. Live with a lover of wisdom, a zealous lover of justice, and a faithful keeper of friendship. Seneca too: It is best, he says, to follow in the footsteps of our elders, if they have gone before us rightly. [[13:20|a friend of fools|Amicus stultorum]], that is, one who loves the vain and wicked not because they are men capable of happiness, and for God's sake, but because they are vain and foolish, jesting and playful, [[13:20|shall become like to them|similis illis efficitur]]: because he shares with them in their vices by consenting; nor does he rebuke them as is just, but smiles on them. Against this the Apostle commands: [[Eph 5:11|have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness: but rather reprove them|Nolite communicare infructuosis operibus tenebrarum; magis autem redarguite]]. By no means, then, are spectacles to be watched with complacency, laughter or delight, but rather to be wept over.

paras.t: Peccatores persequitur malum, id est, propria eorum malitia undique sequitur eos, et remordens conscientia ipsos non deserit, pœna quoque justæ ultionis ipsos vastabit. Ideo Seneca dixit : Nullum conscium peccatorum tuorum magis timueris, quam te ipsum : alium namque effugere poteris; te, nunquam. Et Leo Papa : Rea, inquit, conscientia patitur quidquid Dei pietate differtur. Atque, ut asserit Augustinus, Animus inordinatus sibi ipsi pœnalis est. Et justis retribuentur bona, id est præmia gloriosa. In præsenti etiam infunduntur eis gratiosa charismata, consolatio spiritualis, conscientiæ quies, alacritas cordis, prælibatio futuræ salutis. Unde, ut Antisiodorensis in Summa sua, et Eusebius Emisenus in homilia testantur, virtuosi in hac vita magnam suæ remunerationis portionem desuper sortiuntur. Magna quippe justitiæ merces est, tempus fructuose expendere, sanctæ puritati operam dare, Deo in tranquillitate ac sinceritate vacare, vilissimum jugum vitare peccati, et servitutem evadere hostis maligni.
paras.en: [[13:21|Evil pursueth sinners|Peccatores persequitur malum]], that is, their own wickedness follows them everywhere, and a gnawing conscience does not leave them, and the penalty of just vengeance will lay them waste. Therefore Seneca said: Fear no witness of your sins more than yourself: for another you can escape, yourself never. And Pope Leo: A guilty conscience, he says, suffers whatever is put off by the mercy of God. And, as Augustine declares, A disordered mind is its own punishment. [[13:21|and to the just good shall be repaid|Et justis retribuentur bona]], that is, glorious rewards. In the present life too gracious gifts are poured into them: spiritual consolation, quiet of conscience, eagerness of heart, a foretaste of salvation to come. Hence, as Antisiodorensis [that is, William of Auxerre] in his Summa, and Eusebius of Emesa in a homily, testify, the virtuous receive from above in this life a great portion of their reward. For it is a great reward of justice to spend one's time fruitfully, to give oneself to holy purity, to be free for God in peace and sincerity, to shun the most vile yoke of sin, and to escape the slavery of the evil enemy.

paras.t: Bonus homo relinquet hæredes suos filios et nepotes. In veteri Testamento inter cetera, justis promittebatur fecunditas prolis, et semen copiosum relinquere post se. Istud tamen non fuit omnibus justis concessum. Melius ergo spiritualiter sumitur, quod scilicet homo virtuosus, idoneusque prælatus relinquet post se bonos discipulos, suarum virtutum imitatores : sicut et Christus reliquit gloriosos Apostolos gratiæ suæ participes. Unde fuit prædictum : Si posuerit pro peccato animam suam, videbit semen longævum. Et custoditur justo substantia peccatoris. Interdum contingit, quod temporalia impiis juste ablata, justis præstantur. Christo autem Sancto Sanctorum incorporati sunt gentiles, qui olim fuerunt servi diaboli. De quo Dominus ait per Isaiam : Dispertiam ei plurimos, et fortium dividet spolia, pro eo quod in mortem tradidit animam suam. Unde ipsemet in Evangelio loquitur : Quum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum, in pace sunt ea quæ possidet ; si autem fortior eo supervenerit, vasa ejus diripiet. Ipse enim Salvator ascendens in altum, captivam duxit captivitatem. Denique substantia peccatoris custoditur justo, quia opera meritoria a reprobis quandoque in caritate exsistentibus facta, non ipsis finaliter, sed electis justis communicantur ac proficiunt ad salutem.
paras.en: [[13:22|The good man leaveth heirs, sons, and grandsons|Bonus homo relinquet hæredes suos filios et nepotes]]. In the Old Testament, among other things, fruitfulness in offspring was promised to the just, and that they would leave a numerous seed after them[[Deut 7:14||]]. Yet this was not granted to all the just. It is better, then, taken spiritually: namely, that a virtuous man and a fit prelate will leave good disciples after him, imitators of his virtues: as Christ too left the glorious Apostles, sharers in His grace. Hence it was foretold: [[Is 53:10|if he shall lay down his life for sin, he shall see a longlived seed|Si posuerit pro peccato animam suam, videbit semen longævum]]. [[13:22|and the substance of the sinner is kept for the just|Et custoditur justo substantia peccatoris]]. It sometimes happens that temporal goods justly taken from the wicked are given to the just. But to Christ, the Holy of Holies, the gentiles have been incorporated, who were once slaves of the devil. Of Him the Lord says through Isaias: [[Is 53:12|will I distribute to him very many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he hath delivered his soul unto death|Dispertiam ei plurimos, et fortium dividet spolia, pro eo quod in mortem tradidit animam suam]]. Hence He Himself says in the Gospel: [[Luke 11:21|When a strong man armed keepeth his court, those things are in peace which he possesseth.|Quum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum, in pace sunt ea quæ possidet]] [[Luke 11:22|But if a stronger than he come upon him|si autem fortior eo supervenerit]], he will [[Matt 12:29|rifle his goods|vasa ejus diripiet]]. For the Saviour Himself, [[Eph 4:8|Ascending on high, he led captivity captive|ascendens in altum, captivam duxit captivitatem]][[Ps 67:19||]]. Lastly, the substance of the sinner is kept for the just, because meritorious works done by the reprobate while they were for a time in charity profit not them in the end, but are shared with the elect just and profit them for salvation.

paras.t: Multi cibi sunt in novalibus patrum, id est novis agris seu campis noviter cultis a patribus ; et aliis congregantur absque judicio, id est sine ratione. Hoc corporaliter sæpe sic accidit, quod novalia patrum copiosum proferunt fructum, quem alii interdum irrationabiliter occupant. Spiritualiter autem, in novalibus, id est libris, doctrinis, exemplisque patrum, sunt multæ alimoniæ spirituales, quæ aliis sine judicio congregantur, dum quis talia prædicat proximis, nec tamen proficit inde, neque reficitur mente.
paras.en: [[13:23|Much food is in the tillage of fathers|Multi cibi sunt in novalibus patrum]] [*novalia*: land newly broken and tilled], that is, in new lands or fields newly cultivated by the fathers; [[13:23|but for others it is gathered without judgment|et aliis congregantur absque judicio]], that is, without reason. In the bodily sense this often happens so: the new-tilled lands of the fathers yield abundant fruit, which others sometimes seize without reason. Spiritually, however, [[13:23|in the tillage|in novalibus]], that is, in the books, teachings and examples of the fathers, there is much spiritual nourishment, which is gathered by others without judgement, when someone preaches such things to his neighbours, and yet does not profit by it himself nor is refreshed in mind.

paras.t: Qui parcit virgæ, odit filium suum, id est, spiritualiter eum non amat, quem incorrectum et indisciplinatum relinquit. Similiter qui subditum suum non corripit nec castigat, eum odire magis quam diligere comprobatur. Qui autem diligit illum vero et spirituali amore, instanter erudit eum verbis, exemplis, flagellis : intelligendo per filium sobolem totam. Quum enim amare, sit alicui bonum velle atque impendere, qui sobolem suam non erudit nec castigat, non diligit eam, sed odit, quam immorigeratam indomitamque relinquit. De hoc in Ecclesiastico multa conscripta sunt. Qui diligit, inquit, filium suum, assiduat illi flagella. Non des filio potestatem in juventute sua, sed curva cervicem illius, et tunde latera ejus. Hinc ait et Apostolus : Patres, educate filios vestros in disciplina et correptione Domini. Parentes quippe filiis suis tria tenentur, scilicet educationem corporalem, instructionem in moribus, et correctionem pro culpis.
paras.en: [[13:24|He that spareth the rod, hateth his son|Qui parcit virgæ, odit filium suum]], that is, he does not love him spiritually, since he leaves him uncorrected and undisciplined. Likewise he who does not rebuke or chastise his subject is shown to hate him rather than love him. [[13:24|but he that loveth him|Qui autem diligit illum]] with a true and spiritual love [[13:24|correcteth him betimes|instanter erudit]] [*instanter erudit*: "instructs him earnestly"] by words, examples and stripes: understanding by *son* all one's offspring. For since to love is to will good to someone and to bestow it, he who does not instruct and chastise his offspring does not love it, but hates it, since he leaves it unruly and untamed. On this much is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 30:1|He that loveth|Qui diligit]], it says, [[Ecclus 30:1|his son, frequently chastiseth him|filium suum, assiduat illi flagella]]. [[Ecclus 30:11|Give him not liberty in his youth|Non des filio potestatem in juventute sua]], but [[Ecclus 30:12|Bow down his neck|curva cervicem illius]], and [[Ecclus 30:12|beat his sides|tunde latera ejus]]. Hence the Apostle too says: [[Eph 6:4|fathers|Patres]], [[Eph 6:4|bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord|educate filios vestros in disciplina et correptione Domini]]. For parents owe their children three things: bodily upbringing, instruction in morals, and correction for faults.

paras.t: Justus comedit, et replet animam suam, id est, moderate se reficit, juxta rationabilem animæ appetitum, cujus discreto desiderio satisfacit; venter autem impiorum insaturabilis est, id est, tam gulosi sunt iniqui, quasi satiari non valeant; nova quoque et exquisita expetunt fercula. Spiritualiter vero, justus spiritualibus se reficit alimentis, et animam suam replet piis affectibus. Venter autem impiorum insaturabilis, id est, cor eorum terrenis rebus non satiatur : imo instar hydropicorum, quo plura acquirunt, plura desiderant, ita quod sicut hydropicis crescit ex potu sitis, sic ipsis ex adeptione affectio. Propter quod Seneca : Inopi, inquit, parva desunt; avaro, omnia. Restringendus est igitur venter, nec minus desiderium cordis, quum dicat Gregorius : Dominante vitio gulæ, totum quod homines fortiter egerint, perdunt; et dum venter non restringitur, cunctæ virtutes pariter obruuntur. Sed heu, quanta est carnalium, vel potius brutalium hominum insania! Nam, ut ait Innocentius, Initium vitæ hominis, aqua et panis : gulosis autem non sufficiunt arborum fructus, leguminum genera, radices herbarum, pisces maris, pecora terræ, volucres cæli; sed quæruntur pigmenta, parantur aromata, nutriuntur altilia, capiuntur obesa, quæ ministrorum obsequio exquisite coquuntur.
paras.en: [[13:25|The just eateth and filleth his soul|Justus comedit, et replet animam suam]], that is, he refreshes himself in moderation, according to the reasonable appetite of the soul, whose discreet desire he satisfies; [[13:25|but the belly of the wicked is never to be filled|venter autem impiorum insaturabilis]], that is, the wicked are so gluttonous that they seem unable to be satisfied; and they seek out new and exquisite dishes. Spiritually, however, the just man refreshes himself with spiritual food, and fills his soul with devout affections. [[13:25|But the belly of the wicked is never to be filled|Venter autem impiorum insaturabilis]], that is, their heart is not satisfied with earthly things: rather, like the dropsical, the more they acquire the more they desire, so that as thirst grows in the dropsical from drinking, so in them desire grows from getting. For this reason Seneca says: The needy man lacks little things [the margin gives the reading *pauca*, "few things", for *parva*]; the avaricious, everything. The belly, then, must be restrained, and no less the desire of the heart, since Gregory says: When the vice of gluttony has the mastery, men lose all that they have done bravely; and while the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are overwhelmed together. But alas, how great is the madness of carnal, or rather brutish, men! For, as Innocent says, [[Ecclus 29:27|The chief thing for man's life is water and bread|Initium vitæ hominis, aqua et panis]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xxix, 28, the Vulgate's numbering; Denis has *Initium*, "the beginning"]: but for gluttons the fruits of the trees, the kinds of pulse, the roots of herbs, the fishes of the sea, the beasts of the earth and the birds of the air are not enough; but sauces are sought, spices prepared, fowls fattened, fat beasts caught, which are cooked with care by the service of attendants.

14.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI QUARTIDECIMI : SAPIENS MULIER ÆDIFICAT DOMUM SUAM.
14.title_en: Elucidation of the fourteenth chapter: A wise woman buildeth her house.

paras.t: Sapiens mulier ædificat domum suam, id est, sobolem ac familiam suam instruit verbis atque exemplis. Ideo parentes Saræ uxoris junioris Tobiæ, docuerunt filiam suam regere domum, gubernare familiam, et se ipsam irreprehensibilem exhibere. Abigail quoque familiam suam et virum de manu David irati salvavit, ut legitur primo Regum. Insipiens autem mulier exstructam quoque manibus destruit: quoniam verbis et factis suos scandalizat domesticos, et in temporalibus male regit. Spiritualiter, sapiens mulier, est Ecclesia catholica, Christi sponsa, quæ sibi commissos ædificat, efficaciterque gubernat. Insipiens vero mulier, est hæreticorum ecclesia, quæ subvertit pro posse Catholicos.
paras.en: [[14:1|A wise woman buildeth her house|Sapiens mulier ædificat domum suam]], that is, she instructs her offspring and her household by words and examples. So the parents of Sara, the wife of the younger Tobias[[Tob 10:12||]], taught their daughter [[Tob 10:13|to take care of the family, to govern the house, and to behave herself irreprehensibly|regere domum, gubernare familiam, et se ipsam irreprehensibilem exhibere]]. Abigail too saved her household and her husband from the hand of the angry David, as we read in the first book of Kings[[1 Kings 25:18||]]. [[14:1|but the foolish will pull down with her hands that also which is built|Insipiens autem mulier exstructam quoque manibus destruit]]: for by her words and deeds she scandalizes those of her house, and rules badly in temporal things. Spiritually, the wise woman is the Catholic Church, the bride of Christ, who builds up those committed to her and governs them effectively. But the foolish woman is the church of the heretics, which overthrows Catholics as far as it can.

paras.t: Ambulans recto itinere, id est in observantia præceptorum, quæ ducit ad gloriam, et timens Deum filiali aut saltem initiali timore, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via, id est, scandalose ac turpiter conversatur, præsertim quando talis iniquus ex conversatione justi putat se aliquod incommodum consequi, puta contemptum, dejectionem, diffamiam. Nam sicut similitudo est causa dilectionis, sic dissimilitudo causa est aversionis et aspernationis. Sed in hoc casu debet vir bonus et timoratus, patiens esse et gloriari in Domino. Nam, ut in Proverbiis suis Seneca loquitur, Malis displicere, est laudari. Et rursus fatetur: Misera est fortuna quæ inimico caret. Quamvis id agas, ut ne quis merito tuo te oderit, erunt tamen semper qui te odient.
paras.en: [[14:2|He that walketh in the right way|Ambulans recto itinere]], that is, in the keeping of the commandments, which leads to glory, [[14:2|and feareth God|et timens Deum]] with a filial or at least an initial fear [that is, the fear of one beginning to love God, between servile fear of punishment and the filial fear of offending him], [[14:2|is despised by him that goeth by an infamous way|despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via]], that is, who lives scandalously and shamefully; above all when such a wicked man thinks that some harm comes to him from the just man's way of life, such as contempt, being cast down, or ill repute. For as likeness is the cause of love, so unlikeness is the cause of aversion and disdain. But in this case the good and God-fearing man must be patient and glory in the Lord. For, as Seneca says in his Proverbs, To displease the wicked is to be praised. And again he declares: Wretched is the fortune that has no enemy. Although thou act so that no one hates thee by thy desert, yet there will always be some who hate thee.

paras.t: In ore stulti, virga superbiæ, id est contumeliosa et injuriosa ac animosa locutio, qua audientes affliguntur. Stultus enim, ut asserit Isaias, fatua loquetur. Labia autem sapientium custodiunt eos: id est, ipsi sapientes per sua sapientialia et doctrinalia verba, se ipsos custodiunt, ne ex verbis stultorum turbentur, et ut agant quod docent; vel, custodiunt stultos, dum eos sua probitate emendant. Sapientia enim vincit malitiam. Ideo ait Apostolus: Libenter suffertis insipientes, quum sitis ipsi sapientes.
paras.en: [[14:3|In the mouth of a fool is the rod of pride|In ore stulti, virga superbiæ]], that is, insulting, injurious and passionate speech, by which those who hear it are afflicted. For [[Is 32:6|the fool|Stultus enim]], as Isaias declares, [[Is 32:6|will speak foolish things|fatua loquetur]]. [[14:3|but the lips of the wise preserve them|Labia autem sapientium custodiunt eos]]: that is, the wise themselves, by their words of wisdom and teaching, guard themselves, so as not to be troubled by the words of fools, and so as to do what they teach; or, they guard the fools, while they amend them by their own uprightness. For [[Wis 7:30|no evil can overcome wisdom|Sapientia enim vincit malitiam]] [Denis turns the verse about: 'wisdom overcomes malice']. Therefore the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 11:19|you gladly suffer the foolish: whereas yourselves are wise|Libenter suffertis insipientes, quum sitis ipsi sapientes]].

paras.t: Ubi non sunt boves, præsepe vacuum est; ubi autem apparent plurimæ segetes, ibi manifesta fortitudo bovis. Hoc primo superficialiter accipi potest de bobus et bladis, quantum ad illos in quorum terris soli boves arant: quod antiquitus communiter ita fuit. Unde et in Job inducitur: Boves arabant. Itaque, Ubi non sunt boves, præsepe vacuum est, quum agri non colantur ibidem; ubi vero terra copiose fructificat, constat quod boves fortiter araverunt.
paras.en: [[14:4|Where there are no oxen, the crib is empty: but where there is much corn, there the strength of the ox is manifest|Ubi non sunt boves, præsepe vacuum est; ubi autem apparent plurimæ segetes, ibi manifesta fortitudo bovis]] [Denis reads *ubi autem apparent plurimæ segetes*, 'but where much corn appears']. This can be taken first, at the surface, of oxen and crops, as regards those in whose lands only oxen plough, as was commonly so in ancient times. Hence in Job too it is said: [[Job 1:14|The oxen were ploughing|Boves arabant]]. So, [[14:4|Where there are no oxen, the crib is empty|Ubi non sunt boves, præsepe vacuum est]], since the fields are not tilled there; but where the land bears fruit abundantly, it is plain that the oxen have ploughed strongly.

paras.t: Spiritualiter autem, per boves designantur prædicatores, doctores, prælati, sicut ad Corinthios docet Apostolus, illud ex Deuteronomio introducens, Non alligabis os bovi trituranti. Hi enim in agro Dei, id est in Ecclesia, laborant, fidelium corda verbo prædicationis aperiendo ad suscipiendum semen gratiæ Spiritus Sancti, quod inserunt eis, et ea cooperando fecundant. Unde Corinthiis loquitur Paulus: Adjutores Dei sumus; Dei agricultura estis. Itaque, Ubi non sunt boves, id est boni prælati ac prædicatores, præsepe vacuum est, id est, corda populi gratia atque virtutibus carent, quia magistrum et ducem non habent; ubi autem plurimæ segetes, id est abundantia actuum virtuosorum, ibi manifesta fortitudo bovis, id est, efficacia doctrinæ prælati seu prædicatoris evidenter relucet in hujusmodi fructu, tanquam in suo effectu.
paras.en: Spiritually, however, the oxen signify preachers, doctors and prelates, as the Apostle teaches the Corinthians, bringing in that saying from Deuteronomy[[Deut 25:4||]]: [[1 Cor 9:9|Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn|Non alligabis os bovi trituranti]]. For these labour in God's field, that is, in the Church, opening the hearts of the faithful by the word of preaching to receive the seed of the grace of the Holy Ghost, which they sow in them, and by working together with it they make them fruitful. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 3:9|we are God's coadjutors. You are God's husbandry|Adjutores Dei sumus; Dei agricultura estis]].
