So, [[14:4|Where there are no oxen|Ubi non sunt boves]], that is, good prelates and preachers, [[14:4|the crib is empty|præsepe vacuum est]], that is, the hearts of the people lack grace and virtues, because they have no master and leader; [[14:4|but where there is much corn|ubi autem plurimæ segetes]], that is, an abundance of virtuous acts, [[14:4|there the strength of the ox is manifest|ibi manifesta fortitudo bovis]], that is, the effectiveness of the prelate's or preacher's teaching shines out clearly in such fruit, as in its effect.

paras.t: Testis fidelis non mentietur, falsum testimonium proferendo; profert mendacium testis dolosus, qui per preces et munera, aut ex timore, amore vel odio faciliter a veritatis tenore divertit.
paras.en: [[14:5|A faithful witness will not lie|Testis fidelis non mentietur]] by bearing false witness; [[14:5|a deceitful witness uttereth a lie|profert mendacium testis dolosus]], who through entreaties and gifts, or out of fear, love or hatred, easily turns aside from the course of the truth.

paras.t: Quærit derisor sapientiam, non a Deo per orationem devotam, nec ex Scripturis per studium bonum, nec a veris Catholicis per humilitatem, sed ex proprio intellectu, et ab hæreticis, philosophorumque libris; et non invenit sapientiam salutarem, quæ extra Ecclesiam non habetur, nec invenitur. Doctrina prudentium facilis, id est, faciliter potest addisci, quantum requiritur ad salutem. Prudentes quoque juxta audientium capacitatem loquuntur, et clare, non intricate, exprimunt suæ mentis conceptum, sicut ait Apostolus: Quasi parvulis in Christo lac dedi, id est facilem humilemque doctrinam, non solidum cibum.
paras.en: [[14:6|A scorner seeketh wisdom|Quærit derisor sapientiam]], not from God by devout prayer, nor from the Scriptures by good study, nor from true Catholics by humility, but from his own understanding, and from heretics and the books of the philosophers; [[14:6|and findeth it not|et non invenit]], the wisdom of salvation, that is, which is not had nor found outside the Church. [[14:6|the learning of the wise is easy|Doctrina prudentium facilis]], that is, it can easily be learned, as far as is required for salvation. The prudent also speak according to the capacity of their hearers, and express the thought of their mind clearly, not in a tangled way, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 3:1|As unto little ones in Christ|Quasi parvulis in Christo]] [[1 Cor 3:2|I gave you milk|lac dedi]], that is, easy and humble teaching, not solid food.

paras.t: Vade contra virum stultum, ut eum refrenes a malo, atque corripias, et nesciet, id est, caritatem tuam et piam intentionem non advertet, sed indignabitur magis. Aliqui autem verba sequentia includunt huic versiculo, ut sit sensus, quod nesciet labia prudentiæ, id est prudentiam labiorum tuorum. Vel versus hic incipit: Labia prudentiæ, sapientia, id est, in labiis prudentis sapientia resonabit. Vel verbum hoc, Sapientia, nectendum est clausulæ subsequenti.
paras.en: [[14:7|Go against a foolish man|Vade contra virum stultum]], to restrain him from evil and to rebuke him, [[14:7|and he knoweth not|et nesciet]] [Denis reads the future, *nesciet*, 'he will not know'], that is, he will not notice thy charity and loving intention, but will be the more indignant. Some, however, include the following words in this verse, so that the sense is that [[14:7|he knoweth not the lips of prudence|nesciet labia prudentiæ]], that is, the prudence of thy lips. Or the next verse begins: [[14:7|The lips of prudence|Labia prudentiæ]], wisdom, that is, in the lips of the prudent wisdom will resound. Or this word, Wisdom, is to be joined to the clause that follows.

paras.t: Sapientia callidi, id est astuti et circumspecti, est intelligere viam suam, id est propriam conversationem rite considerare, et pericula laqueosque sibi expositos bene perpendere ac vitare: et sic nomen, Callidi, sumitur hic in bono. Et imprudentia stultorum errans ab itinere ultimi finis.
paras.en: [[14:8|The wisdom of a discreet man|Sapientia callidi]], that is, of one shrewd and circumspect, [[14:8|is to understand his way|est intelligere viam suam]], that is, to consider his own way of life rightly, and to weigh well and avoid the dangers and snares laid for him: and so the word *callidi* [that is, 'of the crafty, the cunning', which the Douay-Rheims renders 'discreet'] is taken here in a good sense. [[14:8|and the imprudence of fools erreth|Et imprudentia stultorum errans]], straying from the road to the last end.

paras.t: Stultis illudit peccatum, id est, sua delectatione decipit homines vitiosos: qui hic passim stulti vocantur, quoniam stulti sunt coram Deo, et ab increata ejus Sapientia se avertunt, donoque sapientiæ carent, atque stultitia, quæ dono sapientiæ contrariatur, id est vitio puerilitatis, replentur. Stultis ergo illudit peccatum, sicut esca in hamo decipit pisces. Delectat namque peccare. Nam si non delectaret, non fieret, ut asserit Augustinus. Non, inquam, fieret tam multum ut modo. Aliqui legunt: Stultus illudit peccatum, id est, per risum et ludum operatur iniquitatem, et pro nihilo reputat Deum offendere, imo lætatur quum male fecerit. Et inter justos morabitur gratia, id est, in eorum mentibus dona gratiæ requiescunt, et ipsi ad invicem gratiose se habent, acceptabilesque consistunt.
paras.en: *Sin mocketh fools*[[14:9||]] [Denis reads *Stultis illudit peccatum*, 'sin makes sport of fools'; the Douay-Rheims follows the other reading he gives below], that is, it deceives vicious men by its delight: they are everywhere here called fools, since they are fools before God, and turn away from his uncreated Wisdom, and lack the gift of wisdom, and are filled with folly, which is contrary to the gift of wisdom, that is, with the vice of childishness. Sin, then, mocks fools, as the bait on the hook deceives fish. For sinning delights; for if it did not delight, it would not be done, as Augustine declares. It would not, I say, be done as much as it is now. Some read: [[14:9|A fool will laugh at sin|Stultus illudit peccatum]], that is, he works iniquity with laughter and sport, and counts it nothing to offend God; nay, he is glad when he hath done evil[[Prov 2:14||]]. [[14:9|but among the just grace shall abide|Et inter justos morabitur gratia]], that is, the gifts of grace rest in their minds, and they bear themselves graciously towards one another, and are acceptable.

paras.t: Cor quod novit amaritudinem animæ suæ, id est, quod advertit propter quid anima sua merito debeat intra se amaricari, videlicet propter sua peccata per veram contritionem, et propter difficultatem obtinendi salutem, et quia tot defectuositatibus plenum est, et propter incertitudinem sui status, quoniam nescit an amore sit dignus, an odio, et propter aliorum peccata, et maxime propter quotidianam inhonorationem, multiplicemque Dei offensam gravissimam; in gaudio ejus non miscebitur extraneus, id est, consolationem a Deo percipiet, reprobis et impœnitentibus inexpertam. Beati enim qui taliter lugent, et cum pio Ezechia dicere possunt, Recogitabo omnes annos meos in amaritudine animæ meæ: quoniam ipsi consolabuntur. Jam equidem consolantur de spe veniæ, et indulgentia culpæ, infusioneque gratiæ, et de gratiosa visitatione ac illustratione Spiritus Sancti, qui post tempestatem tranquillum facit, et post fletum exsultationem infundit. Qui ergo vult gaudium istud salubriter experiri, peccata sua digne deploret, indignas quoque consolationes jugiter detestetur, ac impœnitentium vitet consortia.
paras.en: [[14:10|The heart that knoweth the bitterness of his own soul|Cor quod novit amaritudinem animæ suæ]], that is, which notices why its soul ought rightly to be embittered within itself: namely for its sins, by true contrition; and for the difficulty of obtaining salvation; and because it is full of so many failings; and for the uncertainty of its state, since it [[Eccles 9:1|knoweth not whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|nescit an amore sit dignus, an odio]]; and for the sins of others; and above all for the daily dishonouring of God and the manifold and most grievous offence given him: [[14:10|in his joy the stranger shall not intermeddle|in gaudio ejus non miscebitur extraneus]], that is, it will receive from God a consolation unknown to the reprobate and the impenitent. For [[Matt 5:5|Blessed are they that mourn|Beati enim qui taliter lugent]] in this way, and can say with the devout Ezechias, [[Is 38:15|I will recount to thee all my years in the bitterness of my soul|Recogitabo omnes annos meos in amaritudine animæ meæ]]: [[Matt 5:5|for they shall be comforted|quoniam ipsi consolabuntur]]. Indeed they are comforted even now, by the hope of pardon, the forgiveness of guilt and the pouring in of grace, and by the gracious visitation and enlightening of the Holy Ghost, who after the storm makes a calm, and after weeping pours in exultation[[Tob 3:22||]]. Whoever then wishes to taste this joy to his salvation, let him worthily bewail his sins, let him constantly detest unworthy consolations, and avoid the company of the impenitent.

paras.t: Domus, id est cognatio seu posteritas, impiorum delebitur: quæ patrum suorum peccata sectatur. Unde tertio Regum, domus Jeroboam, Baasa, Amri, Achab, et consimilium, leguntur ob scelera sua deletæ. Tabernacula, id est congregationes, justorum germinabunt, id est, fructum virtutum producent, juxta illud Psalmi: Justus ut palma florebit, sicut cedrus Libani multiplicabitur. Et apud Osee dicitur: Ero quasi ros; Israel germinabit sicut lilium, et erumpet radix ejus ut Libani.
paras.en: [[14:11|The house|Domus]], that is, the kindred or posterity, [[14:11|of the wicked shall be destroyed|impiorum delebitur]], the house that follows the sins of its fathers. Hence in the third book of Kings the houses of Jeroboam[[3 Kings 15:29||]][[3 Kings 15:30||]], Baasa[[3 Kings 16:12||]][[3 Kings 16:13||]], Amri[[3 Kings 16:28||]], Achab[[4 Kings 9:7||]][[4 Kings 10:11||]][[4 Kings 10:17||]] and the like are read to have been destroyed for their crimes. [[14:11|but the tabernacles|Tabernacula]], that is, the congregations, [[14:11|of the just shall flourish|justorum germinabunt]], that is, they will bring forth the fruit of virtues, according to that saying of the Psalm: [[Ps 91:13|The just shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow up like the cedar of Libanus|Justus ut palma florebit, sicut cedrus Libani multiplicabitur]]. And in Osee it is said: [[Osee 14:6|I will be as the dew, Israel shall spring as the lily, and his root shall shoot forth as that of Libanus|Ero quasi ros; Israel germinabit sicut lilium, et erumpet radix ejus ut Libani]].

paras.t: Est via, quæ videtur homini justa, id est, quædam, imo et multiplex est actio seu conversatio et observantia, quam homines reputant justam: novissima autem ejus deducunt ad mortem, id est, ipsa cum suis effectibus atque demeritis, tandem trahit ad gehennalem interitum, eo quod non sit vere bona, virtuosa et meritoria, sed apparenter duntaxat. Multa etenim vitia habent speciem seu apparentiam et colorem quemdam virtutum: sicut dissolutio reputatur alacritas et spiritualis lætitia, mœror quoque maturitas, et zelus amarus fervor justitiæ. Sic immoderatam abstinentiam, et proprii sensus immansionem, multi putant temperantiæ actum atque constantiam. Hinc in Proverbiis suis Seneca loquitur: Timidus cautum se vocat, sordidus parcum. Necesse est ergo radium discretionis habere, sapientioribus credere, singularitatem vitare, atque sanctorum Patrum sectari exempla ac documenta, nec proprium sequi sensum, quum dicat Philosophus: Qualis unusquisque est, talia dicit, talia operatur, et taliter vivit. Et iterum disseruit: Desiderium pueri, id est imperfecti, oportet esse secundum præceptum doctoris. Denique, teste divino Dionysio, Nihil desideratur aut agitur, nisi sub ratione aut apparentia boni. Idcirco et vitiosi viam suam æstimant bonam.
paras.en: [[14:12|There is a way which seemeth just to a man|Est via, quæ videtur homini justa]], that is, there is a certain action, nay many a one, or way of life and observance, which men reckon just: [[14:12|but the ends thereof lead to death|novissima autem ejus deducunt ad mortem]], that is, it, with its effects and demerits, draws at last to destruction in hell, because it is not truly good, virtuous and meritorious, but only in appearance. For many vices have the look or appearance and a certain colour of virtues: as dissipation is reckoned eagerness and spiritual joy, gloom as gravity, and bitter zeal as fervour for justice. So too many think immoderate abstinence and the clinging to one's own opinion [Latin *proprii sensus immansionem*, 'abiding in one's own sense'] to be an act of temperance and constancy. Hence Seneca says in his Proverbs: The timid man calls himself cautious, the mean man thrifty. It is necessary, then, to have the ray of discretion, to trust those wiser than oneself, to avoid singularity, and to follow the examples and teachings of the holy Fathers, and not to follow one's own opinion; since the Philosopher says: As each man is, such things he says, such things he does, and so he lives. And again he taught: The desire of a child, that is, of one not yet perfect, must be according to the teacher's precept. Lastly, on the witness of the divine Dionysius, Nothing is desired or done except under the aspect or appearance of good. Therefore the vicious too think their way good.

paras.t: Risus dolore miscebitur: id est, vanam lætitiam pœna sequitur, et dolor remordentis conscientiæ, dissolutioni risuum sociatur. Ideo ait Salvator: Væ vobis qui ridetis, quia plorabitis et flebitis. Ad quod applicari potest quod sanctus Job contestatur: Versa est in luctum cithara mea, et organum meum in vocem flentium. Et extrema gaudii luctus occupat, id est, desolatio infernalis consequitur finem gaudiorum inanium sæculi hujus, juxta illud beati Job: Tenent tympanum et citharam, et gaudent ad sonitum organi; ducunt in bonis dies suos, et in puncto ad infernum descendunt. Ideo ait Filius Dei: Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis. De hoc luctu iterum ait: Ibi erit fletus et stridor dentium.
paras.en: [[14:13|Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow|Risus dolore miscebitur]]: that is, punishment follows vain joy, and the pain of a gnawing conscience goes with the dissipation of laughter. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that now laugh: for you shall mourn and weep|Væ vobis qui ridetis, quia plorabitis et flebitis]]. To which may be applied what holy Job declares: [[Job 30:31|My harp is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of those that weep|Versa est in luctum cithara mea, et organum meum in vocem flentium]]. [[14:13|and mourning taketh hold of the ends of joy|Et extrema gaudii luctus occupat]], that is, the desolation of hell follows on the end of the empty joys of this world, according to that saying of blessed Job: [[Job 21:12|They take the timbrel, and the harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ|Tenent tympanum et citharam, et gaudent ad sonitum organi]]; [[Job 21:13|They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment they go down to hell|ducunt in bonis dies suos, et in puncto ad infernum descendunt]]. Therefore the Son of God says: [[Luke 13:5|except you do penance, you shall all likewise perish|Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis]]. Of this mourning he says again: [[Matt 8:12|there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth|Ibi erit fletus et stridor dentium]][[Matt 13:42||]][[Matt 13:50||]][[Matt 24:51||]][[Matt 25:30||]][[Luke 13:28||]].

paras.t: Viis suis replebitur stultus, id est, iniquus implebitur retributione ac pœnis demeritorum actionum suarum, sicut per Ezechielem Dominus dixit: Unumquemque secundum viam suam judicabo. Et super eum erit vir bonus: id est impio præferet Deus justum, et virtuosos qui nunc conculcantur ab iniquis, in futuro judicio erunt super illos. Sæpe etiam et a multis justus iniquo præfertur.
paras.en: [[14:14|A fool shall be filled with his own ways|Viis suis replebitur stultus]], that is, the wicked man will be filled with the requital and punishments of his ill-deserving actions, as the Lord said through Ezechiel: I will [[Ezech 18:30|judge every man according to his ways|Unumquemque secundum viam suam judicabo]][[Ezech 33:20||]]. [[14:14|and the good man shall be above him|Et super eum erit vir bonus]]: that is, God will set the just man before the wicked, and the virtuous, who are now trampled on by the wicked, will be above them at the judgment to come. Often too the just man is preferred to the wicked by many.

paras.t: Innocens, id est inexpertus et nondum discretionem adeptus, seu bonus et simplex in se, putans alios esse qualis ipse est, credit omni verbo, non suspicans malum de alio. Hinc Assuerus rex loquitur: Quidam aures principum simplices, et ex sua natura alios æstimantes, callida fraude decipiunt. Sed, sicut in libro de Consideratione sanctus scribit Bernardus, Credendi facilitas, præsertim in præside aliorum, est valde periculosa, et horribilia mala sequuntur ex ea, videlicet suspiciones perversæ, indignationes, detractiones, injuriæ ac persecutiones justorum. Hinc inducit Joannes: Nolite omni spiritui credere, sed probate spiritus, si ex Deo sint; Ecclesiasticus quoque, Qui cito credit, levis corde est. Seneca quoque in epistola tertia: Neutrum faciendum est, et utrumque vitium est, et omnibus credere, et nulli. Pensandum est ergo qualis sit ipse qui dicit. Ideo sequitur: Astutus considerat gressus suos, id est, actus suos perpendit, qualiter debeat se habere, et ne incauta ac facili credulitate fallatur. Hinc in Proverbiis suis docet Cyrillus: Velociore aure est audiendum, et gravi corde credendum. Oportet enim diligenter advertere, quid et cui credatur. Revera minus provide amico et inimico pariter creditur, quum amore et odio, libra linguæ, pondere affectionis fallacis in obliquitatem trahatur. Verum nulli securius, quam amico de malis, et inimico de bonis accommodatur auditus. De te vero nunquam credas inimico tuo in æternum: quia si bene dicit, sophista est, de bono tendit ad malum; si male dicit, facit quod suum est.
paras.en: [[14:15|The innocent|Innocens]], that is, one inexperienced who has not yet gained discretion, or one good and simple in himself, who thinks others are such as he is, [[14:15|believeth every word|credit omni verbo]], not suspecting evil of another. Hence King Assuerus says: Some [[Esth 16:6|with crafty fraud they deceive the ears of princes that are well meaning, and judge of others by their own nature|aures principum simplices, et ex sua natura alios æstimantes, callida fraude decipiunt]]. But, as St. Bernard writes in his book On Consideration, Readiness to believe, above all in one set over others, is very dangerous, and dreadful evils follow from it: perverse suspicions, indignation, detraction, wrongs and persecutions of the just. Hence John brings in: [[1 John 4:1|believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God|Nolite omni spiritui credere, sed probate spiritus, si ex Deo sint]] [the margin gives John 4:1; the words are from the first Epistle of John]; and Ecclesiasticus too: [[Ecclus 19:4|He that is hasty to give credit, is light of heart|Qui cito credit, levis corde est]]. Seneca too, in his third letter: Neither is to be done, and both are a fault, to believe all and to believe none. One must weigh, then, what sort of man he is who speaks. Therefore there follows: [[14:15|the discreet man considereth his steps|Astutus considerat gressus suos]], that is, he weighs his acts, how he ought to bear himself, and that he be not deceived by an incautious and easy credulity. Hence Cyril teaches in his Proverbs: One must listen with a quicker ear, and believe with a weightier heart. For one must notice carefully what is believed, and whom. Indeed it is unwise to believe friend and enemy alike, since by love and hatred the balance of the tongue is drawn awry by the weight of deceitful affection. But to no one is a hearing given more safely than to a friend about evils, and to an enemy about good things. But about thyself never believe thine enemy: for if he speaks well, he is a sophist, tending from good to evil; if he speaks ill, he does what is his own.

paras.t: Sapiens timet Deum offendere, et declinat a malo, id est a peccato et occasione peccati, et ab omni specie mali, secundum doctrinam Apostoli, ne aliquem scandalizet. Stultus transilit, id est, imprudens præcipitanter in mala culpæ se ingerit, ac periculo se exponit; et confidit evadere, diuque vivere, et postea pœnitere. Circa hoc dicit Glossa: Sicut stulti est, de sua velocitate confidere, torrentemque rapidum aut voraginem saltu velle transire; sic sapientis est, ad planum vel ad pontem divertere. Ita qui culpam pro posse declinat, timens ne malis involvatur, est sapiens. Stultus vero est qui contemnit et peccat, blandiens sibi quod postea pœnitebit, aut pœnas fortiter sustinebit.
paras.en: [[14:16|A wise man feareth|Sapiens timet]] to offend God, [[14:16|and declineth from evil|et declinat a malo]], that is, from sin and the occasion of sin, and from [[1 Thess 5:22|all appearance of evil|omni specie mali]], according to the teaching of the Apostle, lest he scandalize anyone. [[14:16|the fool leapeth over|Stultus transilit]], that is, the imprudent man throws himself headlong into the evils of guilt and exposes himself to danger; [[14:16|and is confident|et confidit]] of escaping, and of living long, and of repenting afterwards. On this the Gloss says: As it belongs to a fool to trust in his own swiftness and to want to cross a rushing torrent or a whirlpool at a leap, so it belongs to a wise man to turn aside to level ground or to a bridge. So he who avoids guilt as far as he can, fearing to be entangled in evils, is wise. But he is a fool who despises and sins, flattering himself that he will repent afterwards, or will bear the punishments bravely.

paras.t: Impatiens operabitur stultitiam, id est, stulte, irrationabiliter et inhoneste se habet in apparatu, verbis ac gestu, eo quod impatientiæ passio rationem ejus obtenebret, et ipsum impetuose exagitet. Sustinenda sunt ergo adversa absque tristitia; et quo laudabilior est patientia, eo impatientia vituperabilior est. Et vir versutus, id est fraudulentus, hypocrita, simulator, odiosus est, in quantum talis. Estque impatiente deterior, juxta Glossam: quia impatiens palam ostendit stultitiam suam; versutus vero, quum sit corde perversus, simplicitatem simulat, atque humano judicio sanctus inter reprobos æstimatur. Sed, ut Cicero fatur, pleniusque Cyrillus, Non est prudentia vera, nisi quæ simplicitatis innocentia decoratur. Prudentia namque est ars præclarissima recte vivendi cum simplicitate, quæ est nescientia quemquam lædendi.
paras.en: [[14:17|The impatient man shall work folly|Impatiens operabitur stultitiam]], that is, he bears himself foolishly, unreasonably and unbecomingly in his bearing, words and gestures, because the passion of impatience darkens his reason and drives him violently about. Adversities, then, are to be borne without sadness; and the more praiseworthy patience is, the more blameworthy is impatience. [[14:17|and the crafty man|Et vir versutus]], that is, the deceitful man, the hypocrite, the dissembler, [[14:17|is hateful|odiosus est]], in so far as he is such. And he is worse than the impatient man, according to the Gloss: for the impatient man shows his folly openly; but the crafty man, though perverse at heart, feigns simplicity, and by human judgment is reckoned a saint among the reprobate. But, as Cicero says, and Cyril more fully, There is no true prudence unless it is adorned with the innocence of simplicity. For prudence is the most excellent art of living rightly with simplicity, which is not knowing how to hurt anyone.

paras.t: Possidebunt parvuli stultitiam. Hoc de parvulis sensu, id est intellectu, est accipiendum, et etiam de parvulis ætate, qui ante annos discretionis ad inania inclinantur. Unde scriptum est infra: Stultitia colligata est in corde pueri. Apostolus quoque: Nolite, inquit, fieri parvuli sensu. Et exspectabunt astuti, id est sagaces, scientiam: quia in scientiis student proficere.
paras.en: [[14:18|The childish shall possess folly|Possidebunt parvuli stultitiam]]. This is to be taken of those who are children in sense, that is, in understanding, and also of those who are children in age, who before the years of discretion are inclined to empty things. Hence it is written below: [[Prov 22:15|Folly is bound up in the heart of a child|Stultitia colligata est in corde pueri]]. The Apostle too: [[1 Cor 14:20|do not|Nolite]], he says, [[1 Cor 14:20|become children in sense|fieri parvuli sensu]]. [[14:18|and the prudent shall look for|Et exspectabunt astuti]], that is, the shrewd, [[14:18|knowledge|scientiam]]: for they are eager to make progress in the sciences.

paras.t: Jacebunt mali ante bonos, et impii ante portas justorum. Hoc sæpe contingit in vita hac, in qua rei a judicibus justis damnantur. Verumtamen in sæculo isto sæpius contingit oppositum, ita quod justi impiis subjiciuntur et opprimuntur ab eis, sicut asserit Habacuc: Quia impius prævalet adversus justum, propterea egreditur judicium perversum. Sed in die judicii, coram electis et justis erunt prostrati reprobi et injusti: qui et in inferno positi, præbebunt Beatis spectaculum, qui lætabuntur visa vindicta atque miseria iniquorum, juxta illud: Egrediemini, et salietis quasi vituli de armento, et calcabitis impios. Et alibi: Egredientur, et videbunt cadavera virorum qui prævaricati sunt in me; et erunt usque ad satietatem visionis omni carni. Egredientur autem Beati, non tam corporeo exitu, quam intellectuali intuitu.
paras.en: [[14:19|The evil shall fall down before the good: and the wicked before the gates of the just|Jacebunt mali ante bonos, et impii ante portas justorum]]. This often happens in this life, in which the guilty are condemned by just judges. Yet in this world the opposite happens more often, so that the just are made subject to the wicked and oppressed by them, as Habacuc declares: [[Hab 1:4|because the wicked prevaileth against the just, therefore wrong judgment goeth forth|Quia impius prævalet adversus justum, propterea egreditur judicium perversum]]. But on the day of judgment the reprobate and unjust will lie prostrate before the elect and the just: and, set in hell, they will offer a spectacle to the Blessed, who will rejoice at the sight of the vengeance[[Ps 57:11||]] and the misery of the wicked, according to that saying: [[Mal 4:2|you shall go forth, and shall leap like calves of the herd|Egrediemini, et salietis quasi vituli de armento]], and [[Mal 4:3|you shall tread down the wicked|et calcabitis impios]]. And elsewhere: [[Is 66:24|they shall go out, and see the carcasses of the men that have transgressed against me|Egredientur, et videbunt cadavera virorum qui prævaricati sunt in me]]; [[Is 66:24|they shall be a loathsome sight to all flesh|et erunt usque ad satietatem visionis omni carni]] [Latin *usque ad satietatem visionis*, 'to the full sating of sight']. The Blessed will go out, however, not so much by a bodily going forth as by the gaze of the understanding.

paras.t: Etiam proximo suo pauper odiosus erit. Quidam enim sunt tam elati, crudeles et impii, quod aspernantur et odiunt pauperes, et de pauperibus suis cognatis verecundantur. Amici vero divitum, multi: qui applaudunt divitibus, quos beatificant corde, et ab eis commodum vel honorem consequi sperant.
paras.en: [[14:20|The poor man shall be hateful even to his own neighbour|Etiam proximo suo pauper odiosus erit]]. For some are so proud, cruel and impious that they spurn and hate the poor, and are ashamed of their poor kinsfolk. [[14:20|but the friends of the rich are many|Amici vero divitum, multi]]: who applaud the rich, whom they count happy in their hearts, and from whom they hope to gain profit or honour.

paras.t: Qui despicit proximum suum, peccat. Præsertim si spernit illum quoniam pauper est, aut in quantum homo. Si autem spernit eum in quantum iniquus est, et tamen personam ejus spiritualiter amat, non peccat. Hinc loquitur Isaias: Quum videris nudum, operi eum, et carnem tuam ne despexeris. Etiam Malachias propheta ait: Nonne Pater unus omnium nostrum? nonne Deus unus creavit nos? Quare ergo despicit unusquisque fratrem suum, violans pactum patrum nostrorum? Qui autem miseretur pauperis, beatus erit: juxta illud, Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. Qui credit in Domino, fide quæ per dilectionem operatur, misericordiam diligit: quia appetit sibi a Deo misericordiam fieri, et proximis suis misericors est. Nam tali fidei pietas est conjuncta.
paras.en: [[14:21|He that despiseth his neighbour, sinneth|Qui despicit proximum suum, peccat]]. Above all if he spurns him because he is poor, or in so far as he is a man. But if he spurns him in so far as he is wicked, and yet loves his person spiritually, he does not sin. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 58:7|when thou shalt see one naked, cover him, and despise not thy own flesh|Quum videris nudum, operi eum, et carnem tuam ne despexeris]]. The prophet Malachias too says: [[Mal 2:10|Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why then doth every one of us despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers?|Nonne Pater unus omnium nostrum? nonne Deus unus creavit nos? Quare ergo despicit unusquisque fratrem suum, violans pactum patrum nostrorum]] [[14:21|but he that sheweth mercy to the poor, shall be blessed|Qui autem miseretur pauperis, beatus erit]]: according to that saying, [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy|Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur]]. [[14:21|He that believeth in the Lord|Qui credit in Domino]], with [[Gal 5:6|faith that worketh by Charity|fide quæ per dilectionem operatur]], [[14:21|loveth mercy|misericordiam diligit]]: for he desires that mercy be shown him by God, and he is merciful to his neighbours; for loving-kindness is joined to such faith.

paras.t: Errant, qui operantur malum: quia rationis judicium in eis est obscuratum, et a rectitudine æquitatis divertunt se, atque ab ultimo deviant fine. Misericordia et veritas præparant bona, id est, ad omne bonum aptum faciunt hominem. Justus enim vivit ex fidei veritate; et qui misericordiam exhibet proximo, misericordiam sortitur a Deo, qui ait in Evangelio: Estote misericordes, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis misericors est. Mensuram bonam et confertam et coagitatam et supereffluentem, dabunt in sinum vestrum. Potest quoque per veritatem justitia designari, quæ debet misericordiam temperare.
paras.en: [[14:22|They err that work evil|Errant, qui operantur malum]]: for the judgment of reason is darkened in them, and they turn aside from the rightness of equity, and stray from the last end. [[14:22|but mercy and truth prepare good things|Misericordia et veritas præparant bona]], that is, they make a man fit for every good. For the just man lives by the truth of faith[[Hab 2:4||]][[Rom 1:17||]]; and he who shows mercy to his neighbour obtains mercy from God, who says in the Gospel: [[Luke 6:36|Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful|Estote misericordes, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis misericors est]]. [[Luke 6:38|good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom|Mensuram bonam et confertam et coagitatam et supereffluentem, dabunt in sinum vestrum]]. By truth, too, justice may be signified, which ought to temper mercy.

paras.t: In omni opere bono erit abundantia, id est præmium copiosum, affluentia gratiæ, et spiritualis profectus, dummodo homo toto suo conatu faciat illud: et per bonum opus intelligendum est hic omnis actio virtuosa, interior sive exterior. Ubi autem verba sunt plurima, id est superflua, ibi frequenter egestas, id est defectus sapientiæ ac virtutis. Sapientes namque et virtuosi, in verbis sunt moderati ac parci; et qui minus scientifici sunt, magis solent se verbis jactare ac sermonibus abundare. In multiloquio quoque non deest peccatum: et qui multis utitur verbis, lædit animam suam. Ideo ait Bernardus: Væ nobis, qui spiritum habemus in naribus, qui pleni rimarum effluimus undique. Et Seneca testatur: Locutum me aliquando pœnituit, tacuisse nunquam.
paras.en: In every good work [[14:23|there shall be abundance|erit abundantia]] [Denis reads *In omni opere bono*, 'in every good work'; the Douay-Rheims has 'In much work'], that is, a plentiful reward, an outpouring of grace, and spiritual progress, provided a man does it with all his effort: and by good work is to be understood here every virtuous action, inward or outward. [[14:23|but where there are many words|Ubi autem verba sunt plurima]], that is, superfluous ones, [[14:23|there is oftentimes want|ibi frequenter egestas]], that is, a lack of wisdom and virtue. For the wise and virtuous are moderate and sparing in words; and those who know less are wont to boast more in words and to abound in talk. [[Prov 10:19|In the multitude of words there shall not want sin|In multiloquio quoque non deest peccatum]] too: and [[Ecclus 20:8|He that useth many words shall hurt his own soul|qui multis utitur verbis, lædit animam suam]]. Therefore Bernard says: Woe to us, who have the spirit in our nostrils, who, being full of cracks, leak out on every side. And Seneca declares: I have sometimes repented of having spoken, never of having kept silent.

paras.t: Corona sapientium, divitiæ eorum: id est, spiritualis opulentia seu copia meritorum hominum virtuosorum, est causa et ratio æternæ felicitatis ipsorum. Similiter divitiæ quæ virtuose expenduntur, eis proficiunt ad salutem. Fatuitas stultorum, imprudentia: quia non dirigunt actus suos recte ad ultimum et beatificum finem; sicque carent vera prudentia, cujus est media ad finem congruentia apte disponere.
paras.en: [[14:24|The crown of the wise, is their riches|Corona sapientium, divitiæ eorum]]: that is, the spiritual wealth or store of merits of virtuous men is the cause and ground of their eternal happiness. Likewise riches that are spent virtuously profit them for salvation. [[14:24|the folly of fools, imprudence|Fatuitas stultorum, imprudentia]]: for they do not direct their acts rightly to the last and beatifying end; and so they lack true prudence, whose work it is fitly to order the means suited to the end.

paras.t: Liberat animas testis fidelis. Talis enim in foro judicii eruit innocentes a morte, sicut S. Nicolaus tres juvenes morti adjudicatos, deinde tres principes innocentes morti addictos; Daniel quoque propheta, Susannam. Maxime autem, qui tempore persecutionis testimonium perhibet fidei christianæ, multos eruit a morte perfidiæ ac gehennæ, ut patuit de S. Sebastiano et innumerabilibus aliis. Et profert mendacia, imo et falsa testimonia, versipellis, id est dolosus, qui est quasi pellis eversa, quoniam aliud habet in corde, aliudque in ore: et juxta aliorum favorem ac commoda sua, et juxta passionum suarum alternationem, variat propriam vocem. Contra quos loquitur Seneca: Perhibe testimonium veritati, non amicitiæ.
paras.en: [[14:25|A faithful witness delivereth souls|Liberat animas testis fidelis]]. For such a one in the court of judgment rescues the innocent from death, as St. Nicholas did three young men condemned to death, and then three innocent princes sentenced to death; and the prophet Daniel, Susanna[[Dan 13:45||]]. But above all he who in time of persecution bears witness to the Christian faith rescues many from the death of unbelief and of hell, as was seen in St. Sebastian and countless others. And [[14:25|the double dealer|versipellis]] [[14:25|uttereth lies|profert mendacia]], nay, false testimonies too, that is, the deceitful man, who is like a skin turned inside out [*versipellis*, literally 'skin-turner'], since he has one thing in his heart and another in his mouth: and according to others' favour and his own advantage, and according to the changes of his passions, he alters his own voice. Against such Seneca says: Bear witness to the truth, not to friendship.

paras.t: In timore Domini consistit fiducia fortitudinis, id est firma et fortis confidentia mentis in Deo. Qui enim sibi conscius est se coram Deo timorate vixisse, et ipsum filialiter timuisse, rite confidit in eo, ejusque auxilio sperat suæ salutis adversariis prævalere. Talis enim timor facit peccata sincera intentione vitare, et bonam utique conscientiam parit. Ideo timoratus Job dixit: Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo. Et Tobias, qui ab infantia sua timuit Deum, magnam passus adversitatem, scilicet excæcationem, atque ab amicis ac conjuge irrisionem, nequaquam a sua motus fiducia, dixit: Noli timere, fili mi; pauperem quidem vitam gerimus, sed habebimus multa bona, si timuerimus Deum. Hinc ait Gregorius: Timor Domini fiduciam fortitudinis præstat: quia mens nostra tanto validius terrores rerum temporalium despicit, quanto veriori formidine earum Creatori se subdidit. Et filiis tuis, scilicet Dei (seu filiis ejus, puta divini timoris), erit spes efficax et beata, id est, efficaciter et condigne sperabunt in Domino, sperantes ex ejus pietate ac meritis propriis adipisci salutem, juxta illud: Timenti Deum bene erit in extremis, et in die defunctionis benedicetur. Porro, filii timoris vocantur, qui valde intenti sunt ei, et enutriti in eo, ac juxta inclinationem ipsius vivunt et operantur, sicut in simili ait Apostolus: Quicumque Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi filii sunt Dei. Et secundum hunc modum, quidam dicuntur filii sapientiæ ac virtutum.
paras.en: [[14:26|In the fear of the Lord is confidence of strength|In timore Domini consistit fiducia fortitudinis]], that is, a firm and strong confidence of the mind in God. For he who is conscious of having lived in fear before God, and of having feared him as a son, rightly trusts in him, and hopes by his help to prevail over the enemies of his salvation. For such fear makes a man avoid sins with a sincere intention, and certainly brings forth a good conscience. Therefore the God-fearing Job said: [[Job 13:15|Although he should kill me, I will trust in him|Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo]]. And Tobias, who [[Tob 2:13|feared God from his infancy|ab infantia sua timuit Deum]], having suffered great adversity, namely blindness[[Tob 2:11||]], and mockery from his friends and his wife[[Tob 2:15||]][[Tob 2:16||]][[Tob 2:22||]][[Tob 2:23||]], was in no way moved from his confidence, and said: [[Tob 4:23|Fear not, my son: we lead indeed a poor life, but we shall have many good things if we fear God|Noli timere, fili mi; pauperem quidem vitam gerimus, sed habebimus multa bona, si timuerimus Deum]]. Hence Gregory says: The fear of the Lord gives confidence of strength: for our mind despises the terrors of temporal things the more stoutly, the more truly it has submitted itself in fear to their Creator. And for thy children, namely God's (or [[14:26|for his children|filiis ejus]], that is, of the divine fear), [[14:26|there shall be hope|erit spes]], effective and blessed: that is, they will hope in the Lord effectively and worthily, hoping to obtain salvation from his loving-kindness and from their own merits, according to that saying: [[Ecclus 1:13|With him that feareth the Lord, it shall go well in the latter end, and in the day of his death he shall be blessed|Timenti Deum bene erit in extremis, et in die defunctionis benedicetur]]. Further, those are called children of fear who are wholly intent on it and brought up in it, and live and act according to its bent; as the Apostle says in a like case: [[Rom 8:14|whosoever are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God|Quicumque Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi filii sunt Dei]]. And in this way some are called children of wisdom and of the virtues.

paras.t: Timor Domini, fons vitæ: quia conservat mentem in vita gratiæ, et actiones meritoriæ procedunt ex isto timore, sicut rivi ex fonte; ut declinet a ruina mortis, id est, ipsum timentem faciat a morte peccati ac inferni divertere. Quum enim expellat peccata et conservet in gratia, recte vocatur fons vitæ, imo quodammodo causa totius boni. Nam, ut asserit Isaias, Hic est omnis fructus, ut auferatur iniquitas: quam sine infusione gratiæ ac virtutum certum est non auferri. Ideo dixit Psalmista: Timete Dominum, omnes sancti ejus, quoniam nihil deest timentibus eum.
paras.en: [[14:27|The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life|Timor Domini, fons vitæ]]: for it keeps the mind in the life of grace, and meritorious actions proceed from this fear as streams from a fountain; [[14:27|to decline from the ruin of death|ut declinet a ruina mortis]], that is, so that it make the one who fears turn aside from the death of sin and of hell. For since it drives out sins and keeps a man in grace, it is rightly called a fountain of life, nay, in a manner the cause of all good. For, as Isaias declares, [[Is 27:9|this is all the fruit, that the sin thereof should be taken away|Hic est omnis fructus, ut auferatur iniquitas]]: and it is certain that iniquity is not taken away without the pouring in of grace and the virtues. Therefore the Psalmist said: [[Ps 33:10|Fear the Lord, all ye his saints: for there is no want to them that fear him|Timete Dominum, omnes sancti ejus, quoniam nihil deest timentibus eum]].

paras.t: In multitudine populi, dignitas regis: id est, ad regis pertinet dignitatem, quod multos habet populos et ministros sibi subjectos; et præsertim ad laudem et gloriam pertinet præsidentis, quod multos habet subditos compositos moribus, neque ordinatos. Sic et dignitas Christi resplendet in hoc, quod totus orbis terrarum ad ipsum conversus fuit, et convertetur. Hinc jussit: Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cælis est. Et e converso, in paucitate plebis, ignominia principis: quia ignominiosum est principi, paucos habere subjectos et inordinatos ministros. Exemplaritas namque et honestas, prudentia et virtus servorum ac subditorum, cedit in domini sui honorem. Propter quod quotidie oramus: Pater noster qui es in cælis, sanctificetur nomen tuum. Similiter inordinatio, perversitas, insipientia ministrorum, cedit in dedecus domini ac pastoris. Propter quod ait Apostolus ad Romanos: Nomen Dei per vos blasphematur in gentibus. Unde per Jeremiam Dominus dixit Judæis: Commaculastis nomen sanctum meum. Princeps quoque Apostolorum in prima sua hortatur Canonica: Conversationem vestram inter gentes habentes bonam, ut in eo quod detrectant de vobis, tanquam de malefactoribus, ex bonis operibus vos considerantes, glorificent Deum.
paras.en: [[14:28|In the multitude of people is the dignity of the king|In multitudine populi, dignitas regis]]: that is, it belongs to a king's dignity that he has many peoples and ministers subject to him; and above all it belongs to the praise and glory of one who presides that he has many subjects of settled character and well ordered [the print has *neque ordinatos*, 'nor ordered', apparently a slip for *atque*]. So too the dignity of Christ shines out in this, that the whole world has been converted to him, and will be converted. Hence he commanded: [[Matt 5:16|let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven|Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cælis est]]. And conversely, [[14:28|in the small number of the people the dishonour of the prince|in paucitate plebis, ignominia principis]]: for it is a disgrace to a prince to have few subjects and disorderly ministers. For the good example and uprightness, the prudence and virtue of servants and subjects, redound to their lord's honour. For this reason we pray daily: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name|Pater noster qui es in cælis, sanctificetur nomen tuum]]. Likewise the disorder, perversity and folly of ministers redound to the shame of their lord and shepherd. For this reason the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 2:24|the name of God through you is blasphemed among the Gentiles|Nomen Dei per vos blasphematur in gentibus]]. Hence through Jeremias the Lord said to the Jews: You [[Jer 34:16|have defiled my name|Commaculastis nomen sanctum meum]] [Denis reads 'my holy name']. The Prince of the Apostles too exhorts in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 2:12|Having your conversation good among the Gentiles: that whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may, by the good works which they shall behold in you, glorify God|Conversationem vestram inter gentes habentes bonam, ut in eo quod detrectant de vobis, tanquam de malefactoribus, ex bonis operibus vos considerantes, glorificent Deum]].

paras.t: Qui patiens est, multa gubernatur sapientia. Hoc enim est effectus et signum sapientiæ magnæ, quod homo intuitu æternorum, contemplatione divinorum, amore Christi, zeloque probitatis, et ad proximorum ædificationem, servat patientiam in adversis. Propter quod ait Philosophus, quod soli sapientes vincunt passiones. Qui autem impatiens est, exaltat stultitiam suam, id est, irrationabilem motum animi sui effundit præcipitanter, et quam inordinatus sit intus, stulte ostendit forinsecus.
paras.en: [[14:29|He that is patient, is governed with much wisdom|Qui patiens est, multa gubernatur sapientia]]. For this is the effect and sign of great wisdom, that a man, looking to eternal things, contemplating divine things, out of love of Christ and zeal for uprightness, and for the edification of his neighbours, keeps patience in adversities. For this reason the Philosopher says that only the wise overcome the passions. [[14:29|but he that is impatient, exalteth his folly|Qui autem impatiens est, exaltat stultitiam suam]], that is, he pours out headlong the unreasonable movement of his mind, and foolishly shows outwardly how disordered he is within.

paras.t: Vita carnium, sanitas cordis. Cor quandoque accipitur pro corporali parte et organo animali: de quo corde dicit Philosophus, quod sit primum vivens, et ultimum moriens. Hujus igitur cordis bona habitudo seu sanitas, est vita carnium, id est corporis animati et membrorum ipsius, quia ex corde sic sumpto procedunt spiritus et actiones vitales, motivæ ac animales ad corpus. Interdum vero, imo et sæpius, sumitur cor pro intellectu vel voluntate: cujus sanitas est virtutum integritas ac gaudium spirituale, ex quibus caro ad exercendum opera meritoria vegetatur. Putredo ossium est invidia: quia est pessima passio, menti corporique nociva, quia ossa mentis, id est virtutes, corrumpit, ossaque corporis labefacit. Ideo invidus jugiter affligit et punit semetipsum: et interior ejus insania, foris monstratur per signa miserrima: quia, ut ait Gregorius, Invidi color pallore afficitur, oculi deprimuntur, mens infelix accenditur, membra frigescunt, fit in cogitatione rabies, in dentibus stridor. Hinc fertur apud Job: Parvulum occidit invidia. Nempe qui invidet, virtutibus destitutum et defectuosum se esse demonstrat. Propter quod Seneca ait: Si invideris, major es; si invides, minor: vir autem bonitate præditus, nemini invidet.
paras.en: [[14:30|Soundness of heart is the life of the flesh|Vita carnium, sanitas cordis]]. The heart is sometimes taken for the bodily part and the organ of the animal life: of which heart the Philosopher says that it is the first thing to live and the last to die. The good condition or soundness of this heart, then, is the life of the flesh, that is, of the living body and its members, because from the heart so taken the spirits and the vital actions, those of movement and of the animal life, go out to the body. But at times, nay more often, the heart is taken for the understanding or the will: whose soundness is the wholeness of the virtues and spiritual joy, by which the flesh is quickened to perform meritorious works. [[14:30|envy is the rottenness of the bones|Putredo ossium est invidia]]: for it is a most evil passion, harmful to mind and body, since it corrupts the bones of the mind, that is, the virtues, and weakens the bones of the body. Therefore the envious man continually afflicts and punishes himself: and his inner madness is shown outwardly by most wretched signs: for, as Gregory says, The colour of the envious man is overcast with pallor, his eyes are downcast, his unhappy mind is inflamed, his limbs grow cold, there is rage in his thoughts, gnashing in his teeth. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 5:2|envy slayeth the little one|Parvulum occidit invidia]]. Indeed he who envies shows himself to be destitute of virtues and defective. For this reason Seneca says: If thou art envied, thou art the greater; if thou envy, the lesser: but a man endowed with goodness envies no one.

paras.t: Qui calumniatur egentem, id est defectuosum in naturalibus donis seu temporalibus rebus, exprobrat factori ejus, scilicet Deo creatori, qui talem fecit egentem, atque ad cujus imaginem factus est egens. Non ergo improperanda est alicui sua naturalis defectuositas aut paupertas, sed pie est dissimulanda, supportanda et adjuvanda. Propter quod subditur: honorat autem eum, videlicet Creatorem, qui miseretur pauperis: quia et Deus præcepit hoc, cujus præceptum implere, est eum honorare. Ipse quoque in sua imagine honoratur. Et Christus in Evangelio protestatur: Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis.
paras.en: [[14:31|He that oppresseth the poor|Qui calumniatur egentem]], that is, one lacking in natural gifts or in temporal goods, [[14:31|upbraideth his maker|exprobrat factori ejus]], namely God the Creator, who made such a one needy, and to whose image the needy man was made. No one, then, is to be reproached with his natural defect or his poverty, but it is to be kindly overlooked, borne with and relieved. For this reason it is added: [[14:31|honoureth him|honorat autem eum]], namely the Creator, [[14:31|he that hath pity on the poor|qui miseretur pauperis]]: for God too commanded this, and to fulfil his commandment is to honour him. He is honoured also in his image. And Christ declares in the Gospel: [[Matt 25:40|as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me|Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis]].

paras.t: In malitia sua expellitur impius, id est, propter sua peccata societate justorum privatur, æterna beatitudine spoliatur, et de membro Christi fit membrum diaboli. Sperat autem justus in morte sua, id est, tempore mortis confidit in Domino, juxta illud, Justus si morte præoccupatus fuerit, in refrigerio erit; et si pro justitia moritur, certus est de præmio talis mortis.
paras.en: [[14:32|The wicked man shall be driven out in his wickedness|In malitia sua expellitur impius]], that is, for his sins he is deprived of the company of the just, stripped of eternal blessedness, and from a member of Christ becomes a member of the devil. [[14:32|but the just hath hope in his death|Sperat autem justus in morte sua]], that is, at the time of death he trusts in the Lord, according to that saying, [[Wis 4:7|the just man, if he be prevented with death, shall be in rest|Justus si morte præoccupatus fuerit, in refrigerio erit]]; and if he dies for justice, he is sure of the reward of such a death.

paras.t: In corde prudentis requiescit sapientia, tanquam habitus intellectus, decor mentis, opulentia rationis: prudentia quoque et sapientia quæ est donum, non separantur ab invicem; et indoctos quosque erudiet verbo et opere, quibus datam sibi gratiam administrat.
paras.en: [[14:33|In the heart of the prudent resteth wisdom|In corde prudentis requiescit sapientia]], as the habit of the understanding, the beauty of the mind, the wealth of the reason: and prudence, and the wisdom that is a gift [that is, the gift of the Holy Ghost], are not separated from each other; [[14:33|and it shall instruct all the ignorant|et indoctos quosque erudiet]] by word and deed, to whom it ministers the grace given it.

paras.t: Justitia elevat gentem. Regnis enim et politiis justis prospere solet succedere: quod in veteri Testamento, tempore regum et subditorum justorum sic fuit. Justitia quoque, quum sit præclarissima virtus, valde dignificat justos, et Deo conformat, atque de isto exilio ad altitudinem et salutem regni cœlestis erigit ipsos. Miseros autem facit populos peccatum. Nam efficit eos viles et diaboli membra ac servos, deinde ad infernum deprimit eos: et sicut filii Israel tempore judicum ac regum suorum, varias pertulerunt calamitates et clades, propter sua peccata; ita et Christiani a Turcis et Sarracenis ac Tartaris, imo et mutuo miserabilius a se ipsis. Denique ipsa culpa est miseria major quam pœna, quia a salute magis elongat et impedit, ac felicitati magis contrariatur.
paras.en: [[14:34|Justice exalteth a nation|Justitia elevat gentem]]. For it is wont to go well with just kingdoms and commonwealths: as it was in the Old Testament in the time of just kings and subjects. Justice too, being a most excellent virtue, greatly ennobles the just, and makes them like God, and raises them from this exile to the height and salvation of the heavenly kingdom. [[14:34|but sin maketh nations miserable|Miseros autem facit populos peccatum]]. For it makes them vile, members and slaves of the devil, and then thrusts them down to hell: and as the children of Israel, in the time of their judges and kings, suffered various calamities and defeats for their sins, so too have Christians from the Turks, the Saracens and the Tartars, nay more wretchedly still from one another. Lastly, guilt itself is a greater misery than punishment, because it removes a man further from salvation and hinders it more, and is more contrary to happiness.

paras.t: Acceptus est regi minister intelligens: quia domino suo reverenter obedit, et causas sibi commissas fideliter ac prudenter exsequitur. Sic et Regi omnipotenti placet sapiens servus, idoneusque vicarius et prælatus. Unde ait Salvator: Quis putas est servus fidelis et prudens, quem constituit dominus super familiam suam? Iracundiam ejus inutilis sustinebit: id est, servo pigro, infideli, insipienti, dominus suus juste irascetur, præsertim negligenti et infructuoso prælato ac prædicatori, in quem subditorum quoque peccata redundant. Unde in Evangelio ait judex: Servum inutilem mittite in tenebras exteriores.
paras.en: [[14:35|A wise servant is acceptable to the king|Acceptus est regi minister intelligens]]: for he obeys his lord with reverence, and carries out faithfully and prudently the matters committed to him. So too a wise servant, and a fit vicar and prelate, pleases the almighty King. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 24:45|Who, thinkest thou, is a faithful and wise servant, whom his lord hath appointed over his family|Quis putas est servus fidelis et prudens, quem constituit dominus super familiam suam]]? [[14:35|he that is good for nothing shall feel his anger|Iracundiam ejus inutilis sustinebit]]: that is, with the slothful, unfaithful and foolish servant his lord will justly be angry, above all with the negligent and fruitless prelate and preacher, upon whom the sins of his subjects too fall back. Hence in the Gospel the judge says: [[Matt 25:30|the unprofitable servant, cast ye out into the exterior darkness|Servum inutilem mittite in tenebras exteriores]].

15.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI QUINTIDECIMI : RESPONSIO MOLLIS FRANGIT IRAM.
15.title_en: Declaration of the fifteenth chapter: A mild answer breaketh wrath.

paras.t: Responsio mollis frangit iram : id est, humilis ac modesta responsio hominis ab alio increpati, interrogati, aut comminationem perpessi, exstinguit aut mitigat iram corripientis aut comminantis seu interrogantis, qui videns sibi deferri, placatur. Malitia etenim vincitur bonitate, peccatum virtute, improbitas exemplaritate, ira mansuetudine. Ad quod admonens nos Apostolus : Noli, inquit, vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum. Tanta etenim, Seneca teste, est vis et laus probitatis, ut omnes ejus efficacia moveantur. Sic Abigail sua molli responsione fregit iram David; et Gedeon, Ephratæorum.
paras.en: [[15:1|A mild answer breaketh wrath|Responsio mollis frangit iram]]: that is, the humble and modest answer of a man who is rebuked, questioned or threatened by another quenches or softens the wrath of the one who rebukes, threatens or questions him; for he, seeing deference shown him, is appeased. For malice is overcome by goodness, sin by virtue, wickedness by good example, wrath by meekness. To this the Apostle admonishes us: [[Rom 12:21|Be not|Noli]], he says, [[Rom 12:21|overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good|vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum]]. For so great, as Seneca witnesses, is the force and the praise of uprightness, that all are moved by its power. So Abigail by her mild answer broke the wrath of David[[1 Kings 25:24||]]; and Gedeon that of the Ephratæans[[Judg 8:2||]] [the margin gives 1 Reg. xxv, 24–35 and Judic. viii, 2, 3].

paras.t: Sermo durus suscitat furorem. Qui enim alium dure et superbe alloquitur, provocat eum, quantum in se est, ad iram intensam. Aliqui tamen sunt ita perfecti, quod ex aliorum improbitate non concitantur ad passionem; quidam vero sunt boni, quamvis nondum perfecti, qui dum improbe offenduntur, graviter irascuntur. Propter quod Seneca in Proverbiis suis ait : Bonus animus læsus multo gravius irascitur. Denique fertur in Vitis Patrum, quod Abbas S. Macarius ad ecclesiam pergens, fecit discipulum suum præcedere : qui obvianti sibi sacerdoti idolorum, dixit : Quo curris, dæmon? Quo audito, sacerdos ille percussit discipulum B. Macarii, seminecem reliquit, atque pertransiit. Cui obvians S. Macarius, salutavit eumdem, dicens : Salve, laborator, salve. Ex cujus tam benevola salutatione admirans et compunctus sacerdos, conversus est. Quo facto, dixit sanctissimus pater Macarius : Sermo pius et dulcis duras mentes provocat ad virtutes; verba vero pungitiva, amara, superba, etiam bona corda provocant ad peccandum.
paras.en: [[15:1|A harsh word stirreth up fury|Sermo durus suscitat furorem]]. For he who speaks to another harshly and proudly provokes him, as far as in him lies, to intense wrath. Some, however, are so perfect that they are not roused to passion by the wickedness of others; but some are good, though not yet perfect, who are gravely angered when they are wickedly offended. Wherefore Seneca says in his Proverbs: A good mind, when wounded, is angered far more gravely. Lastly, it is related in the Lives of the Fathers that the Abbot St. Macarius, going to church, had his disciple go before him; and the disciple said to a priest of the idols who met him: Where are you running, demon? Hearing this, that priest struck the disciple of Bl. Macarius, left him half dead, and passed on. St. Macarius, meeting him, greeted him, saying: Hail, toiler, hail! Wondering at so kindly a greeting, and pierced with compunction, the priest was converted. When this had happened, the most holy father Macarius said: A kind and gentle word provokes hard minds to virtue; but stinging, bitter and proud words provoke even good hearts to sin.

paras.t: Lingua sapientium ornat scientiam, id est, ordinate et pulchre eam proponit, ita quod magis ab audientibus reputatur; os fatuorum ebullit stultitiam, id est, stolida verba impetuose indeliberateque evomit : per quæ interior manifestatur eorum fatuitas, quia ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. Sic hæretici et quidam philosophi suas effuderunt stultitias per verba et scripta contra doctores catholicos, præsertim Porphyrius, Julianus, Averroes et Celsus.
paras.en: [[15:2|The tongue of the wise adorneth knowledge|Lingua sapientium ornat scientiam]], that is, sets it forth in order and beautifully, so that it is the more esteemed by those who hear it; [[15:2|the mouth of fools bubbleth out folly|os fatuorum ebullit stultitiam]], that is, spews out stolid words impetuously and without deliberation, by which their inward folly is laid bare, for [[Matt 12:34|out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh|ex abundantia cordis os loquitur]]. So heretics and certain philosophers poured out their follies in words and writings against the Catholic doctors, especially Porphyry, Julian, Averroes and Celsus.

paras.t: In omni loco oculi Domini contemplantur bonos per approbationem, et malos per detestationem, sicut in Psalmo cantatur : Oculi Domini super justos, et aures ejus in preces eorum; vultus autem Domini super facientes mala. Hoc contra eos qui dixerunt divinam providentiam non pertingere usque ad ista terrena determinate cognoscenda, nec cognoscere actus humanos, nec privativa et vitia. De quibus Dominus ait Ezechieli : Dixerunt : Reliquit Dominus terram, et Dominus nos non videt. Unde et apud Sophoniam : Visitabo, inquit, super viros defixos in fæcibus suis, qui dicunt : Non faciet Dominus bene, et non faciet male. Atque Psalmista : Dixerunt, Quomodo scit Deus? et, Si est scientia in Excelso? Contra quos subtiliter arguit Propheta, dicendo : Intelligite, insipientes in populo, et stulti, aliquando sapite. Qui plantavit aurem, non audiet? aut qui finxit oculum, non considerat?
paras.en: [[15:3|The eyes of the Lord in every place behold the good|In omni loco oculi Domini contemplantur bonos]] by approving them, [[15:3|and the evil|et malos]] by detesting them, as is sung in the Psalm: [[Ps 33:16|The eyes of the Lord are upon the just: and his ears unto their prayers.|Oculi Domini super justos, et aures ejus in preces eorum]] [[Ps 33:17|But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things|vultus autem Domini super facientes mala]]. This is against those who said that divine providence does not reach so far as to know these earthly things determinately, nor knows human acts, nor privations [that is, defects, things that consist in the lack of some good] and vices. Of whom the Lord says to Ezechiel: [[Ezech 9:9|they have said: The Lord hath forsaken the earth, and the Lord seeth not|Dixerunt : Reliquit Dominus terram, et Dominus nos non videt]] [Denis reads nos, "seeth us not", as at Ezech 8:12]. And so in Sophonias: I, he says, [[Soph 1:12|will visit|Visitabo]] [[Soph 1:12|upon the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their hearts: The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil|super viros defixos in fæcibus suis, qui dicunt : Non faciet Dominus bene, et non faciet male]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 72:11|they said: How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?|Dixerunt, Quomodo scit Deus? et, Si est scientia in Excelso?]] Against whom the Prophet argues subtly, saying: [[Ps 93:8|Understand, ye senseless among the people: and, you fools, be wise at last.|Intelligite, insipientes in populo, et stulti, aliquando sapite]] [[Ps 93:9|He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? or he that formed the eye, doth he not consider?|Qui plantavit aurem, non audiet? aut qui finxit oculum, non considerat?]]

paras.t: Lingua placabilis, id est pacifica, quæ orando et laudando placat Deum sibi ac proximis, et discordantes reconciliat invicem, lignum vitæ, id est, vitaliter reficit corda pacificorum; quæ autem immoderata est, id est inconsiderata, præceps, superflua ad loquendum, conteret spiritum, id est, gratiam Spiritus Sancti aufert a mente, et spiritum seu animam loquentis, interdum etiam audientis, spiritualiter destruit, proferendo verba detractoria et mendosa, seminativa discordiæ, et consimilia, quæ ex suo genere sunt peccata mortalia. Hinc Hugo : Lingua dicitur, quoniam lingit adulando, mordet detrahendo, occidit mentiendo, ligat et ligari non potest, labitur ut anguilla, penetrat ut sagitta, tollit amicos, multiplicat inimicos, movet rixas, seminat discordias, uno ictu multos percutit et occidit, blanda est et subdola, lata et parata ad bona exhaurienda, commiscendaque mala.
paras.en: [[15:4|A peaceable tongue|Lingua placabilis]], that is, a peacemaking one, which by praying and praising appeases God toward itself and its neighbours [placabilis, "peaceable", comes from placare, "to appease"], and reconciles to one another those at variance, [[15:4|is a tree of life|lignum vitæ]], that is, refreshes with life the hearts of the peacemakers; [[15:4|but that which is immoderate|quæ autem immoderata est]], that is, inconsiderate, headlong, given to too much talk, [[15:4|shall crush the spirit|conteret spiritum]], that is, takes the grace of the Holy Spirit away from the mind, and spiritually destroys the spirit or soul of the speaker, and sometimes also of the hearer, by uttering detracting and lying words, words that sow discord, and the like, which in their kind are mortal sins [that is, grave sins of their nature, though in a particular case they may be venial]. Hence Hugh: The tongue (lingua) is so called because it licks (lingit) by flattering, bites by detracting, kills by lying; it binds and cannot be bound, slips away like an eel, pierces like an arrow, takes away friends, multiplies enemies, stirs up quarrels, sows discords, strikes and kills many at one blow; it is smooth and crafty, wide and ready to drain away good things and to mix in evil ones.

paras.t: Stultus, id est incorrigibilis, indocilis, et obstinatus in vitiis, irridet disciplinam patris sui carnalis ac spiritualis, imo et Dei Patris, quia salubrem correptionem ac justam castigationem abhorret ac despicit. Hinc de rebellibus Israelitis ait Dominus : Ego erudivi eos, et in me cogitaverunt malitiam : reversi sunt ut essent absque jugo. Qui autem custodit increpationes, eas patienter suscipiendo, memoriter retinendo, seque emendando, astutior, id est sagacior, fiet : quia vitando peccata, meretur illuminari a Deo, propriamque fragilitatem limpidius pensat, et deinceps cautius se habet, ex memoriis præteritorum perpendens ac vitans pericula futurorum. Unde in Jeremia, ubi nostra habet translatio, Erudire, Jerusalem, Septuaginta transtulerunt : Per omnem dolorem et flagellum erudieris.
paras.en: [[15:5|A fool|Stultus]], that is, one incorrigible, unteachable and obstinate in vice, [[15:5|laugheth at the instruction of his father|irridet disciplinam patris sui]], his father in the flesh and in the spirit, nay, even of God the Father, since he loathes and despises wholesome correction and just chastisement. Hence the Lord says of the rebellious Israelites: [[Osee 7:15|I have chastised them|Ego erudivi eos]] [erudivi means both "I have instructed" and "I have chastised", as disciplina in the verse treated means both "instruction" and "chastisement"], [[Osee 7:15|and they have imagined evil against me|et in me cogitaverunt malitiam]]: [[Osee 7:16|They returned, that they might be without yoke|reversi sunt ut essent absque jugo]]. But [[15:5|he that regardeth reproofs|Qui autem custodit increpationes]] [custodit, literally "keepeth"], receiving them patiently, keeping them in memory and amending himself, [[15:5|shall become|fiet]] [[15:5|prudent|astutior]], that is, more shrewd: for by avoiding sins he deserves to be enlightened by God, and he weighs his own frailty more clearly, and thereafter bears himself more warily, weighing and avoiding the dangers of the future from the memory of the past. Hence in Jeremias, where our translation has [[Jer 6:8|Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem|Erudire, Jerusalem]], the Septuagint translated: By every pain and scourge shalt thou be instructed.

paras.t: In abundanti justitia virtus maxima est, id est præcipua fortitudo et confortatio justi. Nam ipsa justitia est virtus præclara, justum in Deo confortans, sicut præhabitum est, Justus autem quasi fundamentum sempiternum : et infra habebitur, Justus quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit. Idcirco, abundans justitia est maxima animæ fortitudo. Potest tamen per abundantem justitiam, adimpletio consiliorum et exhibitio operum supererogationis intelligi : in quibus est præcipua fortitudo, hominisque perfectio, sicut asserit Christus : Si vis perfectus esse, vende omnia quæ habes, et da pauperibus, et sequere me. Cogitationes autem impiorum eradicabuntur, id est, ab effectu optato impedientur, atque a Judice summo condemnabuntur, juxta illud Psalmi : In illa die peribunt omnes cogitationes eorum.
paras.en: [[15:5|In abundant justice there is the greatest strength|In abundanti justitia virtus maxima est]] [virtus, "strength", is also the word for "virtue"], that is, the chief fortitude and strengthening of the just man. For justice itself is an excellent virtue, strengthening the just man in God, as was said above: [[Prov 10:25|The just is as an everlasting foundation|Justus autem quasi fundamentum sempiternum]]; and as will be said below: [[Prov 28:1|the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|Justus quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit]]. Therefore abundant justice is the greatest strength of the soul. Yet by abundant justice may also be understood the fulfilling of the counsels and the performance of works of supererogation [that is, good works beyond what the commandments require], in which lies the chief strength and the perfection of man, as Christ declares: [[Matt 19:21|If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor|Si vis perfectus esse, vende omnia quæ habes, et da pauperibus]], and [[Matt 19:21|follow me|sequere me]]. But [[15:5|the devices of the wicked shall be rooted out|Cogitationes autem impiorum eradicabuntur]], that is, they shall be hindered from the effect they desire, and condemned by the supreme Judge, according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 145:4|in that day all their thoughts shall perish|In illa die peribunt omnes cogitationes eorum]].

paras.t: Domus justi, plurima fortitudo. Domus justi est, vel cor ipsius, in quo per cogitationem et affectionem moratur; vel ejus domestici, vel posteritas, aut congregatio populi sibi subdita et commissa. In corde autem justi, est fortitudo sapientiæ ac virtutum; similiter in ejus domesticis et posteris, informationi et correctioni ejus acquiescentibus. Conformiter justus prælatus ac præsidens virtuosus, solet virtuosos habere subjectos. Et in fructibus impii, conturbatio. Fructus impii, sunt ejus delectationes inordinatæ et opera prava : in quibus est conturbatio, id est carentia pacis internæ, rebellio sensualitatis contra rationem, rationis quoque a Deo aversio, atque demeritum ad infernalem turbationem perducens. Hinc octavo Ethicorum docet Philosophus, quod vitiosus pacem non habet. Et in Isaia propheta habetur : Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus.
paras.en: [[15:6|The house of the just is very much strength|Domus justi, plurima fortitudo]]. The house of the just man is either his heart, in which he dwells by thought and affection; or his household, or his posterity, or the congregation of people subject and committed to him. In the heart of the just man is the strength of wisdom and of the virtues; and likewise in his household and his descendants, when they yield to his instruction and correction. In the same way a just prelate and a virtuous ruler commonly has virtuous subjects. [[15:6|And in the fruits of the wicked is trouble|Et in fructibus impii, conturbatio]]. The fruits of the wicked man are his disordered pleasures and evil works, in which is trouble: that is, the lack of inward peace, the rebellion of sensuality against reason, the turning of reason itself away from God, and demerit [that is, guilt that deserves punishment] leading to the turmoil of hell. Hence the Philosopher teaches in the eighth book of the Ethics that the vicious man has no peace. And in the prophet Isaias we have: [[Is 48:22|There is no peace to the wicked, saith the Lord.|Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus]]

paras.t: Labia sapientium disseminabunt scientiam, alios instruendo, utilia et doctrinalia proferendo : quod Christus et Apostoli summe fecerunt; cor stultorum dissimile erit cordi ac labiis sapientium, quoniam vanitatem et errores cor stulti disseminat, ut de hæreticis et aliis constat. Est quoque cor stulti sibi ipsi dissimile, quia diversis phantasiis ac vitiis variatur, et nunquam in eodem permanet statu. Quocontra de Anna legitur : Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati. Denique stultus, id est iniquus, non conatur imaginem Creatoris sui reformare in se; imo quotidie eam magis deturpat ac mundo conformat : sicque cor impii est suo Creatori dissimile, et mundo dæmonibusque conforme. Quamquam per naturam sit immateriale ac intellectuale, per propriam culpam est mundanum atque carnale. Contra quod hortatur Apostolus : Nolite conformari huic sæculo, sed renovamini in novitate sensus vestri.
paras.en: [[15:7|The lips of the wise shall disperse knowledge|Labia sapientium disseminabunt scientiam]], by instructing others, by uttering useful and instructive things, as Christ and the Apostles did in the highest degree; [[15:7|the heart of fools shall be unlike|cor stultorum dissimile erit]] the heart and lips of the wise, since the heart of the fool scatters vanity and errors, as is plain in heretics and others. The heart of the fool is also unlike itself, for it is varied by diverse fancies and vices, and [[Job 14:2|never continueth in the same state|nunquam in eodem permanet statu]]. Whereas of Anna we read: [[1 Kings 1:18|her countenance was no more changed|Vultus ejus non sunt amplius in diversa mutati]]. Lastly, the fool, that is, the wicked man, does not strive to reform in himself the image of his Creator; nay, daily he disfigures it more and conforms it to the world: and so the heart of the wicked is unlike its Creator, and conformed to the world and the demons. Although by nature it is immaterial and intellectual, by its own fault it is worldly and carnal. Against which the Apostle exhorts: [[Rom 12:2|be not conformed to this world: but be reformed in the newness of your mind|Nolite conformari huic sæculo, sed renovamini in novitate sensus vestri]] [Denis reads renovamini, "be renewed", where the Vulgate has reformamini].

paras.t: Victimæ impiorum abominabiles Domino. Hoc de sacrificiis legis evidenter verificatur, quia non erant in se ipsis seu ex parte operis operati, Deo accepta, sed solum ex fide, devotione et caritate offerentium ea. Unde in Psalmo Dominus testatur : Non accipiam de domo tua vitulos, neque de gregibus tuis hircos. Et Michæas propheta ait : Quid dignum offeram Domino? Numquid placari potest Dominus in millibus arietum, aut in multis millibus hircorum pinguium? Similiter, spiritualia sacrificia impiorum, scilicet orationes et consimiles actiones, quæ ex suo genere bonæ sunt, non sunt Deo accepta, quum scriptum sit : Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis. Verumtamen sacrificium evangelicæ legis, in se et per se acceptissimum est Deo Patri. Orationes quoque ministrorum Ecclesiæ iniquorum, non in quantum sunt particulares personæ, sed ut sunt publici ministri et officiati Ecclesiæ, efficaces sunt coram Deo, non tamen meritoriæ ipsis ministris hujusmodi. Vota justorum placabilia, id est, promissiones et desideria, ac votiva sacrificia virtuosorum hominum complacent Deo, qui respexit ad Abel et ad munera ejus, non autem ad Cain, neque ad munera ejus.
paras.en: [[15:8|The victims of the wicked are abominable to the Lord|Victimæ impiorum abominabiles Domino]]. This is plainly verified of the sacrifices of the Law, since they were not acceptable to God in themselves, or on the part of the work performed [that is, ex opere operato, by the mere performance of the rite, as the sacraments of the New Law give grace], but only through the faith, devotion and charity of those who offered them. Hence the Lord testifies in the Psalm: [[Ps 49:9|I will not take calves out of thy house: nor he goats out of thy flocks.|Non accipiam de domo tua vitulos, neque de gregibus tuis hircos]] And the prophet Micheas says: [[Mich 6:6|What shall I offer to the Lord that is worthy?|Quid dignum offeram Domino]] [[Mich 6:7|May the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams, or with many thousands of fat he goats?|Numquid placari potest Dominus in millibus arietum, aut in multis millibus hircorum pinguium?]] Likewise the spiritual sacrifices of the wicked, namely prayers and like actions, which are good in their kind, are not acceptable to God, since it is written: [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination.|Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]] Yet the sacrifice of the Gospel law is in itself and of itself most acceptable to God the Father. The prayers also of wicked ministers of the Church, not inasmuch as they are private persons, but as they are public ministers and officers of the Church, are effective before God, though not meritorious for such ministers themselves. [[15:8|The vows of the just are acceptable|Vota justorum placabilia]], that is, the promises and desires and votive sacrifices of virtuous men are pleasing to God, who [[Gen 4:4|had respect to Abel, and to his offerings|respexit ad Abel et ad munera ejus]], but not [[Gen 4:5|to Cain and his offerings|ad Cain, neque ad munera ejus]].

paras.t: Abominatio est Domino vita impii. De quo in Deuteronomio legitur, Aversatur Dominus omnem impietatem; et in Psalmo, Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus. Nam quanto quis sanctior ac justior est, tanto plus detestatur omnem iniquitatem. Quum ergo Deus essentialiter et incircumscriptibiliter sanctus et justus sit, constat quod incomparabiliter vitia abominetur. Qui sequitur justitiam, quæ est virtus communis et omnis virtus, id est, qui virtutes amplectitur, diligetur ab eo. Etenim justus Dominus, et justitias dilexit. Quicumque autem actualiter seu habitualiter justus est, diligetur a Deo, secundum præsentem justitiam, non tamen secundum prædestinationem æternam, nisi sit de numero electorum. Porro justus est qui observat præcepta. Ideo loquitur Christus : Qui diligit me, sermones meos servabit, et Pater meus diliget eum.
paras.en: [[15:9|The way of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord|Abominatio est Domino vita impii]] [Denis reads vita, "the life", where the Vulgate has via, "the way"]. Of which we read in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 25:16|He hateth all injustice|Aversatur Dominus omnem impietatem]] [Denis has "the Lord hateth all impiety"]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man the Lord will abhor|Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus]]. For the holier and more just anyone is, the more he detests all iniquity. Since, then, God is holy and just essentially and without bound, it is plain that He abhors vices beyond all comparison. [[15:9|He that followeth justice|Qui sequitur justitiam]], which is general virtue and all virtue [that is, justice in the wide sense, which takes in every virtue], that is, he who embraces the virtues, [[15:9|is beloved by him|diligetur ab eo]] [Denis has the future, "shall be loved"]. For [[Ps 10:8|the Lord is just, and hath loved justice|justus Dominus, et justitias dilexit]]. But whoever is just, actually or habitually, shall be loved by God according to his present justice, though not according to eternal predestination unless he be of the number of the elect. Now he is just who keeps the commandments. Therefore Christ says: [[John 14:23|If any one love me, he will keep my word. And my Father will love him|Qui diligit me, sermones meos servabit, et Pater meus diliget eum]].

paras.t: Doctrina mala deserentium viam vitæ. Frequenter impii prælati et prædicatores iniqui, qui viam vitæ, id est arctam viam salutis, relinquunt, docent bona, vera, salubria, sicut de Scribis et Pharisæis dixit Salvator : Super cathedram Moysis sederunt Scribæ et Pharisæi; quæcumque ergo dicunt vobis, facite. Quomodo igitur doctrina deserentium viam vitæ est mala? Est respondendum, quod mala est eis, quoniam peccant mortaliter evangelizando, et ea quæ prædicant non implendo.
