Est etiam mala, id est minus reputata, quoniam cujus vita despicitur, restat ut ejus prædicatio contemnatur. Ideo Seneca in suis ait Proverbiis : Omnis doctor in ratione vitæ peccans, est turpior ob hoc, quod in officio, cujus magister esse vult, labitur. Qui increpationes odit, morietur in sæculo isto per culpam, deinde per damnationem æternam : talis enim non cessat peccare. Et frequenter tales incorrigibiles, capitalia agunt facinora, propter quæ corporaliter occiduntur.
paras.en: [[15:10|Instruction is grievous to him that forsaketh the way of life|Doctrina mala deserentium viam vitæ]] [mala, "grievous", is literally "evil" or "bad", and Denis takes it so]. Wicked prelates and evil preachers, who forsake the way of life, that is, the narrow way of salvation, often teach good, true and wholesome things, as the Saviour said of the Scribes and Pharisees: [[Matt 23:2|The scribes and the Pharisees have sitten on the chair of Moses|Super cathedram Moysis sederunt Scribæ et Pharisæi]]; [[Matt 23:3|whatsoever they shall say to you, observe and do|quæcumque ergo dicunt vobis, facite]]. How then is the teaching of those who forsake the way of life evil? It must be answered that it is evil for them, since they sin mortally in preaching the Gospel and not fulfilling what they preach. It is evil also, that is, less esteemed, since when a man's life is despised, it follows that his preaching is scorned. Therefore Seneca says in his Proverbs: Every teacher who sins in the conduct of his life is the more disgraceful for this, that he falls in the very office of which he would be master. [[15:10|He that hateth reproof shall die|Qui increpationes odit, morietur]] in this world by sin, and afterwards by eternal damnation: for such a man does not cease to sin. And often such incorrigible men commit capital crimes, for which they are put to death in the body.

paras.t: Infernus et perditio coram Domino, id est, nota sunt ei, cujus oculis omnia nuda sunt et aperta : cui ait Propheta, Si descendero in infernum, ades. Quanto magis corda filiorum hominum Deo sunt cognita? Qui testatur : Scient omnes Ecclesiæ quia ego sum scrutans renes et corda. Unde Jeremias ait : Pravum est cor hominis et inscrutabile : quis cognoscet illud? Ego Dominus scrutans cor et probans renes. Cui specialis cura ac providentia est de rationalibus et intellectualibus creaturis.
paras.en: [[15:11|Hell and destruction are before the Lord|Infernus et perditio coram Domino]], that is, they are known to Him to whose eyes [[Heb 4:13|all things are naked and open|omnia nuda sunt et aperta]]; to whom the Prophet says: [[Ps 138:8|If I descend into hell, thou art present|Si descendero in infernum, ades]]. [[15:11|How much more the hearts of the children of men|Quanto magis corda filiorum hominum]] are known to God? Who testifies: [[Apoc 2:23|all the churches shall know that I am he that searcheth the reins and hearts|Scient omnes Ecclesiæ quia ego sum scrutans renes et corda]]. Hence Jeremias says: [[Jer 17:9|The heart is perverse above all things, and unsearchable, who can know it?|Pravum est cor hominis et inscrutabile : quis cognoscet illud?]] [Denis reads cor hominis, "the heart of man", where the Vulgate has cor omnium, rendered "above all things"] [[Jer 17:10|I am the Lord who search the heart, and prove the reins|Ego Dominus scrutans cor et probans renes]]. For He has a special care and providence over rational and intellectual creatures.

paras.t: Non amat pestilens, id est scandalose et publice male vivens, seu false docens, eum qui se corripit. Talis enim sedet in pestilentiæ cathedra, et habituatus est in sua malitia. Nec ad sapientes graditur, ut emendetur ab eis.
paras.en: [[15:12|A corrupt man loveth not|Non amat pestilens]] [pestilens, literally "pestilent"], that is, one who lives evilly, in scandal and in public, or teaches falsely, [[15:12|one that reproveth him|eum qui se corripit]]. For such a man sits in [[Ps 1:1|the chair of pestilence|pestilentiæ cathedra]], and is hardened by habit in his malice. [[15:12|Nor will he go to the wise|Nec ad sapientes graditur]], to be amended by them.

paras.t: Cor gaudens exhilarat faciem. Nam sive quis spiritualiter, sive carnaliter delectetur in corde, signa interioris jucunditatis relucent in facie, præsertim in oculis. In mœrore animi dejicitur spiritus, id est, anima ita deprimitur, quod signa internæ desolationis relucent in vultu, juxta illud : Cur vultus tuus tristis est, quum te ægrotum non videam? Non est hoc frustra, sed malum, nescio quod, in corde tuo est.
paras.en: [[15:13|A glad heart maketh a cheerful countenance|Cor gaudens exhilarat faciem]]. For whether one delights in heart spiritually or carnally, the signs of inward gladness shine out in the face, especially in the eyes. [[15:13|By grief of mind the spirit is cast down|In mœrore animi dejicitur spiritus]], that is, the soul is so weighed down that the signs of inward desolation shine out in the countenance, according to that word: [[2 Esd 2:2|Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou dost not appear to be sick? this is not without cause, but some evil, I know not what, is in thy heart|Cur vultus tuus tristis est, quum te ægrotum non videam? Non est hoc frustra, sed malum, nescio quod, in corde tuo est]].

paras.t: Cor sapientis quærit doctrinam : quia non solum vult alios informare, sed etiam informari ab aliis per verba aut scripta, et cupit semper proficere; et os stultorum pascitur imperitia, id est, stulti et garruli propria loquacitate, imperitisque colloquiis delectantur.
paras.en: [[15:14|The heart of the wise seeketh instruction|Cor sapientis quærit doctrinam]]: for he wishes not only to inform others but also to be informed by others, through words or writings, and he desires always to make progress; [[15:14|and the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness|et os stultorum pascitur imperitia]] [imperitia, literally "unskilfulness" or "ignorance"], that is, fools and chatterers delight in their own talkativeness and in ignorant conversations.

paras.t: Omnes dies pauperis, mali : id est, qui in temporalibus pauper est, dies habet laboriosos, propter necessaria conquirenda; et si paupertas sua displicet sibi, in assiduis afflictionibus tædiisque consistit. Porro qui pauper est spiritu, et voluntarie inops, Deoque serviens, persecutionibus, tentationibus et afflictionibus quotidianis non caret. Multæ enim tribulationes justorum. Et omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patiuntur. Et, sicut ait Gregorius, Abel esse renuit, quem Cain malitia non exercet. Insuper, in multis offendimus omnes. Et sic dies nostri pleni sunt malis culpæ et pœnæ. Unde et quotidiana contritione ac pœnitentia indigemus. Ideo ait Apostolus : Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt. Hinc Jacob patriarcha : Dies, inquit, peregrinationis meæ super terram, centum triginta annorum sunt, parvi et mali. Dicitur autem tempus malum, non quod in se malum sit, sed propter ea quæ sunt et fiunt in tempore, a quibus sumit denominationem multiplicem. Unde scriptum est : Videns Jonathas quia tempus eum juvat.
paras.en: [[15:15|All the days of the poor are evil|Omnes dies pauperis, mali]]: that is, he who is poor in temporal things has toilsome days, because of getting what he needs; and if his poverty displeases him, he lives in continual afflictions and weariness. Again, he who is poor in spirit and needy of his own will, and serves God, is not without daily persecutions, temptations and afflictions. For [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|Multæ enim tribulationes justorum]]. And [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution|omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patiuntur]]. And, as Gregory says, he who is not tried by the malice of Cain refuses to be Abel. Moreover, [[Jas 3:2|in many things we all offend|in multis offendimus omnes]]. And so our days are full of the evils of guilt and of punishment; hence we need daily contrition and penance. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:16|redeeming the time, because the days are evil|Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt]]. Hence the patriarch Jacob: [[Gen 47:9|The days|Dies]], he says, [[Gen 47:9|of my pilgrimage|peregrinationis meæ]] upon earth [[Gen 47:9|are a hundred and thirty years, few, and evil|centum triginta annorum sunt, parvi et mali]]. Now time is called evil, not because it is evil in itself, but because of the things that are and are done in time, from which it takes many names. Hence it is written: [[1 Mach 12:1|Jonathan saw that the time served him|Videns Jonathas quia tempus eum juvat]].

paras.t: Secura mens, quæ scilicet inordinatis anxietatibus, immoderata sollicitudine, passionumque immoderantia caret, est quasi juge convivium : quia assidue lætificat hominem. At vero mens bene secura est, quæ vere adhæret Deo, et bonam conscientiam possidet, ac pacem internam habet cum Creatore. Quæ dicere ex sententia potest : Dominus illuminatio mea, et salus mea : quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ : a quo trepidabo? Sunt autem quidam intimorati, qui etiam in quadam vivunt securitate, non pensantes sua pericula et peccata : quibus et sua securitas dulcis est, sed admodum periculosa.
paras.en: [[15:15|A secure mind|Secura mens]], that is, one free of disordered anxieties, immoderate care and the unruliness of the passions, [[15:15|is like a continual feast|est quasi juge convivium]]: for it gladdens a man continually. But that mind is well secure which truly cleaves to God, possesses a good conscience, and has inward peace with the Creator; which can say from the heart: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?|Dominus illuminatio mea, et salus mea : quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ : a quo trepidabo?]] [the margin gives Ps. xxvii, 1, the Hebrew numbering] There are, however, some without fear [intimorati: those who lack the fear of God] who also live in a kind of security, not weighing their own dangers and sins; to them too their security is sweet, but exceedingly perilous.

paras.t: Melius est parum de temporalibus, scilicet simplicem victum et vestitum habere, cum timore Domini filiali, quam thesauri magni et insatiabiles. Imo timor Dei per se incomparabiliter cunctis terrenis opibus exstat præstantior; utilius quoque est ad bene vivendum, necessaria sola habere, quam temporalibus abundare, quoniam multa vitia assequuntur divitias. Ideo monet Apostolus : Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. Hinc et multi philosophi divitias contempserunt, quatenus philosophiæ vacarent liberius. Ideo in secunda epistola ad Lucilium Seneca testatur : Honesta res est, læta paupertas; imo jam non est paupertas, sed opulentia cordis, si læta est. Denique non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit, pauper est. Quid enim refert, quantum illi in arca, quantum in horreis jaceat, quantum pascat aut feneretur, si imminet alieno, si non acquisita, sed acquirenda computet? Quis sit divitiarum modus quæris? primus, habere quæ necesse est; secundus, quod satis est. Dicuntur autem thesauri insatiabiles, quasi active, hoc est insatiativi, quoniam appetitum non satiant, sed irritant.
paras.en: [[15:16|Better is a little|Melius est parum]] of temporal things, that is, to have simple food and clothing, [[15:16|with the fear of the Lord|cum timore Domini]], filial fear, [[15:16|than great treasures without content|quam thesauri magni et insatiabiles]] [insatiabiles, literally "insatiable"; see below]. Nay, the fear of God in itself surpasses all earthly riches beyond compare; and it is more profitable for living well to have only what is necessary than to abound in temporal things, since many vices follow upon riches. Therefore the Apostle warns: [[1 Tim 6:8|having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]. Hence many philosophers too despised riches, so as to be freer for philosophy. Therefore Seneca testifies in the second letter to Lucilius: A cheerful poverty is an honourable thing; nay, it is no longer poverty but wealth of heart, if it is cheerful. Lastly, not he who has little, but he who craves more, is poor. For what does it matter how much lies in his strong-box, how much in his barns, how much he pastures or lends at interest, if he hangs upon what is another's, if he counts not what he has gained but what he has yet to gain? Do you ask what is the measure of riches? The first, to have what is necessary; the second, what is enough. Now the treasures are called insatiable in an active sense, as it were, that is, unsatisfying, since they do not satisfy the appetite but provoke it.

paras.t: Melius est vocari ad olera cum caritate, quam ad vitulum saginatum cum odio : id est, salubrius et desiderabilius est ad cibum sobrium, non pretiosum nec lautum, ex caritate invitari, quam ad fercula copiosa et lauta, ex rancore. Qui enim ex odio invitat, frequenter molitur malum ei quem invitavit, quemadmodum Ptolemæus filius Abobi, Simoni; et Absalon Amnon suo fratri. Nemo igitur desiderio divitiarum relinquat Dei timorem et competentiam strictam, nec ad delicata convivia appetat cum periculo invitari.
paras.en: [[15:17|It is better to be invited to herbs with love, than to a fatted calf with hatred|Melius est vocari ad olera cum caritate, quam ad vitulum saginatum cum odio]]: that is, it is more wholesome and more desirable to be invited out of love to a sober meal, neither costly nor sumptuous, than out of rancour to plentiful and sumptuous dishes. For he who invites out of hatred often plots evil against the one he has invited, as Ptolemee the son of Abobus did against Simon[[1 Mach 16:15||]], and Absalom against Ammon his brother[[2 Kings 13:27||]] [the margin gives 1 Mach. xvi, 15, 16 and 2 Reg. xiii, 27–29]. Let no one, then, for desire of riches abandon the fear of God and a strict sufficiency [competentia: a bare competence, just what is enough], nor seek to be invited to delicate banquets at the peril of it.

paras.t: Vir iracundus provocat rixas. Cito enim movetur ad iram : qua accensus, profert verba injuriosa, ex quibus rixæ nascuntur; vel mox ad ultionem prorumpit. Qui patiens est, mitigat suscitatas, id est, discordantes et corrixantes reconciliat. Ad quod hortatur sanctus pater Bernardus, dicendo : Et tu tanquam angelus pacis, sollicitus esto auferre scandala, turbationes sedare, dissentientes et litigantes pacificare. Unde in Proverbiis suis Seneca est locutus : Semper dissensio ab alio incipiat, a te reconciliatio.
paras.en: [[15:18|A passionate man stirreth up strifes|Vir iracundus provocat rixas]]. For he is quickly moved to anger; and, inflamed by it, he utters injurious words, from which quarrels arise; or he straightway bursts out into revenge. [[15:18|he that is patient appeaseth those that are stirred up|Qui patiens est, mitigat suscitatas]], that is, he reconciles those who are at variance and quarrelling with one another. To this the holy father Bernard exhorts, saying: And do thou, like an angel of peace, be careful to remove scandals, to calm disturbances, to make peace between those who disagree and contend. Hence Seneca has said in his Proverbs: Let disagreement always begin from another, reconciliation from thee.

paras.t: Iter pigrorum, quasi sepes spinarum : id est, pigris et acediosis tam molestum est virtuosos aggredi actus, ac immorari ac proficere in eisdem, ac si per spinosam sepem essent ituri. Varia quoque allegant et confingunt impedimenta bene agendi, sicut et infra habetur : Dicit piger : Leo est in via. Hinc ait Bernardus : Perniciosa tepiditas, quoniam periculosa est et molestissima, plena miseriæ et doloris, infernoque proxima, et umbra mortis jure censetur. Sane invenire est homines sub onere deficientes, pusillanimes et remissos, virga atque calcaribus indigentes : quorum est remissa lætitia, pusillanimisque tristitia; quorum brevis et rara compunctio, animalis cogitatio, tepida conversatio; quorum obedientia sine devotione, lectio sine ædificatione, sermo sine circumspectione, oratio sine attentione; quos vix gehennæ metus inhibet, pudor vix cohibet, vix frenat ratio, vix disciplina coercet. Via justorum absque offendiculo, id est, justi in via virtutum procedunt ferventer et expedite, absque Dei offensa, proximorumque scandalo; nec sibi confingunt prætacta obstacula, imo divino innitentes auxilio, dicunt Deo : Quoniam in te eripiar a tentatione, et in Deo meo transgrediar murum.
paras.en: [[15:19|The way of the slothful is as a hedge of thorns|Iter pigrorum, quasi sepes spinarum]]: that is, to the slothful and the listless [*acediosis*, those given to *acedia*, sloth in spiritual things] it is as irksome to undertake virtuous acts, and to abide and make progress in them, as if they had to go through a thorny hedge. They also allege and invent various hindrances to doing good, as is also found below: [[Prov 26:13|The slothful man saith: There is a lion in the way|Dicit piger : Leo est in via]]. Hence Bernard says: Tepidity is ruinous, since it is perilous and most irksome, full of misery and sorrow, next door to hell, and is rightly reckoned the shadow of death. Truly, one may find men fainting under the burden, faint-hearted and slack, needing the rod and the spur: whose joy is slack and whose sadness faint-hearted; whose compunction is brief and rare, their thinking animal [that is, of the senses, not of the spirit], their way of life tepid; whose obedience is without devotion, their reading without edification, their speech without circumspection, their prayer without attention; whom the fear of hell scarcely restrains, shame scarcely checks, reason scarcely bridles, discipline scarcely constrains. [[15:19|the way of the just is without offence|Via justorum absque offendiculo]], that is, the just go forward in the way of the virtues fervently and readily, without offence to God and without scandal to their neighbours; nor do they invent for themselves the obstacles mentioned above, but rather, leaning on the divine help, they say to God: [[Ps 17:30|For by thee I shall be delivered from temptation; and through my God I shall go over a wall|Quoniam in te eripiar a tentatione, et in Deo meo transgrediar murum]].

paras.t: Filius sapiens lætificat patrem suum carnalem ac spiritualem, imo et Deum Patrem, complacendo ei. Istud tamen supra plenius fuit expositum. Et stultus homo despicit matrem suam : non quod omnes iniqui suas despiciant matres carnales ; sed quicumque despicit matrem suam, insipiens est, nisi forsan contemnat eam zelo justitiæ, in quantum inexcusabiliter vitiosam. Porro omnes iniqui despiciunt matrem suam Ecclesiam, non obediendo ejus jussionibus ac doctrinis.
paras.en: [[15:20|A wise son maketh a father joyful|Filius sapiens lætificat patrem suum]], both his father in the flesh and his spiritual father, nay, even God the Father, by pleasing him. This, however, was expounded more fully above[[Prov 10:1||]]. [[15:20|but the foolish man despiseth his mother|Et stultus homo despicit matrem suam]]: not that all the wicked despise their mothers according to the flesh; but whoever despises his mother is foolish, unless perhaps he contemns her out of zeal for justice, in so far as she is inexcusably vicious. Further, all the wicked despise their mother the Church, by not obeying her commands and teachings.

paras.t: Stultitia, gaudium stulto : id est, iniquo qui est assuefactus et habituatus in vitiis, delectabile est vanis et illicitis verbis ac factis intendere. Habitus namque est quasi altera natura, et vehementer inclinat, secundum Philosophum secundo Ethicorum. Ideo secundum habitum operari, est delectabile operanti. Propter quod rursus Aristoteles ait, quod delectatio fiens in opere, signum est habitus acquisiti. Et vir prudens dirigit gressus suos, id est, actus suos ordinat ad debitum finem. Prudentia namque est recta ratio agibilium, ut habetur sexto Ethicorum, et est de mediis, non de fine.
paras.en: [[15:21|Folly is joy to the fool|Stultitia, gaudium stulto]]: that is, to the wicked man who is accustomed and habituated to vices it is delightful to give himself to vain and unlawful words and deeds. For a habit is as it were a second nature, and inclines strongly, according to the Philosopher in the second book of the Ethics. Therefore to act according to a habit is delightful to the one acting. On which account Aristotle says again that the delight arising in the deed is a sign of a habit acquired. [[15:21|and the wise man maketh straight his steps|Et vir prudens dirigit gressus suos]], that is, orders his acts to their due end. For prudence is right reason about things to be done, as is found in the sixth book of the Ethics, and is concerned with the means, not with the end.

paras.t: Dissipantur cogitationes, id est, faciliter errant, et ab effectu impediuntur, ubi non est consilium : quod est actus prudentiæ, estque inquisitio quid expediat fieri, et quid non. Ideo dirigit cogitationes, ut bonæ sint, et refrenat inutiles. Unde subjungitur : ubi vero plures sunt consiliarii, confirmantur : ita quod solidæ sunt et honestæ. Nempe, ut asserit Cassianus, mens humana est similis molæ, cui si nihil ad molendum imponitur, se ipsam suis circumvolutionibus demolitur. Sic mens hominis, suarum cogitationum instabilitate ac vanitate lædit et consumit se ipsam, nisi in suis cogitationibus per prudentiam atque consilium gubernetur ac refrenetur.
paras.en: [[15:22|Designs are brought to nothing|Dissipantur cogitationes]] [*cogitationes*, “thoughts”, where the Douay-Rheims has “designs”], that is, they easily go astray and are hindered from taking effect, [[15:22|where there is no counsel|ubi non est consilium]]: which is an act of prudence, and is an inquiry into what it is expedient to do and what not. Therefore counsel directs the thoughts, that they may be good, and curbs the useless ones. Hence it is added: [[15:22|but where there are many counsellors, they are established|ubi vero plures sunt consiliarii, confirmantur]]: so that they are solid and honest. Indeed, as Cassian asserts, the human mind is like a mill: if nothing is put into it to grind, it wears itself away by its own turning. So the mind of man harms and consumes itself by the instability and vanity of its thoughts, unless it is governed and bridled in its thoughts by prudence and counsel.

paras.t: Lætatur homo in sententia oris sui. Humanum etenim est, de propria sententia, tanquam prudenter prolata, lætari. Verumtamen hoc non est semper laudabile. Si autem quis glorietur de vera et salubri oris sui sententia ac doctrina, sed in Domino, non in se, et in quantum sententia sua confert ad Dei honorem, proximorumque utilitatem et sui ipsius salutem; commendabile est. Si vero lætetur in sententia oris sui ex privato amore, et in quantum est a se prolata, sicut homo communiter immoderate appretiatur ac reputat sua ; vituperabile est. Sicque multi delectantur in sua sententia : propter quod pertinaciter eam defendunt, et a sui errore judicii queunt vix revocari. Sicque, ut dicit Thomas in secunda secundæ, ex detractione sequitur excæcatio cordis, quia detractor lætatur in sententia oris sui, quam profert de alio : unde judicat se vera dixisse de eo cui detraxit, quamvis non vera, sed falsa de eo evomit. Et sermo opportunus, id est suo loco et tempore pronuntiatus recta intentione, et ex rationabili causa, est optimus. Ideo sapiens non solum advertit oris sententiam, sed et circumstantias in omni actu virtutis servandas.
paras.en: [[15:23|A man rejoiceth in the sentence of his mouth|Lætatur homo in sententia oris sui]]. For it is human to rejoice in one’s own sentence [*sententia*, a judgement or opinion delivered], as though it had been wisely uttered. Yet this is not always praiseworthy. If someone glories in the true and wholesome sentence and teaching of his mouth, but in the Lord, not in himself, and in so far as his sentence contributes to the honour of God, the profit of his neighbours and his own salvation, it is commendable. But if he rejoices in the sentence of his mouth out of private love, and in so far as it was uttered by himself (as a man commonly prizes and esteems his own things beyond measure), it is blameworthy. And thus many take delight in their own opinion: on which account they defend it obstinately, and can scarcely be called back from the error of their judgement. And thus, as Thomas says in the Secunda Secundæ, blindness of heart follows from detraction, because the detractor rejoices in the sentence of his mouth which he utters about another: whence he judges that he has spoken true things of the one he has detracted, although what he vomits out about him is not true but false. [[15:23|and a word in due time|Et sermo opportunus]], that is, uttered in its proper place and time, with a right intention and for a reasonable cause, [[15:23|is best|est optimus]]. Therefore the wise man pays heed not only to the sentence of the mouth, but also to the circumstances to be observed in every act of virtue.

paras.t: Semita vitæ super eruditum, id est, actio ex vita gratiæ oriens, et ad vitam gloriæ ducens, est in homine vere docto : in quo non solum est lumen scientiæ, sed et probitas morum ; qui vitat insipientiam, tam interiorem quam exteriorem, omnem videlicet culpam dono sapientiæ repugnantem, atque ab increata Sapientia separantem. Ut declinet de inferno novissimo, id est ab omni peccato mortali, quod suo pondere ac reatu trahit ad infernum damnatorum : de quo in Psalmo, Eruisti animam meam ex inferno inferiori. Vel, De inferno novissimo, id est infernali damnatione. Summitur autem infernus quatuor modis. Primo, pro purgatorio : de quo in Missæ officio cantatur, Libera animas fidelium defunctorum de pœnis inferni. Secundo, pro limbo patrum : de quo Jacob in Genesi, Descendam, inquit, ad filium meum lugens in infernum. Tertio, pro limbo puerorum. Quarto, pro loco damnationis animarum.
paras.en: [[15:24|The path of life is above for the wise|Semita vitæ super eruditum]] [*super eruditum*, literally “upon the instructed man”], that is, action springing from the life of grace and leading to the life of glory is in the man who is truly taught: in whom there is not only the light of knowledge but also uprightness of life; who shuns folly, inward as well as outward, namely every fault that is contrary to the gift of wisdom and separates from the uncreated Wisdom. [[15:24|that he may decline from the lowest hell|Ut declinet de inferno novissimo]], that is, from every mortal sin, which by its weight and guilt drags down to the hell of the damned: of which it is said in the Psalm, [[Ps 85:13|thou hast delivered my soul out of the lower hell|Eruisti animam meam ex inferno inferiori]]. Or, [[15:24|from the lowest hell|De inferno novissimo]], that is, from infernal damnation. Now hell [*infernus*, literally “the lower place”] is taken in four ways. First, for purgatory: of which it is sung in the office of the Mass, Deliver the souls of the faithful departed from the pains of hell. Secondly, for the limbo of the fathers: of which Jacob speaks in Genesis: [[Gen 37:35|I will go down|Descendam]], he says, [[Gen 37:35|to my son into hell, mourning|ad filium meum lugens in infernum]]. Thirdly, for the limbo of children. Fourthly, for the place of the damnation of souls.

paras.t: Domum superborum, id est cognationem atque familiam elatorum, demolietur Dominus, et firmos faciet terminos viduæ, id est, bona viduarum custodiet et augebit. Est enim Dominus miserabilium personarum specialis protector et consolator, juxta illud Psalmi : Dominus custodit advenas: pupillum et viduam suscipiet. Etiam dicitur alibi : Facit judicium pupillo et viduæ, amatque peregrinum. Viduis quoque, quæ, secundum Apostolum, vere sunt viduæ, dat Dominus firmam mansionem in regno cœlesti. Rursus, termini viduæ, sunt fines Ecclesiæ : quæ in hac vita quodammodo vidua est, quia nondum cupitis et fruitivis ac beatificis fruitur sui Sponsi amplexibus. De cujus terminis fertur in Psalmo : Qui posuit fines tuos pacem. Et Isaiæ sexagesimo legitur : Non audietur ultra iniquitas in terra tua, vastitas et contritio in terminis tuis.
paras.en: [[15:25|the house of the proud|Domum superborum]], that is, the kindred and household of the haughty, [[15:25|The Lord will destroy|demolietur Dominus]], [[15:25|and will strengthen the borders of the widow|et firmos faciet terminos viduæ]], that is, he will guard and increase the goods of widows. For the Lord is the special protector and comforter of persons deserving pity, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 145:9|The Lord keepeth the strangers, he will support the fatherless and the widow|Dominus custodit advenas: pupillum et viduam suscipiet]]. It is also said elsewhere: [[Deut 10:18|He doth judgment to the fatherless and the widow, loveth the stranger|Facit judicium pupillo et viduæ, amatque peregrinum]]. To widows also who, according to the Apostle, [[1 Tim 5:3|are widows indeed|vere sunt viduæ]], the Lord gives a firm dwelling in the heavenly kingdom. Again, the borders of the widow are the bounds of the Church, which in this life is in a manner a widow, because she does not yet enjoy the longed-for, fruitive and beatific embraces of her Bridegroom. Of whose borders it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 147:3|Who hath placed peace in thy borders|Qui posuit fines tuos pacem]]. And in the sixtieth chapter of Isaias we read: [[Is 60:18|Iniquity shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction in thy borders|Non audietur ultra iniquitas in terra tua, vastitas et contritio in terminis tuis]].

paras.t: Abominatio Domini, cogitationes malæ, id est, pravæ cogitationes sunt abominabiles Deo, qui ait : Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis; et alibi, Væ qui cogitatis inutile. Et ex hoc ostenditur error Josephi, asserentis non esse peccatum in cogitationibus, quamdiu non procedunt in opus iniquum. Et purus sermo pulcherrimus firmabitur ab eo : id est, omnis sermo verus et justus, nil culpæ habens admixtum, est purus, et placet Deo, ac roboratur ac approbatur ab eo tanquam pulcherrimus. Sed et ipse Christus, qui est Verbum æternum, et increatus sermo Dei Patris, juxta illud ad Hebræos, Vivus est sermo Dei et efficax, a Patre firmatus est in corde credentium per fidem et caritatem. De quo Pater testatus est : Hic est Filius meus dilectus, ipsum audite. Item, sermo iste purus, evangelica est doctrina vere pulcherrima, quam Christus et ejus prædicaverunt Apostoli, Domino cooperante, et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis.
paras.en: [[15:26|Evil thoughts are an abomination to the Lord|Abominatio Domini, cogitationes malæ]], that is, depraved thoughts are abominable to God, who says: [[Is 1:16|take away the evil of your devices from my eyes|Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis]]; and elsewhere, [[Mich 2:1|Woe to you that devise that which is unprofitable|Væ qui cogitatis inutile]]. And from this is shown the error of Josephus, who asserts that there is no sin in thoughts so long as they do not go forth into a wicked deed. [[15:26|and pure words most beautiful shall be confirmed by him|Et purus sermo pulcherrimus firmabitur ab eo]]: that is, every word that is true and just, having no fault mixed in it, is pure, and pleases God, and is strengthened and approved by him as most beautiful. But Christ himself also, who is the eternal Word and the uncreated Word [*sermo*, the word used in the verse] of God the Father, according to that to the Hebrews, [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living and effectual|Vivus est sermo Dei et efficax]], has been confirmed by the Father in the hearts of believers through faith and charity. Of him the Father bore witness: [[Matt 17:5|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]], [[Matt 17:5|hear ye him|ipsum audite]]. Again, this pure word is the gospel teaching, truly most beautiful, which Christ and his Apostles preached, [[Mark 16:20|the Lord working withal, and confirming the word with signs that followed|Domino cooperante, et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis]].

paras.t: Conturbat domum suam, id est propriam mentem et conscientiam, qui sectatur avaritiam : quia non solum variis vitiis, sed et multis afflictionibus implet cor suum. Propter quod Christus divitias vocat spinas. Talis quoque scandalizat et molestat domum suam, id est familiam, quam non reficit sufficienter, et multum facit laborare, ac male remunerat pro suo labore. Porro avarus, ut Climacus ait, est Evangelii subsannator, quoniam terrenorum contemptum Christus exemplo et verbo præcipue commendavit. Qui autem odit munera, id est injustam et periculosam munerum acceptionem, scilicet ad subvertendum justitiam, vivet per gratiam. Ideo Dominus jussit: Non accipias munera quæ excæcant etiam prudentes, et subvertunt verba justorum. Hinc Moyses dixit ad Dominum: Tu scis quod nec asellum unquam acceperim ab eis. Sic Samuel loquitur: Si munus de manu cujusquam accepi. Istud ergo judicibus familiaribusque eorum est præcipue observandum.
paras.en: [[15:27|troubleth his own house|Conturbat domum suam]], that is, his own mind and conscience, [[15:27|He that is greedy of gain|qui sectatur avaritiam]]: because he fills his heart not only with various vices but also with many afflictions. On which account Christ calls riches thorns. Such a man also scandalizes and troubles his house, that is, his household, which he does not feed sufficiently, and makes to labour much, and pays badly for its labour. Further, the avaricious man, as Climacus says, is a mocker of the Gospel, since Christ especially commended contempt of earthly things by example[[Matt 8:20||]] [the margin gives Matth. xviii, 20, which does not fit; Matt 8:20 is probably meant] and by word[[Matt 19:29||]][[Luke 14:33||]]. [[15:27|but he that hateth bribes|Qui autem odit munera]], that is, the unjust and perilous taking of gifts, namely for the overthrowing of justice, [[15:27|shall live|vivet]] by grace. Therefore the Lord commanded: [[Ex 23:8|Neither shalt thou take bribes, which even blind the wise, and pervert the words of the just|Non accipias munera quæ excæcant etiam prudentes, et subvertunt verba justorum]]. Hence Moses said to the Lord: [[Num 16:15|thou knowest that I have not taken of them so much as a young ass at any time|Tu scis quod nec asellum unquam acceperim ab eis]]. So Samuel speaks: [[1 Kings 12:3|if I have taken a bribe at any man's hand|Si munus de manu cujusquam accepi]]. This, then, is especially to be observed by judges and those of their household.

paras.t: Per misericordiam, id est opera misericordiæ spiritualia et corporalia, imo et per compassionem internam, etiamsi desit facultas operis, et fidem, quæ est fundamentum totius ædificii spiritualis; vel, Fidem, id est fidelitatem: de qua loquitur David, Dominus reddet unicuique secundum justitiam suam et fidem; purgantur peccata, id est dimittuntur, sicut in Evangelio ait Salvator: Quod superest, date eleemosynam; et ecce omnia munda sunt vobis; et rursus, Beati misericordes, quia ipsorum miserebitur Deus. Et quoniam opera bona ex hoc præcipue efficaciam habent merendi, quia in fide fundantur, et invisibile præmium quod sola fide agnoscitur, præstolantur; idcirco per fidem quæ est virtus theologica, purgantur peccata. Unde ait beatissimus Petrus: Fide purificans Deus corda eorum. Rursus, qui fidelitatem servat Deo et proximo, meretur purgari ab omni peccato. Hinc eleemosyna vocatur pars satisfactionis. Verumtamen non purgatur homo a peccati remissione, quantum ad culpam, sine prævia contritione et confitendi proposito. Peccata autem venialia quotidiana, per quotidiana misericordiæ opera potissime dimittuntur, quamquam caritatis fervor, absolute loquendo, summe consumat peccati rubiginem, sicut asserit Christus: Dimittuntur ei peccata multa, quia dilexit multum. Per timorem autem Domini declinat omnis homo a malo. Nam timor servilis retrahit a peccatis horrore pœnarum, timor filialis amore virtutis, timor initialis utroque modo, ut dictum est sæpe.
paras.en: [[15:27|By mercy|Per misericordiam]], that is, by the works of mercy, spiritual and corporal, nay, even by inward compassion, though the means for the work be lacking, [[15:27|and faith|et fidem]], which is the foundation of the whole spiritual building; or, *faith*, that is, faithfulness [*fides* means both], of which David speaks: [[1 Kings 26:23|the Lord will reward every one according to his justice, and his faithfulness|Dominus reddet unicuique secundum justitiam suam et fidem]]; [[15:27|sins are purged away|purgantur peccata]], that is, are forgiven, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 11:41|that which remaineth, give alms: and behold, all things are clean unto you|Quod superest, date eleemosynam; et ecce omnia munda sunt vobis]]; and again, [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful|Beati misericordes]], for God will have mercy on them [so Denis; the Gospel has: for they shall obtain mercy]. And since good works have their power of meriting chiefly from this, that they are founded on faith and look for an invisible reward that is known by faith alone, therefore sins are purged through faith, which is a theological virtue. Hence the most blessed Peter says: [[Acts 15:9|purifying their hearts by faith|Fide purificans Deus corda eorum]] [Denis adds *Deus*: God purifying their hearts by faith]. Again, he who keeps faithfulness to God and to his neighbour merits to be purged from every sin. Hence almsgiving is called a part of satisfaction. Yet a man is not purged by the remission of sin, as to the guilt, without previous contrition and the purpose of confessing. But daily venial sins are forgiven chiefly through daily works of mercy, although the fervour of charity, speaking absolutely, most of all consumes the rust of sin, as Christ asserts: [[Luke 7:47|Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much|Dimittuntur ei peccata multa, quia dilexit multum]]. [[15:27|and by the fear of the Lord every one declineth from evil|Per timorem autem Domini declinat omnis homo a malo]]. For servile fear draws back from sins through horror of punishment, filial fear through love of virtue, initial fear [that is, the fear of beginners, partly servile and partly filial] in both ways, as has often been said.

paras.t: Mens justi meditatur obedientiam, id est, sollicite intra se cogitat et proponit obedire cunctis superioribus suis, quantum illorum jurisdictio extendit se super eam, et maxime Deo: hoc enim requirit justitiæ debitum. Unde hortatur Apostolus: Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit; itemque, Obedite præpositis vestris. Hinc Samuel: Melior, inquit, est obedientia, quam victimæ; quoniam quasi scelus idololatriæ est, nolle acquiescere. Et Bernardus: Nec studium bonæ actionis, nec gratia sanctæ contemplationis, nec lacrima pœnitentis extra obedientiam esse potest, nec Deo placet. Os impiorum redundat malis, id est, verbis rebellionis ac ceteris vitiosis verbis abundat: quæ ex abundantia perversi cordis erumpunt. Unde talibus dixit Salvator: Quomodo potestis loqui bona, quum sitis mali?
paras.en: [[15:28|The mind of the just studieth obedience|Mens justi meditatur obedientiam]], that is, he carefully thinks over and resolves within himself to obey all his superiors, as far as their jurisdiction extends over it [that is, over his mind], and above all God: for the debt of justice requires this. Hence the Apostle exhorts: [[Rom 13:1|Let every soul be subject to higher powers|Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit]]; and likewise, [[Heb 13:17|Obey your prelates|Obedite præpositis vestris]]. Hence Samuel: [[1 Kings 15:22|obedience is better|Melior]], he says, [[1 Kings 15:22|than sacrifices|est obedientia, quam victimæ]]; for it is [[1 Kings 15:23|like the crime of idolatry, to refuse to obey|quasi scelus idololatriæ est, nolle acquiescere]]. And Bernard: Neither zeal for good works, nor the grace of holy contemplation, nor the tear of the penitent can be outside obedience, nor does it please God. [[15:28|the mouth of the wicked overfloweth with evils|Os impiorum redundat malis]], that is, it abounds in words of rebellion and other vicious words, which burst forth from the abundance of a perverse heart. Hence the Saviour said to such men: [[Matt 12:34|how can you speak good things, whereas you are evil?|Quomodo potestis loqui bona, quum sitis mali]]

paras.t: Longe est Dominus ab impiis, non loco, quia ubique præsens est incircumscriptibilis Deus, sed per dissimilitudinem. Unde et longe a peccatoribus salus. Est ergo longe ab eis, quia displicent ei: et quo per vitiorum deformitatem ac fœditatem dissimiliores sunt Deo, eo longius distant ab eo. A Deo quippe, non corporis gressu, sed mentis affectu receditur. Ipse tamen essentialiter omnibus adest, omnia penetrat, et ipsis essentiis rerum illabitur. Unde loquitur divinus Apostolus: Non longe est ab unoquoque nostrum: in ipso enim vivimus, movemur et sumus. Et orationes justorum exaudiet: dummodo orent sicut oportet, puta salubriter et constanter, prout ait Salvator: Oportet semper orare, et non deficere. Qui rursus fassus est: Si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Deus itaque, qui invitat et exhortatur ut ipsum oremus, paratus est utique exaudire; sed aliqua differt, et paulatim exaudit, ut dona ipsius gratantius accipiamus, diligentius custodiamus, ac diu appetendo, frequentiusque et ardentius orando, copiosius tempore opportuno exaudiamur.
paras.en: [[15:29|The Lord is far from the wicked|Longe est Dominus ab impiis]], not in place, since God, who cannot be circumscribed, is present everywhere, but by unlikeness. Hence also [[Ps 118:155|Salvation is far from sinners|longe a peccatoribus salus]]. He is far from them, then, because they displease him; and the more unlike God they are through the deformity and foulness of their vices, the farther they stand from him. For one withdraws from God not by a step of the body but by the affection of the mind. Yet he is present to all things by his essence, penetrates all things, and enters into the very essences of things. Hence the divine Apostle says: [[Acts 17:27|he be not far from every one of us|Non longe est ab unoquoque nostrum]]: [[Acts 17:28|For in him we live and move and are|in ipso enim vivimus, movemur et sumus]]. [[15:29|and he will hear the prayers of the just|Et orationes justorum exaudiet]]: provided they pray as they ought, that is, wholesomely and constantly, as the Saviour says: [[Luke 18:1|we ought always to pray and not to faint|Oportet semper orare, et non deficere]]. Who also declared: [[John 16:23|if you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you|Si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis]]. God, therefore, who invites and exhorts us to pray to him, is surely ready to hear; but he defers some things and hears little by little, so that we may receive his gifts more gratefully and guard them more carefully, and that, by long desiring and by praying more often and more ardently, we may be heard more abundantly at the fitting time.

paras.t: Lux oculorum lætificat animam. Potest hoc primo exponi de luce sensibili : quam corporalibus oculis intueri delectabile est, juxta quod in Ecclesiaste legitur : Dulce lumen, et delectabile est oculis videre solem. Similiter lux visiva existens in pupilla, exhilarat animam, quia per eam fit visio, et per exteriorem visum anima multa addiscit. Visus etenim plurium rerum differentias nobis ostendit, secundum Philosophum. Hinc cæcatus Tobias : Quale, inquit, mihi gaudium erit, qui in tenebris sedeo, et lumen cœli non video? Secundo, exponitur de luce intelligibili, id est de gratia Dei, de veritate, de illustratione divina, quæ interiores lætificat oculos. Contemplatio etenim veritatis valde delectat. De hac luce ait Michæas : Quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est, id est causa et dator lucis, et illuminationis animæ meæ. Ideo subdit : Deducet me Dominus in lucem, et videbo justitiam ejus. Tertio, exponitur de lumine gloriæ, increataque luce : cujus clara et beatifica visio summe exhilarat et plene contentat, sicut ait Psalmista : Adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo. Iis expositionibus concordat antiqua translatio, quæ sic habet : Videns bona oculus delectat cor. Nempe ex unione potentiæ cum objecto convenienti, delectatio oritur.
paras.en: [[15:30|The light of the eyes rejoiceth the soul|Lux oculorum lætificat animam]]. This can be expounded, first, of sensible light, which it is delightful to behold with the bodily eyes, according to what is read in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 11:7|The light is sweet, and it is delightful for the eyes to see the sun.|Dulce lumen, et delectabile est oculis videre solem]] Likewise the visual light that is in the pupil gladdens the soul, because through it sight takes place, and through outward sight the soul learns many things. For sight shows us the differences of a great many things, according to the Philosopher. Hence the blinded Tobias: [[Tob 5:12|What manner of joy|Quale]], he says, [[Tob 5:12|shall be to me, who sit in darkness and see not the light of heaven?|mihi gaudium erit, qui in tenebris sedeo, et lumen cœli non video?]] Secondly, it is expounded of intelligible light, that is, of the grace of God, of truth, of the divine enlightening, which gladdens the inward eyes. For the contemplation of truth delights greatly. Of this light Micheas says: [[Mich 7:8|when I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light|Quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est]], that is, the cause and giver of the light and enlightenment of my soul. Therefore he adds: [[Mich 7:9|he will bring me forth into the light, I shall behold his justice|Deducet me Dominus in lucem, et videbo justitiam ejus]] [Denis reads *Deducet me Dominus*, “the Lord will lead me”, where the Vulgate has *Educet me*]. Thirdly, it is expounded of the light of glory and of the uncreated light, whose clear and beatific vision gladdens supremely and contents fully, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 15:11|thou shalt fill me with joy with thy countenance|Adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo]]. With these expositions the ancient translation agrees, which reads thus: The eye that sees good things delights the heart [the old Latin version made from the Greek]. For delight arises from the union of a power with a fitting object.

paras.t: Fama bona impinguat ossa, id est, valde oblectat. Naturale enim est homini delectari in hoc, quod bonæ est famæ. Unde et alibi dicitur : Curam habe de bono nomine; itemque, Melius est nomen bonum quam unguenta pretiosa. Itaque, si homo delectetur in bona fama de ipso volante, in quantum fama illa est ad Dei honorem, ædificationemque proximorum; bona est delectatio illa, præsertim si fama vera sit. Si autem delectetur in fama sua, in quantum est ad sui ipsius honorem, laudem et commodum; vana est talis lætitia, et maxime si fama sit falsa. Sic hypocritæ et alii multi delectantur in sua fama. Propter quod Seneca in suis fatur Proverbiis : Plerique famam, conscientiam pauci verentur. Sed utrumque simul curandum, quum dicat Hieronymus : Opera salutis, sine fama boni odoris, non satis relucent auditoribus; nec sine opere proficit fama.
paras.en: [[15:30|a good name maketh the bones fat|Fama bona impinguat ossa]] [*fama*, “report, repute”, where the Douay-Rheims has “name”], that is, it greatly delights. For it is natural to man to take delight in being of good repute. Hence it is also said elsewhere: [[Ecclus 41:15|Take care of a good name|Curam habe de bono nomine]]; and likewise, [[Eccles 7:2|A good name is better than precious ointments|Melius est nomen bonum quam unguenta pretiosa]]. And so, if a man takes delight in the good report that flies abroad about him, in so far as that report serves the honour of God and the edification of his neighbours, that delight is good, especially if the report is true. But if he takes delight in his repute in so far as it serves his own honour, praise and advantage, such gladness is vain, and most of all if the report is false. Thus hypocrites and many others take delight in their repute. On which account Seneca says in his Proverbs: Most men fear for their repute, few for their conscience. But both are to be cared for together, since Jerome says: Works of salvation without the report of a good odour do not shine out enough to the hearers; nor does repute profit without the work.

paras.t: Auris quæ audit, id est, gratanter acceptat, increpationes vitæ, id est correptionem caritativam et justam, ad vitam gratiæ et salutem ordinatam ac disponentem, in medio sapientium commorabitur, id est, inter sapientes merito computatur, et eis se sociat, ut ex eorum increpatione proficiat : sicque fit sapiens, et digna in cathedra doctorali ad alios informandos sedere. Sicut enim ineptus et indignus est alios regere, qui subesse et regi despexit; sic indignus est alios increpare ac informare, qui corripi et informari abhorruit. Denique qui vere cognoscit se ipsum et proprias defectuositates, atque innumerabiles culpas saltem veniales, etiam quotidianas increpationes sumit jucunde, quamvis forsan conscius sibi non sit de eo quod sibi objicitur, sciens se in aliis innumerabiliter esse culpabilem, ultra propriam cognitionem. Si tamen enorme et scandalizativum aliorum aliquid objiciatur, potest se correptus humiliter excusare. Hinc in Proverbiis suis sanctus ait Cyrillus : Pone te in libra justitiæ, et sic perspicies quantus sis. Si parvi pendis te ipsum, ubique totus eris : quia humilitas parit timorem, timor securitatem, quæ custodit salutem. Quæso te, sequere jus commune, quod præcipit ut in judicio non uni credatur, nec alicui minus quam sibi ipsi de bonis. Immoderate ergo te diligens, injustissime tibi credes. Aliis igitur crede de te, præsertim de malis tuis.
paras.en: [[15:31|The ear that heareth|Auris quæ audit]], that is, gladly accepts, [[15:31|the reproofs of life|increpationes vitæ]], that is, charitable and just correction, ordered to the life of grace and to salvation and disposing for them, [[15:31|shall abide in the midst of the wise|in medio sapientium commorabitur]], that is, is deservedly counted among the wise, and joins himself to them, so as to profit by their reproof: and so he becomes wise, and worthy to sit in the doctor’s chair to instruct others. For as he is unfit and unworthy to rule others who has scorned to be subject and to be ruled, so he is unworthy to reprove and instruct others who has shrunk from being corrected and instructed. Lastly, he who truly knows himself and his own defects, and his innumerable faults, at least venial ones, accepts even daily reproofs cheerfully, although perhaps he is not conscious of what is laid to his charge, knowing that in other things he is blameworthy in countless ways beyond his own knowledge. If, however, something enormous and scandalous to others is laid to his charge, the one corrected may humbly excuse himself. Hence holy Cyril says in his Proverbs: Put thyself in the scale of justice, and so thou shalt see how great thou art. If thou esteem thyself little, thou shalt be whole everywhere: for humility begets fear, fear security, which guards salvation. I beg thee, follow the common law, which prescribes that in a trial one witness is not to be believed, and that no one is to be believed less than a man about himself, concerning his good points. Therefore, loving thyself immoderately, thou wilt most unjustly believe thyself. Believe others, then, about thyself, especially about thy evils.

paras.t: Hinc subditur : Qui abjicit disciplinam, id est informationem et correptionem ac justam castigationem, despicit animam suam, id est, contemptibilem eam facit Deo et omnibus Sanctis ejus; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis, id est, sano rationis judicio fulget, et suo intellectu salubriter utitur, atque, ut asserit Christus, in patientia sua possidet animam suam. Talis enim rite advertit, quod increpatio sit opus misericordiæ, eleemosyna spiritualis, medela salubris, caritatis indicium, dilectionis internæ ac justitiæ sanctæ effectus.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[15:32|He that rejecteth instruction|Qui abjicit disciplinam]], that is, instruction, correction and just chastisement, [[15:32|despiseth his own soul|despicit animam suam]], that is, makes it contemptible to God and to all his Saints; [[15:32|but he that yieldeth to reproof, possesseth understanding|qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis]] [*possessor est cordis*, literally “is the possessor of his heart”], that is, he shines with the sound judgement of reason and uses his understanding wholesomely, and, as Christ asserts, [[Luke 21:19|In your patience you shall possess your souls|in patientia sua possidet animam suam]] [Denis puts it of such a man: in his patience he possesseth his soul]. For such a man rightly considers that reproof is a work of mercy, a spiritual alms, a wholesome medicine, a sign of charity, an effect of inward love and of holy justice.

paras.t: Timor Domini, disciplina sapientiæ: id est, filialis timor Domini inducit ad impendendum proximo, præsertim subjecto, disciplinam sapientialem et quæ ad sapientiæ prodest augmentum. Qui enim sincere metuit Deum, non audet negligere impletionem divini præcepti, quo proximos delinquentes jubemur corripere, et subjectos reos corrigere. De quo ait Salvator : Si peccaverit frater tuus in te, id est te sciente, corripe eum inter te et ipsum solum. Et sicut pauci sunt veraciter timorati, ita perpauci sunt, qui istud implent præceptum. Propter quod Antisiodorensis in sua asserit Summa, quod propter duorum transgressionem præceptorum, quasi totus perit mundus, videlicet propter prævaricationem præcepti caste vivendi, et fraternaliter corripiendi.
paras.en: [[15:33|The fear of the Lord is the lesson of wisdom|Timor Domini, disciplina sapientiæ]] [*disciplina*, “lesson”, also “discipline, correction”]: that is, the filial fear of the Lord leads one to bestow on one’s neighbour, especially on a subject, a wise discipline, such as helps the increase of wisdom. For he who sincerely fears God does not dare to neglect the fulfilling of the divine precept by which we are commanded to rebuke neighbours who offend and to correct subjects who are at fault. Of which the Saviour says: [[Matt 18:15|if thy brother shall offend against thee|Si peccaverit frater tuus in te]], that is, with thy knowledge, [[Matt 18:15|rebuke him between thee and him alone|corripe eum inter te et ipsum solum]]. And as few are truly God-fearing, so very few are they who fulfil this precept. On which account Antisiodorensis [that is, William of Auxerre] asserts in his Summa that because of the transgression of two precepts almost the whole world perishes, namely the breaking of the precept of living chastely, and of that of correcting one’s brother.

paras.t: Et gloriam præcedit humilitas : id est, per humiliationem sui ipsius virtuosam spontaneam, meretur homo ad gloriam et salutem pertingere, virtutum perfectionem acquirere, cœlestisque regni altitudinem obtinere, sicut in Evangelio Filius Dei testatus est : Qui se humiliat, exaltabitur. Ideo ait Scriptura : Qui humiliatus fuerit, erit in gloria. Oportet enim in primis propriam vilitatem, defectuositatem et culpam agnoscere, sicque ad Deum pro auxiliante gratia, compuncto corde confugere. Hinc secundo libro Proverbiorum suorum ait Cyrillus : Crede mihi, quia maxime se vilifacit, qui magnum se reputat : sicut qui se judicat sapientem, fit amens. Lux quidem luce confunditur, et altitudo altitudine incurvatur. Ubi ergo profunda humilitas, ibi excelsa est dignitas; et ubi ex te ipso dejectio magna, ibi ex virtute dignificatio maxima : dumque mundanis cardinibus nos judicamus indignos, sempiternis atque cœlestibus mansionibus reddit humilitas mox nos dignos. Hinc quoque beatus ait Ambrosius : Quisquis cupit divinitatis tenere fastigia, humilitatis ima sectetur. Quicumque vult fratrem suum prævenire regnando in cœlis, prius illum præveniat obsequendo in terris, sicut ait Apostolus : Honore invicem prævenientes. Vincat eum officiis, ut possit vincere sanctitate.
paras.en: [[15:33|and humility goeth before glory|Et gloriam præcedit humilitas]]: that is, through the virtuous and willing humbling of himself a man merits to attain to glory and salvation, to acquire the perfection of the virtues, and to obtain the height of the heavenly kingdom, as the Son of God bore witness in the Gospel: [[Luke 14:11|he that humbleth himself shall be exalted|Qui se humiliat, exaltabitur]][[Luke 18:14||]]. Therefore Scripture says: [[Job 22:29|he that hath been humbled, shall be in glory|Qui humiliatus fuerit, erit in gloria]]. For one must first acknowledge one’s own vileness, defectiveness and guilt, and so flee with contrite heart to God for his helping grace. Hence Cyril says in the second book of his Proverbs: Believe me, he most abases himself who reckons himself great: as he who judges himself wise becomes a fool. Light indeed is confounded by light, and height is bowed down by height. Where, then, there is deep humility, there is lofty dignity; and where there is great casting down of thyself by thyself, there is the greatest exalting by virtue: and while we judge ourselves unworthy of the world’s high places [*cardinibus*, literally “hinges”], humility soon makes us worthy of the everlasting and heavenly mansions. Hence also blessed Ambrose says: Whoever desires to hold the heights of the Godhead, let him pursue the depths of humility. Whoever wishes to go before his brother in reigning in heaven, let him first go before him in serving on earth, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 12:10|with honour preventing one another|Honore invicem prævenientes]]. Let him overcome him in services, that he may be able to overcome him in holiness.
